20800-london-lectures-of-1907:
Sharp lines divide psychism from true spiritual growth in the London Lectures of 1907. The speaker wants each hearer free to choose which path to unfold within. Clear terms, he says, must come before any wise choice of that kind.

Annie Besant, the famed theosophist, gave lectures of this sort to London crowds. Her talks treat karma, rebirth, and the growth of the soul. Theosophy then drew seekers who found old churches too narrow. These lectures show its appeal in plain form: big claims, calm tones, and a promise that hidden laws can be grasped by study.
22905-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Punch looks back thirty thousand years in its issue of April 7, 1920, from volume 158. A weekly journal reports, the magazine notes, that the seas around England then stood at a higher level than at present. Nothing much can be done about the matter now, Punch concedes, but it deserves a mention all the same.

That deadpan manner fills the whole number. Jokes, verses, cartoons, and mock reports treat postwar Britain with weary good humor. The Great War had ended, and the magazine's readers were learning peacetime again. A single issue preserves that mood in amber. It also shows Punch's long-lived formula, topical, tidy, and determined to find the small absurdity in every large event.
23056-the-rendezvous-1907:
Ivan Turgenev paints a birch grove in The Rendezvous, his sketch dated 1907 in this translation. Birch leaves in the grove still hold their green, though it has paled with the season. Here and there stood a solitary young birch, all red or all golden. One should have seen how brightly these flushed in the sun, its rays gliding through branches washed by sparkling rain.

Inside that shining wood, a hunter waits and watches a meeting he was never meant to see. A peasant girl and a valet from the great house keep the rendezvous of the title, and class speaks in every gesture. The piece comes from Turgenev's Sportsman's Sketches, the book that quietly indicted serfdom. Nature gets the poetry, people get the truth.
23216-sac-au-dos-1907:
Joris-Karl Huysmans wrote Sac au Dos, a story of the war with Prussia, presented here in a 1907 edition. Its narrator admits he never understood why that butchery of armies was needed. He felt no call to kill others, and none to be killed by them.

Still, he is enrolled in the Seine's Garde Mobile and follows orders. He hunts up an outfit, visits the barber, and reports by seven in the evening to barracks on the Rue Lourcine. Huysmans tells war from inside one reluctant conscript, where duty is routine and the reasons for fighting stay blank.
23219-putois-1907:
Anatole France's Putois, presented in a 1907 edition, is a family tale passed down with care. A parent hands the story on so it will not die with the older generation. The teller's grandfather, Eloi Bergeret, was a man not amused by trifles, yet he set a high value on this piece.

Bergeret called it the Anatomy of Putois, after its central figure. He even said he preferred that anatomy, in some respects, to the anatomy of Quaresmeprenant, a giant from older French tales. France wraps a small household legend in mock learning, and lets family pride do much of the storytelling.
23222-the-fe-te-at-coqueville-1907:
Émile Zola's The Fête at Coqueville, presented in a 1907 edition, tells of a small coastal village and the family that founded it. Coqueville began with the Mahés. That family settled there and grew strong at the foot of the cliff. For a long time, they prospered.

The Mahés married among themselves for centuries, so that the village holds none but Mahés. Then, under Louis XIII, a man named Floche appeared. No one knew much about where he came from. Zola sets a closed, inbred village against one outsider, and lets that contrast drive the fête-day tale.
a-vanished-arcadia-being-some-account-of:
A Vanished Arcadia, published in 1901 by R B Cunninghame Graham, gives an account of the Jesuits in Paraguay between 1607 and 1767. Graham describes the Christian commonwealth of the Jesuit missions between the Paraná and Uruguay rivers. There the Jesuits built their famous reductions, towns where the Guaraní lived under mission rule, until the order was expelled.

Graham examines whether the work the Jesuits did among the Indians was beneficial, the question that has hung over the missions ever since. His account weighs the protection and order of the reductions against their control and their sudden end. The book, issued with a map, remains a readable English history of that lost world.
abbott-behind-scenes-mediums-1907:
David Abbott lifts the veil on seer craft in Behind the Scenes with the Mediums, his book of 1907. Abbott was a stage mage in Omaha who spent years in dark rooms as a guest. He learned each trick from the in side: slate writes, rope ties that slip, forms made of gauze, and the code talk of mates hid in the crowd of guests.

He prints the whole craft in clear, wry prose. Fans of the faith cursed his name for it. Busters cite the book more than most. It is the best guide to the tricks of its age.
adams-education-henry-adams-1907:
Henry Adams, grandson and great-grandson of American presidents, wrote his life story in the third person, as if watching a student fail. First printed in a small private edition in 1907, the book reached the public after his death. It is now counted among the great American life stories.

Adams says his schooling left him unready for a world of banks, machines, and raw power. His famous chapters set the Virgin of the old cathedrals against the dynamo of the new factories. That contrast still frames how readers think about faith, force, and modern life.
alchemy-and-the-alchemists-giving-the-se:
Alchemy and the Alchemists, published in 1907 by R Swinburne Clymer, argues a bold thesis about the old art. Its full title promises the secret of the philosopher's stone, the elixir of youth, and the universal solvent. It then claims that the true alchemists did not seek to transmute base metals into gold at all, but sought the highest initiation, the development of the spiritual nature in man.

Clymer reads the furnaces and metals of the alchemical books as symbols of an inner work. On his account, knowing the stone means knowing oneself, and the gold is a perfected human nature. The book belongs to the occult revival of its decade, and it preserves that movement's spiritual reading of alchemy in full.
arabian-nights-burton-1885-vol-07:
Volume seven of the Thousand Nights and a Night, in Burton's translation of 1885, continues the great cycle. Shahrazad's tales by now fill years of nights, and the king has children by his storyteller. The frame's danger has cooled into habit, wonder, and a kind of education for the throne.

Burton keeps his method steady: literal text, full verse, and notes that range from grammar to geography. Sailors, slaves, caliphs, and demons share the stage in turn. The Arabic book had grown for centuries by accretion, and Burton honors that layered growth. Readers step in anywhere, yet the long arc rewards those who persist. Volume seven is deep water, well stocked.
arxiv-2509-00107:
Chuanbo Liu and Jin Wang propose in 2025 that deep networks learn through joint action of a key set of neurons. Networks now beat humans on many hard tasks, yet how training works inside them stays murky. The authors argue that strongly active, task-bound neurons, called critical neurons, couple in step to drive learning.

That coupling yields Hebbian-like correlation graphs, where linked firing strengthens links. Early in training, the graph passes a sharp shift in how it connects. Weights among critical neurons are reinforced and shuffled at once, which strikes a fine balance. The picture frames training as self-organization in an adaptive system, not mere curve fitting. Such insight could guide leaner network designs.
arxiv-2509-00707:
Daehoon Gwak leads seven authors in total, with Minseo Jung, Junwoo Park, Minho Park, ChaeHun Park, Junha Hyung, and Jaegul Choo, in improving masked diffusion language models. Such models generate text by unmasking tokens in parallel, a non-autoregressive approach, meaning tokens are not produced strictly one by one, yet standard decoding often falls back into a sequential order.

Gwak and his co-authors propose Reward-Weighted Sampling, which uses an external reward model to judge each whole intermediate sequence during generation. The scores rescale token logits, the model's raw preferences, boosting tokens that support global coherence. Theory shows the scaling induces helpful rank reversals and raises expected reward, and experiments improve both non-autoregressive order and overall metrics.
arxiv-2509-00907:
Jediah Tau and one co-author, John T Whelan, investigate hardware injections in LIGO's third observing run. Simulated continuous gravitational wave signals were physically added to the detectors through auxiliary laser actuation on test-mass mirrors, before any data cleaning, to validate search methods.

Two periodic signals mimicked a spinning neutron star in a low-mass X-ray binary like Scorpius X-1. Tau and Whelan searched with the model-based cross-correlation pipeline, using an orbital parameter region sized like the plausible range for Scorpius X-1 but containing each injection. Their self-blinded analysis confidently detected one injection. The other, made with lower amplitude in a costlier frequency region, was not detected, though a deeper targeted search at its true parameters verified its imprint.
arxiv-2509-01307:
How fast a galaxy turns gas into stars follows a known relation, but its fine detail inside galaxy centers is less clear. K Sruthi, with five co-authors, examines that relation in three nearby barred spiral galaxies that host active nuclei. They combine ultraviolet images from AstroSat with carbon monoxide maps from the ALMA telescope array.

The data trace recent star formation and molecular gas at a sharp scale of about one hundred twenty to one hundred thirty-two parsecs. The fitted relation was sublinear in all three galaxies, with slopes from about zero point one seven to zero point seven one in plain terms. One galaxy showed a firm relation matching past work, while the other two were weaker, likely due to fewer star-forming regions and dense central gas. The study refines how gas feeds stars near galaxy cores.
arxiv-2509-01407:
A phylogenetic tree maps how species are related through evolution, and gene sequences give molecular evidence for building such trees. S M Rafiuddin proposes a model that fuses existing tree-building methods with a genetic algorithm, a population-based search that breeds candidate solutions toward better ones. The goal is an independent platform for estimating trees from sequence data.

Gene data are drawn from the NCBI Entrez databases, a major public store of biological records. A modular parallel design handles the data set efficiently, splitting the work across parts that can run at once. Benchmark approaches for tree populations supply the search techniques to be combined. Rafiuddin presents the model as a way to search the huge space of possible trees and settle on the best estimate for a given set of gene sequences.
arxiv-2509-01707:
Ao Sun, Zhihan Wang, and Jinxin Xue study the singular set of mean curvature flow, a process that moves a surface by its bending. Singular points are spots where the flow breaks down and the shape pinches. The authors focus on singular sets shaped like cylinders in higher dimensions. They ask how smooth and structured those sets must be.

The team proves the sets sit inside a smooth curved sheet of the same dimension, once thin lower parts are removed. When the set itself forms such a sheet, its bending is fixed by the flow shape near the pinch. They also give a close profile of the flow and a size estimate near these points. The proof rests on a new distance bound that filters out slow fading modes.
arxiv-2509-01807:
Smbat Grigoryan extends a model he built for particle spectra from collider crashes to also cover sideways flow patterns. The model blends a blast wave picture, where matter expands like an explosion, with flexible statistical terms. Earlier work fit how many particles emerge at each sideways momentum in Large Hadron Collider data. The extension now targets elliptic flow, which measures how flow strength varies with direction.

The extended model fits both spectra and flow for many particle types, from light pions to heavy charmed states. Data cover lead and xenon crashes at several energies and crash alignments. Predictions for oxygen crashes at a stated energy are also given. The model even works at much lower energies from an older collider, widening its reach.
arxiv-2509-02007:
Shreyash Adappanavar leads four co-authors with mFARM, a fairness audit for language models in clinical decision support. Models in high stakes medical use can inherit and amplify social biases. Simple fairness metrics miss the multi sided nature of medical harm. Worse, they can reward models that stay clinically inert and safe but wrong.

Two large controlled benchmarks are built from a public intensive care database. Each holds tens of thousands of prompts varied by race and gender across context tiers. The audit scores allocational, stability, and latent disparity, then blends them into one mark. A balance score pairs fairness with accuracy to expose trade-offs. Four open models and tuned variants are tested under compression and context cuts.
arxiv-2509-02107:
Shaoshuai Chu and Michael Herty build high order schemes for random flow laws that keep mass and push. Such laws rule how fluids move, and random inputs add doubt to the flow. Young measures are tools that can hold wavy, spiky answers to those laws. A past first order scheme turned the task into a straight equation solved by linear programming.

A second order form comes from straight line rebuilds of point values on each side. A fifth order form adapts a weighted scheme that steers clear of fake waves. Tests on both random and fixed cases show much more sharp breaks in the flow. Cases span Burgers flow, Euler flow for light gas, and gas with no push. The new forms keep the good build of the first scheme.
arxiv-2509-02707:
Daciberg Lima Gonçalves, John Guaschi, and Carolina de Miranda e Pereiro wrote a 2025 topology paper. It studies mixed braid groups. Such groups describe braids whose strands come in several labelled families on a surface. They ask when a classic exact sequence for such braids splits.

The surfaces treated are the torus and the Klein bottle. Splitting means a projection admits a consistent way back, called a section. For projections that drop the last family, a section exists exactly when the first family's strand count divides every other family's count. Other cases get partial conclusions. The proofs compute suitable mixed braid groups and key quotient groups. Splitting questions reveal how braid groups decompose into simpler pieces.
arxiv-2509-03307:
Marta Silva and 3 co-authors tested machine learning inference for hunting anomalous Higgs couplings in 2025. The Higgs boson's links to W bosons could hide deviations from the Standard Model, and such deviations might relate to the cosmic surplus of matter over antimatter. The authors study one Higgs production channel ending in a lepton, a neutrino, and bottom quarks.

Two simulation-based inference methods are compared: one estimates a likelihood ratio for each event, the other builds an optimized observable for the target parameters. Both are also checked against traditional histograms of motion and angle variables. The learning methods beat one-dimensional histograms and matched two-dimensional ones. Cutting to a cleaner signal region sharpened sensitivity to one class of couplings without losing the other. Robustness fixes for the ratio method are a clear next step.
arxiv-2509-03607:
Ignacio Magaña Hernandez and one co-author's 2025 research paper measures cosmic expansion with spectral sirens, gravitational-wave events whose distance comes from the waves alone. Most sirens need a visible counterpart or a complete galaxy catalogue to fix redshift, the stretching of light by expansion. Spectral sirens instead use bumps in the black hole mass distribution as a ruler.

Their data come from GWTC-4.0, the latest gravitational-wave transient catalogue, holding 153 strong binary black hole candidates. Three population models are fitted: two parametric shapes with power laws and peaks, and a flexible Gaussian process model that lets the data draw the shape. All give broadly consistent values for the Hubble constant, which sets the expansion rate. The Gaussian process result, combined with the bright event GW170817, reaches about ten percent precision, the tightest in the study.
arxiv-2509-03907:
Subhojit Roy and three co-authors' 2025 physics paper takes up a pairing mechanism for unconventional superconductivity in single layers of transition metal dichalcogenides. These atom-thin materials show several odd traits under Ising spin-orbit coupling, where electron spins are pinned by the lattice. Experiments report collective Leggett modes, a nodal energy gap, an unusually large in-plane critical field, and a twofold gap anisotropy.

Their mechanism pairs electrons through spin and charge fluctuations. For monolayer tantalum disulfide, they identify its dominant instability. An added electron-phonon term is then tested against experiments. The theory stabilises a ground state whose density of states looks nodal, matching tunnelling microscope results. The large in-plane critical field follows from Ising coupling combined with mixing of even and odd parity pairing. A magnetic field applied in the plane splits the ground state's degeneracy, yielding the twofold pattern behind the anisotropy.
arxiv-2509-04107:
Ozgu Goksu and one co-author, Nicolas Pugeault, tackle uneven training data in federated learning for a 2025 computer science paper. Federated learning trains one shared model across many devices without gathering their private data in one place. Trouble starts when each device sees very different examples, or only a few, so merged models generalize poorly. Their method, FedQuad, works directly on how examples are arranged inside the model.

Similar examples are pulled closer together while different classes are pushed farther apart, across all devices. That tidier layout reduces the damage done when local models are averaged. Tested on two standard image data sets under many lopsided splits, FedQuad beat earlier approaches. The authors also map where this style of training helps most.
arxiv-2509-04407:
Roman Krcmar and two co-authors calculate the magnetic field made by straight wires spread across a hyperboloid in a 2025 physics paper. A hyperboloid is a saddle-like surface curving away in opposite directions. Currents run steadily, or nearly so, along identical wires placed at equal spacings on that surface. The authors work out how the resulting magnetic field distributes through space, and what force each wire feels from all the others.

A dense limit, where wires crowd into a continuous sheet, receives the same treatment. The discussion closes with an application: shaping current paths this hyperbolic way as a route to generating high magnetic fields. Magnet designers gain a new geometry to consider.
arxiv-2509-05707:
Families of hyperbolic complex manifolds can change only in an all-or-nothing way, Mu-Lin Li, Sheng Rao, and Mengjiao Wang prove in a 2025 complex geometry paper. A hyperbolic complex manifold is one whose geometry forbids certain maps from the complex plane, making it rigid in spirit.

For a smooth family over a disk, the set of parameters where the fibre equals a fixed hyperbolic manifold is either discrete or the whole base. Over a compact Riemann surface the set is finite or everything. For the projective line and elliptic curves the authors conjecture the set is empty or everything. Deformation questions of this kind measure how special hyperbolic manifolds are among all complex manifolds.
arxiv-2509-05907:
Offloading computing tasks from moving vehicles to roadside edge servers is optimized in a 2025 paper by Qianren Li and three co-authors. Vehicles hand jobs to base stations, which pass them to an edge server, but random speeds make future positions unknowable. Planning must therefore balance cell choice, upload time, and throughput under uncertainty.

The authors frame a scheduling period as a finite-horizon Markov decision process and solve it on two time scales. At the start of each super slot, deterministic optimization yields a reference plan and an approximate value function. Within the super slot, each small slot improves its action against that approximation, a scheme with a proven cost bound. Tests driven by a high-fidelity traffic simulator show clear gains over baseline schedulers.
arxiv-2509-06207:
Families of sets where the biggest intersecting subfamilies sit at single points are the Erdős-Ko-Rado property, and J. B. Ebrahimi and A. Taherkhani prove it by composition in a 2025 paper. Their framework builds the property for large systems from smaller subfamilies already known to have it, including the strong form where point stars are the only maxima.

The method streamlines proofs of classic results from Katona's cycle method, admissible orderings, permutations, and perfect matchings. Its new power shows on copies of a fixed hypergraph inside a complete hypergraph: for large enough ground sets, that family has the strong property. Cycle families in complete and complete bipartite graphs get a series of related results.
arxiv-2509-06807:
Safer language models that stay useful instead of refusing everything are the target of a 2025 paper led by Yanrui Du, with five co-authors. Security tuning often makes models overly conservative, trading usability away. The authors aim to push the balance point itself, the Pareto frontier, rather than slide along it.

Their framework, MoGU, routes each layer's work between a security-tuned and a usability-tuned variant, with routers that sense hidden states and allocate weights dynamically. The second version tightens that coupling: routers sit only in layers carrying clear security features, and backbone modules join router training for two-way adaptation. Results hold across mainstream, on-device, and reasoning models. Even after instruction fine-tuning weakens safety, a simple data-mixing step restores security without losing task gains.
arxiv-2509-07207:
Mack Dowell Komba Moudoumou and 2 co-authors give a new variational principle in 2025 for a gas of sticky particles that start out accelerating. Sticky particle models track grains or matter clumps that merge when they collide, forming clusters. Such models help solve pressureless gas equations, a system where particles move without pressure pushing them apart, even under an outside force.

The authors characterize clusters that form when the acceleration function decreases over time. Their principle rests on how mass is spread over particle velocities and on the shape of that acceleration. Momentum conservation requires care, since the force on each particle must be counted as clusters form. The result gives a fresh solution route for the forced pressureless gas system. It may help model flows where outside forcing and clumping act together.
arxiv-2509-07507:
Saad Lahlali and 4 co-authors present MVAT in 2025, a method for detecting 3D objects when only 2D box labels are available. Labeling 3D data is costly, while 2D boxes drawn on camera images are far cheaper. The catch is projection ambiguity: one 2D box can match many 3D poses, and a single viewpoint often hides part of an object.

MVAT aggregates object point clouds across time in sequential data to build fuller 3D representations. A teacher network learns from single views but is trained toward targets built from those aggregated objects. The teacher then creates high-quality pseudo-labels, stand-in labels, that a student learns to predict from one view for both still and moving objects. A multi-view projection loss ties predicted 3D boxes to all 2D labels. Tests use the nuScenes and Waymo Open driving datasets.
arxiv-2509-08607:
Mapping gravity around asteroids and comets is the goal of Pietro Fanti and 1 co-author in a 2025 paper introducing MasconCube. Spacecraft fly close to these irregular bodies, where older spherical models fail. Polyhedral models assume even density, and neural methods can be slow to train.

MasconCube places point masses, called mascons, on a regular three-dimensional grid and learns their values directly. Known shape data limits the possible answers. Tests on Bennu, Eros, Itokawa, and synthetic bodies beat rival methods on several measures. Training runs about forty times faster than GeodesyNets, while the mass layout stays easy to read.
arxiv-2509-08707:
Ada Fang and 3 co-authors introduce Igloo, a tokenizer for antibody loops, in a 2025 paper. Antibody loops called CDRs bind to antigens and shape new drug design. Older grouping methods cover only part of loop diversity and fit poorly with protein foundation models.

Igloo encodes both backbone angles and sequence, trained so similar loops sit close in latent space. It retrieves matching loops better than prior methods and assigns tokens to all loops. Added to protein language models, it improves binding prediction on most targets tested. It also samples new loops that are diverse in sequence yet consistent in structure.
arxiv-2509-09007:
A supersolid flows like a superfluid while keeping a crystal's order, and it has only been made with ultracold atoms. J. L. Figueiredo, J. T. Mendonça, and H. Terças predict a version made of light in a 2025 research paper. Their setting is a semiconductor microcavity filled with plasma. Inside it, photons gain effective mass and interact through the plasma.

The authors derive the governing equation with a tunable photon-photon interaction. Under steady laser driving, the cavity light can crystallize spontaneously into a supersolid lattice through an instability. The effect needs only weak light-matter coupling and no hybrid light-matter particles. They identify realistic electron densities and light intensities for an experiment. A photonic supersolid would give physicists a new, comparatively accessible platform for studying quantum order that usually demands extreme cooling.
arxiv-2509-09107:
Pritam Sen and 2 co-authors present CryptGNN for secure inference with graph neural networks in a 2025 paper. Clients may use a third party graph model in the cloud as a service. Input data, graph structure, and model parameters all need protection from other parties.

Secure message passing and feature transformation layers use distributed secure multi-party computation. No trusted server is required, and the system works with any number of computing parties. Security is proved even if all but one party collude. Analysis and experiments demonstrate both security and efficiency. The design lets sensitive graph data be used without exposing it to the cloud.
arxiv-2509-09307:
Zhengzhao Lai and 7 co-authors present MatCha, a benchmark for materials characterization image understanding, in a 2025 paper. Characterization images reveal links between processing, microstructure, and properties in materials. Multimodal models show promise in materials science, but their grasp of real characterization data was untested.

MatCha holds fifteen hundred questions demanding expert level knowledge across four research stages and twenty-one tasks. Leading multimodal models score far below human experts. Performance degrades further on questions needing higher expertise and finer visual perception. Few-shot and chain of thought prompting do not close the gap. The benchmark aims to spur work on material discovery and autonomous science agents.
arxiv-2509-10007:
Samuli Soutukorva and 3 co-authors present, in a 2025 paper, a system for teaching robots paths by showing them. Rather than code a route, a person demonstrates a path shape, and the system stores it as a Gaussian path model, a statistical summary of the curve. Many such models, of many shapes, form a library the robot can draw on.

New demonstrations can be matched against the library to classify which known path a person is showing. The authors also give a way to reshape an existing model through a fresh demonstration, using geometric analysis of the new path. The aim is intuitive motion programming: people who cannot code can still teach a robot how to move.
arxiv-2509-10107:
Dmitrii S. Bespalov and 60 co-authors benchmark how scientists read X-ray scattering data from warm dense matter in this 2025 paper. Warm dense aluminium, squeezed to extreme pressure, is hard to diagnose, and the standard analysis leans on uniform electron gas models. The team fired femtosecond X-ray pulses through aluminium shocked to high pressure at the European XFEL facility and recorded scattering over many angles.

The measured plasmon signal showed the standard models overshoot the resonance energy by a clear margin. A first-principles treatment matched the data within error, once the disorder created by the shock was taken into account. The authors conclude that reliable readings of such experiments need that fuller treatment, at least for aluminium in this state.
arxiv-2509-10607:
Nahuel Mirón-Granese and Claudia G. Scóccola study a subtle bias in cosmology measurements in this 2025 paper. The tensor-to-scalar ratio, usually called r, measures the strength of gravitational waves from the early universe, read from polarization patterns in the cosmic microwave background. Dark radiation that interacts with itself can quietly change that pattern.

In their model the dark radiation behaves like a light particle with self-interactions. Those interactions reduce the damping of gravitational waves, which boosts the expected signal. Running mock data through standard analysis, they find that ignoring the interactions can shift the inferred r by about as much as the error bars of coming experiments. Careful modeling, they argue, is essential for unbiased results.
arxiv-2509-10707:
Sajjad Abdoli and 2 co-authors study how AI models judge each other's work in this 2025 paper. Their test material was image descriptions written by a vision-language model, graded by three members of the GPT family. The question was whether each grader has a stable style of its own, an evaluation personality, rather than a neutral yardstick.

Clear personalities emerged. One model graded with tight consistency, one was best at catching errors, and the largest was strict yet erratic. Control tests with a different model writing the questions confirmed the styles belong to the graders. The GPT models also showed a shared tilt toward negative judgments, about two to one, which did not appear in the other family tested.
arxiv-2509-11507:
Jared Zhu and Junde Wu design an agent-based operating layer for digital health in a 2025 paper called MedicalOS. Clinical software has eased routine work, yet clinicians still juggle many tools, repeat manual steps, and work through complex screens instead of caring for patients.

MedicalOS turns plain language orders into predefined health commands that follow trusted clinical rules. Tasks such as patient inquiry, history lookup, exam handling, report writing, referrals, and treatment planning are wrapped as ready-made tools. The authors checked the system on hundreds of patient cases across many specialties. It showed high diagnostic scores, sound exam requests, and steady structured reports and medication advice. The design aims at trustworthy, scalable workflow automation.
arxiv-2510-00007:
Gilead Levy studies lists of whole numbers that add up to one fixed total. Such a list is called a partition. A partition is graphical when its numbers match the link counts of the points in a simple graph. Levy works with partitions whose parts face broad limits on the values they may take.

He counts the graphical partitions of an even total and finds a compact formula for their share of all such partitions. At its largest, that share shrinks like one over the square root of the total as the total grows. For each set of limits, he finds a floor for the size of the parts. Past that floor, the limits have little effect on the share. For parts kept to powers of two, the floor is one half of the total raised to the power log 2, plus a small error term.
arxiv-2510-00107:
Olga Garcia-Gallego and three colleagues published this 2025 cosmology paper on how the early universe became ionized again. A key number, the optical depth, sums up how much starlight-era gas blocks the oldest light we can see. That number is usually measured from the cosmic microwave background. The team instead derived it from the Lyman-alpha forest, the pattern of absorption in distant quasar light.

The forest traces the gas temperature, which ties back to when ionization happened. Solving the heating and chemistry of hydrogen and helium links the two quantities. Their result puts the optical depth near a value well below some recent high claims. A value nearly twice as large is ruled out with strong confidence in their analysis. Future larger quasar samples could sharpen this independent check on the reionization era.
arxiv-2510-00407:
Jade Kandel and colleagues at the University of North Carolina published this 2025 study on augmented reality motion guidance. AR headsets can coach exercise and physical therapy with cues placed right on the body. Prior design advice covered mostly simple upper-body moves in plain view. The team tested guidance for moves that vary in visibility and in their plane of motion.

Participants performed three isolation exercises under eight visualization designs. Four encodings showed the motion as a path, an object, a line, or a human figure. Each encoding appeared from both first-person and third-person viewpoints. The best viewpoint depended on how visible the moving body part was. Showing more of the overall motion did not always improve how well people moved. The authors distill the results into evidence-based guidelines for AR guidance systems that handle whole-body movement.
arxiv-2510-00807:
Mueller and Pu study the spatial behaviour of solutions to a stochastic heat equation in this 2025 arXiv paper on probability theory. The equation drives a field with space-time white noise multiplied by a power of the solution. For powers between zero and one the noise coefficient is Hölder continuous, which breaks the Lipschitz theory. Nonnegative solutions exist, but uniqueness in law is known only in special cases, so the authors work with the solution set.

They establish associativity and spatial ergodicity for solutions, then prove a central limit theorem for spatial averages. In the square-root case, which corresponds to the density of super-Brownian motion, they derive a limit for the moment generating function of the integral. They bound how fast the solution's maximum grows across space. The results extend fluctuation theory for stochastic equations to a regime where tools fail.
arxiv-2510-00907:
Phan, Ma, Nguyen, and Do present BoMGene in this 2025 arXiv paper, a hybrid feature selection method for gene expression classification. Gene expression datasets measure thousands of genes in few samples, so most genes are redundant or irrelevant noise. Good feature selection shrinks the input, speeds training, and often improves accuracy. The authors combine two established selectors with complementary instincts: Boruta, which tests features against shadow copies, and mRMR, which maximizes relevance while minimizing redundancy.

Across twenty-five public gene expression datasets, the hybrid chose fewer features than mRMR alone. Training ran faster as a result, while accuracy held steady or improved against each individual method. Four standard classifiers, from support vector machines to gradient boosting, all showed the same pattern. The authors report clearer stability across datasets as well. Future work targets better redundancy measures and augmentation against class imbalance.
arxiv-2510-01107:
Hathcock and Ravi prove when proportional allocations can realize perfect fractional matchings, in this 2025 arXiv paper on bipartite graphs and online allocation. Online systems, such as ad impression assignment, need allocation rules that are extremely simple to apply as items arrive. A proportional allocation gives each right-side node a positive weight, and every left node splits itself among neighbours in proportion to those weights. The question is when those splits assemble into a fractional perfect matching.

Using a classical matrix scaling result, the authors prove such an allocation exists exactly when the graph is matching covered. They also extend the result with simple proportional schemes for graphs that are not matching covered. The tail of the paper stress-tests the idea under two capacity constraints, where a complete bipartite example forces large violations. Whether richer simple schemes handle that case stays open.
arxiv-2510-01207:
Kaushik and co-authors dissect the 2022 outburst of a millisecond pulsar using two space telescopes' data together. The neutron star spins hundreds of times per second while stealing gas from a companion. Understanding which structures emit its X-rays tests how accretion works at extreme speeds.

A soft disk plus a hard, patchy corona explains the spectra through the whole outburst. Disk and corona temperatures stayed in narrow ranges while overall brightness evolved. Absorbing gas inside the system changed substantially and systematically over time. Two broad timing features, one with a clear hard lag, round out the picture of the flow. NICER and AstroSat watched the same outburst from different strengths. A partially covering corona explains why some hard light escapes and some scatters. Uniform modeling across the outburst lets parameters be compared honestly. Absorption became the most dramatic mover.
arxiv-2510-01307:
Varglund and co-authors survey the radio voices of nearly four thousand narrow-line Seyfert galaxies, the largest clean sample yet. These active galaxies were long supposed to be radio quiet, yet some launch powerful relativistic jets. Four major sky surveys at different frequencies supply the measurements.

About forty percent of the sample showed detectable radio emission, most of it faint. Star formation explains much of the low-frequency glow in the typical source. Extreme sub-populations stand out against that quiet background, including strongly jetted cases. Population-wide statistics replace the anecdote-driven picture this class grew up with. Low-frequency surveys caught the most sources by a wide margin. Most detections are faint and steady rather than flaring. Optical spectral parameters accompany the radio measurements for context. Star formation's share grows toward lower frequencies in the data. Jets in supposedly quiet galaxies remain the headline curiosity.
arxiv-2510-01507:
Duerinckx and Jabin build the first systematic grip on correlations in crowds of particles that push each other harshly. Mean-field theory treats each particle as feeling only the average crowd, and corrections live in correlation functions. For gentle forces those corrections are well measured, but for singular, spiky forces they had resisted all proof attempts.

The authors linearize the correlation functions and bound them for forces that are merely square-integrable. A standard hierarchy then sharpens some bounds afterward, even recovering the known best results for gentle forces. Two payoffs follow, covering a classic correction to mean-field behavior and a central limit theorem for the crowd's spread. Both results enter the singular regime for the first time. Brownian motion in the model keeps particles jiggling while the singular forces act. Robust bounds matter because real colloids and plasmas rarely offer gentle forces.
arxiv-2510-01607:
Zeng and co-authors collect robot manipulation training data from people working freely, with no robot in the room. A portable virtual-reality kit and sensorized controllers mirror the robot's grippers, so human demos transfer cleanly. Crucially, the headset records deliberate head movements, capturing where a person looks while acting.

Most datasets ignore this active looking and bolt cameras to wrists instead. Policies trained only on the collected data handled six hard two-handed tasks with solid success. Performance held up respectably on new objects and in new rooms. Teaching robots where to look may matter as much as teaching them how to move. Wearable computing keeps the kit self-contained outside laboratory walls. Precise pose alignment bridges the gap between human hands and robot grippers. Egocentric video shows the scene as the actor saw it. Data collection escapes the lab at last.
arxiv-2510-02107:
Kladny, Schölkopf, and Muehlebach rework the exponential loss behind AdaBoost into a trainable objective in this 2025 paper. AdaBoost punishes mislabeled points harshly through exponential loss, yet it generalizes puzzlingly well as weak learners pile up. The classical multi-class form resists gradient-based optimization. Their replacement, PENEX, is built for first-order methods from the start.

Theory shows PENEX implicitly maximizes the margins of data points, which explains the regularization effect. Its gradient steps implicitly parameterize the weak learners of the boosting framework. Across computer vision and language tasks, PENEX regularized as well as or better than established methods at similar cost. The authors pitch it as an AdaBoost-inspired alternative for training and fine-tuning deep networks. Margin maximization, long a post-hoc story about boosting, becomes a design principle here. The work bridges classical ensemble theory and modern deep learning practice.
arxiv-2510-02307:
He and co-authors fix a quiet flaw in text-to-image models asked for small pictures. Their 2025 paper shows that noise schedules treat resolutions unfairly. The same noise level erases more signal from a small image. A model trained at large sizes then faces a mismatch. Its small outputs look washed out or broken. The fix, NoiseShift, adjusts the noise setting by output size. It needs no retraining and no model changes. It plugs into existing generators as they are.

The team applied NoiseShift to three leading generators. Quality at low resolution rose sharply in their tests. One model gained nearly sixteen percent on a standard photo set. Another gained more than eight percent. Small images matter for phones and cheap previews. Users on tight budgets gain a real option. The method also stacks with other schedule and design improvements.
arxiv-2510-02607:
Martínez and Henry build a logic that respects homotopy. Homotopy theory studies shapes up to smooth deformation. In that world, strict equality between objects is the wrong tool. A classic result showed that statements avoiding object equality survive swaps of equal categories. The authors extend that idea to weak model categories. These are the standard homes for homotopy theory. Each such home gets its own language of first-order formulas.

The formulas concern the well-behaved objects of the category. Their truth does not change under homotopies. It also survives weak equivalences, the maps the theory treats as sameness. The construction covers many settings at once. It covers 2-categories, bicategories, chain complexes, and Kan complexes. It also covers quasi-categories and Segal spaces. The work gives logicians a uniform way to state homotopy-safe claims. It ties model categories to dependent type theory as well.
arxiv-2510-02707:
Wimalasuriya and Tragoudas detect adversarial attacks on neural networks without training for any specific attack. Their 2025 machine learning security paper builds a statistical detector. Crafted inputs can fool networks while looking harmless. Existing detectors often fail on attacks they never saw. The method sets a detection baseline before deployment. It compares a network against a compressed twin of itself. Adversarial inputs disturb the pair's agreement measurably. That disagreement becomes a metric of attack presence. The baseline needs no examples of attacks at all.

Tests spanned many attack types and datasets. Detection stayed near perfect across the range. False positives dropped sharply versus rival methods. Real time checking fits sensitive deployments well. Attack agnostic defense matters because attacks keep evolving. A baseline fixed in advance cannot be outpaced by novelty. Security teams gain a practical early warning signal.
arxiv-2510-02907:
Prakash and co-authors study the brightest X-ray source in the sky. Scorpius X-1 is a neutron star pulling gas from a companion. India's XPoSat satellite carries an instrument called XSPECT. Its fast readout, near one millisecond, copes with the brightness. The team tracked the source across its three known branches. Those branches trace a Z shape on a color diagram.

Soft emission fit a multicolor disk model well. Inner disk heat stayed in a modest band across branches. A hotter cloud of electrons scattered part of the light. Its heat and thickness shifted along the track. Iron lines appeared near two clear energies. During flaring, both disk and scattered flux rose steeply. The neutron star's surface also grew hotter then. The authors tie the Z-track motion to the scattering cloud. Its thickness, flux, and the disk heat drive the changes.
arxiv-2510-03107:
Alpizar-Chacon and colleagues survey computing students about generative AI. The tools have swept into classrooms faster than the rules. Teachers debate whether they lift or hollow out learning. Prior studies tracked use, but rarely across school levels. This team polled four hundred ten students in computing programs. Twenty-three schools took part, from high schools to research universities. Usage habits differed clearly by institution type.

Warm feelings toward the tools were shared across all levels. Excitement, optimism, and gratitude showed up everywhere. Older students voiced more worry and skepticism, though. High schoolers trusted the tools more and faulted them less. Ethics views also split by level. Younger students held more permissive views on classroom use. Heavier users, in turn, held warmer views overall. The AI hype barely swayed high schoolers' choice of computing. The team shares its survey tools for reuse abroad.
arxiv-2510-03207:
Song, Rohatgi, Singh, and Bagnell ask when learning from a privileged expert beats learning from scratch. Partially observable agents cannot see the full state directly. Simulators, though, know that hidden state during training. Distillation lets a student imitate the expert who sees everything. The authors study the trade-off in a stylized model. A perturbed block model captures decodability versus belief contraction.

Theory says latent stochasticity tips the balance between methods. Controlled locomotion experiments confirmed that prediction. Noisy hidden dynamics erode the value of perfect state access. Calm dynamics let distillation shine as theory expects. A second finding surprised more than the first. A top latent policy can be the wrong one to teach from. Distilling a slightly different policy can serve the student better. Guidelines for using privileged information emerge from the analysis. Practitioners should probe dynamics noise before choosing the route.
arxiv-2510-03607:
Olabiyi presents a 2025 arXiv paper in functional analysis on multiplication operators acting on spaces of Banach lattice valued functions. The functions are continuous, take values in a Banach lattice, and vanish at infinity over a locally compact space. A multiplication operator scales each function by a multiplier, and flowing those operators gives a semigroup. The paper asks which multipliers generate strongly continuous semigroups of this kind. Earlier answers covered only scalar valued functions, the C0 setting.

Olabiyi's characterization extends those scalar results to the vector valued lattice setting. The conditions pin down when the semigroup behaves for analysis to proceed. Multiplication operators are the infinite dimensional cousins of diagonal matrices, and they model many systems. A criterion for the lattice valued case supports work in ordered Banach spaces and operator theory. The classification connects to the center of a Banach lattice, the algebra of its well behaved multipliers.
arxiv-2510-03907:
Brown and colleagues wrote this 2025 arXiv paper on bouncing universe models and a trick for keeping them smooth. In these models a bounce replaces the big bang, as contraction turns into expansion. During contraction, shear grows fast and threatens to make the universe lumpy and uneven near the bounce. An ekpyrotic field, whose pressure can exceed its energy density, should tame that shear.

The authors study the trick inside loop quantum cosmology and a modified version of it. Their inflaton potential has two parts, one for inflation and one ekpyrotic near the bounce. Numerical runs show the ekpyrotic part dominates near the bounce and solves the shear problem. After the bounce, the inflationary part takes over and drives a long expansion phase. That phase lasts long enough to address the classic big bang problems. Two favored mechanisms can thus share one universe without ruining each other.
arxiv-2510-04307:
Csajbók and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper improving a lower bound on the minimum weight of dual codes built from finite projective geometry. These geometric codes are generated by incidence vectors of points and higher-dimensional subspaces. Their dual codes correspond geometrically to point multisets meeting every line in a number of points divisible by the characteristic. Small dual codewords are hard to rule out, and the best previous bound came from Bagchi and Inamdar in 2002.

A reduction by Lavrauw, Storme, and Van de Voorde converts the subspace problem to the point-line case in a smaller projective space. The authors exploit that geometric viewpoint with polynomial techniques developed for codes whose weights and length share a divisor. They obtain a substantial improvement of the Bagchi-Inamdar bound when the field is a proper extension and both dimension and characteristic exceed two.
arxiv-2510-04507:
Min Wang and six coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on teaching AI agents to cope with changing worlds. Real settings shift over time, through weather, traffic, and other forces that never sit still. An agent then faces a sequence of related but distinct tasks. Older methods leaned on patterns that evolve in regular ways, which breaks in wild settings. The team turned to wavelets, a tool that reads signals at many scales at once.

Their system, WISDOM, turns a sequence of task descriptions into the wavelet domain. Wavelet coefficients capture both broad trends and fine wiggles in how tasks evolve. A new update rule, modeled on temporal difference learning, tracks and predicts that evolution. The authors prove the rule converges and that the representations improve the learned policy. On varied benchmarks, WISDOM beat existing baselines on both learning speed and final scores. The margin held in settings with stochastic, irregular change.
arxiv-2510-04607:
Yuan Wang, Mingyu Li, and Haibo Chen wrote this 2025 paper on giving AI computer agents a better interface. Agents that drive software must click through screens built for human eyes. Each goal breaks into long chains of actions, and errors pile up along the chain. The team built a layer called GOI that reshapes an interface into three primitives. The primitives cover access, state, and observation in a declarative style.

The split is deliberate: the language model plans, and GOI handles the clicking and navigation below. No source code changes or private APIs are needed for the layer to work. Tests ran on the Microsoft Office suite under Windows against a screen based agent. Success rates rose by about two thirds with GOI. The number of interaction steps fell by about forty four percent at the same time. More than three fifths of the wins finished in one model call.
arxiv-2510-04707:
David Seery wrote this 2025 cosmology paper on the rare, extreme ripples left by the early universe inflation era. Inflation theory predicts how density ripples are distributed, and the middle is nearly bell shaped. The tail, where ripples could seed black holes, is much harder to compute. Seery builds a method for that tail using instantons, the best paths of a random process. The framework grows out of a path integral view of the stochastic theory.

It connects to the quantum field theory machinery for open systems. That link lets the method go past the slow roll limit and handle fields at once. He tests it on linear potentials, ultra slow roll, and constant roll cases. The answers match published results. In one case, noise that fades fast over time, the tail returns to a bell shape. Rare event math decides how many black holes inflation could have made.
arxiv-2510-04907:
Jan Naumann, Jens Eisert, and Philipp Schmoll wrote this 2025 physics paper on simulating quantum magnets that live on a triangular lattice. Tensor network states are the workhorse for quantum matter. The approach maps a triangular lattice onto a square one with diagonal links. That detour misrepresents how entanglement sits on the triangles. The authors build an algorithm native to the triangular geometry. Automatic differentiation turns it into an energy minimizer.

At the bond dimension, the native method reached better variational energies than the mapped one. The gain comes from a truer entanglement picture and more parameters to tune. They tested the method on the antiferromagnetic Heisenberg model, a frustrated magnet. Both the triangular and the kagome lattice served as benchmarks. Results lined up well against numerical studies. Frustrated magnets are candidates for spin liquid phases, so sharper energies matter. Native geometry tools could shift what physicists conclude about these materials.
arxiv-2510-05007:
Giovanni Cerulli and Francesco Caracciolo bring a safety-first idea into public policy design in this 2025 arXiv paper. Standard policy learning assigns each person the treatment with the best average outcome. That rule ignores how wildly outcomes can swing. The authors instead maximize the chance that outcomes clear a social minimum.

Their rule ranks treatments by the ratio of average outcome to its spread. They test the framework on farm data from Italy's Farm Accountancy Data Network. The case study covers subsidy allocation under the EU Common Agricultural Policy. Data-driven policies beat the actual allocation under every risk attitude they tried. Welfare fell as risk aversion rose, which prices the cost of insuring against uncertainty.
arxiv-2510-05307:
Jieyu Zhou and four co-authors ask how often users should check an AI agent's work in this 2025 arXiv paper. Most agents ask for confirmation only at the very end. One early error can then cascade and force a full restart. Checking every step avoids disasters but exhausts the user.

A formative study with eight users revealed a recurring confirmation, diagnosis, correction, and redo pattern. The authors turned that pattern into a decision-theoretic model of confirmation timing. The model picks check-in points that minimize expected total time. In a study with 48 participants, intermediate confirmation cut task time by about 13.5 percent. A strong 81 percent of participants preferred it over confirming only at the end.
arxiv-2510-05407:
Ram Manohar and S. M. Mallikarjuaniah build a self-refining simulator for shattering materials in this 2025 arXiv paper. Phase-field models smear cracks into a smooth damage field, avoiding explicit crack tracking. Their model couples elastic wave motion with the Ambrosio-Tortorelli fracture energy. Damage irreversibility is enforced strictly through a variational inequality.

A residual-based estimator drives mesh adaptation toward the evolving fracture zone. The authors prove the adaptive scheme's discrete solutions converge to a critical point of the energy. That convergence guarantee is the first for this class of adaptive dynamic fracture algorithms. In two-dimensional tests with an edge crack under shear, the method captured crack branching and tortuous paths. Adaptive refinement delivered those details with significant savings over uniform meshes.
arxiv-2510-05507:
Tukharyan and colleagues study a way to disarm the most stubborn nuclear waste. Six long-lived fission products cause most of the lasting radioactivity in spent fuel. The team asks whether a proton accelerator could transmute those isotopes into safer forms. Their 2025 study simulates the full process at reactor scale.

In the design, a proton beam strikes a heavy target and sprays out neutrons. Those neutrons then strike the waste isotopes placed around the target. Lead and depleted uranium emerged as the leading target materials, with different trade-offs. Technetium, iodine, and selenium transmuted well in the simulations. Tin resisted partly, while zirconium barely reacted and cesium gained little net benefit. Cost results split sharply by isotope, with technetium cheapest and cesium and zirconium costly. The findings overall can guide target and blanket designs for future waste systems.
arxiv-2510-05707:
Boetius and colleagues teach robots motions that are stable by design on curved state spaces. Robot poses and stiffness live on Riemannian manifolds, not flat space. Learned motion laws there rarely carry stability promises. Their 2025 framework, sNMODE, bakes Lyapunov stability into neural manifold ODEs.

The method projects the neural vector field so it meets a Lyapunov test. That check holds at every state, not just along training paths. Both the base field and the Lyapunov function use flexible neural forms. Paths evolve on the manifold itself, staying on its shape constraints. Tests cover quaternion and positive-definite matrix manifolds from the LASA data sets. Motions on place-plus-pose space also succeed in tests. The framework beats older stable-system learners on these benchmarks. A real robot trial confirms real-world use and scale. Steady approach matters most in safety-first robot uses.
arxiv-2510-05807:
Piper and colleagues reconcile blockchain permissioning with both privacy and regulation. Decentralized finance apps must enforce know-your-customer rules without exposing user attributes. Existing permissioned designs leak private data or smuggle in trusted parties. Their 2025 framework combines self-sovereign identity with zero-knowledge proofs.

Users hold credentials in personal wallets under decentralized identifiers. Attribute-based policies are decided transparently by smart contracts on chain. Proofs cover equality, range, membership, and time-dependent conditions. A commit-and-prove scheme moves credential authenticity checks outside the proof circuit. That split makes proof generation considerably faster than baseline approaches. Compliance then holds throughout the system, not only at fund entry and exit. Transparency of policy decisions survives because contracts record them publicly. Privacy survives because proofs reveal nothing beyond the policy verdict. Verifiable credentials keep the whole flow user-centric and auditable.
arxiv-2510-06107:
Bhatia and three University of Aberdeen co-authors trace where hallucinations form inside language models in a 2025 interpretability paper. Their framework, Distributional Semantics Tracing, combines established tools into a causal map of model reasoning. Meaning is tracked as a pattern shaped by context, layer by layer.

Tracing finds a commitment layer where the internal state locks onto a falsehood and cannot recover. The authors blame a clash between two pathways: a fast associative route and a slower contextual route. When the fast route wins, they call the failure a reasoning shortcut hijack. Their coherence score for the contextual pathway tracks hallucination rates closely, with a strong negative correlation in their tests. Hallucinations thus look like predictable products of weak semantics, not random glitches. That diagnosis points toward monitoring tools that catch failures before the model commits.
arxiv-2510-06307:
Deng and five co-authors stabilize consensus in multi-agent language systems with BCCS in a 2025 artificial intelligence paper. Multi-agent systems solve hard language tasks by collaboration, with consensus-seeking at the core. Existing approaches judge consensus by voting, ignoring contradictions in internal beliefs. They also make every agent collaborate with everyone indiscriminately.

The authors first build theory for choosing optimal collaborators that maximize consensus stability. BCCS then selects those collaborators and calibrates consensus judgments by internal beliefs. On MATH and MMLU, the framework beat the best existing results. Accuracy improved roughly two percent on MATH and roughly four percent on MMLU. Whom an agent talks to matters as much as how votes are counted. The authors release their code and data publicly for reuse. Belief-aware consensus could make multi-agent pipelines more reliable for reasoning-heavy work.
arxiv-2510-06407:
Öhman and three co-authors build a materials-modeling framework for predicting molecular single-photon emitters in a 2025 quantum physics paper. Single-photon sources are essential building blocks for quantum technology. Molecules are attractive because chemists can tailor them, but the space of possible molecules is vast and poorly mapped.

Their approach integrates database analysis with microscopic predictions. A well-studied system, dibenzoterrylene in an anthracene host, benchmarks the pipeline. Databases supply the candidate pool, and the benchmark-first design keeps predictions honest before the search widens. Screening identifies promising new emitter candidates beyond the benchmark. Among them sits a chiral molecular emitter, an interesting find for quantum optics. The authors envision coupling the framework to machine learning next. Such integration could search chemical space far faster. The work opens a route toward unlocking molecular light–matter interfaces computationally.
arxiv-2510-06507:
Wang and five co-authors stage a dinner theater where guests eat a biohybrid flying robot in a 2025 human-computer interaction paper. The tangible design fiction unfolds in a 2052 Paris restaurant. Diners consume the robot instead of banned ortolan bunting. Performance, ritual, and multisensory immersion replace textual speculation.

The scenario asks what changes when a machine occupies the delicacy's place at the table. Six creative-industry participants played diners and role-players. Their responses mixed curiosity, discomfort, and philosophical debate. They found the biohybrid meal plausible and unsettling. Questions of sentience, symbolism, and adoption dominated. Those concerns exceed synthetic meat's usual sustainability framing. The authors claim three contributions. The artifact demonstrates robots as food. The session yields insight into negotiating cultural and ethical boundaries in post-natural eating. It advances embodied, multisensory design fiction methodologically.
arxiv-2510-07407:
Le Conte and co-authors trace how galactic bars emerged over the last twelve billion years. Their 2025 paper uses deep near-infrared imaging from the James Webb telescope. Bars are the elongated stellar spines crossing many disc galaxies today, including our own. The team visually classified a nearly mass-complete sample of disc galaxies across cosmic noon. Classifications ran independently in short and long wavelength channels to check for bias. Both channels agreed on the overall bar share, which lends the trend credibility against dust and resolution worries.

The bar fraction falls steadily with distance: roughly sixteen percent nearby in the sample, down to about seven percent at the far end. Mean bar length, by contrast, barely changes across the era in the cleaner channel. Bar-driven internal evolution thus began surprisingly early, only about two billion years after the Big Bang.
arxiv-2510-07507:
Cherenson and Panagou design a unified controller for robots that cannot directly command every motion they make. Their 2025 paper treats underactuated, uncertain systems whose response to inputs is nonlinear and state-dependent. The architecture exploits time-scale separation: fast dynamics act as virtual inputs steering the slow subsystem. Dynamic control allocation then picks the actual actuator commands that best realize those virtual inputs under input constraints. A state predictor drives an adaptive law that learns the unknown dynamics online, compensating for disturbances and modeling error without a prior model of either.

Singular perturbation theory and Lyapunov analysis prove stability and bounded tracking of reference paths. The test platform is a VTOL quadplane, an aircraft that hovers like a drone and cruises like a plane. One controller handled cruise, the tricky landing transition, and hover, regimes usually given separate controllers.
arxiv-2510-07707:
Zhao and five coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on detecting hate speech across writing styles. Open slurs are easy for software to catch. Hate hidden in sarcasm, irony, stereotypes, or coded words is harder. Detection models often lean on wording, so they fail when style changes. Different platforms mix styles with different target groups, creating clues. The authors tackle both problems with a causal approach.

Their framework, CADET, treats hate speech as the product of a causal graph. Context, motive, target, and style become separate factors in the model. CADET pulls those factors apart in its internal representation and controls the confounders. It can also reason counterfactually by swapping style while holding intent fixed. In experiments, CADET generalized across styles better than rivals and stayed interpretable. The work suggests causal thinking can make content moderation fairer and more reliable as hate keeps changing form.
arxiv-2510-07907:
Scattaglia and Pratelli wrote this 2025 paper in geometric measure theory on isoperimetric problems, which ask which shapes minimize perimeter at fixed volume. A key tool is a small-change property: adjusting volume slightly should cost little perimeter. Without it, proofs fall apart. The classical version covers one set with standard volume. Weighted problems use varying densities, and clusters split volume among regions.

The property first appeared for single sets in the classical setting. The authors extend the property, in power-law form, to clusters with a double density. Volume and perimeter each carry a density. The extension is delicate because weighted perimeter reacts badly to pushes. Their result supplies the readjustment step that cluster arguments need. With it, competitors can have volumes corrected without wasting the gain. That step supports regularity results for optimal clusters.
arxiv-2510-08007:
Lahs, Comparat, Kirk, and Roberts wrote this 2025 paper mapping which atomic measurements can reveal hypothetical cosmic fields. Many theories predict light bosons filling space, possibly forming dark matter, coupling weakly to atoms. Precision atomic measurements rank among the most sensitive detectors available. The authors ask, systematically, which atomic observable responds to which kind of coupling.

They consider five coupling types, from scalar to tensor, deriving the nonrelativistic potential for each. Symmetry arguments then show which moments each coupling can induce. The list covers electric and magnetic dipole moments, electric quadrupole moments, and the nuclear Schiff and anapole moments. Every observable turned out to have some sensitivity to every coupling type. The paper also discusses how the terms scale, since none wins universally. The map helps experimentalists choose atoms and measurements that maximize their reach for new physics.
arxiv-2510-08107:
Heuer and five coauthors wrote this 2025 climate modeling paper moving a machine-learned convection scheme from one Earth system model into another without destabilizing it. Learned schemes often shine offline yet crash long simulations. Their network was trained on high-resolution simulation data with radiative tendencies removed. Crucially, it also predicts its own error. The host model mixes the learned scheme with a conventional one whenever confidence runs low.

That mixing makes the hybrid tunable against observations and yields interpretable regime patterns. In atmosphere-only setups, several hybrid configurations beat the default convection scheme, including on precipitation statistics. Adding input noise during training kept runs stable and physically consistent for at least twenty years of simulation. The proof of concept advances the long-term usability of learned physics in climate models.
arxiv-2510-08307:
Cristina Sardón and Xuefeng Zhao study Hamiltonian systems in a non-standard geometric setting in a 2025 arXiv paper. Hamiltonian systems describe motion through energy functions and bracket rules for how variables interact. Generalized Poisson geometry supplies those bracket rules, but some brackets cannot be split into simpler parts. The authors focus on such non-decomposable brackets and the dynamics they support.

They study Hamiltonian systems, and their quasi-Hamiltonian cousins, within this frame. Their main result concerns systems that enjoy suitable invariance, such as Lie symmetries or conserved quantities. Any such system, they show, can be written as a quasi-Hamiltonian system under a well-built bracket. In favorable cases it becomes genuinely Hamiltonian in the same frame. They present this as a unified way to treat multi-Hamiltonian and higher-order dynamics.
arxiv-2510-08507:
Xuanqiang Zhao, Benchi Zhao, and Giulio Chiribella measure the communication power of indefinite causal order in a 2025 arXiv paper. Quantum theory allows processes with no definite order of events, and such setups beat ordered ones at some information tasks. Whether they help communication itself, the most basic task, stayed controversial and hard to prove. The authors build a rigorous framework for communication links assembled from quantum devices.

In the one-shot setting, sending a single classical message, they establish a clear-cut advantage for indefinite order. But the advantage is not generic across communication tasks, they also show. In the asymptotic setting, with many repeated uses of the same device, indefinite order beats shared entanglement by nothing. Entanglement alone matches whatever indefinite order provides there. The results map nontrivial relations among entanglement, causal order, communication, and no-signaling resources.
arxiv-2510-08707:
Yossef Zenati, Conrado Albertus Torres, Joseph Silk, and M. Ángeles Pérez-García compute the neutrino flash when a neutron star turns into a quark star in a 2025 arXiv paper. If a neutron star's core grows dense enough, ordinary hadrons may deconfine into quark matter. That conversion should release a distinctive burst of neutrinos. The team simulates it in one-dimensional general relativistic hydrodynamics.

Deconfinement triggers once central density passes roughly three times nuclear saturation density. Equations of state combine the DD2 hadronic model with the MIT Bag model for quark matter. Neutrino emission includes pair annihilation, plasmon decay, Urca processes, and bremsstrahlung, plus a leakage scheme after the transition. The light curve generically develops a short, spectrally harder feature near deconfinement, lasting about ten to fifty milliseconds. It appears as a prompt shoulder or as a separate second peak, with heavy-lepton neutrinos delayed.
arxiv-2510-08807:
Zhao and a large team of roboticists release a dataset for teaching humanoid robots everyday manipulation, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Most robot training data comes from fixed arms in fixed rooms, which leaves walking, human-shaped machines underrepresented. Humanoid Everyday instead covers tasks that use the whole body. It includes nimble object handling, direct interaction with people, and jobs that mix walking with carrying or reaching.

Human operators drove the robots remotely through a supervised pipeline, recording rich sensor streams. The data pairs camera views with depth, laser scans, touch signals, and spoken-style task labels. In total it holds more than ten thousand demonstration runs and over three million frames across two hundred sixty tasks in seven categories. The team also benchmarked leading learning methods on the data and opened a cloud platform where others can test their own policies under fixed conditions.
arxiv-2510-09007:
Wang and co-authors ask whether a language model can still unlearn something when the examples of what to forget are messy, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Unlearning removes the influence of sensitive or harmful training data from a finished model. Standard methods assume the forget set is clean and complete. In practice, it may be partial, rewritten by other software, or stamped with watermarks, any of which might break the process.

The team benchmarked two leading unlearning methods on such noisy forget sets, degrading the data in controlled ways. Forgetting stayed surprisingly robust, as long as the core meaning of the examples survived the damage. Their explanation rests on saliency, a measure of which parts of an example drive the forgetting. The key semantic components stayed influential even when surface wording changed a lot. Unlearning, they conclude, is steered by deep meaning rather than shallow wording.
arxiv-2510-09107:
Perera and Thayasivam read chest CT scans with a three-branch neural network built to catch faint signs of disease, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The test case is COVID-19, whose scans can look nearly identical to healthy ones without expert eyes. Their architecture extends a modern convolutional design by summarizing each image through three parallel lenses at once. Two lenses take the average and the peak response across each feature map, while a third, new lens lets learned attention decide what to emphasize.

Training followed a strict pipeline of preprocessing, augmentation, and a two-phase schedule built on transfer learning. The combined data held two thousand six hundred nine scan slices from two public sources. On validation data it reached about ninety-eight percent accuracy and near-perfect separation of cases, ahead of prior models on this dataset. They present the design as a template for other subtle pathologies.
arxiv-2510-09307:
Tomashenko and co-authors tackle a privacy problem call centers know well: disguising one voice in a conversation while leaving the other voices untouched, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Speaker anonymization rewrites a voice so the speaker cannot be identified, while keeping the words intelligible. Almost all research assumes a lone speaker. A customer-service call, though, has at least two voices, and only the customer's needs protection; the agent's voice must stay natural for the recording to remain useful.

The study explores strategies for anonymizing one target speaker inside multi-speaker conversational audio. Conventional methods, tuned for solo recordings, often fail here, blurring speakers or under-protecting the target. The authors also argue that current evaluation cannot properly score the privacy-utility trade-off when several speakers are present. They highlight development pitfalls and propose improved evaluation methods to match, framing targeted anonymization as its own problem.
arxiv-2510-09807:
R Thapa, E Mustermann, H Jain, V Dierolf, and M McKenzie report crystals that rotate while growing inside glass in a 2025 arXiv paper. A seed crystal growing in a glass matrix was seen to turn under some torque, which contradicts the assumption that the surrounding amorphous glass is uniform and directionless. The authors seek the atomistic origin of the effect.

Molecular dynamics simulations of lithium niobate glass, with and without added silica, reproduce the phenomenon. The glass is not uniform at the scale of the crystal interface: its inhomogeneity exerts uneven forces on the seed, and those forces supply the torque. Higher growth temperatures amplify the rotation through faster atomic motion. Added silica slows growth by thickening the glass, but barely affects the rotation. The findings challenge the picture of glass as isotropic during early crystallisation and offer guidance for tailoring glass-ceramic microstructures.
arxiv-2510-10007:
Huenemoerder and co-authors report X-ray observations of the star V750 Ara in this 2025 arXiv paper in stellar astrophysics. V750 Ara is a gamma Cas-type star, a class known for unusually hard and bright X-ray emission. The team observed it with two space telescopes.

Chandra's HETG grating gathered 197 kiloseconds of high-resolution spectra, and NuSTAR added 95 kiloseconds at higher energies. The spectra show the target resembles other members of its class. That similarity is itself informative, since the cause of the gamma Cas behavior is still debated. Each well-measured member tightens the pattern any theory must match, including how the star's disk and magnetic field may produce the X-rays.
arxiv-2510-10307:
Liao and co-authors link space-time accessibility to leisure participation in this 2025 arXiv study of urban life. Accessibility shapes whether people join leisure activities, a core part of inclusive, lively cities. Standard measures judge access from a fixed home location, as if days began and ended there.

Real days are chains of obligations, and leisure must fit inside them. The authors measure accessibility through space and time together, capturing the chances a daily routine actually leaves open. That view should explain participation better than home-based scores. The findings can guide planners who place parks, venues, and transit, since a facility that is near on the map may still be unreachable in a packed day.
arxiv-2510-10407:
Shaolun Liu and co-authors present PrediQL in this 2025 arXiv paper on API security testing. GraphQL lets clients ask for exactly the data they need, but its flexible queries and nested dependencies expose APIs to complex, context-dependent flaws. Conventional fuzzers generate random payloads or follow rigid mutation rules, and they miss such flaws.

PrediQL uses large language models to test GraphQL APIs automatically. A model can read a schema and craft queries that respect its structure while probing for weaknesses. Adaptive generation follows the API's responses, going deeper than fixed heuristics allow. The authors aim at vulnerabilities that only appear when queries are shaped by the schema's own relationships.
arxiv-2510-10607:
Jaime E Pineda and a large team of co-authors present the final data release of a major star formation survey, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The Green Bank Ammonia Survey used the Green Bank Telescope to map every Gould Belt star forming region visible from the northern hemisphere. It targets dense gas traced by ammonia emission, in regions spanning Taurus, Perseus, Ophiuchus, and Orion. This release covers every region observed.
