The winner is plain but strict: ensure every target property appears past a set threshold in training. Data, code, and results are released for others to check. The guidance helps teams that need complete graph extraction, not just the easy, frequent facts.
arxiv-2511-03907:
Liam Bakar and six colleagues designed SnappyMeal, a multimodal artificial intelligence app for logging food. Interviews with nutrition experts and regular trackers showed paper and app journals are inflexible, weakly followed, and often inaccurate. Flexible logging matters because diet records underpin links between food, medicine, fitness, and health.

SnappyMeal accepts several input types, asks goal-dependent follow-up questions when context is missing, and pulls detail from grocery receipts and nutrition databases. Benchmark tests were joined by a three-week real-world deployment with over five hundred logged items. Users praised the input options and perceived accuracy strongly, suggesting a more context-aware path for dietary tracking tools.
arxiv-2511-04007:
Zhiming Shuai, Xiangdong Zhang, and Gui-Rong Liang numerically study superradiance of a charged scalar field around charged black-bounce spacetimes. They cover both scattering setups and black hole bomb models, where a mirror traps amplified waves. A quantum parameter in the geometry shallows the effective potential.

That shallowing weakens superradiant amplification in both settings. Field mass suppresses gains at all frequencies, while black hole and field charge suppress low frequencies yet enhance high ones. In one bomb arrangement a distinct new eigenmode appears at large quantum parameter values, absent in a second arrangement. Heavy-field cases add another eigenfrequency at the same setting, without superradiant amplification.
arxiv-2511-04107:
Chengu Wang, writing alone, builds sorting networks of depth thirteen for twenty-seven and twenty-eight channels, improving the best known bound of fourteen. Sorting networks sort any input through a fixed pattern of comparators, and lowering depth for a given channel count is a long-running combinatorial contest.

The twenty-eight-channel network uses reflectional symmetry. High-quality prefixes from sixteen- and twelve-channel networks are combined, extended greedily one comparator at a time, and a SAT solver completes the remaining layers. Cutting one layer at these sizes is a concrete record step, and the hybrid hand-plus-solver construction shows how search can finish designs that pure greedy building stalls on.
arxiv-2511-04707:
Rishi Rajesh Shah leads six authors with NINJA, a jailbreak attack for long-context language models. Million-token inputs opened new powers, but their safety effects were unclear. NINJA hides a harmful goal inside a haystack of benign, model-written content.

Where the harmful goal sits in that long context turns out to matter greatly. Tests on the HarmBench suite raised attack success sharply across leading models. Open and proprietary systems alike were affected, including LLaMA, Qwen, Mistral, and Gemini. The finding warns that long context is not just a feature; it is also a new attack surface.
arxiv-2511-04807:
Matthew D. Kvalheim and his co-author map what topology allows and forbids in autoencoders. An autoencoder squeezes data through a small latent space and rebuilds it. The round trip should act like the identity on the data manifold itself.

Continuous encoder and decoder maps face hard topological limits, they show. Some manifolds simply cannot be compressed into a given latent shape faithfully. The authors also describe what autoencoders can do for dynamical systems. When the data manifold is invariant under the dynamics, those capabilities shape how learned models can track motion without leaving the manifold.
arxiv-2511-04907:
Lunjia Hu and co-authors speed up swap multicalibration, a fairness-linked test that asks if a forecast is right when checked within many overlapping groups. Prior work tied this test for a trait like a mean or median to whether that trait can be drawn out by regression.

In the online set-up, the known method reached its error bound but ran too slowly to use. The authors give a faster swap version and widen the result beyond group flags. Their work keeps the same style of error growth while it cuts the cost of each round.
arxiv-2511-05207:
Ryuji Hashimoto and co-authors build a market simulation where trader agents both learn and differ in taste, to see what price patterns emerge. Agent models have long split those two traits into rival camps, so their joint effect was unknown.

In their multi-agent learning frame, each trader has its own risk aversion, time discount, and access to information. Prices form from their linked choices, not from a set rule. The study checks which known market facts appear when both traits act at once, a step toward more true-to-life tests of market rules and shocks.
arxiv-2511-05307:
Akua Dickson and co-authors build a framework that keeps soft robot arms within safe force limits when they touch fragile things near them. Soft arms suit delicate work, but past obstacle methods track position only and ignore how hard the arm may push.

Their maps turn force safety rules from task space, points along the arm, into configuration space, the arm's joint angles. That lets the robot check force safety in real time as it moves. The work aims at safe use in homes, labs, and care sites where a hard push could do harm.
arxiv-2511-05407:
Yahui Fu and co-authors model user satisfaction in dialogue systems with an eye on minority users, whose ratings can differ from the crowd's for the same reply style. One-size alignment tends to fit the majority and miss those users.

Their frame learns both personal and group-level tastes for satisfaction scores. A chain of personalized reasoning feeds a preference-adaptive reinforcement step. The aim is a system that can tell when a minority user needs an unlike reply. It should not just grind toward broad consensus. That should lift fit for users at the edges of a user base.
arxiv-2511-05907:
Archit Agarwal, Meghali Garg, and Bibekananda Maji derive an exact formula for counting partitions that obey two restrictions at once. A partition splits a number into a sum of parts. Here the parts must avoid multiples of a fixed step, and each part may carry one of several colors.

The work extends a line running from Hardy and Ramanujan's circle method through Rademacher's exact series and later formulas for special partition families. Using the circle method, the authors get a Rademacher-type exact series for the combined family for any number of colors. As an application they prove higher-order Turán inequalities for the counting function. Bonus results cover colored distinct-part partitions and sums of minimal excludants over ordinary partitions and overpartitions.
arxiv-2511-06107:
David Kaplan and co-authors project whether countries will meet the United Nations goal for basic reading and math skills by 2030. The indicator tracks the share of children reaching minimum proficiency, with a focus on lower secondary students. Five years remain to the deadline member states agreed.

Past reporting used measures not built for forecasting the pace of progress. The team combines Bayesian latent growth curve modeling with Bayesian model averaging to estimate each country's rate well. Data come from the OECD's PISA study plus indicators from the World Bank, UNDP, and UNESCO. The method yields probabilistic projections for all countries in the analysis. Four case study countries show how single-country forecasts work in practice.
arxiv-2511-06207:
Jian Li, Xinsheng Wang, and Jianjie Zhao work in linear dynamics, studying sequences of bounded linear operators acting between Banach spaces. Their topic is mean Li-Yorke chaos, a form of chaotic behavior judged by average separation of points over time rather than by single steps. Two companion notions, mean equicontinuity and mean sensitivity, frame the analysis.

The paper proves a dichotomy: for such operator sequences, the system falls on one side or the other of that pair of properties. It then studies mean Li-Yorke chaos for plain operator sequences and for submultiplicative ones. Several usable criteria for when mean Li-Yorke chaos occurs are established along the way.
arxiv-2511-06407:
Takashi Hayakawa and Satoshi Asai make a powerful sampling method practical for layered Gaussian process models. Such Bayesian models capture tangled nonlinear patterns in real data, but drawing samples from their posteriors has stayed slow outside simple cases. Riemannian-manifold Hamiltonian Monte Carlo adapts its geometry to the model, yet standard toolkits run it sluggishly.

The speedup comes from reordering computation to match the model's structure and caching matrix decompositions through dynamic programming. A naive automatic differentiator inside existing toolkits cannot deliver that gain. Tests on simulated logistic regression and on national medical spending data showed effective posterior sampling and evidence values, laying groundwork for better Gaussian process software.
arxiv-2511-06507:
Harrison Horn and co-authors report lab evidence that dry, hydrogen-rich planets can manufacture their own water deep inside. Sub-Neptune planets are common, and models read them as either hydrogen blankets or water layers over rocky cores. Water-rich worlds were assumed to form far from their stars and wander inward later.

High-pressure experiments reacted warm dense hydrogen fluid with molten silicate rock. Silicon left the melt to form alloys and hydrides, freeing oxygen that combined with hydrogen into water reaching tens of percent by weight. That yield far exceeds older low-pressure estimates. Finding abundant water on a close-in planet may therefore say little about where the planet was born.
arxiv-2511-06907:
Ilias Papalamprou and four co-authors optimize matrix multiplication, the workhorse of scientific computing and deep learning, for AMD's Versal ACAP chips. These chips mix AI engines, programmable logic, and processors, which suits edge computing but makes mapping the computation across them complex. Earlier work largely ignored the trade-off between speed and energy.

Their automated system searches for mappings tuned either for performance or for energy efficiency. Instead of relying on analytical models, it trains a machine learning model on roughly six thousand measured on-board tests to guide the search. On the Versal VCK190 board, the resulting designs improved throughput by about 1.23 times on average and energy efficiency by about 1.25 times over leading systems, with larger gains in the best cases.
arxiv-2511-07007:
Duc Nguyen and six co-authors introduce TrueCity, a benchmark for understanding three-dimensional city scenes from point clouds. Models need labeled real-world data to generalize, but labeling is scarce, and synthetic data, though perfectly labeled, misses real sensor noise and complexity. No earlier benchmark offered matched real and simulated point clouds of the same place for studying that synthetic-to-real gap.

TrueCity supplies centimeter-accurate labeled real point clouds, semantic 3D city models, and labeled simulated point clouds representing the same city. Its classes follow international 3D city modeling standards, enabling consistent comparison across the two domains. Extensive tests with common baselines quantify how large the domain shift is and test plans for using synthetic data to strengthen real-world scene understanding. Data, code, and models are public.
arxiv-2511-07707:
Manonmani Sekar and Nasim Nezamoddini schedule factories that rebuild themselves for each product change. Reconfigurable manufacturing systems swap hardware settings quickly, but planning must keep pace in real time amid shifting demand and supply disruptions. Static schedules collapse under that variability.

Negotiating software agents, trained with multi-agent reinforcement learning, bid and bargain over jobs and machines. Deep Q-network agents learn under centralized training, then act flexibly as conditions change. The soft planning layer adapts without stopping the line. Smarter dynamic scheduling could let reconfigurable plants deliver their promised agility instead of choking on complexity.
arxiv-2511-08307:
Aranyak Acharyya, Joshua Agterberg, Youngser Park, and Carey Priebe prove closeness bounds for response based vectors of black box maker models. Vector each model as a vector, built from its answers to shared queries, lets analysts compare systems like language and image generators. The Data Kernel View Space method gives one such vector, but users need to know how many sample responses make it trustworthy.

Under stated regularity assumptions, the sample vector stays close to its population version with high probability. The bounds state exactly how many responses a desired accuracy requires. The algebraic tools also extend to classic multidimensional scaling vectors when dissimilarities are observed with noise.
arxiv-2511-08407:
Apimuk Sornsaeng, Itai Arad, and Dario Poletti test the superposition of product states ansatz for many body quantum spin systems from one to three dimensions. Tensor networks dominate this field but lose power outside one dimensional local models and make extracting information approximate. The superposition ansatz, related to canonical polyadic decomposition, trades compression strength for exact information extraction, geometry independence, easy parallelization, and analytic shortcuts.

The authors first chart typical properties of the ansatz for spin half systems, including entanglement entropy and trainability. Ground state searches on tilted Ising models, in one and three dimensions with short and long range couplings plus a random network, then show the method can reach high accuracy.
arxiv-2511-08707:
Zhuojun Tian and Mehdi Bennis design a learning scheme for teams of agents that each see the world from a different viewpoint. Their framework rests on the maximal coding rate reduction principle, a rule that shapes learned representations to be compact within classes yet diverse across them.

Each agent periodically factors its learned subspaces and sends truncated basis matrices to its peers. Fused subspaces emerge from the exchange, and a projection step pulls every agent's outputs toward the shared result. The authors prove the coding-rate change stays bounded and that basis fusion is consistent across agents. Simulations show high classification accuracy while the agents' representations stay diverse. Baseline methods, by contrast, collapse toward correlated subspaces and tangled representations.
arxiv-2511-08807:
Juan José Montellano-Ballesteros and Christian Rubio-Montiel study a coloring number for directed graphs built around mutual reachability between color classes. In a dib-coloring, each color class must contain a vertex that points toward every other class and a vertex that all other classes point toward, while the coloring stays acyclic.

The dib-chromatic number is the largest number of colors such a coloring can use. The authors first answer a basic question that the definition leaves open: whether this number always exists. They then work out the dib-chromatic number for bipartite digraphs, the two-sided directed graphs that model many matching and ordering problems. The paper is a contribution to structural graph theory, where new coloring invariants are tested on the graph families that reveal their behavior.
arxiv-2511-08907:
Patrick Mayeda proves a structural theorem about exit path categories, a tool from stratified topology that records how paths can leave the singular layers of a space. The setting is a smooth manifold carrying an action of a finite group, and the question is how the exit path category of the manifold relates to that of the quotient space.

The functor between the two categories turns out to be a right fibration, a well-behaved kind of map between categories. The entering-path category of the quotient is classified by a natural functor into the group's orbit category. The technical core is a maneuver that replaces arbitrary exit paths with immediately exiting ones, which lets homotopies downstairs lift to homotopies upstairs. Such results help compute invariants of quotient spaces from the better-understood spaces above them.
arxiv-2511-09607:
Abhijit Banerjee and three co-authors carry a classic uniqueness theory for meromorphic functions into several complex variables. The Yang-Hua theorems describe when two meromorphic functions must coincide, given how they share values. Their paper studies a nonlinear differential equation coupling two functions through a directional derivative, in several complex variables.

The authors extend the Yang and Hua results from 1997 to this higher-dimensional setting. They also prove new uniqueness theorems that extend those conclusions further. As one use, they derive explicit solutions of certain nonlinear partial differential equations in several variables. Physical readings of those solutions are collected in tabular form, linking the abstract uniqueness theory to concrete equations.
arxiv-2511-09707:
Ajaykrishnan E S and three co-authors give a quasi-polynomial time algorithm for three-coloring circle graphs. Circle graphs arise as intersection graphs of chords of a circle. Whether three-coloring them is solvable in polynomial time is a well-known open problem.

Their algorithm runs in quasi-polynomial time. It produces a proper three-coloring whenever one exists. As a consequence, the same bound decides whether an ordered graph has a three-page book embedding. The authors call the result a partial resolution of the open problem. Quasi-polynomial is far below exponential, but the polynomial question remains open.
arxiv-2511-10407:
Jia-Hua Zou and nine co-authors design a way to link superconducting quantum processors through optical networks. Processors in separate refrigerators cannot share quantum states directly, and turning microwave signals into light is hard to do well. Their module uses a nonlinear circuit element called a SNAIL to connect light converters with long-lived 3D microwave cavities.

Simulations include noise from laser heating, signal loss, and imperfect detection. Raw entangled states reach a fidelity around 0.8 at rates of thousands per second across thirty kilometers of fiber. A tailored pumping step, matched to the dominant error type, lifts fidelity to about 0.94 at slower rates. The cavity based design beats transmon based schemes in their tests, offering a practical route toward linked quantum machines.
arxiv-2511-10607:
Trung Hoa Dinh and Nhat A. Nghiem add to the growing list of quantum information quantities that quantum computers can estimate. Recent work has produced quantum algorithms for entropies and matrix means, and this paper targets two broader objects: maximal quantum f-divergences and Kubo-Ando means.

The authors present quantum algorithms for computing both. The maximal f-divergence generalizes familiar distance measures between quantum states, while Kubo-Ando means formalize averages of positive operators. Because Rényi entropies and ordinary matrix means appear as special cases of their targets, the pair argue their framework is universal, subsuming several earlier quantum algorithms under one approach.
arxiv-2511-10907:
Leonard Susskind publishes a short correction to a claim he made in his own recent papers and lectures about where entropy resides in a holographic model of de Sitter space. The setting is the DSSYK and JT gravity description of the static patch, and the question is how far the stretched horizon, where the entropy lives, sits from the mathematical horizon.

Susskind had argued the distance was a string-scale length. He now states that conclusion rested on a misconception about the confinement-deconfinement transition in the 't Hooft model. With that error corrected, the right answer is of order the Planck distance, which differs from the string distance by a factor tied to the square root of the model's size parameter. The note is a self-correction of the earlier claim.
arxiv-2511-11307:
Saptarshi Neil Sinha, Julius Kühn, and their colleagues estimate the full 3D pose of strawberries using only synthetic training data, aimed at robotic fruit picking. Automated selective harvesting matters where seasonal labor is scarce and costly, but real training photos of fruit in place are hard to gather at scale. Their pipeline renders photorealistic fake strawberries from 3D models through a procedural Blender process.

A single-shot pose algorithm built on a fast detection backbone predicts position and orientation at once and can run on edge hardware. Models scored comparably on a desktop graphics card and a small Jetson board across pose metrics. The desktop ran faster, while the Jetson suited tight field settings.
arxiv-2511-11407:
Manyu Li, Ruian He, and their colleagues introduce MicroVQA++, a large data set for training multimodal models to reason about microscopy images. Biomedical models are increasingly asked science questions about such images, yet high-quality training data for microscopy reasoning are scarce. The corpus is drawn from the BIOMEDICA archive through a three-stage pipeline built for quality control.

Stage one draws supervision from expert-validated figure and caption pairs in peer-reviewed papers. Stage two filters inconsistent samples with a heterogeneous graph that fuses text entailment checks, vision-language alignment, and agent signals. Stage three has a model agent draft choice questions, screened by humans. The release pairs a large training split with a human-checked test split.
arxiv-2511-12107:
Tianxiang Zhang and five co-authors improve face forgery detection, as deepfakes pose a growing threat to trust in images and video. The vision model DINOv2 looks promising for this task, but plain fine-tuning treats all fakes as one class. That misses the distinct traces left by different forgery methods.

Their adapter adds small trainable modules to each transformer block and trains two tasks at once: is the face real, and which forgery method made it? A shared branch passes forgery cues into the real-or-fake decision. With only a small number of trainable parameters, the method matches or beats larger state-of-the-art systems in their tests.
arxiv-2511-12407:
Nivedina A. Sarma and twelve co-authors map how inverse surfactants, molecules with water-hating heads and water-loving long tails, assemble into tunable nanostructures. Natural hierarchical materials often form by self-assembly of similar two-sided molecules, and synthetic versions of these inverse molecules show promise for uses such as drug delivery. Which shapes form, and why, was not fully mapped.

Scattering experiments, simulations and statistical theory together show that head-group size is a key control knob for shape changes. A simple ratio, the size of the hydrophobic part against the hydrophilic part, emerges as the deciding quantity for micelle structure and for the jump to larger aggregates. A minimal theory captures the behavior quantitatively.
arxiv-2511-12807:
Giuseppina Nigro and six co-authors model why some fast-rotating late M dwarf stars show steady magnetic fields while others show restless ones. Stars in the same range split into two branches: stable dipole fields, or strongly varying ones, both run by an alpha-squared dynamo. The authors use a low-dimensional shell model of thermally driven magnetoconvection that captures the dynamo's essential nonlinear dynamics while leaving out density stratification.

To check the model, they compare its pattern of magnetic polarity reversals with Earth's paleomagnetic record, the richest reversal data available for such a dynamo. The key finding: stronger convective heat transport brings more frequent reversals and thus more variable fields. That suggests the two branches of M dwarfs may differ mainly in how efficiently they move heat. The authors stress the model is qualitative.
arxiv-2511-13407:
S. V. Trofymenko and I. V. Kyryllin simulate K-shell ionization and the resulting X-rays when fast electrons and positrons cross oriented silicon crystals. The study follows how the angular pattern of X-rays from the crystal's entry face changes with beam angle and energy. Energies span a wide range, from one to one thousand giga-electronvolts in the simulations.

Their simulation method is described in full, and the results show the angular pattern usually shifts in a non-monotonic way. The authors discuss the physical causes behind that behavior. Special attention goes to dechanneling, the process where electrons leave guided crystal paths, and how it shapes the X-rays they emit.
arxiv-2511-13807:
Andreas Kamilaris and 7 co-authors report three years of running GAEA, a country-scale environmental digital twin for Cyprus. The twin hosts twenty-seven geospatial services over the whole island, serving urban planners, policymakers, farmers, property owners, and forestry workers, plus insurers and banks with property portfolios. Few digital twins have run at national scale long enough to teach operational lessons.

Their account covers what worked, what strained, and what comes next for large environmental twins. Data upkeep, service design, and user trust all surface as live challenges at this scale. The paper gives agencies weighing similar national systems a grounded record of costs, benefits, and pitfalls from a real deployment.
arxiv-2511-14207:
Antonio De Felice and Shinji Tsujikawa show how adding an electric ingredient rescues a class of exotic stars. In k-essence theories, where matter depends on a scalar field and its motion, a no-go result forbids healthy static compact objects with positive energy density. Extending the theory to depend also on a gauge field's strength escapes that verdict.

Within Einstein-scalar-Maxwell theory with a scalar-vector coupling, the authors construct charged compact stars that are flat at infinity and have vanishing density and pressure at the center. They solve the field profiles analytically and compute masses and radii. Electric versions pass stability checks everywhere, while magnetic ones suffer strong coupling near the center.
arxiv-2511-14407:
The ExoClock project presents an updated catalogue of transit times for six hundred and twenty exoplanets. Hundreds of contributors, led by A. Kokori and co-authors, combine ground and space telescope data. Precise transit times tell observers when a planet will cross its star. Old predictions drift, so regular updates are vital for future missions.

The catalogue merges thirty thousand measures from small ground telescopes, past papers, and major space missions. It improves prediction precision by about tenfold for many planets. Nearly half the planets needed a correction. The team also flag planets whose transit times vary. The open catalogue supports planning for the Ariel space mission and beyond.
arxiv-2511-14607:
Agustin Olivares, Paul Leger, and Rodrigo Poblete model sludge management for vinasse treatment in the Chilean pisco industry. Making one liter of alcohol leaves ten to fifteen liters of vinasse wastewater. Stored vinasse evaporates and leaves a nutrient rich acidic sludge. That sludge can harm soil and plants if mishandled.

Their system dynamics model compares three strategies on cost and benefit. Options are natural drying, moving sludge to another site, and chemical treatment to speed sludge formation. Scenario analysis shows trade offs for each path. Prior sludge models focused on urban water, not alcohol waste. The study gives local producers a planning tool grounded in their process.
arxiv-2511-15007:
Shehan Irteza Pranto and five co-authors introduce a graphical interface for collecting and viewing vaping behavior data. Puff duration, gaps between puffs, and puffs per session shape exposure to toxicants. A passive monitor device records puffing and touching events from nicotine delivery systems. Raw logs alone are hard for researchers and regulators to interpret.

The Python interface extracts, decodes, and visualizes a full day of puffing data. Tests on experimental data confirm correct time conversion and event decoding. Behavior plots are clear and effective for analysis. The software is open source and freely shared. Better tooling should improve studies that inform regulation of vaping products.
arxiv-2511-15207:
Chaofeng Guan, Gaojun Luo, and three co-authors study repetition codes inside the retransmission protocols that keep messages intact over noisy channels. Every code fails sometimes, so systems check each message and ask for a resend when the check fails. Some protocols resend the identical codeword, while others send a fresh coded version of the same message.

The authors generalize repetition coding across both styles and ask how to maximize the chance of a correct decode within a limited number of rounds. Their framework joins error correction at the physical layer with the integrity check above it. Smarter repetition matters for hybrid retransmission schemes in modern wireless standards, where each extra round costs time and spectrum.
arxiv-2511-15607:
Vincenzo Fiorentino and Stefan Weigert extend a classic quantum theorem to the simplest quantum system, a qubit. Gleason theorem derives the standard probability rule for quantum measurements from basic assumptions, but in its original form it does not cover two-dimensional systems like a qubit alone. Their trick is to treat the qubit as part of a larger combined system.

The combined systems structure, described by a tensor product, lets them derive both the state description and the Born probability rule for a qubit. The key demand is consistency: chances assigned to outcomes must not depend on whether the system is viewed alone or as part of a larger whole. The result also survives in some alternative theories.
arxiv-2511-15707:
Nachiketa Sarkar introduces a statistical framework for finding chemical freeze-out conditions in collisions of heavy nuclei. Freeze-out is the stage when particle abundances stop changing, described by a temperature and a chemical potential. Analysts usually fit ratios of particle yields, but choosing which ratios to use loses information and adds hidden uncertainty, a long-standing ambiguity Sarkar aims to remove.

All possible ratios from a chosen particle set are transformed into an uncorrelated component basis that removes linear redundancy. A thermal gas model is then calibrated in that clean space, energy by energy, using Bayesian methods with a fast emulator. Sensitivity analysis shows which ratio mixes matter most and reveals a shift from chemical-potential control to temperature control at higher energies.
arxiv-2511-15807:
Bhagyesh Kumar and four co-authors introduce TopoReformer, a defense that cleans attacks on text-reading systems. Optical character recognition turns text images into machine text. Tiny, near invisible changes can fool it into wrong output, and some attacks survive photo capture in the real world. That threatens document work, plate reading, and compliance tools.

TopoReformer reforms the input using topology, the study of global shape traits like links and holes that survive bending. An autoencoder enforces consistency in a hidden form, restoring structure while removing the attack. Tests on handwritten character and digit data cover standard attacks, adaptive attacks, and one attack made just for text reading.
arxiv-2511-16107:
Shao-Jun Xia, Huixin Zhang, and Zhengzhong Tu study whether vision-language models can learn a visual task from examples of a different task. Visual in-context learning solves a task from a few demonstration pairs without training, and large models do this well when demonstration and query match. Real cases often mismatch, leaving unclear whether the model should copy the shown transformation or infer a new one.

Their T2T-VICL framework converts mismatched demonstrations into implicit textual guidance without naming the tasks. A large teacher model describes visual changes and task differences across pairs, building a data set of cross-task relations. That skill is distilled into a lightweight student that writes content-dependent prompts, which then guide the answering model on the new query.
arxiv-2511-17107:
Chenhao Jin and Hehu Xie build a solver for a core computational problem in photonics: finding the vibration modes of light inside a photonic crystal made of anisotropic material. The Maxwell eigenproblem behind this has a large null space that stalls naive methods. Their solver uses kernel compensation within Yee's classic grid scheme to remove that null space, and runs matrix-free on graphics processors using fast Fourier transforms.

A new discretization handles permittivity tensors with off-diagonal entries, the signature of anisotropy, and the authors prove the resulting matrix has the symmetry and positivity their method needs. Benchmark tests confirm the scheme is robust and accurate. The work gives designers of optical devices a faster, trustworthy tool for anisotropic crystals.
arxiv-2511-17207:
Kunyi Li and five co-authors present SING3R-SLAM, a system that builds a three-dimensional map of an indoor space from a single moving camera. Simultaneous localization and mapping from one camera is hard because small errors accumulate into drift and inconsistent scale. Recent dense reconstruction methods capture local geometry well but struggle to stay globally consistent when used incrementally.

SING3R-SLAM represents the scene as a global map of Gaussian primitives that acts as a persistent, adjustable memory. Local reconstructions are aligned at the submap level into that global map, and the global map's consistency then refines the local geometry in return. Experiments showed state-of-the-art results in camera pose estimation, reconstruction detail, and novel view rendering, with pose accuracy improved by over ten percent. The map stays compact enough for practical use.
arxiv-2511-17307:
Jonghwan Rhee and nine co-authors solve a data-handling problem for the DINGO survey, which hunts neutral hydrogen gas in distant galaxies with the ASKAP radio telescope. Deep spectral observations create storage demands that next-generation instruments make severe. The default plan, reducing each day's data and stacking images, risks baking in systematic errors; imaging everything jointly is prohibitively expensive. The team tests a middle route on 200 hours of pilot and survey data.

Their method pauses the pipeline at the daily residual visibility grids, stacks those, and deconvolves once, jointly. Against a full traditional reduction, this uv-grid stacking recovered nearly all of the hydrogen flux, while image stacking lost about eight percent and produced artefacts like negative bowls around bright sources. Line widths came back within a few percent. The team will apply the method to the full DINGO survey.
arxiv-2511-17807:
Gilberto Aguilar-Perez, Giovany Cruz, Miguel Cruz, and Efrain Rojas study a gravity model that pictures the universe as a surface, or brane, moving in a higher dimensional space. They look at the model through thermodynamics, the study of heat and energy at the horizon that bounds what observers can see.

Extra terms from the brane picture change the horizon entropy and temperature in the background equations. The authors test whether the horizon and the surrounding bulk can stay in thermal balance for different kinds of matter. Balance turns out to depend strongly on how the matter pressure relates to its density.
arxiv-2511-18007:
Siteng Ma, Honghui Du, Prateek Mathur, Brendan S Kelly, Ronan P Killeen, Aonghus Lawlor, and Ruihai Dong ask whether full labelling is needed for change detection on medical scans taken over time. Labelling such series is slow and costly, since new lesions can be tiny and easy to miss across visits. Active learning, which asks experts to label only the most useful cases, has mostly been tested on still tasks, not on change over time.

The team builds a framework shaped for longitudinal imaging, pairing and differencing two-dimensional slices so change itself becomes the signal the learner queries. The aim is to reach strong detection with far fewer expert labels. For hospitals sitting on large unlabelled scan archives, a method of this kind could cut the cost of building monitoring tools sharply.
arxiv-2511-18107:
Yegon Kim, Hyunsu Kim, Gyeonghoon Ko, and Juho Lee cut the cost of training surrogate models for partial differential equations, fast stand ins for expensive numerical solvers. Making training data with the solver dominates the cost, and existing active learning buys whole solution trajectories even when only some time steps matter.

Their STAP framework buys only the most important time steps from the solver and lets the surrogate approximate the rest, so a fixed budget covers more diverse trajectories. A new acquisition rule estimates how much a chosen set of steps would reduce variance. Benchmark equations confirm the savings in practice.
arxiv-2511-18407:
Adil Belhaj and Maryem Jemri study thermodynamics of charged black holes in a gravity model inspired by non commutative geometry from string theory. They introduce extended derivatives carrying an antisymmetric tensor like those in string fields, then solve the field equations for the resulting black holes.

They analyze stability, critical behavior, and phase transitions, computing a free energy whose shape resembles the classic Van der Waals fluid transition. A pressure and volume style transition appears for suitable ranges of the deformation setting and the charge, which they constrain with graphics processor based methods borrowed from machine learning tools.
arxiv-2511-18507:
Kai Jiang and six co-authors teach large multimodal models new scenes in sequence without wiping old skill. A device model meets shifting views: high air shots, underwater scenes, low air shots, and indoor rooms. Learning each in turn tends to erase the last, a flaw called catastrophic forgetting.

The team build MSVQA, a question set that spans those four scene types and views. Their frame, UNIFIER, grows the vision code space as new scenes come, yet ties views of one scene to stay coherent. Skill thus builds up inside a scene and aids the next. Tests show less forgetting than past continual methods. The work targets models that must keep learning on the move.
arxiv-2511-18607:
Bo-Eun Choi and seven co-authors find that the Magellanic Stream reaches farther than maps had shown. The Stream is a vast gas trail in the Milky Way halo, most of its mass ionized, drawn from the two Magellanic Clouds as they interact with the Galaxy. Sight lines to background quasars probe its extent.

Spectra from the Hubble telescope's cosmic origins tool, in the Plane Quasar Survey, show carbon absorbers that fit the Stream on the north side of the Galactic plane. The gas sits about sixty degrees past the known ionized edge, with matched place and motion. Low ions are absent while high ions show, a sign of hot gas. Ion ratios favor heating by collisions over light. The Stream's ionized reach grows by a wide step.
arxiv-2511-18707:
Sandeep Bajrangi Bari, Sahan Raghava Sykam, Ranojit Das, Rohit Tyagi, and Aditya H Kelkar describe two instruments built for ion collision experiments at a university accelerator in Kanpur, India. When a fast ion strikes an atom or molecule, its charge can change, and measuring that charge after the collision reveals what happened. Their charge state analyser sorts the outgoing ions with an electrostatic parallel-plate deflector, a design they first simulated with ion optics software.

A second build, a programmable bipolar power supply reaching ten kilovolts, biases the analyser's electrodes. Both devices were tested in real collision studies using proton and carbon beams at million-electronvolt energies from the facility's tandem accelerator. The paper is a practical build report for labs equipping similar collision experiments.
arxiv-2511-18807:
Chun-Meng Tang, Chun-Gui Duan, Liang Tang, and Cong-Feng Qiao predict masses for gluonic tetraquark states by QCD sum rules. A tetraquark binds four quarks; a gluonic kind adds a gluon rich core. The team study a color layout that joins two charm pairs with a gluon field in matching color states.

Eighteen current forms cover three spin parity charge sets beyond two sets from past work. An operator expansion with nonperturbative terms to a set depth yields the mass spectrum. Most sets land in a high mass band, with two slightly lower. The values back a gluonic part inside known di-J/psi structures. Sum rule forecasts guide where hunters should look in collider data.
arxiv-2511-19107:
Robert Bredereck, Eva Deltl, Leon Kellerhals, and Jannik Peters prove a negative result about fair clustering. They study grouping where no cluster has a centre, and each member's loss is the largest distance to anyone else in their group. A clustering is in the core if no group of agents can split off and all do better, a stability idea borrowed from game theory. The question is whether such a stable grouping always exists.

For every number of groups from three up, they construct metric examples, with as few as nine agents. Where no clustering lies in the approximate core for any factor below a bound they compute, and they show that bound is tight for their construction. With computer help they also find a flat Euclidean example with a slightly weaker bound. It is, they note, the first proof that the core can be empty here.
arxiv-2511-19207:
Megan H Martinez, Michael S Petersen, Carrie Filion, Rashid Yaaqib, and Claire Larson present a data-driven way to measure how tilted disc galaxies are and which way they face. A galaxy's inclination and position angle are basic inputs for almost any study of its structure, yet they are usually fitted with heavy models. Their method decomposes galaxy images in a Fourier-Laguerre basis, a set of patterns tuned to disc shapes, and reads the tilt from a simple ratio between the fourfold and uniform components.

That ratio maps to inclination through an empirical relation that holds regardless of the galaxy's detailed morphology, while the facing angle comes straight from the phase of the fourfold part. On a benchmark set the method matches published values closely with almost no catastrophic failures. They apply it across the Siena Galaxy Atlas.
arxiv-2511-19407:
Johan Samsing, Lorenz Zwick, Pankaj Saini, and János Takátsy show how gravitational wave lensing can reveal where a black hole merger happened. When a massive object bends the waves, observers see several images of one event. Comparing them gives a stereoscopic view, letting the source's motion across the sky be measured from Doppler shifts.

Acceleration of the source adds a drift in each image over time. Measuring both effects together constrains the dynamics of the home environment, from clusters to triple star systems. Mergers inside active galactic nucleus disks look especially promising, so future lensed catalogs could test that formation channel directly.
arxiv-2511-19507:
M. Mavin De Silva, Callie Clark, Tadachika Nakayama, and Takahiro Yabe measure whether placing an electric vehicle charging station lifts business at nearby shops. Theory models of driver behavior often miss real trip patterns and understate local effects. The authors instead run a quasi-experiment on real deployment history.

Phone location data track visits to businesses in New York City and the California Bay Area, where stations were installed at staggered times. Matching treated shops with similar untreated ones, and comparing three matching strategies, avoids biased control groups. The staggered design also overlaps better in dense areas. Stations are found to raise customer traffic significantly.
arxiv-2511-19707:
Dennis Bodewits and eight co-authors catch a comet breaking apart just after its close pass by the Sun. Comet C/2025 K1 (ATLAS) swung within a third of Earth's orbital distance in October 2025. Daily monitoring then showed a sharp activity jump in early November, with the coma changing shape fast.

Hubble images taken days later resolve five fragments, an unusually early view of a nucleus mid-breakup. Motions show a chain of splits, and both main breakups came one to three days before their bright outbursts. Fresh inner material seems to need warming time before dust escapes well, and spin-up from outgassing is a plausible breakup driver.
arxiv-2511-19807:
R. Negrello and seventeen co-authors steer electron beams with bent silicon crystals at unusually low energies. A crystal bent along its atomic planes can channel particles, guiding the beam while boosting radiation. The team fires beams of three energies from the Mainz Microtron through a very thin bent crystal.

Experiment and simulation together sort out channeling, dechanneling, rechanneling, and volume capture, and weigh each effect on steering and radiation. Steering still works at the lowest energy, with channeling efficiency above fifty percent, a record there. Channeling and volume reflection raise radiation up to sixfold, supporting bent crystals for compact light sources.
arxiv-2511-19907:
Mingyu Zhao and six co-authors present MHB, a system for recognizing continuous American Sign Language. Their method first finds where each sign starts and ends in a sentence video, then recognizes the cut signs. It uses three-dimensional skeletal features, which capture how sign properties bunch near boundaries.

A handshape classifier, pretrained on eighty-seven linguistically defined handshape categories from a newly merged dataset, adds information about shapes expected at sign edges. A fusion module joins the segmentation and handshape models, and the found boundaries feed a recognition model trained on isolated and pre-cut signs. On the ASLLRP corpus, the method improves clearly over earlier work.
arxiv-2511-20507:
Roll and colleagues give language models a clinical language exam adapted from aphasia care. Their 2025 paper introduces the Text Aphasia Battery, or TAB. Aphasia is language loss from brain damage, assessed with standard batteries. Those tests assume speech, hearing, and human pragmatics. Text-only models need a redesigned instrument instead.

TAB adapts the Quick Aphasia Battery into four text subtests. They cover word understanding, sentence understanding, repetition, and connected text. Speech-language pathologists helped develop the benchmark. An automated grader using Gemini 2.5 Flash scores responses at scale. Its agreement with consensus reached a kappa of 0.255 in validation. Human raters agreed with each other at 0.286, a comparable level. The framework probes how linguistic abilities break down in models. It is explicitly not a diagnostic tool for human patients. Released openly, TAB links clinical aphasiology with model analysis.
arxiv-2511-20707:
Salman Sajad Wani and colleagues work out in 2025 how relativity changes the quantum speed limit. That limit is the fastest pace at which a quantum system can change state. Two bounds set it, one by Mandelstam and Tamm, one by Margolus and Levitin, but both ignore relativistic effects. The omission matters for satellite quantum-key links, gravitational-wave detectors, and space clock networks, where timing precision is everything.

Starting from the Foldy-Wouthuysen expansion, the team adds the leading relativistic correction and tracks laser-like and squeezed light states. Relativity slows their evolution by an amount depending on the state's size and squeezing. It also raises the speed-limit bounds and adds a phase drift that dulls timing sensitivity. The effect is small but testable in the lab. For one electron in a 5.4-tesla Penning trap, read out at 149 gigahertz, the drift should appear within 15 minutes, inside holding times.
arxiv-2511-20907:
Sheng Ran argues in 2025 that quantum mechanics is missing half of a symmetry hiding in its own equations. A quantum state can be written in space and time coordinates or, equivalently, in momentum and energy coordinates, the two linked by a Fourier transform. Standard theory treats the second as a mere re-expression: all evolution happens in time, none in energy. Ran enlarges the state space to contain both sectors.

In the enlarged space, the momentum-energy sector gains autonomous evolution, driven by its own generator. The result is a dual-manifold geometry where each domain looks complete inside yet opens onto the other. Remarkably, Ran shows this symmetry alone reproduces two phenomena usually credited to general relativity. One is the uniform dark-energy background filling the cosmos; the other is the exponential mapping at black hole horizons behind Hawking radiation.
arxiv-2511-21107:
Tongkai Lu, Shuai Ma, and Chongyang Tao improve in 2025 the neural branching decisions inside mixed-integer linear programming solvers. Branch-and-bound search lives or dies by which variable it splits on at each node. Learned branching policies imitate strong branching, but they treat all tree nodes alike. Yet nodes near the root differ semantically from deep ones, and expert samples for the scarce upstream nodes are costly to collect. Their SC-MILP framework groups nodes by feature distribution into strata.

A graph convolutional model is then trained with dynamic stratified contrastive learning, pulling same-group nodes together and pushing groups apart, with separation growing along the hierarchy. An upstream augmentation procedure manufactures equivalent and perturbed problem instances, relieving upstream data scarcity without more labels. On MILP benchmarks, the method raised branching accuracy, cut solving time, and generalised to unseen instances, beating traditional branching rules and neural approaches.
arxiv-2511-21307:
Xinyi Zhang, Liang Liang, Anastasia Ailamaki, and Jianliang Xu design a database index meant to stay fast when reads and writes collide, in 2025. Learned indexes predict where a key sits using a model of the data's distribution, beating classical trees on simple lookups. Under mixed workloads, though, they suffer long tail delays, weak range scans, and erratic behavior as data shifts.

Zhang and her coauthors answer with HIRE, a hybrid in-memory index. Its leaf nodes adapt their layout to local data and workload, while model-accelerated internal nodes absorb updates through a log. A non-blocking, cost-driven recalibration keeps the structure honest as data changes, and a smarter bulk-loading routine builds it efficiently. On real-world datasets HIRE reached up to about 42 times the throughput of rival indexes under mixed workloads and cut tail latency by up to 98 percent.
arxiv-2511-21607:
Zarin Tahia Hossain and Mostafa Milani warn that filling in missing data accurately is not the same as knowing how much to trust the fill, in 2025. Modern imputers differ widely in how they express confidence about their guesses, and users rarely check whether that confidence is honest. The team ran a systematic study across three method families: statistical, transport-based, and deep generative approaches.

Six representative methods, including MICE, SoftImpute, and GAIN, were compared across datasets, missingness rates, and all three missingness patterns, from random to value-dependent. Confidence was estimated three ways, repeated runs, model sampling, and predictive distributions, and scored with reliability curves and expected calibration error. The headline result: accuracy and honesty are often misaligned, so the most accurate method may be least trustworthy about its own errors. Methods that directly model uncertainty gave more reliable coverage, and the paper closes with selection guidelines.
arxiv-2511-21707:
Zhuoran Duan and eleven coauthors build a large multimodal model that perceives the world through radio signals, in 2025. Sixth-generation networks aim to fuse communication, sensing, and intelligence, and a wireless-native model could serve billions of users by understanding physical surroundings from the signals networks already exchange. Research on such models is young, and no standard training recipe existed.

Duan and his coauthors first lay out the characteristics such models should have, then propose a two-stage paradigm: modality-specific alignment, then task-specific adaptation. Their GPT-style model trains on a real-world large-scale dataset, using wireless signals as the anchor modality for contrastive learning. In feasibility tests on integrated sensing and communication data, it outperformed both small specialist models and general large multimodal models, with strong cross-scenario generalization.
arxiv-2511-21907:
Cherdantsev and colleagues analyse magnetoelastic materials, the composites in sensors and actuators whose magnetic and mechanical behaviours are coupled. Modelling them is hard because part of the energy lives on the original, undeformed shape and part on the deformed one. The team asks what effective, averaged-out theory emerges when the material's fine periodic structure shrinks away and the elastic response is small.

Working in the rigorous language of Gamma-convergence, they prove that sequences with bounded energy stay compact. They identify the limiting energy exactly: a quadratic homogenized magnetoelastic term plus homogenized exchange and magnetostatic self-energy terms. In plain terms, the mixed model simplifies to a precise linear effective model. The authors note this is, to their knowledge, the first homogenization result for manifold-valued energies with this mixed Eulerian-Lagrangian structure, opening the door to similar results for other coupled-physics materials.
arxiv-2511-22207:
Banerjee, Airon, Vishwakarma, and Debnath, number theorists, compute how large spaces of Siegel modular forms can be. Siegel modular forms generalize classical modular forms to several variables, and knowing the dimension of the space at a given genus, prime level, weight. Nebentypus character is basic data the field lacks in general: no formula covers arbitrary characters, and low weights at or below four resist the trace-formula methods that handle heavier weights.

Their method determines the image of restriction maps for forms with arbitrary characters and weights, and a Java implementation computes Fourier expansions of those images for genus two. From the restriction image the bound follows, giving the first upper bounds for spaces with nontrivial character across all weights, including the stubborn low-weight cases. The algorithm complements formulas assuming trivial character or weight at least five.
arxiv-2511-22707:
Wei and colleagues build a recommender that treats each item as a set of levels. Most generative recommenders blend an item's ID, category, title, and text into one code, which flattens those levels. Shoppers start broad, then narrow to a type and one product. CoFiRec splits item data into levels, from broad categories down to fine detail and user signals. Each level is tokenized on its own, and the order of levels is kept.

At decode time, the model writes item tokens from coarse to fine. That order tracks how intent narrows from broad tastes to a single item. The team proves the design cuts the gap between items it makes and true items. On several public test sets, CoFiRec beat prior methods across base models. The authors offer level-wise token design as a general lesson.
arxiv-2511-22807:
Nguyen Hong Duc and Vu Trung Hieu give an algorithm for a deceptively basic question: does a polynomial in several variables stay above some floor, or plunge to minus infinity somewhere? Lower-boundedness is a prerequisite for optimisation algorithms computing global minima, yet the only complete method was quantifier elimination, whose cost grows doubly exponentially in the number of variables. A recent tangency-value characterisation suggested another route but yielded no algorithm.

They introduce the given polynomial's non-critical tangency value polynomial at a point, a single-variable polynomial with Puiseux series coefficients whose roots encode the tangency values. At a generic point, deciding lower-boundedness reduces to counting certain roots of it, a job Sturm's classical theorem handles. The resulting probabilistic algorithm decided test cases efficiently and, in experiments, outperformed quantifier elimination, especially on dense polynomials. A full complexity analysis is left as the key open problem.
arxiv-2511-22907:
Houshiar and colleagues give the contact binary EM Tucanae its first multiband workup. W UMa systems are star pairs so close they share a common envelope; EM Tuc had never had a multiband light curve analysis. The team combined ground-based observations in B, V, Rc, and Ic filters with TESS data, modelled the light curves with PHOEBE, and refined fits by Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling.

The O-C diagram, built from all available eclipse timings, curves upward parabolically. The orbital period is increasing, corresponding to mass flowing from the less massive star to the more massive one at about 4.62 hundred-millionths of a solar mass per year. Modelling confirms an overcontact configuration with mass ratio 3.987, needs a cool starspot to explain the light curve's asymmetry, and with Gaia DR3 parallax pins the masses at 0.24 and 0.97 solar masses, temperatures differing by 338 kelvin.
arxiv-2511-23007:
Wang tackles a quiet risk in software projects: requirement documents hold tens of thousands of individual requirements. And some quietly conflict with each other, such as one demanding a Java compiler while another assumes a Python interpreter. Finding those clashes by hand is slow, and automatic detectors struggle with imbalanced data and with documents from new domains.

The proposed framework, TSRCDF-SS, reads each requirement pair through two different sentence encoders, SBERT and SimCSE, and merges their views with a six-part combined representation before a classifier decides. A hybrid training loss, mixing a focal loss variant with domain constraints and a confidence penalty, keeps rare conflict cases from being swamped. And transfer learning carries knowledge across domains. Experiments report gains of 10.4 percent in F1 scores within a domain and 11.4 percent in macro-F1 when moving across domains, over mainstream comparison models.
arxiv-2511-23307:
Spotorno and colleagues build neural models for cyber-physical systems that cannot afford to break physics. Embedding the known equations directly into the network's structure instead of penalizing violations in the loss. Their Hybrid Recurrent Physics-Informed Neural Network places the known physics inside a recurrent integrator as a hard constraint. So the learned part only has to capture the unknown residual dynamics, like friction, wear, and thermal effects.

A projected extension adds a predict-then-project step that strictly enforces algebraic invariants at every step by construction. And the authors prove the architecture keeps the representational capacity of standard physics-informed networks in their analysis. They validated the base model on a real battery prognostics problem, a differential-algebraic system from NASA's lithium-ion battery collection. And the projected version on standard constrained benchmarks, reporting high accuracy and data efficiency alongside honest trade-offs in cost and numerical stability.
arxiv-2512-00207:
Language models store facts inside their multilayer perceptron layers, arranged like key-value pairs. Owen Dugan and co-authors, including Chris Ré, study how to construct efficient fact-storing perceptrons for transformers in 2025. Earlier work proposed explicit weight constructions for such storage.

Understanding the construction improves knowledge of how models hold factual information in their parameters. Efficient storage designs could make models smaller for the same knowledge, or reveal how to edit facts deliberately. The work sits between theory and practice, treating a trained network as engineered memory rather than a black box. Explicit constructions complement statistical arguments about what trained networks probably do. They also show how much memory a given set of facts requires.
arxiv-2512-00307:
Social networks carry signed ties: friendships pull nodes together, while hostility pushes them apart. Haobin Ke and co-authors study adversarial signed graph learning with differential privacy in 2025. Balance theory lets learning methods infer edge signs from multi-hop pairs of nodes.

Training on sensitive signed graphs raises privacy concerns, because model parameters may leak private link information. The authors combine adversarial training with privacy guarantees so embeddings preserve structure and sign without exposing relationships. The work matters for platforms that analyze trust and conflict while owing their users real confidentiality. Adversarial training hardens the embeddings against attempts to extract the hidden links. Signed graphs are also the natural language of trust networks and political blocs.
arxiv-2512-00507:
Glassy materials relax toward equilibrium with a stretched exponential curve that is awkward to analyze. Shuli Chen and co-authors study the inverse spectral problem for that relaxation in 2025, using a Prony series approximation. The stretched exponential has a singularity at the origin, which makes data analysis inconvenient.

The Prony series replaces it with a sum of simple exponentials, an approach tied to the extended Burgers model of viscoelasticity. The inverse problem asks which spectrum of relaxation times produced the observed data. Recovering that spectrum helps materials scientists connect a glass's behavior to its internal structure. Prony series are sums of exponentials, each with its own relaxation time.
arxiv-2512-00607:
Simulating a Turing machine raises a basic question: how much information must be stored to certify a moment of its run? Logan Nye studies the holographic geometry of deterministic computation in 2025. Standard simulations suggest a linear relationship between a run's duration and the storage needed.

Certifying, verifying, or regenerating the configuration at a given time are the tasks Nye measures. A holographic viewpoint, borrowed from physics, asks whether the run's history can be encoded on a smaller boundary-like structure. The question links computability theory to information geometry in an unusual way. The holographic phrasing borrows from physics, where bulk information lives on a boundary. Deterministic computation is the cleanest setting for such storage questions.
arxiv-2512-00707:
Inocent Calist and Minseok Kim wrote a 2025 paper on radio channel models for future wireless networks. As networks move from 5G toward 6G, models must stay smooth and physically sound across a wide band, from FR1 up through FR3. Gaps in knowledge are worst in the mid-range band now studied for new rules.

Their approach builds a frequency-continuous model for city macro and micro cells, anchored at a mid-band frequency. Macro cells cover wide areas, while micro cells serve small hotspots. A model that bridges the bands helps engineers plan 6G service that works across all of them, not just in pieces.
arxiv-2512-00807:
Yujie Lin, Jiayao Ma, Qingguo Hu, Derek Wong, and Jinsong Su study gender fairness in vision-language models in a 2025 paper. These models learn from huge image and text collections and inherit social biases from that data. Gender bias in how people are shown is a known problem.

Many fixes take a difference-unaware stance, treating every group exactly the same. The authors argue that this can backfire. Some settings need strict neutrality, while others hold real group-specific traits that should be preserved. Their difference-aware approach, BioPro, tries to tell those cases apart. Fairer models would avoid both erasing real differences and repeating stereotypes.
arxiv-2512-01107:
Sanjog Misra introduces the idea of a foundation prior in a 2025 paper. Large language models can generate highly informative responses to prompts about people, markets, and behavior. Interest is growing in using those synthetic outputs as data in empirical research and decision-making, as if they were survey responses.

Misra argues the outputs should not be treated as real observations. Instead, they are draws from a foundation prior, the prior predictive distribution induced by the model. That framing tells researchers how much weight such synthetic data deserves. Getting this right matters as firms begin to substitute model output for costly human data.
arxiv-2512-01307:
Hongyu Liu and Zhihui Liu ask if a random process can be rebuilt from its long-run pattern. Many systems drift and spread at once. Over time they settle into a steady spread of states. That steady spread can be measured in real tests.

The pair study the reverse task. Given just the steady spread, can the drift and spread terms be found? They check when the answer is one clear process and not many. A firm yes would let staff infer hidden rules of a system from long-run data alone, a gain for science and health work.
arxiv-2512-01407:
Alexandre Sac-Morane and co-authors model how cement hardens at tiny scales. As cement paste takes in water, its inner form shifts. That form sets how strong the final paste will be. Tracking the shift helps design mixes that last.

Their phase-field model tracks growth and melt of grains in the paste. It rests on the heat rules for those changes. The model forecasts both inner form and strength traits as cure goes on. Good forecasts can cut lab trials and guide greener mixes with less waste and lower carbon cost.
arxiv-2512-01507:
Daniel Armstrong and co-authors pull strategy tips from language models for chemistry. Planning a synthesis is more than picking valid steps. Good plans join parts in a smart order. They guard key groups and form rings at the right time. Most software misses that strategy layer.

Their method, SynthStrategy, asks a model to state its latent strategy. Those tips are then turned into code that planners can use. Coded tips make the strategy clear and reusable. The work aims to lift machine plans closer to how expert chemists think through a route.
arxiv-2512-01707:
Daeun Lee and co-authors build StreamGaze for streaming video sense with gaze. Streaming tools process each frame as it comes in. They must also guess user intent for uses like AR glasses. Past streaming tests score time reasoning alone. None score use of human gaze.

Their system uses gaze signals to guide temporal thought. Gaze tells the model where the user cares. Proactive answers can then arrive before a full query. Gaze-guided streaming could make AR aids feel less like tools and more like attentive partners. Benchmark design is part of the work, since gaze use in streaming video had no shared test before this system set one out.
arxiv-2512-01807:
Guillermo Diaz-Camacho and co-authors benchmark emulators for distributed quantum computing. Big quantum tasks need linked small processors, not one giant chip. Quantum links let nodes compute jointly. Emulators let teams test that vision before hardware matures.

Their benchmark scores emulator platforms on set tasks. Feasibility studies need such scores to pick tools. Emulators also expose where protocols break at scale. Fair benchmarks guide both software teams and hardware planners toward workable distributed designs. Emulator scores span speed and fidelity together, since a fast but loose emulator misleads protocol design as surely as a slow exact one.
arxiv-2512-01907:
Boron aluminum nitride is a candidate material for the next generation of electronic and light-based devices, thanks to its ultra-wide bandgap and heat tolerance. Cody L. Milne and Arunima K. Singh use first-principles calculations in 2025 to map how its energy bands line up with those of related materials.

Band alignment decides how easily charge flows across the junctions inside a device, so designers need these numbers before building anything. The authors cover both polar and nonpolar crystal orientations and compare the alloy against aluminum nitride and gallium nitride. Their results fill a gap that had left this promising alloy hard to engineer with confidence.
arxiv-2512-02107:
Partition functions count the states of a physical theory, and for four-dimensional supersymmetric gauge theories they hide surprising mathematical structure. Palash Singh's 2025 paper proves that a class of these generalized Schur partition functions equals a very different-looking object from two-dimensional conformal theory.

On the other side of the equality stand contour integrals of vector-valued modular forms, which arise in rational conformal field theories. Bridging the four-dimensional gauge theory and the two-dimensional forms lets each side borrow the other's tools. Such equivalences are the working machinery of modern mathematical physics, where dualities turn hard counts into easy ones.
arxiv-2512-02307:
In dynamical systems, a Gibbs measure describes where a system spends its time, weighted toward expanding directions. Vítor Gomes and Bruno Santiago prove in 2025 new rigidity results for the entropy of such measures in partially hyperbolic systems, where some directions expand, some contract, and some do neither.

They show that when such a measure admits an unstable Margulis family, a kind of evenly spread structure along the expanding direction, the unstable Jacobian data must be constant. Rigidity means soft assumptions force hard structure, narrowing what these systems can do. Results like this anchor the ergodic theory of chaotic systems, where entropy is a central fingerprint.
arxiv-2512-02507:
Huadi Qu studies repeating paths in maps that preserve area, a clean model of motion on a surface. Each periodic orbit, a path that returns to its start, carries two numbers of interest. One is its action, drawn from a global function; the other is its rotation number, which tracks winding.

Qu extends recent work by Machel Hutchings on such surface maps, called diffeomorphisms. The results prove that orbits exist with certain chosen action and rotation values. Results of this kind help mathematicians map out what motions a system allows, a question with roots in classical mechanics. Such paths are the beats to which the whole map keeps its time over long runs.
arxiv-2512-02907:
Justin Gruber and three co-authors propose boosting quantum light emission with acoustic graphene plasmons. Plasmons, ripples of electrons on a surface, can greatly speed how fast an emitter radiates. That speed up, the Purcell effect, helps single photon sources shine brighter and faster.

Acoustic graphene plasmons squeeze light into very small volumes near graphene. The team proposes tunable, giant Purcell enhancement for single photon, entangled photon, and multipolar emitters. Tunable bright sources are core parts for quantum communication and sensing, where every photon counts. Tuned boosts let one source serve more than one job, a thrift that counts when each photon takes time and coin to make and catch.
arxiv-2512-03107:
Language models can sound sure while saying things with no support. Mainak Singha calls those answers hallucinations and offers a way to catch them in this 2025 work. The risk is high in finance, where wrong facts can cost money.

His framework, ECLIPSE, treats a hallucination as a gap between a model's doubt and the proof at hand. It groups many sample answers to gauge doubt, and splits a score that shows how proof is used. The author reports a large drop in hallucination rates in tests. Safer checks could help banks use these models with more care. Reported gains aside, the core value lies in a check that runs before answers reach clients or traders.
arxiv-2512-03307:
Models for table data are getting a foundation-model upgrade. Matthew Peroni, Franck Le, and Vadim Sheinin study robust tabular foundation models in this 2025 work. These models aim to beat classic methods on structured data like spreadsheets and records.

A key finding is that such models can be pretrained entirely on synthetic data. That opens room to design data generators that build in good traits, like robustness. Strong table models matter for business, health, and science, where most data sit in rows and columns, not text or images. Synthetic pretraining also lets builders stress-test models on rare table patterns safely.
arxiv-2512-03407:
Materials near jamming behave like both solid and liquid. Kumpei Shiraishi and Hideyuki Mizuno study elastic fluctuations in jammed solids in this 2025 work. They look at how the shear modulus varies from sample to sample near the jamming transition.

The average modulus scales in ways that depend on the particle potential. The fluctuations, by contrast, follow a critical exponent that does not depend on the potential. That independence hints at a universal rule. It may guide design of foams, gels, and granular materials. Universal fluctuation exponents suggest a shared mechanism hides beneath differing particle models.
arxiv-2512-03507:
Old methods from India can make computing classes more open to all. Aalok Thakkar presents that teaching approach in this 2025 work. Lessons on methods in code often lack roots and lean on Europe alone, despite calls for fair, open teaching.

Thakkar brings ancient methods from India into core computer science courses. A study with mixed methods covered many students across four class sections. He reports that teaching with history raised student interest and skill in method-based thinking. It also gave students a wider view of where computing began. Students in the study came from four class sections in all.
arxiv-2512-03707:
Robots that work beside people sometimes need to touch them, as when handing over a small object. Sundas Rafat Mulkana and co-authors tackle that safety problem in a 2025 robotics preprint. Simply avoiding all collision is not enough for handovers, because the useful action itself involves gentle, deliberate contact.

Their framework, ContactRL, folds contact safety directly into the reward used during reinforcement learning, using measured force as feedback. The robot learns motion profiles that keep forces on the person low while still finishing the task. In simulation it broke safety limits rarely while succeeding in most trials. For real use, the learned policy is guarded by an energy-based safety shield. Tests on a UR3e arm across hundreds of handovers kept normal contact forces below ten newtons.
arxiv-2512-04107:
Judging an AI tutor by accuracy alone misses whether it respects learners, context, and ethics. Shi Ding and Brian Magerko propose a broader yardstick in a 2025 preprint. Their TEACH-AI framework evaluates generative AI helpers for education through ten parts, built from a wide literature synthesis.

The framework's full name spells out its ambition: trustworthy and effective AI classroom heuristics. It is deliberately independent of any single school subject and aligned with the stakeholders who live with these tools, from designers and developers to researchers and policymakers. Alongside it comes a practical checklist toolkit with measurable indicators. The authors argue that what counts as good AI in schools must be rethought through social, theoretical, and applied lenses together. They invite the community to design evaluations rewarding co-creation, inclusivity, and long-term human impact, not just test scores.
arxiv-2512-04307:
Andy Chung and five co-authors built a test for how well web agents think across long chats with a user. Agents built on large language models now help with daily tasks online. Good help needs memory of what came before, across many sessions. Yet no one had mapped how such agents cope when the trail grows very long. Their 2025 arXiv paper fills that gap with a fresh benchmark.

The benchmark chains subtasks that depend on each other, so later steps need facts from far back. Between linked steps, the team slips in off-topic task trails as clutter. Context lengths run from tens of thousands of tokens to over a hundred thousand. Four leading models faced the test, from Claude and GPT to Llama. The results show where long-context skill holds up and where it cracks, guiding builders of web agents that must stay sharp over time.
arxiv-2512-04707:
Qinghai Huo, Guangbin Ren, and Irene Sabadini announce a breakthrough in the theory of operators on octonionic Hilbert spaces, a problem open for more than sixty years. Octonions are the largest of the normed number systems, but they refuse to associate: grouping changes products. That quirk wrecks standard linear operator theory, which leans on associativity at every step. Their 2025 arXiv paper builds a new frame, called para-linearity, that bends linearity to fit the octonionic rules.

Inside that frame, the authors define a careful operator algebra and an adjoint operation. Together they restore the analytic properties that theory needs. A geometric object, the slice cone, emerges as the home of spectral data. With it, self-adjoint operators in this setting gain a spectral decomposition. The result opens octonionic quantum models and related analysis to the same rigorous tools that complex spaces enjoy.
arxiv-2512-04907:
Björn Garbrecht and Nils Wagner prove that two classic ways of computing quantum tunneling rates, long taught as separate worlds, are in fact the same theory in disguise. One approach uses resonant states: wave patterns that leak steadily, with decay widths set by outgoing boundary rules. The other, the instanton method, sums over imaginary-time paths, and its physical meaning has stayed murky. Their 2025 arXiv paper draws the exact bridge between them.

The authors show that the contour-bending rule Callan and Coleman gave for the path integral matches, step for step, the outgoing Gamow-Siegert conditions that define resonant states. What looked like a formal trick is the boundary condition in another notation. Unifying the two views clears a conceptual fog around tunneling, from particle decays to false vacuum decay in cosmology, and lets results pass freely between the camps.
arxiv-2512-05407:
D. P. Goronzy and a large team of co-authors compare two metals' surface oxides as suspects in the energy loss that limits superconducting qubits. Transmon qubits are usually wired with niobium, but tantalum wiring has recently performed better. The thin pentoxide layers that form natively on each metal are prime suspects for soaking up microwave energy at millikelvin temperatures. The team deposited niobium and tantalum pentoxides at three thicknesses onto identical waveguide resonators and measured the loss each adds for single photons.

The niobium oxide's loss from two-level-system defects comes out roughly a third higher than the tantalum oxide's. That indicates niobium-wired qubits suffer extra loss from the native pentoxide, on top of losses from suboxide compounds that tantalum avoids. For engineers, the measurement turns a hunch about materials into a number, strengthening the case for tantalum in the next generation of quantum processors.
arxiv-2512-05907:
Abrar Hossain and four co-authors put large language models to work choosing mutual fund portfolios. The models tested, including Microsoft Phi 2, Mistral 7B, and Zypher 7B, were asked to build risk aware allocations across economic sectors.
