A retrieval pipeline let each model check current data, and large economic signals were fed in as context. Standard financial optimization methods then turned language into allocations.

One model separated itself from the field. Zypher 7B consistently produced strategies with the strongest returns and the best risk adjusted results, beating its rivals across the tests. The authors credit its handling of complex relationships and context. Against basic allocation methods, the generative approach improved performance broadly. The study is an early, optimistic datapoint for language models in asset management. The groundwork, the authors argue, is laid for professional tools built this way.
arxiv-2512-06507:
H Abele and a large team from the NUCLEUS group report a first sighting: two distinct recoil peaks when neutrons are captured in an aluminum oxide crystal kept near absolute zero. The crystal is a detector built to catch reactor neutrinos through a faint coherent scatter off whole nuclei. To trust such a detector, its response to a nucleus recoiling must be calibrated exactly, and neutron capture gives a clean, known kick.

Data taken with a radioactive source showed a main recoil line at the expected energy, from nuclei that shed one gamma ray. Beside it sat a new, lower peak from nuclei that shed several gamma rays in a cascade, the first direct measure of such a line. Simulations say it appears when the nucleus stops between gamma rays. The result supports a calibration method for these detectors and sharpens models used in neutrino and dark matter hunts.
arxiv-2512-06607:
Humzah Merchant and Bradford Levy fix a bias that blocks language models from honest work in finance. A model trained on text up to today already knows how stories ended, so testing it on past market calls is rigged: it can peek at the future it was trained on. Retraining a big model with a cutoff date is far too costly to be practical.

Their method steers the model at answer time instead. Two small specialist models are trained, one on the facts that must be forgotten and one on those that may stay. Their scores adjust the big model's word choices as it generates, canceling the leaked knowledge. The authors report the steering removes both exact and paraphrased knowledge, corrects the bias, and beats prior fixes, all fast and cheap. The trick could open backtesting, and other time bound tasks, to ready made models.
arxiv-2512-06907: S Yu Orevkov and N D Puchkova study how real algebraic curves can sit beside one another in the plane. Their focus is a quartic curve, one step above a cubic in complexity, whose oval loops around a second curve like a snake. Under that coiling condition they prove the combined picture can be deformed into a simpler one, where the quartic is replaced by a perturbed doubled conic. They also prove matching statements for real pseudoholomorphic curves, under extra assumptions.
arxiv-2512-07007:
Tulsi Dass revisits Bohmian mechanics, the interpretation of quantum theory in which particles are real points that follow definite paths. That picture dissolves the measurement problem, since outcomes are just where particles end up. Yet it has long sat awkwardly beside the standard Hilbert space machinery, and it struggles with spin and relativity. Dass builds a formalism that keeps the standard state-and-observable framework and adds Bohmian paths inside it.

The wave function is read as describing an ensemble of systems. From its starting values Dass defines a probability space, then a random process tied to the position operator whose paths obey the Bohm guidance equation. Those paths are the trajectories of individual ensemble members. Spin and other discrete quantities are handled by enlarging the arena to include their value spaces, with Pauli's equation as a worked example.
arxiv-2512-08207:
Jeremias Garay, David Nolte, and Cristobal Bertoglio, applied mathematicians, posted a methods paper on arXiv in December 2025. Their topic is simulating blood flow through coronary arteries, where three dimensional flow models are often coupled to simpler reduced models of the wider circulation. That coupling is tricky: the implicit form adds nonlocal terms, the explicit form can go unstable, and inertia effects make calibration harder.

The authors propose a new boundary condition, called the duct boundary condition, built from a method that folds part of the domain into the boundary itself. It keeps coupling local in the implicit case and captures both viscous resistance and inertia with a single physical parameter. They also derive a time marching scheme including the new condition. Coronary simulations show it at work, including estimating its parameter from noisy velocity data, promising more stable, easier to tune heart flow models.
arxiv-2512-08307:
Wee Teck Gan, a mathematician in representation theory, posted a research paper on arXiv in December 2025. His subject is the adjoint lifting, a way of moving automorphic representations from the group GL three up to GL eight. He treats cuspidal representations that have a discrete series component at some place, a well behaved local ingredient that makes the global argument run.

Gan works through the stable twisted trace formula, using the triality automorphism as his main tool. He then describes how the lifted representations on GL eight can split into isobaric pieces. Two applications follow. One points toward Ramanujan bounds for GL three, a famous measure of how small certain coefficients must be. The other bears on the strong Artin conjecture for a class of three dimensional Galois representations.
arxiv-2512-08907:
Alex Vargas, Ranjiangshang Ran, and Justin Burton present a model for the slow creep of polycrystalline ice. Ice creep controls glacier flow and thus sea level rise, yet its transient behavior is poorly understood. The classic flow law makes strain rate a simple function of stress, so it cannot capture the time dependent response seen in experiments.

Their rheological model combines a series of spring dashpot elements that produce power law creep with a single viscous element that captures grain reorientation under stress. The interplay of those parts produces a minimum in strain rate at about one percent strain. That minimum is a universal feature in experiments that had lacked an explanation. The model also shows fractional power law exponents at the minimum, which had been read as signs of separate processes. The compact framework can feed into ice sheet models and may generalize to other polycrystalline materials.
arxiv-2512-09007:
Wen Ge Wang develops a method to study a small quantum system coupled locally to a large chaotic environment. The environment is assumed to satisfy the eigenstate thermalization hypothesis, a key ansatz for how isolated quantum systems thermalize. The approach is built on environmental branches of the total state, whose overlaps give the reduced density matrix of the small system.

To follow that matrix over a finite time, the interval is split into short pieces. Within each piece, a formal solution for the branch evolution is used, then simplified by the thermalization ansatz and by decay of phase correlations from chaotic dynamics. That yields a generic route to a master equation. In the simplest nontrivial case, the derived equation predicts a decoherence rate matching random matrix theory. The framework also justifies the Born approximation used in standard derivations and shows an effective Markovian character for the evolution.
arxiv-2512-10107:
Ellis Buckminster and Samuel J. Taylor show that a natural geometric construction is less unique than its name suggests. A universal circle organizes the ideal boundaries of a foliation's leaves into one circle with a group action. Think of a layered three dimensional shape whose sheets each end on a circle at infinity. Calegari and Dunfield proved every taut foliation of a suitable three manifold has one. Whether different constructions give the same circle was mysterious. The authors study the two foliations tied to an Anosov flow, a chaotic, well structured flow on the manifold.

They prove that several universal circles from the literature are typically distinct for these foliations. Stronger, the group action on one prominent construction is generally not even conjugate to the action from the flow space boundary, meaning no change of coordinates can identify them.
arxiv-2512-10207:
Kazutaka Yanagihara and colleagues optimize the internal lattice of a heat exchanger by designing its flow pattern first. Their exchanger uses a triply periodic minimal surface lattice, a sponge like geometry that distributes flow evenly and stirs boundary layers, aiding heat transfer. But a uniform lattice is not necessarily optimal for moving heat between two fluids. The authors build a macroscopic model of the whole device: flow follows Darcy-Forchheimer theory, and heat transfer is captured by a volumetric coefficient. The lattice's isosurface threshold, which sets channel widths for hot and cold streams, becomes the design variable.

Optimizing that distribution for a planar exchanger with U shaped flow paths produced a graded, nonuniform lattice. The team printed the design in metal by laser powder bed fusion and tested it. The optimized exchanger clearly beat the uniform lattice, with heat exchange performance improved by roughly a quarter on average in experiments.
arxiv-2512-10407:
Christian Soize proposes a probabilistic framework where the neural network itself is random. Instead of fixing an architecture and learning only its weights, he lets a hidden random field, defined on a compact curved surface with holes in it, generate the whole network. Neuron positions, connections, and weights all grow out of that one latent field.

Neurons are scattered by a Poisson process whose density the field controls, input and output neurons are picked by the field's extreme values. And links follow closeness along the surface plus local field agreement. A masking step thins the network for scale. Learning then means inferring the few numbers that govern the field, using a likelihood loss estimated by Monte Carlo sampling. The forty-six page paper proves basic properties such as well-posedness and begins a theory of geometry-driven stochastic learning.
arxiv-2512-10507:
Dominik Kuzinowicz and co-authors study a practical trick in optimisation: rounding the numbers in a binary program's objective to fewer significant bits. Solvers often run faster on rounded problems, and one suspected reason is symmetry, since rounded values create more ties that symmetry-aware solvers can exploit. The original problem, meanwhile, may hide almost-symmetries that rounding exposes.

The team tested the idea on facility location and knapsack problems plus a mixed set of other instances, using the SCIP and CP-SAT solvers. Across every problem class, rounding produced faster algorithms while the answers still carried a guaranteed quality relative to the original objective. How much symmetry mattered depended on the instance type and the solver, a nuance the eight-page study documents carefully.
arxiv-2512-10907:
Challenger Mishra and Justin Tan compute a quantity string theory needs and analysis struggles to supply: solutions of the Hermitian Yang-Mills equations on holomorphic vector bundles. Those solutions fix the geometry of gauge bundles in heterotic string compactifications. And from them flow the physically normalised Yukawa couplings, the numbers that set particle masses and interactions in the resulting physics.

Their method is an alternating optimisation procedure rooted in geometric machine learning. It is fully general in the bundle's rank and structure group, asking only that one can list a basis of global sections. With it, the authors carry out the full computation for a heterotic compactification whose gauge bundle has a non-Abelian structure group, a case beyond the reach of earlier specialised tools. The fifty-one page paper comes with open-source code, so other compactifications can be fed through the same machinery.
arxiv-2512-11207:
A team of astronomers test a standard method for measuring magnetic field strength in the pillars of gas at the edges of glowing star forming regions. The Davis Chandrasekhar Fermi method infers field strength from how much polarised dust emission wobbles, assuming turbulence causes the wobble. Pillars like those in the Eagle Nebula, though, are being squeezed from outside by expanding ionised gas.

Combining three dimensional simulations with fake polarisation and molecular line observations, the authors extract every input the same way an observer would. The synthetic maps reproduced the pillar's large scale field pattern faithfully, so polarimetry traces field geometry well. Field strength was another matter: the classic method overestimated it several fold, and a modified version did little better. External compression organises the field while driving gas motions that are not turbulence, breaking the method's core assumption.
arxiv-2512-11707:
John Mahlon Scott and Hsin-Hsiung Huang tackle a tracking puzzle for ships at sea. Ships broadcast their spots through the Automatic Identification System, but IDs sometimes go missing, leaving loose track pieces. The team works on the hard case: nationwide US waters, with sparse, thinned out reports.

Their pipeline first uses plain motion physics to project track ends forward and shortlist matches for each new report. A trained neural classifier then picks the best match or starts a fresh track, using space, time, and motion clues. On held out data the hybrid beat pure rule based rivals. The work shows simple physics plus learning can relabel ship tracks at national scale.
arxiv-2512-11807:
Evan Redden writes a short comment on a bold claim about physics and simulation. Faizal and co-authors had argued that Gödel style undecidability in physics makes a full formal simulation of the universe impossible. Redden says that claim mixes two unlike things.

One thing is what can be proven inside a formal system. The other is what can exist or run. Using Conway Game of Life, a fully computable yet undecidable system, Redden shows undecidable facts can arise while every step still runs fine. Unless nature needs hypercomputation, beyond any machine, loose ends in proof do not block simulation. The comment is three pages and asks for hard evidence before such sweeping claims stand.
arxiv-2512-11907:
Daniel Platnick, Marjan Alirezaie, and Hossein Rahnama bring order to a trade off in personal AI agents. An agent serves better with more user data, but each added fact costs privacy. Added value tends to taper off, which suits greedy picking. Real life, though, adds hard structure: some facts need others, quotas cap categories, and rules nest inside rules.

The team compiles a user knowledge graph into grouped macro facets. They then prove that common quota and hierarchy rules over those facets form a laminar matroid, a clean constraint type. That turns personalization into a known problem form with greedy methods that carry firm quality guarantees, up to the best possible factor.
arxiv-2512-12207:
Jiangen He and Jiqun Liu test how search chatbots show their sources in a 2025 study. Such systems now add citations, but it is unclear which layout helps users engage. The team ran an online experiment with 394 people and four designs: folding lists, hover cards, footer lists, and sidebars.

High visibility layouts drew far more hovering over sources, though clicks stayed rare in all groups. Layout had small effects on ease and trust ratings, but it changed knowledge, interest, and shifts in agreement. High visibility first cut knowledge gain, then helped as source use rose. The sidebar alone raised shifts in agreement.
arxiv-2512-12407:
Fernando De Teran and Froilan M Dopico find the generic canonical forms for matrix congruence in a 2025 math paper. Canonical forms are the simplest shapes a matrix can take under a change of basis. Congruence and star congruence are two such moves, tied to bilinear and sesquilinear forms, which are pairing rules for vectors.

For plain congruence, one generic form suffices: nearly all complex square matrices reduce to a single shape family, split only by whether size is even or odd. Star congruence is different: it needs n over 2 plus 1 generic forms. That contrast, the authors show, marks a strong split between the two relations.
arxiv-2512-12807:
Anil Khachi studies neutron alpha elastic scattering with the variable phase approach in a 2025 paper. When neutrons bounce off helium nuclei, the scattering pattern reveals the nuclear force between them. The variable phase approach tracks how the scattering phase builds up with distance, giving a direct view of how the interaction generates it inside the finite interaction region.

Using the microscopic KKNN potential, Khachi computes distance dependent phase shifts, amplitude functions, and radial wave functions for the S and P partial waves across laboratory energies. The variable phase equations are solved with a fifth order Runge-Kutta method. Phase shifts behaved in physically consistent ways, and amplitudes and wave functions stayed well behaved. The approach also suits inverse scattering problems.
arxiv-2512-13307:
Thomas Baier, Michele Bolognesi, Johan Martens, and Christian Pauly prove that the Hitchin connection for the group SL2 at level four can be rewritten in abelian terms. The Hitchin connection links quantum states over the space of curves. Expressing it through simpler abelian data is a long-standing goal.

They express it via Mumford-Welters connections on bundles of abelian theta functions, built from all unramified double covers of the curve. From that form they show the connection's monodromy is finite. Key tools are equivariant conformal embeddings and an anti-invariant level-rank duality. The work extends earlier results that covered single curves only.
arxiv-2512-13607:
Boxin Wang and co-authors introduce Nemotron-Cascade, a reasoning model trained with cascaded reinforcement learning. Training a general model across domains is hard because tasks vary in response length and check time. Blending all prompts at once adds engineering strain and makes curriculum choices tough.

Their Cascade RL runs domain-wise stages in sequence instead of mixing them. Alignment training as a first step boosted reasoning well past mere preference tuning, and later stages rarely hurt earlier gains. The 14B model beat its teacher, DeepSeek-R1-0528, on LiveCodeBench tests after training. It also earned silver-medal level results at the 2025 International Olympiad in Informatics. The team shares its training and data recipes in full.
arxiv-2512-13707:
Daoyuan Qian, Qiyao Liang, and Ila Fiete show how noisy activity can push neural networks toward modular designs. Brain circuits are modular, which helps them split tasks, generalize in parts, and avoid forgetting. Artificial networks tend to mix all processing, since modular solutions sit in tiny corners of the solution space.

Inspired by fault-tolerant computing and Poisson-like neuron firing, they add activity-dependent noise with nonlinear responses. That noise drives networks to solutions that reflect the true modular task structure. A deterministic regularizer that multiplies weights by activations captures the same effect. Pre-modularized networks then proved more robust to noise and generalized beyond training data better than mixed networks, though emergence needs many training samples.
arxiv-2512-13807:
Hong Liu argues that the large N dual map needs a missing piece: a filter. Holography maps a conformal field theory to gravity in one higher dimension, but Euclidean wormholes and the failure of factorization lack a clear reading in the standard frame. Erratic N-dependence in field theory observables has no clear gravity counterpart either.

Liu's filter projects out erratic N-dependence when mapping to near-classical bulk physics, giving a boundary meaning for gravity averages. It also explains wormhole inputs and predicts their amplitudes, resolving the factorization puzzle. He derives an infinite tower of bounds on wormhole amplitudes. Beyond that, the filter frames closed universes and black hole interiors as quantum volatile structures.
arxiv-2512-14107:
Hisakazu Matsuki and co-authors report high-precision muon Knight shift measurements of the superconductor Sr2RuO4. The Knight shift, the change in a probe's local field, reveals pairing symmetry. The method worked well for heavy-fermion superconductors, but in d-electron systems like this one the shift is intrinsically small and hard to measure.

Using multiple crystal pieces, a common practice, induced a spurious paramagnetic shift below the transition from stray fields of neighboring crystals. With one crystal, they find a normal-state muon Knight shift of minus 116 plus or minus 7 parts per million. Separating the contributions carefully, they confirm a significant drop in the spin Knight shift below the transition. That fits spin-singlet-like pairing, the most precise such muon result for a d-electron superconductor.
arxiv-2512-14307:
Massimo Giovannini studies relic gravitons and large scale magnetism in a 2025 paper on the early universe. Limits on background gravitational radiation come from several bands, from interferometers in the audio range to pulsar timing arrays at very low frequencies.

Giovannini argues the spectral energy density of gravitons is sharply suppressed at the lowest frequencies, even if the high frequency signal is much larger. A modified postinflationary timeline cuts the number of e folds and suppresses the tensor to scalar ratio. The growth of the hypercharge field and the origin of large scale magnetism further bound how fast the young universe could expand. The results still allow a detectable graviton signal between the MHz and THz ranges.
arxiv-2512-14407:
Alessandro Fasano and colleagues report the polarization calibration of TFGI, the Thirty and Forty GHz instrument of the QUIJOTE telescope project. On the ground, they fit instrument data with a reference diode signal, which helped sort out the angles that shape the measured signal.

Sky observations then checked the ground results. Views of Tau A and the Moon confirmed the calibration and tracked how stable it stayed over time. The team also used the Moon data to find the Moon's refraction index. Work of this kind is the groundwork that lets a telescope project trust its polarization measurements.
arxiv-2512-14607:
An abelian fibration maps a complex variety onto a base so that the typical fiber is an abelian variety, a higher-dimensional cousin of an elliptic curve. Some fibers are multiple, splitting into components that each carry a multiplicity, and the smallest of those numbers is the subject here.

The main theorem is clean: the minimum component multiplicity always equals the greatest common divisor of all the component multiplicities. In other words, the smallest value is exactly the shared divisor of the whole list, with no exceptions. Results of this kind help geometers understand degenerate fibers, which often carry the most information in a fibration.
arxiv-2512-14707:
Richard D. Charlesworth clarifies what a boundary means in hypernetwork theory. Boundaries there are non-structural tags: they restrict which parts of a hypernetwork are visible without changing the hypernetwork itself, and they attach to hypersimplices as annotations.

A boundary, he stresses, plays no role in identity, typing, or the alpha and beta semantics of the theory. Projecting over a boundary is filtering only: it selects exactly the hypersimplices carrying that tag and preserves every axiom of the structural kernel. The note fixes the scope of the concept so later work cannot quietly stretch it into something structural.
arxiv-2512-14807:
David Wright and six coauthors present a faster way to merge data in the hunt for gravitational waves with pulsars. Pulsar timing arrays watch many spinning neutron stars for tiny shifts caused by passing waves. In 2023, teams around the world found shared evidence of a background hum of such waves.

Merging each region's data the standard way is slow and costly in expert time. Their method, FrankenStat, grows out of a simpler merge used in an earlier cross check of the shared signal. On test data it matches the old methods in reach and in how well it pins down values. Yet it finishes the full merge in just a few minutes, which could speed up joint work across the global teams.
arxiv-2512-15207:
Neelaksh Singh and four coauthors levitate objects at a distance using magnetic coils alone, with no contact and no onboard power. Electromagnetic navigation systems steer medical tools inside the body with fast, precise fields. The team used an OctoMag system and a custom 13 coil setup to float and control several rigid bodies across large air gaps.

A compact parametric model maps coil currents straight to forces and torques on the floating object, skipping heavy simulations and lookup tables. Linear quadratic regulators steady the position, while a nonlinear controller handles the reduced attitude, since spin about the dipole axis cannot be controlled. Together they stabilize the five controllable degrees of freedom. In tracking tests the controller beat a standard PID baseline and followed angles as large as 65 degrees. The work points toward new medical uses for remote magnetic handling.
arxiv-2512-15307:
Roberto de Capistrano Filho and co authors study the Korteweg de Vries equation on a star graph in a 2025 math paper. The KdV equation models shallow water waves, and a star graph joins several edges at one central point. The team sets up an initial and boundary value problem on a finite star with equal edges.

They use a notion of s compatibility for the coupled conditions at the center. With fixed point arguments and nonlinear interpolation, they prove global well posedness in Sobolev spaces. The result covers smoothness levels from 0 to 3. Special care is needed at the critical levels one half, three halves, and five halves. An auxiliary variable handles the nonlinear condition at the vertex.
arxiv-2512-15407:
Yuchen Ding and four coauthors count how often each integer can be built from a power plus a partner drawn from a matching set. Fix r at least 2, and let S be the set of r-th powers. An additive complement W is a set such that each natural number is a sum of one member of W and one r-th power. The count of such sums is the function f_r(n).

Prompted by a 1993 conjecture of Cilleruelo, the authors prove a lower bound on the total excess of these counts. The sum of f_r(n) up to N, minus N, grows at least like N to the power 1 minus 1/r. Before this, the bound was known only for squares. For squares they sharpen it to N to the 3/4, up to a small loss. That beats the older square root bound of Ding, Sun, Wang, and Xia.
arxiv-2512-15607:
Harsh Sharma and Himadri Shekhar Dhar demonstrate a quadratic power boost in an extended Dicke quantum battery in a 2025 paper. A quantum battery stores energy in quantum systems and aims to charge faster than any classical counterpart. In the Dicke design, many two level systems share a cavity mode.

Here the battery couples N spins to two photonic cavity modes, one of them in the dispersive regime. The charging power grows with the square of N, driven by both quantum correlations and faster evolution, a genuine quantum advantage claim. The hybrid setup is experimentally realistic. It keeps energy efficiency from dropping much, adds tunability, and stays stable under noise.
arxiv-2512-15707:
Yu Wang and co authors present GateFusion for active speaker detection in video in a 2025 paper. The task is to name who is speaking in each frame. Most leading systems fuse audio and visual features only at the end, which can miss fine cross modal cues that matter in messy, unconstrained scenes.

GateFusion pairs strong pretrained single mode encoders with a hierarchical gated fusion decoder. That decoder injects context from one mode into the other at several depths, steered by learnable gates that see both modes. Two auxiliary losses align single mode outputs with fused ones and punish video only false alarms. The system sets new state of the art scores on Ego4D-ASD, UniTalk, and WASD benchmarks.
arxiv-2512-15907:
Tejas Anvekar and co authors present TabReX, a reference free method for scoring tables generated by language models, in a 2025 paper. Judging generated tables is hard: flattening them into text loses structure, while fixed reference tables limit generality. A fair score should track both structure and factual fidelity.

TabReX converts source text and generated tables into canonical knowledge graphs, aligns them with language model guided matching, and computes rubric aware scores. The scores allow sensitivity and specificity trade offs and give cell level error traces. A new benchmark, TabReX-Bench, spans six domains and twelve perturbation types. TabReX shows the highest correlation with expert rankings among tested metrics.
arxiv-2512-16307:
Safwan Shaheer and three co-authors defend small AI models in a paper posted on arXiv during 2025. Prompt injection attacks hide instructions inside user input to hijack a model's goals. The risk grows as small open-source models, especially the LLaMA family, spread onto phones and edge devices with few safeguards.

The team assessed current prompt-based defenses against the latest attacks, then built a framework that grows its own defenses. Starting from a chain-of-thought seed defense, it refines the defense prompt over rounds of testing. Their strategies cut attack success rates and false detection rates while catching goal-hijacking attempts more reliably. The paper argues that automatic, self-improving defenses can make small models safer to deploy in resource-limited settings, where heavyweight security stacks do not fit.
arxiv-2512-16407:
J Sumaya-Martinez and J Mulia-Rodriguez reinterpret light scattering in an arXiv paper from 2025. Tiny rectangular grooves, narrower than a wavelength, scatter electromagnetic waves in ways long studied through field intensity maps. As groove width nears the wavelength, the scattered profile flips from concave to convex, and the reason was unclear.

The authors track the time-averaged Poynting vector, which shows where energy actually flows near the groove. Narrowing the groove creates, moves, and destroys flow singularities such as vortices and saddle points. That topological reshuffle of near-field energy redirects the flux and produces the convex far-field profile. The result links near-field energy topology directly to far-field scattering, giving a unified physical picture of subwavelength groove behavior for TM-polarized light.
arxiv-2512-16507:
Ivan Noden works in algebraic geometry in a 2025 paper on arXiv. The Grothendieck ring collects all varieties into one algebraic system. Varieties are shapes defined by equations. In that ring, cutting and gluing become arithmetic. Zero divisors there can expose varieties that are L-equivalent without being identical. A zero divisor is a nonzero element whose product with another nonzero element vanishes.

Noden follows a construction by Kanemitsu and observations by Rampazzo. He takes zero loci of sections of vector bundles. The bundles sit over two families of Grassmannians, the symplectic kind and the exceptional type F4. Those zero loci supply fresh zero divisors. In turn they yield nontrivially L-equivalent Calabi-Yau varieties. Such shapes are prized in geometry and string theory. The method extends an earlier G2 Grassmannian approach by Ito and collaborators.
arxiv-2512-16607:
Louis Grenioux and coauthors build Boltzmann generators for glasses, which are disordered solids with no repeating pattern. Sampling fair layouts of such particle systems at balance is slow, and past generator tools worked for crystals and large molecules but not for glasses.

Their method folds the needed symmetries straight into flow-based samplers that respect curved spaces and wrap-around edges, using graph networks that treat like particles alike. Tests show that built-in symmetry sharpens accuracy a lot. They also expose a deep flaw: small numeric errors pile up when odds are tracked, breaking exact reweighting. That flaw marks a basic limit for flow-based tools in this field.
arxiv-2512-17007:
Talia Gillis and coauthors compare two US legal tools for judging algorithmic bias in lending: disparate impact doctrine and UDAP, the ban on unfair, deceptive, or abusive acts or practices. Disparate impact has long grounded fair lending law, while regulators now test UDAP as a second path.

The team formalizes both doctrines and runs them in a simulated lending market. They argue UDAP is not a copy of disparate impact but a distinct frame. Its unfairness prong adds tests of avoidable harm and balance of harms and gains, and its deception and abuse prongs can catch harms the older doctrine misses. Gaps remain, so the authors call for clearer regulatory guidance.
arxiv-2512-17107:
Zenan Yang and coauthors diagnose faults in photovoltaic strings with a differentiable physical simulator. Knowing not just that a fault exists but how big it is guides smart upkeep, yet past quantification tools were slow or opaque.

Their fast fault simulation model reproduces current-voltage curves under many faults and gives analytic gradients for fault parameters. A gradient-based identification method with the Adahessian optimizer then sizes partial shading, short circuits, and series resistance decay. On simulated and measured curves, rebuilt curves missed by under 3 percent error, proof that differentiable simulators can power exact, readable fault diagnosis.
arxiv-2512-17707:
Leonardo Grimaldi, Michele Lucente, and Silvia Pascoli link two cosmic mysteries: why matter survived the Big Bang, and what is humming in gravitational waves. Leptogenesis, the leading account of the matter surplus, creates it early and hot. Later, the young universe may have boiled through a violent phase transition, releasing entropy that would water that surplus down.

Pulsar timing arrays recently heard a faint nanohertz gravitational hum, possibly the echo of just such a transition. Feeding the hum's best-fit strength into a standard leptogenesis model, the team finds the allowed settings shrink a great deal. At the strongest fits, every version future experiments could test is ruled out. The hum, if real, becomes a sieve for theories of our own existence.
arxiv-2512-17907:
Byungjun Kim, Taeksoo Kim, Junyoung Lee, and Hanbyul Joo want digital copies of real rooms that hands can act in. Today's 3D copies of spaces are mostly still: you can look around but not open a drawer. Their Dexterous World Model takes a still scene plus a hand motion track and predicts the video that would follow.

The model watches both the scene view and a mesh of the moving hand, so grasps and pushes land in the right places. Training mixes computer made hand clips with real fixed camera footage. Results show objects being grasped, opened, and moved while the room stays steady, a step toward practice worlds for robots.
arxiv-2512-18007:
Yu Fang leads a twelve author team giving robot control models a sense of motion. Vision language action models turn camera views and spoken orders into robot moves, but they mostly copy expert demos. They rarely reason about how the scene is about to move, which caps their judgment.

The team's design adds a second head that dreams up motion images, maps of where pixels will flow next, while the action head still picks the moves. Training both heads together ties control to motion sense, at no cost to test time speed. Scores rose to 97.5 percent on the LIBERO test set and 58.0 percent on RoboTwin, with a 23 percent gain in real world trials.
arxiv-2512-19007:
Konstantin Kaulen and co-authors sum up VNN-COMP 2025, the sixth yearly contest for tools that verify neural networks. Verification proves a network meets a stated property, rather than just testing sample inputs. The contest ran inside a symposium on AI verification held with a major computer-aided verification conference.

Eight teams entered, and their tools ran on shared benchmark sets with standard file formats and equal-cost cloud hardware. Settings were locked before the final test sets were revealed. The report covers the rules, sixteen regular and nine extended benchmarks, the results, and lessons for making future comparisons fairer and more useful.
arxiv-2512-19107:
Zhe Yang, Xiaoshuang Sheng, Zhengnan Zhang, and Jidong Wu read a phone user's intent from the trail of screens they touched. Knowing intent helps interface agents and recommendation systems. Large multimodal models read such trails well, yet they are too heavy for real-time use on a phone and waste effort on repeated frames.

Their framework, FC-MIR, samples key frames and joins them adaptively to cut visual redundancy. A strong multimodal model, closed or fine-tuned, then sums up the trail and predicts intent, and can even suggest the next action or a search. At compression near half, performance held up on their new trajectory dataset.
arxiv-2512-19207:
Jun-Qin Long, Rui-Hui Lin, and Xiang-Hua Zhai solve for flat, layered spacetimes in f(Q) gravity, a theory built on nonmetricity rather than curvature. They look at static plane-symmetric setups, the geometry of infinite slabs and walls. In empty regions, the nonmetricity scalar settles to a constant.

Vacuum solutions then act like Taub spacetimes with a cosmological constant fixed by the chosen model. The authors match those exteriors to a thin shell and to a slab of finite thickness, tying shell density and pressure to the geometry. In a quadratic model, peak slab pressure sits off center, and some parameter choices cannot hold a slab up at all.
arxiv-2512-19507:
Haocheng Yu, Tianyi Chu, and Spencer Bryngelson trace where sound energy goes when a plane wave pushes through a slit. Some of the energy turns into swirling vortical motion, and some dies as viscous heat. Knowing the split guides acoustic absorbers and liners, yet the mechanisms shift with loudness and frequency.

Direct simulations sweep sound pressure, Strouhal number, and Reynolds number widely. Spectral decomposition ranks the coherent structures at each tone, letting the team price kinetic energy against viscous loss mode by mode. Conversion peaks when the acoustic swing matches the slit thickness, as shedding vortices dominate. Viscous loss takes a fifth to three fifths of the converted share.
arxiv-2512-19607:
Measuring very cold temperatures with quantum devices is the problem taken up by Youssef Aiache, Abderrahim El Allati, İlkay Demir, and Khadija El Anouz. Their probe is a single qubit linked to a bosonic bath, modeled as a spin-boson system. Unusually, the two ways the probe couples to its bath do not commute, so pure dephasing and energy loss act together rather than separately.

That interference creates strong memory effects between the probe's populations and coherences, even trapping coherence in place. The payoff is sharper temperature sensitivity, which grows quadratically at low temperature even when the coupling stays weak. Coherence-based readouts, normally second-best, become the most informative early on, while memory effects dominate. The authors frame the coupling design as a practical, tunable resource for precise quantum thermometers.
arxiv-2512-19907:
Gábor Kasza, János Takátsy, and György Wolf use the sky as the sole lab for cold, dense matter. Neutron stars pack matter at many times nuclear density, at near zero temperature. Most of what we can see of them hinges on the equation of state. That is the link between pressure and density. The team gives that link a flexible form. They then let sky data fence in its free values.

Four fences are joined. Perturbative QCD gives results at very high density. The mass of the heaviest known neutron star is a black widow pulsar. The NICER telescope gives mass and radius for five pulsars. The GW170817 merger gives tidal deformability. Star data fence the equation of state in hard. The heaviest masses and the merger tides do most of the work.
arxiv-2512-20007:
Zhihan Huang and Ziang Niu make goodness-of-fit testing cheap enough to use on awkward models. Many statistical models have normalizing constants nobody can compute, so checking whether one actually fits the data is hard: sampling from the fitted model is expensive, and bootstrap checks demand repeated refitting. Their semiparametric test builds on the kernelized Stein discrepancy, which can judge fit using only the model's score function.

They establish the statistic's consistency and its asymptotic null distribution under general nuisance estimation, then propose an influence-adjusted wild bootstrap that produces a valid test without refitting or fresh sampling. The bootstrap's consistency and local power are proven, and simulations from normality testing to intractable likelihoods show competitive power at a fraction of rivals' cost. A lung-cancer protein signaling network provides the applied illustration.
arxiv-2512-20107:
Thanh-Tung Le, Tuan Pham, and four colleagues split the difference between two schools of novel view synthesis. Rendering a scene from unseen camera angles given sparse posed views is easy for deterministic networks where geometry is observed, but those blur whatever was never seen. Diffusion methods hallucinate plausibly instead, at heavy training and inference cost. UMAMI routes each region to the paradigm that suits it.

A bidirectional transformer encodes multi-view image tokens and Plücker-ray embeddings into one shared latent representation. A feed-forward head then renders pixels where geometry is well constrained, while a masked autoregressive diffusion head completes occluded and unseen areas. Trained end-to-end without handcrafted three-dimensional biases, the hybrid reached state-of-the-art image quality while rendering an order of magnitude faster than fully generative baselines. It was accepted to NeurIPS 2025.
arxiv-2512-21007: Milutin Obradovic and Nikola Tuneski work in geometric function theory, the study of univalent functions, which are analytic functions that never take the same value twice on their domain. For several known classes of such functions, they examine the Toeplitz and symmetric Toeplitz determinants formed from the coefficients of the inverse functions. Those quantities encode how the coefficients can grow and interact. Their analysis sharpens bounds obtained in earlier work on these determinants.
arxiv-2512-21107:
Eduard Stefan Dinuta, Iustin Sirbu, and Traian Rebedea ease the labeling burden behind language-model safety filters. Guardrail classifiers are trained on large labeled sets that are costly to build, error-prone, and often synthetic. Semi-supervised learning offers another path, training on a modest labeled core plus plenty of unlabeled text. The authors test what these techniques buy for safety classification on both sides of the conversation, the incoming prompts and the model's responses.

Augmentation turns out to be the lever that matters most, and only when it is designed for the task: safety-specific edits outperform generic text noise by far. For moderation teams, the practical message is that unlabeled traffic plus thoughtful edits can stand in for a good deal of costly label work without losing classifier quality.
arxiv-2512-21407:
Pranav Sampathkumar, Tim Huege, Andreas Haungs, and Ralph Engel address a bottleneck in cosmic ray physics. When a high-energy cosmic ray hits the atmosphere, it creates an extensive air shower, and large radio antenna arrays can detect the shower's radio pulse. Interpreting those pulses normally requires costly microscopic simulations of the radio emission.

The team shows that a simple neural network can simulate the radio pulses instead, learning the large-scale behavior that emerges from the detailed microscopic physics. As a physics test, they use the network for reconstructing the depth at which the shower reaches its maximum size, a key measure of the cosmic ray's identity. The reconstruction keeps a resolution comparable to work based on full Monte Carlo simulations, at far lower cost. The study serves as a proof of concept for using small neural networks on other emergent phenomena.
arxiv-2512-22207:
Ryan Spencer and five co-authors present GamiBench, a benchmark that tests whether multimodal AI models can truly reason about folding paper. Models handle perception and instructions well but struggle to track objects across views and steps. Origami makes an ideal test: a flat crease pattern must be followed mentally through a sequence into a 3D shape.

GamiBench holds 186 regular and 186 impossible crease patterns, each paired with folded shapes shown from six viewpoints. Its three tasks ask models to predict folded forms, judge valid viewpoints, and detect impossible patterns. New metrics track viewpoint consistency and how often models select impossible folds. Even leading systems such as GPT-5 and Gemini-2.5-Pro struggled with single-step spatial understanding in the authors' tests.
arxiv-2512-22407:
Carl Christopher Haynes-Magyar studies gentler on-ramps for learning to program. Parsons problems, where learners drag code blocks into the right order and indentation, are known scaffolding for writing code from scratch. His Codespec environment adds two variants as optional scaffolding: Faded Parsons, with parts of lines blanked, and Pseudocode Parsons, written in plain language. Nine programmers tried them in retrospective think-aloud interviews.

Learners reached for Faded Parsons when wrestling with syntax and structure, and for Pseudocode Parsons when planning at a high level. The optional scaffolds supported checking their own understanding, forming strategies, and refining prior knowledge. Costs included slow drag-and-drop and confusion when a provided solution clashed with the learner's own mental model. Faded Parsons was also enjoyed as a desirable challenge.
arxiv-2512-22507:
Harish Kumarasubramanian and Jayakanth Ravichandran use Auger Electron Spectroscopy (AES) to watch chemistry happen while oxide films grow. The chemical states inside a film, and at the seams where layers meet, decide which prized effects appear. Those effects include 2D electron gases, magnetism at the seams, and phase changes.

AES is keenly sensitive to small shifts in valence electron counts. The team show it can tell apart distinct oxidation states, live as a film grows, in multivalent perovskite manganate and vanadate systems. At the seam between lanthanum manganate and strontium titanate, the readings gave evidence of charge transfer happening live. The authors present in situ AES as a tool for steering seam chemistry while films grow, a step toward building oxide devices atom by atom.
arxiv-2512-23007:
Tobias Gebäck, Ioanna Motschan-Armen, and Irina Pettersson derive a tissue-level account of electropermeabilization, the process where electric pulses open pores in cell membranes to let drugs or genes enter. Their starting point is a cell-level model in a periodic tissue geometry. It tracks electric potential inside and outside cells, while the membrane's potential jump evolves with a porosity variable through a nonlinear law.

After proving the microscopic problem is well posed, the authors pass to the large scale with two-scale convergence arguments. The macroscopic model has memory effects and a nonlinear, time-dependent effective current. Its conductivity drops in the way experiments show, reflecting the capacitive nature of the lipid bilayer, and computations reproduce the sigmoid rise of tissue conductivity with field strength. The work gives a rigorous answer for conductivity dynamics that experiments had long displayed.
arxiv-2512-23107:
Hossein Vaziri, Mohammad Reza Shojaei, and Pere Masjuan map the electromagnetic form factors of the proton and neutron. These functions describe how nucleons respond to photons, and show their internal charge and magnetism spread. Their study works in the spacelike region and unifies three descriptions: two based on generalized parton distributions and one built from vector-meson exchange.

Fitting data fixes the optimal weights and shape parameters blending those components for both nucleons. From local Taylor series the authors then construct global Padé-based fits for four groups of form factors, producing analytic fits that stay stable across the momentum-transfer range analyzed. The combined framework is offered as an accurate, motivated description of nucleon structure inside a controlled, model-dependent setting. Such fits feed into the reading of electron scattering experiments and into calculations that need form factors as input.
arxiv-2512-23707:
Shashwat Goel and ten co-authors train language models to act as research assistants that draft study plans. Given aims and constraints, a good co-scientist should produce a plan a researcher could brainstorm from or even carry out, but today's models routinely miss stated constraints and unspoken requirements. The team's training material comes from the literature itself.

They automatically extracted research goals, each paired with a goal-specific grading rubric, from papers across several domains, building a large and diverse corpus. Models then trained with reinforcement learning, grading their own plans against the rubrics while a frozen copy of the original model judged. Human experts preferred the tuned model's plans for seventy percent of machine learning goals, and the recipe transferred to medical research, where running experiments for feedback is often impossible.
arxiv-2512-23807:
Marco Zank writes a short mathematical note on the wave equation, setting up its variational formulation in space-time all at once rather than stepping through time. He treats the scalar wave equation in its second-order form on bounded Lipschitz domains, with zero initial conditions and a source term that is merely square-integrable over the space-time cylinder. Variational methods need the right pairing of solution and test spaces to work.

Zank investigates a framework pairing a new solution space with the plain square-integrable test space. Uses known existence and uniqueness results in a Sobolev space to prove the setting fits inf-sup theory, with the solution operator an isomorphism. He also shows the new solution space is not contained in the second-order Sobolev space. The result underpins space-time discretizations, least-squares methods, and space-time boundary element methods.
arxiv-2512-23907:
Paul Englefield and Russell Beale argue, with data, that deleting your files is a bad filing strategy. In an age of information overload, knowledge workers juggle tactics for organizing digital material: filing it, pruning it, covering topics broadly, building ontologies, keeping things timely. The authors studied fifty-one knowledge workers through surveys and interviews to see how these tactics relate to actually finding things again, and how satisfied people feel.

Deletion was always the least adopted tactic, and, more surprisingly, it was actively harmful: workers who deleted more had worse retrieval success and lower satisfaction. The paper reviews the literature on personal information management, then presents detailed statistics and clustering analyses supporting the adverse verdict. The title's echo of a famous programming maxim is deliberate: like the goto statement before it, deletion is considered harmful. The moral is simple: keep the files.
arxiv-2512-24207:
Chi Zhang and Mingqian Yao solve two classic lattice problems in p-adic fields. The problems are the longest vector problem and the closest vector problem. P-adic norms are non-Archimedean. That property changes the geometry completely. Distances obey a stronger triangle inequality there.

The authors exploit that structure. They give a polynomial-time algorithm for orthogonal bases of p-adic lattices. The field must be given by a minimal polynomial. Maximal orders supply the needed structure. So do p-radicals in extension fields of the p-adic numbers. Uniformizers and residue field bases are built efficiently. With those in hand, both lattice problems become rapid to solve. The paper also characterizes norms on vector spaces over the p-adics. The notes serve readers working where number theory meets computation.
arxiv-2512-24507:
Samuel Granovsky, Alexander Kosovichev, Irina Kitiashvili, and Alan Wray model white-light flares on the Sun. Most flares shine in ultraviolet and X-rays. A subset also brighten in visible light. Their kernels are compact and short-lived. Standard electron-beam models dump energy high in the chromosphere. Whether they can explain the deep photospheric brightening is an open question.

The team runs three-dimensional radiative magnetohydrodynamic simulations. The StellarBox code follows beam heating in a structured atmosphere. Synthetic iron line profiles are computed for direct comparison with satellite observations. The runs produce strong upper-chromospheric heating and multiple shock fronts. Continuum brightening reaches levels seen in strong X-class white-light flares. Fine-scale structure changes the dynamics compared with one-dimensional models. Multidimensional transport matters for where flare energy lands.
arxiv-2512-24707:
Marek Janasz and Piotr Pokora study arrangements of conics and lines in the plane whose combined curve has strong algebraic properties linked to maximizing curves. They focus on cases where crossings are ordinary and no point has multiplicity above four. Numerical limits on which combinations can exist come first.

Detailed attention goes to arrangements with a single conic plus lines. The authors construct a new example with one conic and eleven lines, prove boundedness for real arrangements of that kind, and note a consequence for the Milnor algebra. Readers in algebraic geometry get both constraints and a concrete new configuration to test further ideas against.
arxiv-2512-24907:
Tung Nguyen resolves a 1985 open problem of Gyarfas about coloring graphs with no induced path on five vertices. For such graphs, he proves the chromatic number is bounded by a polynomial in the clique number, meaning few colors suffice when no large clique forces many. Earlier bounds were far weaker than polynomial.

A chromatic density framework, using chromatic quasirandomness and density increments, carries the proof, deducing the result from the Erdos-Hajnal property for the five-vertex path. Graph theory readers get a long-sought bound. Polynomial bounds are prized because they turn qualitative structure theorems into quantitative coloring guarantees.
arxiv-2512-25007:
Will Barker presents a computer algebra package for fast Poisson brackets and constraint algebras in canonical gravity. Dirac's Hamiltonian constraint algorithm counts propagating modes and gauge symmetries in alternative gravity theories and exposes pathologies such as strongly coupled modes. For gravity, applying it by hand becomes notoriously arduous.

Automating bracket computation and algebra reconstruction speeds that check dramatically. Gravitational theory readers get a practical tool for vetting extended theories of gravity. Faster constraint analysis means more candidate theories can be screened for hidden problems before deeper study, and gauge symmetries can be recovered with far less manual algebra.
arxiv-2601-00007:
Nicholas A Pape uses the dice game Yahtzee as a test bed for reinforcement learning, where an agent learns by trial and reward. Yahtzee mixes luck, many possible scoring choices, and rewards that arrive late. An exact best strategy is known for the solo game, but the multiplayer version is too large to solve exactly, which leaves room for learned approximations.

Pape trains self-play agents with three policy methods and tests how design choices affect learning. Two methods prove touchy and fall short under a fixed training budget. The third trains steadily across settings and reaches a median score close to the exact optimum over many test games. All agents struggle with one scoring bonus, showing limits in long-term credit assignment.
arxiv-2601-00107:
Deepyaman Chakraborty leads five co-authors in introducing a sampling method for estimating rare events in nonlinear systems, from engineering failures to blocked weather patterns. Their 2026 framework recasts rare events as Bayesian inverse problems built around a limit-state function whose zero set marks the event. Because that function is not smooth, they replace it with a smooth version that keeps the failure set intact.

The resulting distribution is explored by an interacting particle system whose affine invariance lets it adapt to stretched, uneven shapes, with no gradients required. Tests climb from two small examples to a point-vortex model of atmospheric blocking. In each case the method concentrates near the critical sets and yields good proposals for importance sampling. The authors present it as a robust, gradient-free option for rare-event estimation in unstable systems where plain simulation almost never visits the event of interest.
arxiv-2601-00207:
Md Ahmed Al Muzaddid and coauthor William J Beksi count crops by rebuilding the field in three dimensions. Counting fruit and bolls guides farm care and harvest choices. Flat images struggle when plants overlap and hide each other. One view cannot split a cluster with confidence. Their framework uses many views of the same plants.

Independent masks from each view feed a neural radiance field. The field joins them into one 3D scene. New visibility and consistency scores guide the split. Instances separate in 3D, and counts come out exact. No crop specific tuning is needed. Tests span cotton bolls, apples, and pears. Color, shape, and size vary widely across them. Counting stays strong throughout, beating prior art. The team also releases a cotton dataset. Other groups can build on the same ground.
arxiv-2601-00407:
Li Chen, Junlan Shi, Jiani Zhang, and Botao Fu design a two-dimensional material with an unusual electronic structure. The material is a type-II nodal line semimetal, where tilted cone-like bands meet along a line rather than at a point. Such states promise odd transport behavior, but tilting is hard to control because it depends on fine details of the lattice and symmetry. Their 2026 paper offers a bottom-up recipe.

Starting from a two-layer form of aluminum nitride, the team inserts fluorine atoms between the layers. Calculations from first principles show a protected nodal loop sitting right at the Fermi level. Electric fields and strain can tune the behavior. A sharp feature in the band structure even drives magnetism, giving a magnetic topological semimetal.
arxiv-2601-00507:
Junhyung Park, Fanny Yang, and Thomas Icard give counterfactual reasoning a new mathematical foundation. Counterfactuals ask what would have happened under different circumstances, and they sit at the top of Pearl's well-known ladder of causation, usually handled through causal models with interventions. Park and colleagues take a different route.

They define counterfactual probability spaces and counterfactual causal spaces, built from products of world-specific measurable spaces. In their account, counterfactuals and interventions are separate ideas rather than nested ones, and the two frameworks combine only when needed. Shared information between worlds, carried entirely by the probability measure and causal kernels, is the heart of the theory. The result is a cleaner axiomatic basis for reasoning about alternative worlds.
arxiv-2601-00707:
Frederik J Thomsen and two co-authors study how large ecosystems sort themselves out, in a 2026 paper. Their model is a stripped-down one: many species with set links, in a random web. Each species grows or shrinks by a simple rule, and none can drop below zero.

The authors show that the states the system can sit in form shrinking zones. These zones match a tool from neural network theory called Gardner volumes. As the share of live species falls, the zones shrink fast. The authors tie that shrink to shifts in the link web over time. The tests say whether all life dies out or growth runs wild. For the wild case, a small tweak to the model leads to a calm end state instead. The work links ecosystem fate to the size of its room to move.
arxiv-2601-01007:
Yusaku Yamamoto and Ken'ichiro Tanaka wrote a 2026 math paper on a very accurate way to solve change equations. Such equations say how a quantity grows or fades over time, from a known start. The method samples the path at set times and fits the whole path at once. Its error shrinks almost exponentially as samples are added, a rare speed. The catch is a big set of linked nonlinear equations to solve.

A simple loop, of Gauss-Seidel type, was known to crack those equations fast. Each pass cuts the error by a factor of ten or a hundred. The authors supply that proof here. They give a condition that makes the loop settle from any start. They also bound how fast it settles, which matches the speed seen in practice. Test cases close the paper. The result puts a trusted shortcut on firm ground.
arxiv-2601-01307:
Ayoub Ghaba and four co-authors study quantum steering in three coupled harmonic oscillators. Steering is a strong form of quantum correlation: measurements on one part can be shown to guide the state of another in a way no classical story can mimic. Exact results for three-body steering are scarce, so the team simplifies the geometry first.

Working in a phase-space picture of the quantum state, they derive exact formulas for steering in every direction between the three oscillators. A key finding is that the ground state shows no steering at all, while adding excitations switches steering on and strengthens it. Which pairs steer which depends on where the excitations sit, not just how large they are. The authors also record symmetry relations among the directions. The work gives a clean reference case for how steering is born and shared in multi-body quantum systems.
arxiv-2601-01407:
Arjhun Sreedar, Rohan Pillay, and Laukik Patade test whether synthetic training data can teach small open language models to reason about emotions, not just label them. Their pipeline uses several agents to write therapy-style conversations, then turns them into structured multiple-choice questions about feelings, each with an explanation. Models are fine-tuned on this material.

The clearest result comes from Mistral 7B. Its emotional understanding score more than doubled, and its emotional awareness score rose by about half, on EmoBench-style tests. The authors argue the gains show emotional reasoning can be induced by data alone, with no change to the model's architecture. That matters for builders of support tools, who need models that follow why a person feels something, not only what the feeling is called. The work also gives a recipe others can copy with open models.
arxiv-2601-01507:
Li and 3 co-authors tackle a hard call in breast care: which early lesions will turn invasive. A finding called DCIS stays inside the ducts, but some cases upgrade to invasive cancer, which changes surgery plans. Ultrasound data are limited, so learning models trained on them alone can generalize poorly.

Their framework first creates extra realistic ultrasound images with a diffusion model guided by several kinds of input. A large teacher network learns from real and made images, then passes its skill to a smaller student. On 1,435 cases from several centers, the student matched senior scan readers and beat junior ones, while running faster with fewer parameters.
arxiv-2601-01807:
Lumpy skin disease is a contagious viral infection of cattle that damages livestock health and threatens food security, so catching it early matters. Ubaidullah and six co-authors present LUMPNet, an image-based system that finds and classifies the skin nodules that are the disease's main visible sign.

The pipeline works in two steps. First, a YOLOv11 model detects and localizes nodules. Then an EfficientNet classifier labels the cropped images as diseased or healthy. A new adaptive hybrid optimizer trains the pair. It is meant to stabilize and speed learning. On a public dataset the system reported ninety-nine percent training accuracy and ninety-eight percent validation accuracy, beating existing schemes and an optimized EfficientNet baseline in a follow-up case study. Automated screening could support faster outbreak response on farms.
arxiv-2601-02007:
Radio signals inside railway tunnels decide whether communication-based train control works, but predicting them at fine resolution with parabolic wave equation solvers is expensive, while coarse solvers smear out the details. Kunyu Wu and six co-authors build PRBPN, a physics-informed recurrent network that rebuilds fine signal-strength fields from coarse solver slices.

The network fuses multiple slices over time. It iterates projection and back-projection steps. Those steps enforce physical consistency. Any pre-upsampling stage is skipped. The design stays data-efficient. Across four tunnel shapes and four frequencies, it tracked fine-mesh references closely. Validation used a real French tunnel, the Massif Central. Robustness was confirmed there. Training had used only a few paired examples. The method promises high-fidelity tunnel coverage planning at a fraction of the usual computing cost.
arxiv-2601-02307:
Dina El Zein and James Henderson tackle a privacy risk in sharing text through transformer embeddings, the lists of numbers a model computes for each word. Those numbers can leak the original text, since an attacker can often rebuild much of the input from them. Sharing embeddings is useful, but sharing them raw is not safe.

Their method, called NVDP, adds a special layer inside the transformer that injects calibrated noise into the embeddings. Training adjusts the noise to the needs of the later task, keeping useful signal while hiding private detail. Privacy is measured with Rényi divergence and a Bayesian form of differential privacy. Tests on the GLUE benchmark of language tasks show the trade off between protection and usefulness can be managed.
arxiv-2601-02507:
Jesse Held, Molly Kaplan, Donald Marolf, and Zhencheng Wang ask whether axion wormholes matter for a deep puzzle in quantum gravity, the factorization problem in the AdS CFT correspondence. A wormhole joining two boundaries seems to link systems that the boundary theory says should factor into independent parts. The authors define the bulk path integral by integrating over a real Lorentzian contour first, then continuing the result as needed, and work in two plus one bulk dimensions for technical control.

With the axion field fixed at opposite values on the two boundary spheres, they find wormholes are subdominant to an ultraviolet sensitive endpoint contribution for boundary values near the real axis. Wormholes dominate only near the negative imaginary axis, and for positive imaginary values they do not contribute at all, because the relevant contour never meets the integration path. The wormhole threat to factorization is thus narrower than often assumed.
arxiv-2601-02607:
Elisio Muchave, Pedro Coutinho, Tiago Oliveira, and Miroslav Krstić design an extremum seeking controller for a system whose actuator behaves like a wave equation. Extremum seeking steers a system in real time toward the best value of an unknown output map, using a small added probing signal. When actuation travels as a distributed wave, that probing signal itself must be reshaped before it can work.

They first solve a path planning problem to reshape the probing signal, then build an edge control law by the backstepping method that offsets the wave dynamics with distributed effects. A Lyapunov analysis shows the averaged closed loop is exponentially stable, and averaging theory for infinite dimensional systems proves the real paths settle near the optimum. Simulations illustrate the method.
arxiv-2601-02807:
Sohini Roychowdhury, Doris Wang, Qian Ge, Joy Mu, and Srihari Reddy present COFFEE. A framework for enriching the embeddings that advertising ranking systems use to represent users and ads, without making the live model slower or more complex to serve. A ranker judges user interest better when it sees engagement both before and after an ad, and when its picture of a user stays fresh. Their framework explores that enrichment along three dimensions at once.

One dimension adds more diverse event sources. A second lengthens the user histories the embeddings draw on. A third adds richer event attributes and multimodal embeddings. Return on investment is measured by comparing organic engagement sources, such as content viewing, against ad impression sources. The authors report gains in ranking quality and in the slope of scaling curves for ad impressions, showing which enrichment spending pays.
arxiv-2601-02907:
Zeyu Gan and eleven co-authors survey what is known about the theory and inner workings of large language models. These systems succeed in practice yet remain black boxes, since the theory behind them lags far behind their engineering. The survey organizes the field by lifecycle, with six stages running from data preparation and model preparation through training, alignment, and inference to evaluation.

Within that frame, the authors review core questions: why certain data mixtures work, what different architectures can and cannot represent, and how alignment methods behave. They close by naming open frontier problems, including the limits of training on synthetic data and the mathematical bounds of safety guarantees. The survey gives researchers a shared map of a fragmented field.
arxiv-2601-03107:
Côme Tabary studies the Landau equation, a kinetic model for how a gas of particles with long-range interactions relaxes over time, in the special case of Maxwell molecules. The question is whether entropy production, the rate at which the gas generates entropy, decreases steadily as the gas settles. Tabary proves that it does, provided the directional temperatures of the gas are well distributed.

From that condition, it follows that for any starting state with finite mass and energy, entropy production is guaranteed to decrease after some explicit time. The paper also shows the entropy production decays exponentially. A further contribution is an explicit formula for its derivative, which the author offers as a starting point toward proving full monotonicity without extra conditions.
arxiv-2601-03307:
Simen Jacobs and four co-authors review how whole biological networks respond to temperature, in the second part of a two-part survey. Part I covered phenomenological and microscopic models; this part moves up a level, to networks of coupled biochemical reactions whose kinetics shift with temperature. It also reviews stochastic frameworks, such as Markov chains, that capture multi-step processes individual rate laws miss.

The central lesson is transformation: Arrhenius-like behavior at the level of single reactions becomes non-Arrhenius scaling, hard thermal limits, and even temperature compensation once reactions are wired into a system. The authors present network models as a mechanistic bridge between measured temperature response curves and the molecular organization behind them. The payoff is predictive insight into robustness, perturbations, and evolutionary constraints on living systems.
arxiv-2601-03407:
Roman Ovsiannikov and four co-authors design a hybrid parametric amplifier. Its two modes live in different physical systems: a microwave cavity mode, and an ensemble of spins, such as nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamond. Such amplifiers boost weak signals. This non-degenerate design can also generate squeezing in either system. The pump comes from modulating the spins' frequency, at the sum of the two mode frequencies.

The effect is surprising. Modulating a spin ensemble alone normally produces neither gain nor squeezing. A naive perturbative analysis says it should merely drive the cavity. With typical cavity parameters, the authors calculate the microwave signal can be amplified by about eighteen decibels, in under two microseconds. The device is meant to work at both room and cryogenic temperatures.
arxiv-2601-03507:
Qiang Zhang and twenty-one co-authors present REFA, a system that animates virtual faces from cameras inside a virtual reality headset. Infrared cameras watch the wearer's eyes and lower face from egocentric views, meaning from the user's own viewpoint. The goal is to drive a virtual character's expressions in real time, without a long calibration step for each person.

Training used a distillation approach that combines data and labels from several sources, including synthetic and real images. The team collected data from eighteen thousand subjects with a phone and a custom headset. A differentiable rendering pipeline extracted expression labels automatically. Systems like REFA could make meetings, games, and remote collaboration in virtual spaces feel far more personal.
arxiv-2601-03907:
Mohammadreza Koolani and seven co-authors built an event-based tactile skin that feels touch with light instead of dense electronic sensors. Two event cameras, which report only brightness changes, look sideways through a flexible silicone optical waveguide. A press bends the guide and changes its light, and the cameras catch that change as events, with positions found by triangulation and a clustering algorithm locating each contact's center.

The system was tested over a probed area of several thousand square millimeters using a meandering scan pattern. For presses visible to both cameras, localization error measured 4.66 millimeters on average in root-mean-square terms, across ninety-five percent of such presses. Event-driven sensing reacts fast and sips power, which suits soft robots and large-area skins that must stay flexible, light, and responsive.
arxiv-2601-04007:
Jacob S. Elford heads a team of eight authors asking whether small black holes follow the same accretion pattern as huge ones. A tight link among millimetre brightness, X-ray brightness, and mass was known for giant black holes in galaxy centres. The team tests that link on stellar-mass black holes in X-ray binary systems.

Using millimetre and X-ray data for five binaries, Elford and his seven co-authors find the small systems also sit on the plane. One source watched over time drifts off the plane after changing state, which hints the link holds only in the hard state. Two kinds of model both predict a plane across all masses, though they differ on exact mass estimates.
arxiv-2601-04407:
Mustafa Bakr and Robin Wopalenski present an exact recipe for turning electromagnetic simulations into quantum models of superconducting circuits, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Designers need the linearized modes of a Josephson junction inside an arbitrary passive environment, and usual extractions are approximate. Their framework starts from the admittance the junction sees looking outward.

By a matrix reduction they show the coupled system obeys a boundary condition at the junction whose solutions are exactly the dressed mode frequencies. that the admittance always has an exact continued-fraction form, realizable as a canonical ladder network with built-in convergence guarantees. The full nonlinear problem keeps the junction's cosine potential intact in the charge basis and couples it to cavity modes. Forming a block structure solvable by matrix continued fractions across every coupling regime. A final result shows high-frequency corrections die away on their own, with no artificial cutoff needed.
arxiv-2601-04507:
Fang Wu tackles the molecules that break machine learning's favourite assumption, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Property predictors rest on similarity: similar molecules should behave alike. Activity cliffs are the exceptions, near-identical molecules with sharply different potency, and they wreck graph-based models exactly where drug hunters care most. Labelled cases near cliffs are scarce, which rules out brute-force teaching.

His system, SemiMol, learns in a partly guided way from the many molecules with no labels instead. A teacher model grades the trustworthiness of pseudo-labels the main model assigns, a step ordinary pseudo-labelling cannot do for regression because it lacks confidence outputs. A self-adaptive curriculum then walks the target model toward the hard examples at a controlled pace. Across thirty activity cliff datasets, SemiMol greatly improved graph-based designs and beat state-of-the-art pretraining and partly guided baselines.
arxiv-2601-04607:
Xiaoyu Liu and six co-authors aim three different neural architectures at the scans where each is strongest, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Radiotherapy planning for head and neck cancers requires outlining every organ at risk, and small, oddly shaped organs defeat single segmentation models. Hybrid systems usually just glue architectures together and waste their distinct strengths in overlap.

Their model, HUR-MACL, first uses a convolutional network to find the regions it is uncertain about, then sends exactly those regions to two specialists. A Vision Mamba network and a deformable convolutional network — that refine them jointly. A distillation loss tailored to mismatched architectures keeps the two specialists teaching each other inside the hard regions. The authors report state-of-the-art results on two public datasets and one private collection, with the gains concentrated where segmentation usually fails.
arxiv-2601-04807:
Explaining why a graph neural network labels a node can take longer than the prediction itself on large graphs. Oscar Llorente and 4 co-authors tackle that bottleneck in a 2026 paper. Graph neural networks use connections between items to classify nodes, find links, and label whole graphs. Node-level explanations, though, grow extremely time-consuming as graphs expand, and batching often weakens explanation quality.

Their approach partitions the graph, splitting it into disjoint subgraphs that can be processed in parallel. Each part's explanations are computed separately, then combined. Faster explanations make these models easier to audit in settings like fraud or biology networks, where users need reasons, not just labels, at realistic scale.
arxiv-2601-04907:
Networks of learners that must agree while whispering compressed messages are the setting for Sifan Yang and 3 co-authors in a 2026 paper. In distributed online convex optimization, many connected learners jointly minimize a changing sequence of loss functions, each seeing local data alone plus compressed messages from neighbours. Compression saves bandwidth but earlier algorithms paid for it with weak regret bounds.

The authors present an improved algorithm together with lower bounds showing how far any method can go. Their analysis tracks how compression quality and the network's spectral gap, a measure of connectivity, limit performance. Tighter bounds guide engineers building federated and sensor systems, where communication, not computation, is the scarce resource being spent.
arxiv-2601-05307:
Ritwik Gupta and Andrew W. Reddie argue that United States AI safety rules chase a mirage in a 2026 paper.
