Charged walls act as conductive channels inside an otherwise insulating ferroelectric, which makes them attractive for reconfigurable electronics. Optical control of domain structure is a long-standing goal in that field.

The authors propose a scenario for the creation process in which the bulk photovoltaic effect plays the key role. Light-driven charge movement provides the screening charge that a charged wall needs to be stable. Phase-field simulations support that account. The results point toward devices whose conductive paths can be written and moved with light, for future electronic and opto-electronic uses.
arxiv-2605-02807:
Fabrizio Canfora, Cristóbal Corral, and Borja Diez introduce an analytic treatment of gravitational lensing when light passes through a medium full of hadrons, the particles made of quarks. The setup mirrors light in a medium with a condensate that gives the photon an effective mass, which can vary from place to place. In such a medium, photons no longer follow the usual null paths of empty space.

Hadrons are modeled by a nonlinear sigma model coupled to electromagnetism. The authors derive a corrected focusing equation with hadronic terms, and the photon paths in the short-wavelength limit. Results match plasma lensing theory, with a plus: transport traits such as the refractive index come out analytically from hadron density, with no fitted model. A worked case covers lensing by a black hole sourced by superfluid pionic vortices.
arxiv-2605-03007:
Salvatore Bottaro and three co-authors build a formalism for spotting late-time injections of energy into the cosmos, such as a dark sector phase change after recombination. Their one assumption is mild: the injection is fast compared with the horizon scale at the time. A hidden sector that stays sequestered from ordinary matter could still leave marks on the cosmic microwave background through gravity alone.

For injections after recombination, they derive how photon paths bend under scalar, vector, and tensor disturbances, and compute the microwave signal through the integrated Sachs-Wolfe effect. The signal, they show, is usually dominated by sudden injections of anisotropic stress. Applied to first-order phase transitions in a sequestered dark sector, current observations limit such energy injections to a tiny fraction of the total. Late, quiet events are not invisible.
arxiv-2605-04007:
Mingjie Jian and six co-authors present PySME version 1.0, an updated Python version of Spectroscopy Made Easy for modeling stellar spectra at survey scale. Stellar abundance analysis depends on flexible, high-performance spectral synthesis, and a central bottleneck is handling very large atomic and molecular line lists: faint lines must be preselected before formal synthesis begins.

PySME revises the line-selection framework around opacity ratio and line depth. It adds dynamic line list construction and control over the wavelength span each line affects. That shrinks what reaches the synthesis core while preserving accuracy. An updated equation-of-state treatment improves hydrogen line modeling and Balmer features, while metal lines stay close to previous results. The interface also supports parameter-dependent derived quantities updated during fitting.
arxiv-2605-04107:
Furkan Sakizli presents TSCG, a deterministic compiler that converts tool schemas for language model agents from JSON into token-efficient structured text. Production agent frameworks transmit schemas as JSON. That format was built for machine parsing rather than model interpretation. The author argues that mismatch causes most tool-use failures for small models at production catalog sizes. TSCG works at the application boundary with no model access, fine-tuning, or runtime search.

Eight composable operators and a formal compression bound of at least half on well-formed schemas make up the compiler. On an agentic benchmark of about nineteen thousand calls, TSCG was tested across twelve models and five scenarios. It raised one fourteen-billion-parameter model's accuracy from zero to over eighty percent at twenty tools. Decomposition experiments attribute the gains mainly to representation change rather than compression alone.
arxiv-2605-04207:
Jinhang Chai and three co-authors study how a seller should set prices over time when demand depends on product features and buyer traits in a partly unknown way. Part of the demand curve follows a flexible function, while the market noise follows an unknown distribution that must also be learned.

Their staged algorithm updates its estimate of the noise from data gathered while selling, rather than paying for separate random price experiments. They prove a general regret bound that works for many utility estimators. They also give rates for linear and sparse cases. These improve the best known results for this pricing setting.
arxiv-2605-04407:
Md Zakir Hossain and four co-authors test whether machine-learning systems for detecting network intrusions keep their accuracy when the network changes. Such systems often score very highly on the data set they were trained on, which can hide a failure to generalise.

Training and testing three standard models on two public data sets, they find random forests lead within each set, reaching very high accuracy. When a model trained on one set is tested on the other, accuracy collapses below forty percent. The authors connect this generalisation gap to broader work on human-centred, behaviour-aware security systems.
arxiv-2605-04507:
Zongqi Cui and Baihan Lin build a negotiation agent whose beliefs about its opponent can be inspected, rather than hidden inside a language model. A good negotiator must infer what the other side values, update those beliefs turn by turn, and act under uncertainty.

Their teacher system scores each dialogue against the six possible orderings of the opponent's priorities and updates a probability distribution over them, then chooses actions from that distribution. A smaller student model is distilled to output both its actions and its beliefs as tagged text. On a standard negotiation data set, the teacher beat prior systems and the student kept much of the belief accuracy.
arxiv-2605-04607:
Franek Stark and four co-authors present a real-time controller for a bipedal walking robot that mixes two models of different fidelity inside one prediction. A detailed whole-body model is accurate but expensive, while a simplified rigid-body model is cheap but coarse, and walking control must decide faster than the detailed model alone allows.

Their scheme uses the detailed model for the near future, where accuracy matters most, and the simplified model for later steps. A standard optimisation framework solves the resulting problem, choosing joint torques from a contact schedule and target speed without pre-planned footstep positions. The controller is validated in simulation on an eighteen-joint bipedal robot.
arxiv-2605-04707:
Samuel H. Ward and three co-authors analyse a supply problem that could slow the global rollout of nuclear fusion power: the lithium isotope lithium-6 is essential fuel for breeding tritium inside a reactor. Each plant consumes little lithium in operation, yet must hold a large enriched inventory on site.

That inventory, fifty to one hundred tonnes, combined with enrichment inefficiency, turns fuel into a major upfront capital cost, further magnified by financing. Today's enrichment technologies are also expensive, hard to scale, and environmentally risky, and highly enriched lithium-6 is a controlled substance. The authors discuss mitigations, including alternative enrichment technologies and reactor designs that ease the requirement.
arxiv-2605-04907:
Ariestotle Raj Maharjan, Jianchen Li, and Jing Liu extend Geant4, a widely used toolkit, so optical runs can be set up without writing C++ code. The plain-text geometry format now carries optical properties for bulk materials and surface interfaces through new tags. Removing code writing and repeated compiling lowers the barrier for new users.

The authors test the extension on key optical processes including Cherenkov radiation, scintillation, Rayleigh scattering, and absorption. They also show how to set up complex optical boundaries using the UNIFIED model in detail. The cases highlight the extension's value for rapid test builds and detector studies.
arxiv-2605-05007:
Zhiqing Cui and thirteen co-authors present Uno-Orchestra, a single policy for routing work inside multi-agent language model systems. Such systems usually commit to flat per-query routing or to hand-built task splitting, so depth, worker choice, and budget are never optimised together. Uno-Orchestra learns both when to split a task and where to send each piece.

The policy was trained on curated trajectories grounded in real worker interactions, choosing among allowed model and tool pairings. Against twenty-two baselines across thirteen benchmarks covering maths, code, knowledge, and tool use, it reached the best overall pass rate. It did so at roughly a tenth of the per-query cost of leading workflow systems.
arxiv-2605-05207:
Zeren Jiang and ten co-authors release Syn4D, a synthetic multiview dataset of moving three-dimensional scenes for computer vision research. Reconstructing and tracking dynamic scenes from a single video remains an open challenge, held back by scarce datasets with dense, accurate geometric labels. Syn4D supplies ground-truth camera motion, depth maps, dense tracking, and parametric human pose for its scenes.

Any pixel can be projected into three dimensions at any time and from any camera, a key feature for training and checking models. The authors evaluate the dataset across four tasks, including scene reconstruction, point tracking, camera retargeting, and pose estimation. Results highlight its potential for dynamic scene understanding and space-time modelling.
arxiv-2605-05407:
Mohamed Salim Aissi and six co-authors present PRISM, a framework for agents that must see, think, and act. A vision-language model alone often misses details that matter for the task at hand. PRISM pairs that model with a language model in a loop of questions and answers.

The language model critiques the scene description and asks goal-focused questions. The vision model answers, and the pair builds a compact, task-driven picture of the scene. On the ALFWorld and Room-to-Room benchmarks, PRISM beat leading image-based systems. The gains came from the interactive questioning, with no hand-written questions needed.
arxiv-2605-05707:
Walking controllers almost always assume a pendulum model of the body, the linear inverted pendulum, by fiat. Lingxue Lyu and Zihui Liu ask whether an optimal controller would choose that behavior on its own. They start from a small centroidal control problem that penalizes how fast angular momentum changes.

With a full-rank stance, the optimum drifts toward a pendular force pattern at a rate set by foot-span geometry, matching experiments closely. With two feet down, as in trotting, friction limits impose a floor on angular momentum rate that no tuning removes. Pendular structure, they argue, is something good control discovers.
arxiv-2605-05907:
Johannes Bertram and four co-authors critique tools used to compare neural representations in brains and deep learning models. Their study asks whether matching similarity scores mean two systems work the same way inside. It focuses on RSA and CKA, two standard measures of how alike two sets of neural activity look.

In a controlled MNIST experiment, changing the internal layout of a model left those scores almost unchanged. Yet the changed models differed in their explanations, weight patterns, and strength on new data. The authors argue that such scores cannot tell shared circuits from merely similar outputs. They propose manifold based checks, and offer a free explorer tool, as extra tests for future claims.
arxiv-2605-06007:
Hyunbae Jeon and Jinho Choi build a testing platform for spoken dialogue systems that play varied social roles. A tutor, a stubborn merchant, and a distracted worker should not all yield in the same way when a user talks over them. Yet most full duplex systems default to one rigid, always yielding policy, which breaks character for firmer roles.

PersonaKit is an open source, low latency web platform for prototyping and user testing such agents. Simple configuration files define each persona and its chances of yielding, holding, bridging, or overriding during overlap. The platform deploys comparative surveys on its own. A field evaluation with eight personas shows it can support end to end studies of these social speech behaviors.
arxiv-2605-06207:
Bowen Zheng and four co-authors rethink how visual tokenizers size their codebooks along a token sequence. Most tokenizers give every position the same codebook, and researchers scale that shared size up for better reconstruction. The authors show a hard information limit behind that habit, which they call the Entropy Cliff.

Early positions in a sequence carry high uncertainty, but the conditional entropy decays so fast that later positions become nearly fixed. On ImageNet, that point arrives within two of 256 positions at a common codebook size, turning the rest into memorization. Their Variable Codebook Size Quantization grows the codebook along the sequence instead. It cut a key generation error score nearly in half and built a coarse to fine semantic order.
arxiv-2605-06307:
Jana Gonnermann-Müller and four co-authors test whether language model students keep stable personas over time. Simulated learners promise a scalable stand in for educational research and teacher training, but the method only works if a persona holds steady across and within conversations. The team measure stability two ways, through self reported traits and through observer rated behavior, across five models and three prompt designs.

Conditions covered three ADHD related intensity levels informed by ICD-11, plus a default persona. Self reports and observer ratings held steadier at high intensity than at moderate intensity. In long unscripted dialogue, observer rated behavior drifted for high and moderate personas, even though self reports stayed stable. Scripted interactions with recurring task prompts cut that drift by up to 97 percent.
arxiv-2605-07107:
Leighton P. Barnes and Alex Dytso strengthen a classic statistical result about maximum likelihood estimation. With large samples, such estimates are known to settle into a bell-shaped distribution. The authors prove stronger forms of that behavior under added assumptions on the score function behind the estimate.

They establish tight sub-Gaussian tail bounds and convergence of all moments for the normalized error. For a smoothed version of the estimator, they prove convergence in relative entropy to the limiting Gaussian law. Under further conditions, the smoothing can be dropped entirely. Their supporting tools, including entropy-control arguments, may interest other researchers.
arxiv-2605-07207:
Nhan Trong Luu and three co-authors convert spiking neural networks from an energy-hungry training format into an efficient event-based one. Spiking networks promise low-power computing, but the direct coding used to train them wastes much of that advantage at run time. Direct-coded models still trail event-based versions badly on energy use.

The team presents the first systematic study of this transfer problem, mapping the challenges that arise when computation switches formats. They propose a set of methods to carry a pretrained direct-coded network into event-based form while preserving performance. The goal is reusing existing pretrained models without giving up the efficiency that makes spiking hardware attractive.
arxiv-2605-07307:
Yi-Chang Chen and three co-authors test whether reasoning chains need their density or their order to yield correct answers. Modern models write long sequential traces assuming every token counts and steps must be read in sequence. The team intervened on model-written chains by removing, masking, shuffling, and corrupting parts of them.

Line-level shuffling barely hurt accuracy, and even heavily reduced traces, stripped of prose and shuffled, kept most of their answers. Masking numbers destroyed accuracy, while masking prose slightly helped. Injecting false answers at triple frequency changed nothing, ruling out simple majority extraction. Answers, they conclude, rest on a sparse, order-insensitive core.
arxiv-2605-07607:
Zhixin Cheng and six co-authors work on registering images to three-dimensional point clouds, lining up a photo with a scanned scene. Viewpoint changes, the gap between camera and scanner data, and repetitive textures create scale confusion and wrong matches. Recent detection-free methods help but suffer attention drift and inconsistencies within each scale.

Inspired by how people first focus, then sweep, the team built a hierarchical focus-sweep interaction module inside a state-space framework, strengthening cross-modal links at several levels. A dynamic layer allocation strategy also chooses how many iterations each case needs, exploiting geometric constraints. On two indoor benchmarks, RGB-D Scenes V2 and 7-Scenes, the approach reached state-of-the-art registration performance.

arxiv-2605-08107:
Bikram Keshari Behera, Rhitabrata Bhattacharyya, and Shyamal Biswas study how Drude metals reflect and absorb light. They cover the whole frequency range in one classical frame. The frame includes bound charges and currents. From it, they derive exact forms for the loss constant, the phase constant, and the reflectivity. The reflectivity matches measured data for plasmas and seawater.

For metals that conduct very well, the loss constant takes a simple form near the plasma frequency. A branch-point kink shows up there. The team calls this opto-critical behavior. They compute its exponents for the loss constant, group velocity, and dielectric response. Quantum fixes are added at the end.
arxiv-2605-08307:
Parul Raghuvanshi and Vishvendra Singh Poonia model spin chemistry inside the heliobacterial reaction center, one of the simplest photosynthetic machines. When light splits charges there, the paired radicals can recombine into triplet states, which waste energy and can damage the cell, so keeping triplets down matters for efficient photosynthesis.

Using Lindblad open-system dynamics for the spin-correlated radical pair, the authors vary hyperfine coupling strengths and recombination rates to see how triplet yield responds. Their focus is chiral-induced spin selectivity, the tendency of chiral structures to filter electron spin, acting as the regulator. The study connects a quantum spin effect to the photophysics of a living system that works without any internal magnetic field.
arxiv-2605-08507:
Otoniel Nogueira da Silva and Manoel Messias da Silva Júnior compare how singularity sameness behaves across linked families of curves. They study a one parameter unfolding of a map from the complex plane into three dimensional space, alongside four families built from its double points, where two source points share one image.

Alongside the comparison, the authors build clear counterexamples to several natural guesses about these families. They also introduce new curve families that stay topologically constant yet fail a stricter sameness test, and extend classic double point formulas to higher dimensions. Singularity theory gains sharper boundaries between notions that look alike but behave differently.
arxiv-2605-08807:
H. Khodabakhshi, Zhi-Chao Li, H. Lu, and F. Shojai link a star's core to the space just past its edge, in both ways. In the Oppenheimer-Snyder fall model, in its broad form, edge rules cut the link to plain algebra. The link ties core density to the metric just past the edge. Builders can thus rebuild still forms of space from the fall. They can also get edge motion, with no need to solve field laws one by one.

Powers in the link act as a test key. Whole powers hint at high energy fixes. Part powers mark models built to fit. The frame makes smooth black holes easier to build. It also gives one shared yardstick for claims on smooth cores and cosmic guards.
arxiv-2605-08907:
Ali Rida Khalife and Cyril Pitrou bound swirl modes of space time with fresh sky data. The data comes from ground and space scopes that map the old light of the Big Bang. Three roots in the young cosmos can seed such swirls. One is a neutrino count flaw. One is a neutrino octupole shape. One is stress that did not match in all ways, from before mass and glow drew even. First waves of space time can ride with them too.

All data sets give tight caps on the swirl share for the count flaw case. The rest allow more, still capped. One set hints at a sign that fits zero. No break from the base model stands.
arxiv-2605-09007:
Jessee Ho, Shweta Khushu, and Shaina Raza say deepfake guards aim at the wrong mark. The mark should be the trick, not the trace. Guards that call real or fake score well on stock sets. They fall hard on new growth tools. In live calls, the harm is the trick act, not a flaw in the sound or sight. The team shows five props of trace work all wear thin as tools grow. They call the false calm the Generalization Illusion.

From speech act thought, from Grice's rules of talk, and from Cialdini's sway rules, they build a mate frame. It checks the line said, the talk as a whole, and how the hearer acts. Guards gain a social layer.

Jinkyo Han and Bahador Bahmani bake constitutive priors into the design process. The 2026 paper keeps AI-designed parts physically honest and manufacturable.
arxiv-2605-09407: Object detectors usually assume RGB images, but depth sensors see the world differently. Woochul Kang, Hyungseop Lee, and Jiho Lee build any-depth detection with a single network — DETR or YOLO flavors. The 2026 paper is one detector for every depth.
arxiv-2605-09507: Summarizing videos means picking the frames that matter, with honest uncertainty about the rest. Omer Tariq, Syed Muhammad Raza, and Jeongbae Son learn uncertainty-aware and decoder-aligned representations for the task. The 2026 paper is video insight that knows its limits.

Tinghao Huang and Shifan Zhao study Ramanujan primes in the context of these forms. The 2026 paper is analytic number theory where arithmetic meets quantum chaos.

Zhen Zhang, Wanjing Zhou, Juncheng Li, and others build RADAR: redundancy-aware spread. The 2026 paper is multi-agent systems with lean, strong, purposeful chatter throughout.

The 2026 paper is smart contract verification for the Move language. It proves tricky functions provably and formally correct.

arxiv-2606-00007:
Johnson designs governance rules for knowledge bases curated jointly by AI agents in this 2026 arXiv paper. Human platforms evolved moderation systems over two decades, but porting them to agents runs into gaps he flags. Agents are stateless, so deterrence-based sanctions lose force. Identical models undermine the variety that makes crowd wisdom work. And sycophancy collapses debate. His curation protocol answers with three layers covering artifact handling, reputation-weighted voting after structured debate, and graduated sanctions adapted for stateless agents.

Simulations with 100 agents drawn from seven archetypes tested the protocol under two adversity scenarios. It traded a little precision in calm conditions for far more strength under attack. Under moderate adversity its precision reached about 0.83 versus 0.79 for majority voting, with the gap widening under stress in their runs. Removing components one at a time showed commit-reveal voting, which hides votes until all are cast, gave the largest improvement.

Zheng-Hui Huang, Zhixiang Wang, Yu-Lun Liu, and Yung-Yu Chuang present a diffusion model in 2026 that splits a photo into two parts. One part is the scene behind glass. The other is the glare on the glass itself.

Earlier methods forced a hard split in one shot, which often failed when the two layers mixed. Their model instead works in rounds. At each round it rebuilds the two images from a shared internal state, then polishes the result. Trials on synthetic and real photos beat prior methods on clarity and on how sharp the edges look. The approach also handled paired captures, where a second shot helps tell the layers apart.
arxiv-2606-04207:
Lukas D'Angelo and colleagues describe in 2026 a real-time testbed that combines wideband radio identification with wireless power transfer, letting batteryless tags both communicate and harvest energy from the same signals. Their rig is an eight-by-eight distributed antenna system running in a common Wi-Fi band.

The testbed excites a backscatter device, a tag that answers by reflecting signals, and reads its reply within two milliseconds of airtime. Channel estimates then serve two applications at once: steering energy toward the tag and locating it indoors in real time. Energy harvesting gains reached up to twelve decibels over unfocused transmission. The authors present the platform as shared infrastructure for experimenting with joint communication, powering, and positioning.
arxiv-2606-04307:
Jun Hu proposes Folded Transport MCMC in 2026, a sampling method that eliminates the label-switching headache in Bayesian mixture models. Because mixture components are interchangeable, the posterior has a factorial number of identical modes, and standard samplers either hop poorly between them or need after-the-fact relabeling.

His sampler restricts the chain to a fundamental domain, a sorted slice of the space holding exactly one copy of each symmetric mode. Proposals come from a learned flow whose density is symmetrized over the label permutations, so the target stays correct on the reduced space. A computable convergence diagnostic comes along, and it sharpens when folding is applied. Across mixture tests and real accelerometer data from a supertall building, improvements ranged from twofold to over a hundredfold.
arxiv-2606-04507:
Zhu and colleagues train AI research assistants whose grader improves alongside the writer, in a 2026 arXiv paper on deep research systems. Producing a research report has no single ground-truth answer. Existing work uses a language model as judge with fixed rubrics. But a static evaluator cannot raise its standards as the solver improves. Optimization pressure then saturates. Their framework, SCORE, couples evaluator and solver in one shared-parameter model. Both improve together.

A meta-harness steers the process. It adjusts the evaluation environment to solver performance. It encourages valid evaluation dimensions and deeper evaluator search. Across deep research benchmarks, SCORE produced consistent improvements in report quality. The authors present co-evolving evaluation and generation as a promising direction. It suits research agents whose outputs cannot be checked against an answer key.
arxiv-2606-04607:
Sevilla and colleagues demonstrate a microscope technique that finds nanoscale defects buried inside silicon carbide wafers without damaging them, in a 2026 arXiv paper. They leave no resolvable surface marks. Standard photoluminescence contrast is quenched by background doping.

The combination yields high-contrast, high-resolution images of dislocations below the surface. So the method identifies as well as locates. The authors describe the approach as simple and tolerant of surface imperfections. It offers a practical route toward industrial in-line inspection of SiC substrates. SiC is central to power electronics. Catching buried defects before device fabrication saves costly failures.
arxiv-2606-04707:
Zhang, Yang, and Jin recalculate how much of the dark matter could be light primordial black holes, paying attention to a modeling choice others glossed over, in a 2026 arXiv cosmology paper. Standard Hawking evaporation disfavors such black holes, but the memory-burden effect can extend their lifetimes by suppressing emission after about half the mass is lost. Earlier cosmological studies modeled the switch into the burden phase as instantaneous. This paper treats the crossover as continuous, comparing additive and multiplicative ways of combining the two evaporation rates through a smoothed profile.

The additive crossover always yields weaker bounds than the multiplicative one, while both are tighter than the instantaneous transition. In the mass range studied, the additive case can allow black holes to be about a tenth of dark matter where the multiplicative case allows only a hundredth. Specifying the combination rule, they conclude, is essential for honest constraints.
arxiv-2606-04807:
Reddy, Yang, and Zhai adapt a reinforcement learning method to the messy job of reducing social bias in language models, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Unlike verifiable tasks, bias has no single ground truth, so rewards are high-variance. Direct Preference Optimization is limited by its offline nature and lack of exploration, while Proximal Policy Optimization can destabilize. Their framework, BiasGRPO, uses group-relative policy optimization, normalizing rewards across a group of sampled completions instead of trusting a learned value function.

Substituting the group-relative baseline reduces instability while keeping the exploration benefits of online training. BiasGRPO outperforms both DPO and PPO across multiple benchmarks. To run it, the authors extend a bias dataset across domains and contexts, and they build and release a custom bias reward model that guides generation without degrading the model's knowledge.
arxiv-2606-05107:
Elouan Gardès and co-authors propose FINO in this 2026 arXiv paper, a label-free way to adapt vision foundation models to specialized scientific domains. Generic vision models degrade on fields like microscopy or Earth observation. The usual fix, supervised fine-tuning, struggles there: labels are scarce, and narrow training can collapse the model's generality. Scientific datasets, however, come with rich metadata that standard pipelines ignore.

FINO adapts representations in a self-supervised way guided by that metadata, handling both discrete labels and continuous values. Its objective encourages the representation to preserve informative factors while suppressing spurious ones, such as sensor or batch effects. Across fluorescence microscopy, Earth observation, wildlife monitoring, and medical imaging, FINO outperformed unsupervised domain adaptation. It even beat fully supervised adaptation. It also exceeded specialized domain systems while using no task labels for the backbone and only lightweight probes on top.
arxiv-2606-05207:
Absos Ali Shaikh and Kamiruzzaman examine pseudosymmetry, Ricci solitons, and curvature inheritance in Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker spacetime in this 2026 arXiv paper. This cosmos is the standard model of a homogeneous, isotropic cosmos, yet its geometry had never had a full curvature examination.

They show it meets a pseudosymmetric-type curvature condition and several related ones on the conformal and conharmonic tensors. Certain Tachibana tensors built from those curvatures depend linearly on a symmetrized combination. It is also a 2-quasi-Einstein manifold of Roter type. Its Ricci tensor is neither cyclic parallel nor of Codazzi type, though it meets several compatibility needs. Studying solitons and inheritance symmetries, they find almost Ricci soliton and eta-Ricci Yamabe soliton forms for the time and radial fields but not the angular one. They close by setting it beside the inhomogeneous Lemaître-Tolman-Bondi spacetime.
arxiv-2606-05307:
Noemi La Bella and colleagues ask how faint a jet base the Event Horizon Telescope can detect around the black hole M87-star in this 2026 arXiv paper. M87 hosts a famous relativistic jet, but spotting jet emission right at horizon scales, next to the bright accretion flow, is hard.

They generated observations for three array configurations, the 2021 and 2022 campaigns plus a near-future one, using semi-analytic accretion-jet models whose jet brightness can be tuned. Jet detectability depended strongly on intensity, array configuration, and imaging method, and the 2022 array's improved short-baseline coverage was a significant step up. The authors conclude the telescope is sensitive to weak horizon-scale jet emission. If post-2021 images show no jet signature, the inner jet must contribute only a small part of the compact flux.
arxiv-2606-05407:
Haofei Lu and colleagues present MoDex in this 2026 arXiv paper, a diffusion policy for sequentially grasping several objects with one dexterous hand without putting any of them down. Most dexterous grasping methods commit the hand's degrees of freedom to a single object, wasting its dexterity and leaving nothing in reserve for the next grasp.

The policy predicts the next gripper pose from observations, conditioned on a point cloud and on an opposition space, a specification of which fingers participate in the current grasp. Training proceeds in two stages: imitation learning on expert demonstrations, then reinforcement learning fine-tuning. That improves success rates over the pretrained policy and eases simulation-to-real transfer. Evaluated on a Franka Panda arm with an Allegro Hand in MuJoCo simulation and on real hardware, MoDex beat the learning-based baselines. The margins were 3 to 18 percentage points in both settings.
arxiv-2606-05907:
Okabe and Komatsu bend a document collection into a curved map where distance means meaning in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their knowledge manifold starts from character-level word-piece frequency vectors for each paper. A constrained layout places papers on a two-dimensional surface, close when semantically near. Smoothed particle interpolation then estimates the knowledge profile at any point on the map, even empty spots.

Directional gradients show how topics shift across the surface. A Gaussian process layer adds uncertainty estimates and each paper's contribution at a query point. Shortest paths on the curved surface, its geodesics, trace how one research area morphs into another. The test corpus held twenty papers on fiber-reinforced composites and aerospace structures. The map recovered meaningful research clusters without being told the groupings. Geodesic paths likewise followed sensible topic transitions. The framework offers analysts a geometry for literature, not just a list.
arxiv-2606-06007:
Haoyang Cao, Chen, Han, and Xu build diffusion models that generate time series without peeking at the future in a 2026 arXiv paper. Synthetic sequential data serves finance, healthcare, energy, and operations, but naive diffusion extensions scramble time dependence. Worse, they can leak future information into earlier steps, which real forecasting forbids. The sequential forward-backward framework adds and removes noise along the sequence itself. Each step conditions on the history built so far, enforcing adaptedness.

A new score-matching objective keeps training efficient and parallel. The theory delivers guarantees in layers: score approximation, score estimation, then distribution fit, with ReLU networks as the worked example. Synthetic tests on ARMA models and Gaussian processes confirmed the approach. A finance demo built mean-variance optimal portfolios from generated data. Code is public. Adaptedness, the authors argue, is not a detail but the defining constraint for honest sequential generation.
arxiv-2606-06107:
Clason and colleagues run quantum key distribution across three hundred kilometers of Swedish fiber in a 2026 arXiv paper. QKD promises information-theoretic secrecy, but deployment faces distance, mixed infrastructure, and classical traffic sharing the glass. The link joins Linköping University to the Stockholm hub of Sweden's national quantum infrastructure. Two hundred seventy kilometers of deployed single-mode fiber form the backbone.

A thirty-three-kilometer multi-core fiber segment stands in for a metropolitan access link, bringing the total past three hundred kilometers. Commercial QKD systems pair with superconducting nanowire detectors to survive the loss. The team switched the quantum channel between cores while Ethernet traffic and injected noise ran alongside. Keys generated en route protected an image transmission with one-time-pad encryption. Image fidelity hinged on the key budget and compression choice. The demonstration targets hybrid quantum-classical networks as they will be built.
arxiv-2606-06207:
Yukiko Kawakami and colleagues hunt for hidden toxicity patterns in Japanese animal drug reports in this 2026 arXiv paper. Pharmacovigilance means watching for harmful drug effects after medicines reach real use. Japan's reporting rules and the differing biology of each species can hide patterns that pooled data would blur. Instead of training a predictor, the team looks for structure directly, in a way regulators can inspect.

They encoded more than four thousand high confidence adverse event reports, covering nine thousand eighty drug and event combinations, by organ system and adjusted for species reporting bias. Clustering found three clear species patterns: liver dominant effects in companion animals, kidney toxicity in ruminants, and skin sensitivity in sheep. Drug clusters matched known pharmacological classes in eighty three percent of cases, and cosine similarity beat rival measures at grouping the sparse reports.
arxiv-2606-06307:
Mohammad Taha Shah and Mohamed-Slim Alouini model networks of stratospheric aircraft in this 2026 arXiv paper on future communications. High altitude platforms circle between twenty and fifty kilometers up, promising broadband for rural, maritime, and island communities. Fleets of them will patrol in rings, so coverage and interference depend on the patrol geometry itself. Standard network analysis tools assume platforms scattered at random, which misses that structure.

They build a stochastic geometry framework on the spherical Earth, with two ring based point processes for patrol fleets. One scatters platforms randomly along each ring; the other fixes the count per ring. They derive coverage formulas and fold in the propulsion cost of circular flight. Under the random model, patrol radius creates clear optima for coverage and energy use. Under the fixed fleet model, performance barely responds to radius once fleet size is set.
arxiv-2606-06507:
Yu Zhong and Luyao Li model a stroke relevant artery with flexible curves in this 2026 arXiv paper on medical geometry. The cervical segment of the internal carotid artery twists in ways that matter for stroke diagnosis and surgical planning, and its centerline must be fitted accurately from scans. Ordinary polynomial fits oscillate, overfit, and force users to hand pick the polynomial order. The authors fit with fractional polynomials instead, allowing non integer powers that bend more naturally.

Choosing the order is automated with the Bayesian Information Criterion. Their effective order idea prunes candidate orders using sample statistics, shrinking the search space. On three hundred seventy nine clinical cases, the method beat traditional integer order fitting in accuracy and noise robustness, staying stable across four noise levels. Computation fell sharply too, from about one hundred fifty three seconds to about twenty three.
arxiv-2606-06607:
Yara do Amaral Coutinho and co-authors hunt a two particle dark sector at the Large Hadron Collider in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their theory has two neutral massive vector particles, both odd under a dark parity symmetry. The lighter is stable and a dark matter candidate. The heavier can decay by emitting a photon. When a collider produces the pair alongside ordinary quark jets, the signature is striking: one photon, jets, and missing momentum carried off by the invisible dark particles.

The team compares two search strategies: a single inclusive selection on missing momentum, and a three bin strategy keeping some shape information. The binned analysis improves the expected reach substantially. It probes regions where freeze out yields exactly the observed dark matter abundance. The authors also discuss a freeze in alternative, and warn their effective theory loses reliability at high masses.
arxiv-2606-06807:
A set function assigns a number to every group in a collection, and an additive one gives each union exactly the sum of its parts. Ho and Kania study functions that are only nearly additive in this 2026 arXiv paper. The Kalton-Roberts theorem promises that any such function sits within a fixed multiple of its error of a truly additive one, and the smallest such multiple is a famous unknown constant.

The original bound was forty four point five, later trimmed to thirty eight point eight. Ho and Kania now prove about nineteen point eight four, more than halving the original. Their proof changes which collections feed a recombination step built on expander graphs. Exact rational arithmetic checks every step, and the proof is formalized in Lean.
arxiv-2606-07007:
Sparse autoencoders promise to name what each neuron in a network has learned. Zhang, Lin, and Lee give that promise a mathematical spine in this 2026 arXiv paper. A concept, they propose, is simply a set of data points. Learning a concept means aligning the model's induced set with the human one.

Three grades of success follow. A neuron may merely detect a concept, separate it cleanly, or approximate it closely. Each grade yields geometric conditions and error bounds. Capacity limits say when one neuron suffices and when teams are needed. The framework explains familiar quirks of these models. Features split, get absorbed, form families, and stack into hierarchies. Formal concept analysis links the two directions of interpretation, which need not agree. Experiments on synthetic data with two autoencoder styles illustrate the theory in action.
arxiv-2606-07307:
Guo and Gordon study how a swirling flow can move the threshold for thermal explosion in this 2026 arXiv paper. The setting is the classic Frank-Kamenetskii model of combustion, where heat from a chemical reaction competes with cooling at a vessel's walls. One parameter controls the balance: below a critical value a steady temperature profile exists; above it, no steady state remains and explosion follows. The authors add a regular vortical flow, meaning a circulating motion inside the vessel.

They prove that when the reaction term grows fast enough, a suitable vortex can reverse the direction in which the threshold shifts. The striking exception is a disk-shaped vessel, where the trick fails. The paper describes the extremal solutions, the borderline profiles exactly at the threshold. Those profiles are always classical: smooth genuine solutions rather than weak limiting objects, a point the authors establish in detail.
arxiv-2606-07407:
Ju and Kim ask how few structured blocks are needed to build an arbitrary matrix, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A Toeplitz matrix is constant along each diagonal, giving it a description. Results say a matrix factors into a product of Toeplitz matrices, but the minimal count depends on the matrix and the structure allowed. The authors generalize the question to families of matrices forming an algebraic variety, a set defined by polynomial equations.

They define factorization varieties capturing products of a number of factors, and a border form based on limits of products. The authors compute dimensions of these varieties for Toeplitz, Hankel, bidiagonal, tridiagonal, skew-symmetric, and companion structures. For lower bounds on length they develop a method based on displacement rank, a measure of near-structure, which yields equations defining them. Upper bounds come from alternating minimization. Geometry provides evidence on the varieties' degrees in an example.
arxiv-2606-07507:
Sabando-Alvarez and Precup write down polynomial equations for the pieces of geometric spaces central to representation theory, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Springer fibers are varieties inside the flag variety, the space of nested chains, attached to nilpotent matrices. For matrices with two Jordan blocks, the fiber's irreducible components correspond both to two-row Young tableaux and to noncrossing matchings. Inspired by work on matrix Schubert varieties, the authors define an explicit polynomial ideal for each noncrossing matching.

They prove those ideals define the components, leaning on descriptions from earlier authors. Examples computed with the ideals then suggest two guessed formulas for each component's cohomology class, an algebraic marker used in Schubert calculus. The authors prove both conjectures for one family of tableaux using algebra methods. Turning abstract pieces into concrete equations makes once-hidden invariants computable, at least across the two-row landscape the paper maps.
arxiv-2606-07607:
Zhou, Huang, and Li accuse genomics of validating its methods with cherry-picked anecdotes, in this 2026 arXiv position paper. Deep learning models predict from DNA, and biologists ask them to explain the mechanisms through interpretable machine learning. The field's habit is to apply one method and publish successes. Benchmarking on transcription factor binding, the authors show 3 risks. Different methods give contradictory accounts for the same prediction. Methods fail to locate regulatory motifs, and explanations fail to reflect the model's internal process.

Their remedy borrows clinical trial culture: strict design, consistency and faithfulness checks, biological validity standards, and reporting failures like adverse events. A tiered framework grades genomic methods by evidence strength. Plausible-looking explanations are worse than none when they misdirect lab work. Genomics, they contend, must move from plausibility to validation before its models can guide laboratory work.
arxiv-2606-08307:
Amal Alqahtani, Salama, and Diab examine how mental health is discussed in Arabic-language online communities in this 2026 arXiv paper. Research in this area has centered mostly on English speakers, leaving Arabic discourse little examined. The authors study more than eight thousand posts on the platform X from over six hundred users, identified by a classifier as likely writing from lived experience. The posts come from three communities devoted to borderline personality disorder (BPD), bipolar disorder, and ADHD.

Using a cultural keyword framework, the team characterizes each community's language patterns. In their corpus, bipolar posts used more religious and medical words. BPD posts leaned toward relational, identity, and emotional-distress words. ADHD posts focused more often on practical symptoms and medication. The authors stress the corpus is imbalanced, so the patterns generate hypotheses rather than confirm them.
arxiv-2606-08407:
El-Yaagoubi, Moo Chung, and Ombao build a framework for mapping directed information flow in brain networks, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Neural circuits are full of recurrent feedback loops, which makes characterizing who influences whom difficult. Many existing tools assume a directed acyclic graph, a network without cycles, and therefore cannot represent the loops that real brains contain. The authors' nonparametric, information-theoretic framework is designed to keep those loops visible instead of assuming them away.

The method couples the discrete Hodge decomposition, a way of splitting flows on a network into independent components, with lead-lag mutual information, which detects which signals precede others. The edge flow separates into three orthogonal parts: a gradient term, a curl term isolating feedback loops, and a harmonic term for cyclic flow. A testing layer then identifies nodes whose flow signatures change between conditions.
arxiv-2606-08607:
Heyi Zhang and colleagues image a young binary star system at fine resolution in this 2026 arXiv paper. The HH 46/47 system is a classic laboratory of star formation, pairing a newborn binary with a striking molecular outflow. Using the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array, the team observed the outflow and its envelope-disk system. The millimeter continuum reveals a compact central source surrounded by a disk around both stars, with substructures.

The companion star is not detected in the millimeter continuum. It coincides with a local intensity minimum, a dip in the disk's emission. Two spur-like features extend from the primary source toward the companion, likely induced by its gravity. Different molecules trace different layers. One carbon monoxide variant maps the extended envelope, while sulfur monoxide probes the inner envelope. The images let teams watch a companion sculpt the disk from which planets may form in time.
arxiv-2606-08807:
Heickal and Lan test whether the form of AI feedback changes how programming students learn, in this 2026 arXiv paper. In a Python course, students who submitted wrong code were randomly assigned one of three kinds of help. The options were natural language hints from a language model, AI-generated failing test cases, or no AI feedback. The recordings became the ProgFeed dataset. It holds 6,693 submissions from 215 students across 17 labs.

Natural language feedback was linked to higher completion rates and faster arrival at correct solutions. Test case feedback was uneven, and its effect hinged on validity: only sixty-six percent of generated test cases were correct. Even valid test cases did not reduce the submissions students needed, suggesting beginners cannot yet exploit counterexamples. Quality checks found the natural language feedback helpful in ninety-two and a half percent of cases.
arxiv-2606-09107:
Inoue and Itaba generalize a cohomology theory from groups to braided quantum-algebraic worlds, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Cohomology measures obstructions in algebra. Symmetric cohomology, Staic's theory for groups, extended to Hopf algebras, uses symmetric-group actions on a cochain complex. Many modern objects, quasi-triangular bialgebras among them, live in braided monoidal categories, where swapping factors twists rather than exchanges.

The authors define the braided cochain complex and cohomology for braided coalgebras in linear monoidal settings, with braidings defined on one object. To compare across settings, they describe relative maps, letting one setting's theory speak to another's. Main theorem: the braided cochain complex of quasi-triangular bialgebras does not change under Morita equivalence, under a condition on the setting. This is automatic in finite dimensions, the usual case. Quantum algebra gains a theory respecting its objects' braided nature, not flattening it into symmetry.
arxiv-2606-09307:
Arashi builds a Bayesian regression framework for data with many outcomes and predictors, where errors break the Gaussian bell curve, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Standard estimators assume Gaussian errors and treat coefficient sparsity separately from dependence sparsity. Macroeconomic series, asset returns, and gene expression show heavy tails, skewness, and outliers biasing both. The framework swaps in flexible error mixtures: multivariate t, skew-normal, and skew-t.

A horseshoe+ prior, a global-local shrinkage prior pulling noise toward zero while sparing real signals, sits on both at once. It covers coefficients and the error precision matrix, coupling the two sparsity patterns. Theory delivers joint posterior contraction, selection consistency, and a guarantee that one huge outlier's influence vanishes under t errors. Simulations show it matches Gaussian methods when errors are Gaussian and wins, often widely, under heavy tails. FRED-MD macro data and S&P 500 returns yield sparse, readable maps.
arxiv-2606-09607:
Yongzhong Xu asks whether cheap clues can prove that a group of attention heads forms a true circuit in a language model in this 2026 arXiv paper. Interpretability work now treats groups of parts, not lone units, as the key objects. A common shortcut groups heads that fire together and calls the group a circuit.

His test is a closure check. He removes the grouped heads and weighs the harm against matched random groups. On two dense models of about a billion parameters, the grouped heads passed: harm clearly topped the random case. In a mixture-of-experts model, one grouped set looked real by the numbers yet failed the check. Cutting it helped the model instead. Two other cheap clues, sharp attention and spread of use, also split from true function. Xu's moral: such clues propose circuits, but only removal tests confirm them.
arxiv-2606-09707:
Gianluca Barmina, Annemette Broch Pirchert, and Andrea Blasi Núñez present a tool for editing trained model weights in a checked, repeatable way in this 2026 arXiv paper. Big checkpoints are hard to inspect and reshape. Teams often patch them with ad-hoc scripts, which break in quiet ways. BrainSurgery swaps scripts for plans.

Each plan is a declarative YAML file that names the edits to run. Regex and structure rules pick out tensors by name or place. Built-in assertions check shapes, data types, and values, so faults surface at once. The tool hides storage formats and memory handling from the user. A demo walks through four examples and three case studies, from model upcycling to LoRA extraction. One check applied a chain of edits and then reversed it. Across fifty prompts, the restored model matched the first one's output, with top pick agreement of one hundred percent.
arxiv-2606-09807:
Thomas Ransford tours function spaces with a freak trait, and ties them to a basic series puzzle that no one has cracked in this 2026 arXiv paper. The spaces hold holomorphic functions on the unit disk, gauged by a norm. Each holds one odd function: sums of polynomials can close in on it in norm, yet its own Taylor partial sums cannot. No blend of those sums works either.

That freak trait sorts spaces into grades. In the best grade, plain partial sums converge for every member. A middle grade needs a summability method, a weighted blend that tames the sums. The worst grade keeps polynomials from filling the space at all. Named spaces land in each grade, from Hardy and Bergman spaces to the Bloch space. The hunt for concrete freak spaces boils down to a plain-looking question about convergent series. That question, Ransford shows, is still open.
arxiv-2606-09907:
Rahman and colleagues tackle two linked problems in learning from patient records over time, in a 2026 arXiv paper on medical AI. Clinical data mixes imaging, text, and records, but at any visit some sources are often missing. A measurement's meaning also depends on the patient's disease trajectory, the path their condition follows across visits. Earlier methods handled missing data or time patterns, rarely both.

Their framework, LongMoE, fills missing modalities with a context-aware imputation module, meaning it estimates absent inputs from what is present. A trajectory-aware encoder models disease progression across irregular visit gaps, and a sparse mixture-of-experts design routes each patient to specialized sub-networks. On the ADNI and OASIS-3 brain study datasets and the MIMIC-IV hospital records, LongMoE stayed robust when current modalities were missing or weak. It also remained competitive when all data was available, supporting longitudinally aware clinical learning.
arxiv-2606-10107:
Stillwagon and his team propose a fairer score for cell segmentation models, in a 2026 arXiv paper on computer vision evaluation. Widely used metrics in biological imaging have mathematical weaknesses. Hard overlap thresholds make scores jump discontinuously, and per-object scaling distorts results when object sizes vary. Greedy matching also pairs predictions with truth in an order-dependent way.

Their metric, Maximum Matching Accuracy, is threshold-free and continuous. It finds a globally optimal one-to-one matching between predicted and ground-truth objects and aggregates total overlap with per-pixel scaling. Across synthetic failure cases, progressive corruption tests, and a model ranking comparison, it produced scores that were more stable, more sensitive, and more interpretable. The beaten rivals included AP at fifty percent overlap, Panoptic Quality, SEG, and AJI. The authors offer it as a principled foundation for benchmarking cell segmentation.
arxiv-2606-10307:
Keramati and his team find that a debating model's opening tokens reveal the quality of reasoning to come, in a 2026 arXiv paper on language model testing. They ask whether built-in confidence signals, the token-level log-probabilities produced during writing, predict reasoning quality as scored by a language-model judge. Using a debate-based essay scoring setup, they compare confidence proxies against rubric-based judge scores across two ASAP essay sets.

Early-token confidence, above all within the first few generated tokens, is steadily the strongest predictor of reasoning quality, beating full-sequence stats. A clear asymmetry appears between agent roles, with confidence aligning more strongly with quality for supportive reasoning than for adversarial critique. The results suggest early decoding dynamics provide a light, strong signal for gauging reasoning trust in multi-agent systems without costly judging passes.
arxiv-2606-10407:
Simen Hexeberg and his team teach object detection models to pinpoint bird calls inside noisy tropical soundscapes, in a 2026 arXiv paper on bioacoustics. Passive acoustic monitoring observes wildlife at scale, but most models only predict species presence within a time window without pinpointing calls exactly in time or frequency, limiting later analysis. They frame call detection as object detection on spectrograms, the time-frequency pictures of sound, and train YOLO11 models to draw boxes around calls in dense Singapore soundscapes.

A scoring metric they propose, Intersection over Minimum, handles fuzzy acoustic edges better than the standard overlap measure. Their best model nearly doubles the baseline's detection score on in-sample Singapore recordings in the reported comparison. The results suggest object detection methods are a promising route to time-frequency spotting of animal calls in complex settings, supporting finer field analysis than presence-only watching.
arxiv-2606-10507:
Diao and colleagues tackle long-horizon tasks for language-model agents in this 2026 arXiv paper, where performance fades as multi-turn jobs stretch out. One cause is long-context interference: the growing history buries the global task state, weakening later decisions. Their method, HIPIF, trains an agent to plan around explicit subgoals and to fold, meaning summarise and shelve, each finished subgoal's history. Reflection checks progress, and subgoal-tied process rewards guide the rest.

The training is end-to-end and needs neither costly helper models nor expert demonstrations written for each task. Across three public agentic benchmarks, HIPIF consistently outperforms competing methods while also improving efficiency. The design mirrors human practice, breaking big jobs into subgoals and compressing finished work, a promising direction for agents that must stay coherent over long tasks.
arxiv-2606-10607:
Li and a large team of co-authors combine rival causal discovery algorithms in this 2026 arXiv paper. Causal discovery tries to recover the cause-and-effect graph among variables from observational data. The trouble is that different algorithms return conflicting graphs, each ignoring what the variables mean. The Causal Ensemble Agent pools the statistical experts' opinions across graph levels, then calls a language model in as referee only when pooled confidence sits near a decision boundary.

The referee reweights experts case by case, using feature descriptions the statistics never saw, and the ensemble composes a fuller graph than any member produced. On synthetic and real-world datasets the framework achieves the strongest overall performance across a wide range of discovery methods. Language models, the authors argue, belong in causal analysis as meta-analysts over evidence, not as oracles.
arxiv-2606-10907:
Iannelli and Ai measure how AI brand mentions steer web behavior in this 2026 arXiv paper. When a chatbot names a brand to a user with no recent engagement, no web log credits the assistant. Joining opt-in clickstream data to the same users' chats with ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini, the authors separate genuine recommendations from incidental name-drops of brands the user already knows.

For true recommendations, same-name Google searches rise by 4.3 percentage points over matched placebos. Visits to the brand's own site rise by roughly two points, and retailer-page visits by about one point. Incidental mentions move behavior far less, and last-click analytics miss the effect entirely.
arxiv-2606-11307:
Cowie and Fender revisit how astronomers estimate the energy of synchrotron sources in a 2026 arXiv paper. Synchrotron self-absorption, SSA, appears across many sources, and its spectral peak is a powerful tool for estimating the emitting region's conditions and minimum energy. Traditional estimates assume the region is quasi-spherical and homogeneous. Many observed spectra, though, show flatter slopes below the peak than that picture predicts.

The authors first re-derive the standard estimates carefully, obtaining the most accurate standard minimum-energy equations. They argue an uneven emitting region best explains the flattened spectra. Using power-law slab and sphere models, they find inhomogeneity can make traditional methods underestimate minimum energy and region size by over an order of magnitude. They derive correction factors depending on the flattened spectral index and its frequency range, plus factors for non-spherical homogeneous regions, and explore polarization and light-curve effects.
arxiv-2606-11407:
Reif, Sahi, Serganova, and Sherman prove a Harish-Chandra isomorphism for supersymmetric spaces in a 2026 arXiv paper. The classical theorem describes the center of the enveloping algebra by Weyl-group-symmetric polynomials on a Cartan subalgebra. Extending it to Lie superalgebras required new invariance conditions, debated since Sergeev and Gorelik-Kac.

They describe the eigenvalue polynomials of invariant operators on such spaces. These satisfy novel conditions the authors call odd. They also prove it for ghost distributions, which obey a square root of those rules. All proofs use algebra alone, via a rank-one reduction and the Chevalley restriction theorem. The work extends the theory from algebras to the spaces built on them, including special linear and orthosymplectic examples.
arxiv-2606-11807:
Balázs Németh, Mohamed Warda and Ronojoy Adhikari develop a geometric theory of active filaments in this 2026 arXiv paper. Slender elastic bodies, from sperm tails to soft robotic arms, often sit in viscous fluid and power themselves. Their internal forces can be nonreciprocal, violating the rule that action and reaction match, so strain produces a net response.

Assuming the physics is unchanged by rotations and translations, the authors derive a shape-space formulation: equations that separate the body's intrinsic deformation from its rigid motion. The result is a reaction-advection-diffusion system, a geometric flow where activity-driven instabilities create patterns. Depending on parameters, it settles into steady shapes, oscillates, or moves chaotically. These regimes appear as rigid, swimming and chaotic motion. The framework unifies recent observations in slender active structures under one theory.
arxiv-2606-12007:
A V Druzhinin and C Cancellieri model how thin films relieve their internal stress in this 2026 arXiv paper. Films deposited far from equilibrium carry residual stress, and its relaxation can damage devices. The mechanism here is plastic: screw dislocations, line defects in the crystal, pile up against the impenetrable interface between film and substrate.

Starting from the initial shear stress, the authors link plastic strain to dislocation density and derive an equation connecting residual stress to that density. Applying force balance gives the dislocation distribution for any non-uniform starting stress profile. They solve it numerically by collocation for constant, linear, parabolic and exponential initial profiles. The relaxed stress depends strongly on the film segment's thickness-to-width ratio. In every case equilibrium demands a pile-up mixing dislocations of both signs of Burgers vector, the measure of a dislocation's strength.
arxiv-2606-12107:
Martin Hasenburger and five colleagues watch an aluminium alloy melt at the nanoscale in this 2026 arXiv paper. Melting of eutectic alloys, mixtures that liquefy at one sharp temperature, is classical metallurgy. The tiny-scale mechanisms were out of reach in experiments until in-situ electron microscopy with micro-heating chips matured.

The team tracked a nanocrystalline aluminium-copper alloy poor in copper in a transmission electron microscope, tracking chemistry and resistance. Melting began in the hotter centre and spread outward, with grain boundaries the main sites for liquid formation through copper enrichment. The compound phase melted before the matrix around it finished melting. Most strikingly, liquid copper travelled over two hundred fifty micrometres, far beyond solid-state diffusion limits, leaving pale rims at the chip's outer edge. The authors promote the method as a platform for studying phase changes in many such materials.
arxiv-2606-12207:
Lai and co-authors survey how test sets for embodied AI, robots and agents acting in physical worlds, get built, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Unlike static datasets, an embodied benchmark bundles tasks, environments, robot data, demonstrations, and scoring rules into one system. The survey follows a five-stage pipeline from task design and data collection through annotation, metric building, and evaluation with diagnostic feedback. Each stage is traced from hand craft through automation to foundation-model help and agentic loops.

The finding: automation rarely deletes cost; it moves it. Savings in human authoring reappear as spending on validation, audit trails, version control, and long-term governance. Agentic closed-loop building promises fresh benchmarks but demands strong audit and rollback discipline. Manual judgment stays necessary where safety and social values are involved. Progress now depends less on bigger suites than on pipelines that stay diagnosable, auditable, and refreshable.
arxiv-2606-12307:
Sougata Bhattacharyya and co-authors find that concentrating entanglement into one strong link backfires under the commonest noise, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A W state spreads one excitation evenly across three qubits, entangling all pairs equally. An asymmetric cousin reshapes the network: two strong vertex-base links and one weak base-base link. The authors track concurrence, an entanglement measure, under several noise types.

Under phase damping the strength hierarchy survives at all noise levels, with no sudden death of entanglement. Under amplitude damping, energy loss, the order flips. The symmetric W state becomes most robust, while the weak base-base concurrence vanishes at a noise threshold. The strong link's structure makes it fragile, an effect the authors name super-link fragility. Under depolarizing noise the asymmetry advantage is erased. Robustness, they conclude, depends jointly on network geometry, excitation sector, and noise symmetry, never on starting entanglement alone.
arxiv-2606-12507:
Rezaei and co-authors fire the judge and let the rubric teach directly, in this 2026 arXiv paper. For open-ended tasks like medical advice, no single right answer exists, so trainers grade model outputs against rubrics, scoring criteria. Standard methods pay an AI judge to score every attempt, which is costly, biased toward the judge's quirks, and yields one sparse score per answer. Their RGSD instead makes the rubric privileged context: the base model, shown the rubric, acts as a teacher.

The student, which never sees the rubric, samples one answer per prompt. Training then matches the student's next-token probabilities to the teacher's, a dense signal replacing the end score. No judge calls occur during training. Across Qwen models from three to eight billion parameters, in medical and science domains, RGSD matches judge-based GRPO on rubric satisfaction. Rubrics enrich the teacher more than self-written reference answers do.
arxiv-2606-13607:
Zach Studdiford and Lupyan compare human and machine reasoning failures in this 2026 arXiv paper, and find them surprisingly alike. When language models generalise poorly or err haphazardly, critics often conclude the models are merely pattern matching, unlike humans who supposedly reason from world models. The authors evaluate human participants and twenty-five language models on common-sense reasoning. Both groups show similar patterns of errors. The team then identifies the attention heads, the internal components routing information, that drive the model responses, and finds they implement a form of pattern matching.

Strikingly, those same heads predict reasoning errors in people, errors triggered by seemingly irrelevant prompt details. The shared mechanism suggests human everyday reasoning also leans heavily on pattern matching, not just abstract principle. The paper reframes the debate: the question is not whether models pattern-match, but whether human cognition differs in kind or only in degree.
arxiv-2606-13707:
Fan Zhang and colleagues present Orchestra-o1 in this 2026 arXiv paper, a framework for agent teams that work across every modality. Agent swarms have shifted language model systems from single agents to teams, making orchestration, the splitting and coordination of tasks, the key layer. Existing frameworks handle only a narrow set of modes and generalise poorly when text, image, audio, and video coexist. Omnimodal cases, such as analysing a recorded meeting or producing multimedia content, expose exactly that weakness.

Orchestra-o1 introduces a mechanism enabling modality-aware teamwork across mixed inputs. Agents specialised by modality can be assigned, sequenced, and combined under one coordination scheme rather than stitched together ad hoc. The authors position the framework for tasks whose inputs arrive in every format at once. As agents move from text-only benchmarks into real media workflows, orchestration that treats modality as a first-class dimension becomes essential.
arxiv-2606-13807:
Rosemeier and Klein design a faster way to compute solutions of equations whose answers wiggle very rapidly. Such oscillatory systems appear in fluid dynamics, mechanics, and plasma physics. Standard solvers must take tiny time steps to follow each wiggle, making long runs expensive. Their 2026 arXiv paper builds a time-stepping scheme linked to the WKB method, a classic tool for wave-like behavior, using a change of variables derived in the paper.

In the transformed variables, the leading rapid oscillations vanish or appear only at higher order, so larger steps stay accurate. The authors test the scheme on several equations, including the van der Pol oscillator, a circuit-like system with self-sustained pulses. They vary the small parameter that sets the scale gap and show how settings must adapt as it shrinks. Across the tests, cost stays bounded even as oscillations grow faster.
arxiv-2606-13907:
Berkesch, Erman, and Favero repair a broken dictionary between geometry and algebra for spaces called toric varieties. For the simpler simplicial kind, Cox's theory links subvarieties to graded ideals in a special ring. For nonsimplicial varieties that link simply fails: distinct ideals can describe the same subvariety. Their 2026 arXiv paper replaces the Cox ring with a variant built only from Q-Cartier divisors, divisors some multiple of which behave well.

With that change, the ideal-variety correspondence is restored in the nonsimplicial case. Subschemes and sheaves gain an explicit classification through multigraded modules. The construction also yields a toric Deligne-Mumford stack, a refined object remembering extra symmetry data. Finally, the authors extend GKZ and Mori theory, the standard combinatorics of toric birational geometry, into this stacky setting. The package removes deficiencies that had confined Cox-style methods to the simplicial world.
arxiv-2606-14007:
Fatunmbi, Gandhi, and Logan move blockchain plot creation onto graphics cards. Proof-of-Space consensus replaces energy-hungry repeated hashing with precomputed storage plots. Making those plots is itself slow because hashing dominates. Their 2026 arXiv paper presents VaultxGPU, extending the VaultX plotter by offloading its Blake3 hashing to the GPU with custom kernels for NVIDIA CUDA and the portable SYCL framework.

The design keeps lookup tables in graphics memory and fuses sorting and matching into one kernel. Across plot sizes K twenty-seven through thirty-one, the SYCL version ran fifty-nine point two times faster than a single-thread CPU. A K thirty-one plot took forty-five point four seconds instead of two thousand six hundred eighty-eight. It beat the best three hundred eighty-four-thread CPU setup too. The remaining bottleneck is disk writing, at fifty-nine to eighty-two percent of pipeline time.
arxiv-2606-14307:
Barberteguy and colleagues teach a 3D reconstruction network to also label what it rebuilds, in one unified model. The input is ordinary photos, with no camera data at all. Feedforward networks now produce dense 3D point clouds from unposed photos, but lack semantic understanding. Earlier add-ons froze the backbone or needed heuristic clustering at inference. Their 2026 arXiv paper presents Pano3D. A set-based mask decoder with learned queries is appended to the backbone. The system is finetuned jointly with geometric and semantic losses, no external models or postprocessing.

The bet: object recognition is already latent in reconstruction features encoding boundaries and 3D coherence. Joint training proved mutually beneficial. Pano3D reached state-of-the-art 3D panoptic results on ScanNet, ScanNet200, and ScanNet++, across online and all-to-all attention backbones.
arxiv-2606-14907:
Ellison Murray trims the cost of correcting satellite power amplifiers in a 2026 arXiv paper. Power amplifiers distort signals, blurring their spectral purity. Digital pre-distortion fixes this by pre-warping the signal to cancel the amplifier's flaws. Full-complexity fixes are too heavy for satellites. Size, weight, and power budgets there are strict.

Murray proposes Least Squares Thresholding for picking a sparse set of correction terms. It is compared with two standard sparse solvers, Orthogonal Matching Pursuit and plain Matching Pursuit. Thresholding matched the stronger method's linearization quality almost exactly. But it cut complexity by a factor of about two point eight. That near-free saving matters on orbit, where every watt and gram counts. The work frames sparse correction as a trade-off to tune, not a fixed recipe. It targets satellite communication systems first.
arxiv-2606-15007:
NVIDIA introduces Nemotron 3 Ultra, an open language model built for long-running agent work, in a 2026 report. The model mixes experts with a hybrid Mamba-attention design to raise speed without losing accuracy. It holds five hundred fifty billion parameters, with fifty-five billion active per token. Context extends to one million tokens for extended tasks.

Pretraining consumed twenty trillion text tokens in low-precision NVFP4 format, in two phases of broad then high-quality data. Post-training adds supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, and distillation from many teacher models. Features such as LatentMoE and multi-token prediction push inference throughput higher. The report claims roughly five to six times the throughput of rival open models at matched accuracy on agentic benchmarks. NVIDIA releases the base, post-trained, and quantized checkpoints on HuggingFace. Training data and the full recipe are released as well.
arxiv-2606-15107:
Chen and coauthors benchmark language models on irregular time series question answering in a 2026 study. Real time series arrive irregularly: sensors log at uneven times and missing values carry meaning. Existing question answering benchmarks assume tidy, regular sampling instead. Random dropout creates fake irregularity that ignores why data went missing.

Their benchmark, IRTS-ToolBench, holds seventeen hundred questions across ten task types and thirteen domains. A language-model-guided pipeline converts regular series into irregular ones in semantically grounded ways. Irregularity follows cause-driven patterns, such as trigger-based or artifact-based sampling gaps. A library of thirty tools supports agent-style solving, with golden tool sets for scoring. Evaluation covers both answer correctness and tool-use behavior. Current models show real reasoning ability on irregular data, especially with context and tools available. Higher-level temporal reasoning still fails often, and agents need strong scaffolding to use tools reliably.
arxiv-2606-15307:
Kmainasi and coauthors train multimodal models to flag hateful and propagandistic memes with explanations, in a 2026 content moderation paper. Memes hide harmful intent in the interplay of image and caption, which neither reveals alone. The team benchmarks off-the-shelf reasoning models on English and Arabic meme datasets. They then extend those datasets with distilled rationales and detailed propaganda labels. Their training recipe applies reinforcement learning with rewards for accuracy and explanation quality. A length penalty keeps the model's reasoning from shrinking away.

On the English Hateful Memes benchmark, accuracy rose by about two points over prior work. On the Arabic ArMeme benchmark, macro-F1 jumped by over seven points. The trained model also produces written explanations for its verdicts. Sequence-classification baselines still win on Arabic accuracy alone. The model balances per-class performance better while explaining itself. Self-supervised training on unlabeled memes added signal.
arxiv-2606-15507:
Dasdan and colleagues audit the moral reasoning of LLaMA 3.1-8B-Instruct in 2026 from the inside, using mechanistic interpretability tools rather than judging only its answers. They run fifty-four moral prompts in four batteries: dilemmas, policy questions, role-play scenarios, and controlled trolley contrasts. Cluster-level and neuron-level metrics track which internal features dominate.

Both families converge on a Situational Anchor Effect: domain-specific representations top the activation list in every battery, whatever the moral content. Ethics-labelled capacity stays near five percent throughout, but its salience swings with prompt framing. In trolley variants, ethics features rise in rank without growing in capacity, and the model attends to whichever surface feature the prompt varies. One candidate ethics neuron stays stable across temperatures. The authors argue that fine-tuning reorders surface text but leaves domain-first frames intact, so output checks alone cannot certify moral reasoning.
arxiv-2606-15707:
Karmakar and colleagues demonstrate a tunable way to transform optical skyrmions in 2026, using the chirality of the medium the light passes through.
