Age, kidney function, medicine count, blood albumin, and overall illness burden ranked as the top drivers, with sharp risk jumps below set kidney and albumin cutoffs. The authors say the blend of accuracy and openness suits bedside risk checks.
pmc-13322907:
Lingshuai Meng and co-authors review the two-way link between the gut barrier and gut microbes in sepsis, in a 2026 article. Sepsis brings whole-body inflammation, organ damage and high death rates, and the intestine sits close to its course.

A leaky gut lining lets microbes and their products drive local and wider immune responses, while a disturbed microbial mix changes disease progress through its chemical output. The authors build a framework for gut-driven body-wide inflammation and note that some standard supportive care can itself harm the intestine. Treatments aimed at gut function, from microbial repair to barrier support, close the review as routes worth testing in practice.
pmc-13323007:
Yanhu Ji and co-authors link daily air pollution to non-accidental deaths in Shantou, China, in a 2026 study of a subtropical coastal city. Daily records from 2016 to 2020 covered deaths, weather and six pollutants, and a Poisson model estimated short-term effects by sex, age and season.

Deaths rose with PM2.5, PM10, sulfur dioxide, nitrogen dioxide and ozone over lags of several days, but not with carbon monoxide in their models. People aged 65 or older showed added sensitivity to ozone alone among the splits tested. Burden estimates used World Health Organization and Chinese air standards as reference levels. The authors argue for tighter control of particle and gas pollution in similar coastal cities.
pmc-13323807:
Joon-Tae Kim leads a Korean registry study on how well stroke risk factors were controlled before an ischaemic stroke, published in 2026. Records from 2011 to 2022 held 63,570 patients with at least one major risk factor among hypertension, diabetes, lipid disorder and atrial fibrillation.

Patients were classed as well, partly or poorly controlled by set treatment and biomarker rules, with roughly a third in each group. Good recovery at three months, meaning independence on the Rankin scale, fell as the number of risk factors rose. The authors test whether fuller pre-stroke control also predicts better recovery within each group, making a case for tighter risk management long before stroke strikes.
pmc-13324307:
Tae-Il Jeon and co-authors show that copper import through CTR1 powers heat production in fat, in a 2026 mouse study. Cold exposure and beta3-adrenergic stimulation raised CTR1 levels and copper build-up in thermogenic fat, linking the metal to the calorie-burning programme.

Mice lacking Ctr1 only in fat cells spent far less energy and turned severely cold during acute chill. Their brown fat showed suppressed oxygen-based energy pathways and weaker fat breakdown signals, and white fat depots also cleared lipid poorly. Brown-fat-only deletion still caused cold intolerance despite near-normal acute drug responses. The copper carrier elesclomol partly restored mitochondrial capacity and cold tolerance in the fat-wide knockout mice.
pmc-13326107:
Zhimei Sun and colleagues compare how stir-frying changes the scent of white and yellow mustard seeds in a 2026 food study. Heat work is a classic step for spice seeds, yet its flavor chemistry is rarely mapped side by side.

Tasters, an electronic nose, and chromatography with ion mobility checks covered raw and fried seeds. Frying shifted the aroma from sharp and mustard-like toward toasted and oily, strongest in yellow seeds. Instrument strength ranked fried yellow first, then fried white, raw white, and raw yellow. Six compounds, including 2-methylpyrazine and octanal, marked variety and frying state. The paired toolkit can verify seed identity and roast level.
pmc-13327807:
Feng-Chin Lee and co-authors measure late harm from radiation in children with brain tumors in a 2026 nationwide Taiwan study. Records covered 815 treated children and 1,630 matched children with brain tumors who had no radiation. The team compared hormone problems, delayed tissue injury, and vessel damage over the long term.

Radiation raised the risk of hormone disorders and late-delayed complications, with one risk 1.796 times the comparison level on their estimates, and overall late effects ran higher even after accounting for surgery and chemotherapy. Risks stood out for gonadotropin deficiency, at 1.602 times, and brain stem necrosis, at 3.208 times the comparison rates. Younger age at diagnosis added risk, so survivors need long hormone and brain follow-up.
pmc-13328007:
Chahyun Oh and co-authors compare non-opioid pain regimens after minor surgery in a 2026 record review. Mixing acetaminophen, anti-inflammatory drugs, and nefopam during surgery is standard, but how many agents are needed was unclear. The single-center study covered 5,601 adults having minor general surgery where opioids are not routine afterward.

Rescue pain relief within four hours was needed by 75.1 percent of single-agent patients, 58.8 percent of dual-agent patients, and 43.8 percent of triple-agent patients in the raw rates. After weighting for group differences, adjusted chances fell to 31.4 percent for triple therapy against 49.1 percent for dual and 67.2 percent for single regimens. More agents, carefully mixed, meant fewer painful first hours.
pmc-13328407:
Weiguo Sun and co-authors review gut microbiome strategies against tuberculosis in a 2026 article. Drug-resistant TB strains keep the disease a severe world threat, and sequencing plus artificial intelligence now tie gut microbes to TB through the gut-lung axis. Patients typically show lower microbe diversity and more inflammatory types, linked to severity and drug response.

The authors weigh microbe-based markers for early diagnosis, AI help in forecasting outcomes, and treatments from probiotics and diet to stool transplants that may boost drug power and ease side effects. Causation proof, privacy worries, and poor access in scarce regions still block the clinic path, so large multi-center trials with real-time monitoring top their agenda.
pmc-13328507:
Xiaoxiang Yan and Shanshan Gong ask in a 2026 study whether trust in government shapes how much people in China will pay to protect nature. They separate trust in the central government from trust in local government. Their data come from the 2021 Chinese General Social Survey, with 1,638 people included.

Both kinds of trust linked to higher willingness to pay, and local trust showed the larger link. City residents leaned more on local trust, while rural residents leaned more on central trust. Use of new media linked to lower willingness to pay, while older media showed no clear link. The authors argue that city and rural areas may need different approaches to gain public support.
pmc-13332407:
Li Zhang and colleagues followed patients with classic fever of unknown origin over the long term in a 2026 study from Peking Union Medical College Hospital. Many such patients leave hospital with no firm cause found, and their outlook has been poorly charted.

Of 739 patients, only 36.8 percent left with a firm cause, while 48.8 percent had a clinical diagnosis and 14.3 percent stayed unexplained. Among 396 undiagnosed patients reached later, just 3.3 percent had died, and 73.0 percent eventually received a firm diagnosis that matched the discharge view in 93.0 percent of cases. Trial tuberculosis treatment succeeded in 79.1 percent of those given it, and among the still-undiagnosed, about a third recovered on their own. The authors advise against overtreating and favor trial therapy plus close follow-up.
pmc-13333307:
Larissa Pessoa and co-authors built MUVY in 2026, a dataset of sports videos filmed by fans from several angles at once. Studying how a single play looks from many viewpoints usually requires staged recordings, while real crowd footage is messy, handheld, and unscripted.

The team mined Creative Commons-licensed YouTube clips and grouped recordings that captured the same action from different seats. The result is 141 recordings across 31 events in seven sports, from athletics and soccer to gymnastics and cricket, totaling about 3 hours and 15 minutes. Each video carries metadata plus frame-level annotations: hand-labeled camera viewpoints and object boxes for players, referees, goalkeepers, and balls, the boxes first drafted by a detection model and then hand-checked. Files are organized by sport, event, and camera, with frames and annotations preserved on Zenodo even if source videos vanish.
pmc-13333407:
Haosong Ma and co-authors report a trap for diagnosticians in a 2026 case of a belly sarcoma that mimicked a muscle tumor and then turned up in the testicle. Dedifferentiated liposarcoma is the commonest sarcoma behind the abdominal organs, but muscle-like versions are vanishingly rare and easily misread.

A 46-year-old farmer from Yunnan arrived with a large right-sided abdominal mass and no testicular sign at first. Surgeons removed the mass with his right kidney and half his colon. Ten days later a right scrotal mass appeared and the testicle was removed. Early tissue reads, positive for the muscle markers desmin and MyoD1, suggested rhabdomyosarcoma. Expert review with gene testing found MDM2 and CDK4 amplification in both specimens, proving dedifferentiated liposarcoma with muscle-style differentiation, and chest scans showed early lung spread. The authors insist on the gene test whenever muscle markers appear in such tumors.
pmc-13333707:
Hexin Zhu and co-authors exposed rats and mice to very humid air for weeks in a 2026 animal study of how damp conditions reshape the gut and blood chemistry. Humidity is a growing climate health risk, but its pathways into the body remain poorly mapped.

Rats and mice lived at about 60 percent relative humidity or about 90 percent for 7, 14, or 28 days. The team sequenced fecal microbes and profiled blood metabolites with mass spectrometry, then linked the two datasets. Humid housing shifted gut microbe makeup and blood chemistry in both species. Disturbed glycerophospholipid handling, ABC transporters, and phenylalanine pathways marked the exposure, and metabolites such as phosphocholine, choline, and taurine tied closely to the microbial changes. The profile offers leads for studying humidity-related illness.
pmc-13334107:
Vittorio Ferrari and co-authors tested whether a single basal blood measurement can stand in for stimulation testing in suspected early puberty, in a 2026 diagnostic study. The GnRH stimulation test is the standard check but is slow and costly.

The team reanalyzed 258 first-time GnRH tests done for suspected central precocious puberty at Edinburgh's Royal Hospital for Children and Young People between 2011 and 2025. Morning basal luteinizing hormone was measured just before testing, with special handling for values below assay detection limits. Basal hormone predicted a pubertal test response with an area under the curve of 0.80 in the analysis. A threshold of 0.5 units per liter balanced sensitivity and specificity, while values at or above 1.0 were always right. Such cutoffs could spare many children the full test.
pmc-13334707:
Majlen A. Dilweg and co-authors built new dopamine reuptake inhibitor candidates in a 2026 drug chemistry study. Blocking the dopamine transporter can treat conditions from depression to substance abuse, yet only one such drug has reached approval, so fresh chemical frames are needed.

The team grew a cycloalkylamine family, making two aliphatic and sixteen aromatic variants and testing them in a fluorescent uptake assay. Three compounds blocked both norepinephrine and dopamine reuptake. Most aromatic versions instead hit the dopamine transporter selectively, with two hydroxyl-bearing compounds, 11e and 11f, reaching nanomolar potency. Docking runs pointed to contacts with residues R85 and D476 as the source of that strength. The series offers starting points for selective dopamine drugs.
pmc-13334807:
Jae Joong Lee and Bedrich Benes introduced A-Occ-Plant, a 2026 computer vision method that fills in missing parts of plant point clouds. Sensors often miss plant surfaces hidden behind leaves, which hobbles trait measurement and 3D reconstruction.

Their pipeline converts a point cloud into images, completes them with two-dimensional amodal segmentation, then rebuilds a full cloud using view-consistent Gaussian splats. A coarse-to-fine transformer with cross-scale attention produces soft masks that fuse into a continuous density field, with no need for external pose estimation. The team built a synthetic dataset from a procedural plant model plus a real-world benchmark with artificial occlusions. Against leading completion methods, A-Occ-Plant improved perceptual scores sharply and recovered leaf count, leaf angle, and plant height, generalizing to soybean.
pmc-13335207:
Nikhil Chowdhary and co-authors set out a 2026 trial protocol pairing sensory electrical stimulation with virtual reality training for people with incomplete spinal cord injury. Trunk instability after such injuries undermines sitting balance, daily function, and quality of life.

The assessor-blind, two-group randomized trial will recruit 22 people with injury levels between T6 and T12 from the rehabilitation department of the Indian Spinal Injuries Centre. One group will receive VR balance training augmented with sensory electrical stimulation while the other receives the comparison program, and sitting balance plus quality of life will be scored. Earlier work supports each technique on its own in nerve-related groups, but their pairing in this group is untested. As a protocol, the article presents design and outcomes, not results.
pmc-13336407:
Ruiqun Chen and co-authors uncovered two brakes that keep interferon production by plasmacytoid dendritic cells from running away in a 2026 immunology study. These cells flood the body with type I interferon against viruses, but overshoot causes immunopathology.

The first brake is SLC44A2, abundant in resting cells and switched down on activation. Without it, cells overproduce interferon, apparently because the protein exports threonine, asparagine, and glutamine, amino acids the interferon program needs. The second brake is interferon itself: excess interferon lowers the migration receptors CCR2 and CCR5, holding the cells back from leaving. The team saw this feedback during viral infection, in autoimmune settings, and in Slc44a2-deficient mice, marking it as a general control circuit.
pmc-13336707:
Robert A. Hegele reviews evidence from the past 18 months in a 2026 article on carrying one faulty copy of genes behind familial chylomicronemia syndrome. Two faulty copies of any of five genes cause that rare, severe fat-clearing disorder. Carriers of a single copy are far more common, and their health effects were long unclear.

Follow-up studies show carriers range from normal fat levels to severe highs that swing over time. Carrying one copy accounts for 15–25% of cases of the broader multifactorial form of the syndrome in the cited work. Some variants actively interfere rather than simply halving function. Hegele draws lessons for family screening, counseling, and picking patients for new apoC-III drugs.
pmc-13336907:
Yingying Ding and colleagues name an RNA-binding protein as a broad virus blocker in a 2026 study. RBM25 works without relying on interferon, the usual alarm pathway. Mice lacking it sickened more from several viruses, while in cells it curbed both RNA and DNA viruses early, at the entry step.

RBM25 teams with a partner, RC3H1, to bind and destabilize the message for Rab22a, a host factor that helps viruses slip inside cells. Infection itself lowers RBM25, letting Rab22a rise and easing viral entry. Restoring or mimicking this brake could yield broad-spectrum antivirals that guard the door rather than chase each virus inside.
pmc-13337107:
Ting Cao and colleagues characterize a selective blocker of a gene-silencing complex in a 2026 study. PRC2, powered by EZH2 or its twin EZH1, tags histones to switch genes off, and overactive EZH2 drives some cancers. Existing approved drugs hit both twins by competing at the fuel site.

Their molecule C36 instead binds a side pocket where several EZH2 parts meet the partner EED, jamming internal communication. It blocks EZH2 complexes hard but spares EZH1 ones. In tumor cells and grafts it cut the silencing mark and target gene activity with low blood toxicity. Pairing C36 with a PD-1 antibody strengthened lung tumor control in mice. Selective allosteric blocking could refine epigenetic cancer therapy.
pmc-13337307:
Kaushik Ragunathan and colleagues recount a hard diagnosis in a 2026 case report of a toddler losing skills. Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, a fatal brain disease from lingering measles virus, usually strikes older children with mental decline and jerking movements. Brain scans are often normal early, which can mislead clinicians.

Their patient, a 24-month-old boy, developed normally until 22 months, then showed twisting postures, daily myoclonic jerks, and steady loss of milestones over 2 months. The picture resembled leukodystrophy, a white-matter disease, rather than infection damage. Fulminant early-onset disease at this age is unusual. The report urges keeping this measles complication in mind when toddlers regress, especially where immunization or early measles exposure is in play.
pmc-13337707:
Yaoyao Zhang and a large team test spinal fluid markers for telling two kinds of meningitis apart in 2026. Bacterial and tuberculous meningitis need different treatment, yet they can look alike. Prior antibiotic use, which is common, makes the call even harder.

A prospective group from 2014 to 2025 included 125 bacterial cases and 56 tuberculous cases, whatever their prior treatment. Spinal fluid procalcitonin and neutrophil share each separated the groups fairly well on their own. Together in one model they performed better, reaching an AUC of 0.849 in the reported analysis. The pair may help clinicians choose treatment sooner, even after antibiotics have started.
pmc-13341607:
Shockwave therapy rescues compressed spinal endplates in a 2026 study by Pan Xiang and colleagues. Cartilage endplate degeneration helps drive disc degeneration, so the team compressed rat tail discs with a custom device and treated cultured endplate cells under load.

Shockwave treatment improved disc height and MRI signal, restored endplate structure, raised sclerostin expression, and calmed the Wnt/β-catenin pathway compared with natural recovery. In dishes, compression had suppressed sclerostin and switched the pathway on, hurting matrix-building markers. Reversing that switch appears to be how the therapy protects the endplate, a mechanism that could guide non-surgical disc care.
pmc-13341807:
Pregnancy hypertension interventions in poorer countries are reviewed by Kristen Riley and co-investigators in a 2026 synthesis. These disorders cause an estimated 16% of maternal deaths, mostly in low- and middle-income countries, and the team gathered literature from 2010 to 2024 across four databases.

Of 212 studies, 56% addressed treatment, 24% prevention, 10% screening, and 10% spanned steps. Fewer than 10% came solely from low-income countries. Most were efficacy trials rather than implementation research, leaving a gap between knowing what works and delivering it at scale. The authors organize findings along a prevention, screening, and treatment continuum to guide implementers.
pmc-13342107:
A natural compound starves cancer cells by jamming a sugar enzyme, in a 2026 study by Yuelong Chai and colleagues. Alternol was already known to kill prostate cancer cells preferentially, and interaction mapping pointed at GAPDH, the glycolysis workhorse cancer cells lean on.

Alternol bound two sites on the enzyme, one overlapping the NAD+ pocket, and shut down purified GAPDH at an IC50 of 5.794 nM. Inside cultured cancer cells it likewise suppressed enzyme activity and cut glycolytic capacity, while benign prostate cells were spared. Metabolic profiling backed the choke point. A nanomolar grip on a central enzyme makes Alternol a notable lead.
pmc-13344307:
Karen J Gibbins, Amy M Valent, and Nicole E Marshall ask whether body mass index alone misjudges pregnancy risk in a 2026 cohort analysis. Using the nuMoM2b first-pregnancy cohort, the team scored cardiovascular health from smoking, activity, diet, cholesterol, blood pressure, and triglycerides, then split obesity risks by that wider score.

Among 2,381 participants, a body mass index of 30 or more roughly doubled or tripled risks for blood pressure disease, severe preeclampsia, big babies, diabetes, and cesarean birth overall. Inside the ideal health group, though, only big babies and diabetes stayed linked to high body mass, while poor cardiovascular health raised blood pressure risk at any size. Full health scoring, they argue, sorts risk far better.
pmc-13350007:
Vishal G Shelat wrote a 2026 commentary on a simple five-item prediction chart for liver cancer survival. The study discussed covered 165 surgically treated patients. It forecast survival at one, three, and five years.

The five inputs are body mass index, the blood protein albumin, a tumour marker, tumour size, and cancer stage. All are easy to gather in clinic. Accuracy was strong early. It faded somewhat by five years. Shelat praises bedside simplicity over complex models. He also places the chart within modern care. There, tumour load, liver reserve, and fitness all shape choices. Two patients at the same stage can fare very differently.
pmc-13351707:
Shuhui Wang and colleagues examine how the FOS gene shapes T-cell activity and heart vessel inflammation in Kawasaki disease, in 2026. The illness is a whole-body vessel inflammation in children that often harms coronary arteries. Gene profiles came from T cells of patients and from a mouse model of vessel inflammation.

FOS levels were higher in T cells during acute illness, with a P value below 0.001, and also rose in the mouse model. Blocking FOS eased vessel inflammation in mice. In cell culture, raising or lowering FOS in JURKAT T cells changed cytokine output and the inflammation those cells triggered in coronary vessel cells. Findings link FOS-driven T-cell activity to artery harm.
pmc-13355407:
Theresa Hunter Gibble and co-authors surveyed 518 United States adults in 2026 who had just started the weight drug tirzepatide. The survey, part of a real-world study, ran four to eight weeks after the first dose. It asked why people started, what blocked them, how they felt, and how easy the drug was to use.

Most said they started to improve overall health, with better movement and confidence also common. Cost worries and insurance blocks were the top barriers, with nine in ten naming coverage. Nearly half had failed to keep weight off with diet and exercise alone. Almost all found the injector or vial easy to use.
pmc-13355707:
Navanita Biswas and co-authors report a 2026 case of a 63-year-old woman whose first clear sign of AL amyloidosis was severe yellow skin from bile backup, without liver enlargement. This rare disease deposits misfolded antibody proteins in organs. She came in for ankle pain and was found jaundiced, with very high liver enzymes but no blocked bile ducts or liver growth on scans.

A liver biopsy showed amyloid deposits, and further tests found an abnormal antibody protein and a plasma cell growth in her marrow. Despite treatment, her liver, heart, and kidneys failed fast, and she chose comfort care and hospice. The authors urge doctors to weigh this disease in unexplained bile backup.
pmc-13355807:
Xun Sun and co-authors present a 2026 method to measure how strongly blockers bind to distinct forms of transthyretin, a protein that can clump into harmful deposits. The protein starts as a four-part unit, then splits into single units that misfold and stack. Blockers may grip either form, but telling the two apart was hard because form amounts shift over time.

Their method pulls separate binding values from a single NMR test that tracks each form. A test drug bound the single form far more strongly in acid conditions, and joining two peptide blockers doubled their grip on both forms. The approach should help design better blockers.
pmc-13356607:
Jonas Böhnlein and co-authors report in 2026 identical twins with a developmental disorder tied to the HNRNPU gene. Whole genome reading found an odd pattern: two nearby single-letter deletions on the same gene copy, never found together on one DNA strand. That means each twin carries three distinct cell lines, a pattern the team names clustered monoallelic mosaicism.

Such a pattern is too unlikely to arise from two separate accidents, so the team argues it came from one early embryo event with divergent fixes on sister strands. Searches of large mutation databases found like cases, hinting at a broader, overlooked path of mutation. The finding may reshape how mosaic cases and recurrence risk are read.
pmc-13357107:
Tianshu Feng and co-authors profiled in 2026 chemokines and their receptors in stomach cancer, signaling proteins that guide cell movement and immune traffic. Stomach cancer varies widely by subtype, and these signals help drive it, but their full pattern was unclear. Using a 371-sample cancer dataset for training and a second dataset for validation, they charted gene changes, grouped patients by signal patterns, and built a risk model.

Thirty-seven signal genes were altered in tumors, and patient groups differed in outlook and tumor surroundings. A nine-gene signature predicted survival well; low-risk patients carried more mutations and seemed likelier to gain from immune therapy. The authors offer it for risk sorting.
pmc-13359707:
Luca Castriota and Patrizia Perzia map an invading sea snail in a 2026 study. The veined rapa whelk, Rapana venosa, is a large predatory snail that has spread far from its home waters. The authors joined published records and citizen science reports with spatial tools to chart its advance across the Black Sea, the Mediterranean, and Atlantic Europe.

The invasion runs furthest in the Black Sea, where the snail favors brackish, nutrient-rich water near river mouths. In the Mediterranean it has lately sped up, led by the north-western Adriatic. In north-west Europe it remains confined. Salinity and river input emerge as the keys to where it can settle.
pmc-13359907:
Andrzej Dzikowski and co-authors examine how Poland manages three returning giants in a 2026 paper. European bison, Eurasian beavers, and moose have all recovered under protection, and their growing numbers now stir conflicts with farming, forestry, and public safety. The authors analyze the legal protection each species holds and how the rules fit the animals' current status.

They propose legal adjustments for management that adapts to local numbers while keeping conservation strong. Under strict conditions, they also consider using meat from culled animals rather than wasting it. The paper treats law as a working tool for balancing wildlife, livelihoods, and safety.
pmc-13360607:
Caden Seraphine and co-authors wrote a 2026 systematic review on immune cells called macrophages in colorectal cancer. This cancer is among the most common and deadly worldwide, yet most patients gain nothing from modern immunotherapy. The tissue around the tumor actively damps the immune response, and macrophages are key players there. They can either help the tumor grow or help fight it.

The review gathers proof on how tumor-helping macrophages shield the cancer from treatment. It also weighs whether these cells can serve as markers that predict how a patient will do. New therapies aim to flip macrophages into their tumor-fighting state. The authors hope such combos can extend immune treatment to the many patients it now leaves behind.
pmc-13361107:
Ke Ye and co-authors built a patient-based lab model to judge eye gene faults in a 2026 study. The gene RPE65 runs a key step in the visual cycle, and its faults cause a severe childhood blindness called Leber congenital amaurosis. Over 115 variant forms are known, but what each one does is mostly unclear. The team studied one patient carrying two different faulty copies of the gene.

Tests in lab cells showed both faults make the RPE65 protein unstable, so the cell chews it up and its eye function falls. The team then grew the patient's own pigment cells from stem cells to model the disease in a dish. They used this model to test whether gene therapy could restore the protein. Such personal models can guide which patients a therapy will help.
pmc-13361307:
Hui Yang and co-authors review camel milk vesicles as health foods in a 2026 paper. Camel milk is prized as a premium food rich in helpful compounds. Its milk carries tiny bubbles, called extracellular vesicles, shed by cells. The review covers how these vesicles are separated and studied, and what health effects they may bring.

The vesicles shield delicate cargo, such as proteins, small RNAs, and active fats, from being broken down in the gut. That makes them fit for baby formula, supplements, and products aimed at long-term inflammation and metabolic disease. In animal and lab models they eased oxidative stress, strengthened the gut wall, and balanced gut microbes. The authors bridge dairy science and disease prevention, while noting most proof is still preclinical.
pmc-13362307:
Ahmet Sencer Ergin and co-authors tested whether simple blood markers can predict rectal cancer response in a 2026 study. Before surgery, patients with locally advanced rectal cancer get chemotherapy and radiation to shrink the tumor. Predicting how much the tumor will regress is still hard. The team reviewed 88 patients with stage II to III cancer treated from 2017 to 2025 at one center.

After treatment and surgery, tumors were graded from complete response to no response: 22 patients responded fully, 50 partly, and 16 poorly. Pre-treatment blood values, including inflammation markers and ratios built from cell counts, were compared across the groups. Cheap, routine blood tests that flag likely responders could help doctors plan surgery timing and spare poor responders needless toxicity.
pmc-13362407:
Ana Šarić Jadrijev and a large team report a 2026 study of death rates in the month after hip fracture surgery. They reviewed 785 patients treated at a hospital in Split, Croatia, in 2021 and 2022. The team weighed age, sex, and prior health, and checked how three common health scoring tools predicted who would die within 30 days.

About one patient in nine died within the month. Older age, male sex, and heavier prior illness all raised the risk, and problems that arose in the hospital went with higher death rates too. The three scoring tools sorted risk about equally well. The study helps teams flag frail patients early and watch them closely.
pmc-13364207:
Akmaral Zh Sarsenbekova and colleagues present a 2026 study on how RAFT polymerization, a chain-taming method, changes the heat breakdown of a copolymer family. The family pairs polypropylene glycol maleate with acrylic acid. They made batches with varied RAFT agent levels and read structure with magnetic resonance, size sorting, and electron imaging. Then they heated the materials while sniffing the gases released and modeling the burn steps.

More RAFT agent meant shorter, more even chains and patchier internal domains with greater swelling. On heating, the RAFT batches broke down in extra stages, with a new low-heat stage from fragile RAFT-born fragments and earlier carbon dioxide release. Computer modeling tied those fragments to the energy of the gas-forming steps. The work guides heat-safe design of such copolymers.
pmc-13364907:
Iván Sanz-Muñoz and co-workers sum up in 2026 the state of high dose flu shots in Spain for old adults. Strong shots beat plain shots in trials and real use for lung and heart harms of flu. Weak age immune response makes the boost key past age 60.

Spain took up the strong shot in the virus years, but each zone set its own rules. Some zones aim first at care home folks, while some add all old adults in town life. The drift is toward wider use and a lower start age. The team backs the strong shot as a broad shield.
pmc-13366607:
Giulio Bordieri and co-workers build in 2026 a clear deep learn model that calls cell life after proton and carbon beam care. Beam care worth rests on how shot traits at many scales shape cell harm. Their model reads traits from three scales, built by sim tools, plus the known beam strength mark.

A step care chain in the model shows which traits swayed each call. Scores run high for both life calls and worth ranks. No one scale rules: small scale traits weigh more, while the beam strength mark weighs less than most hold. Clear calls aid beam plan trust.
pmc-13371107:
Shreyasi Majumdar and co-workers sum up in 2026 scan marks for brain waste ills, from mem loss to shake and stiff forms. Scans can read shape loss, spread paths, sugar burn, and clump loads in the live brain with no cut. Each scan way shows a unlike face of the ill.

The review weighs which marks have proof for care use, set count ways, and fit rules for two clump scans. New marks for a shake clump and cell state, plus blood first paths that send high risk folks to scans, mark the edge. Set form lags still, they note.
pmc-13371507:
Waseem Syed and co-authors report a brain tumor case in a young child in 2026. A girl aged four had a rare fast-growing tumor of the brain and spine, of a type switched on by a gene called FOXR2. Such tumors spread with ease and have a poor outlook if care is not strong.

Her care mixed surgery, strong drug rounds, a stem cell rescue, and proton beam treatment to the brain and spine. Protons were picked to spare her young body some late harm. The report walks through each step and the reasons for it. It may help teams plan care for the next child with this rare tumor.
pmc-13373607:
Barsha and colleagues measure how well hypertension and diabetes trials run through Federally Qualified Health Centers represent underserved Americans, in 2026 research equity work. These community health centers serve diverse, low-income populations, so trials based there might recruit more representatively than typical university trials. Searching six databases for trials published between 2013 and 2023 that engaged at least one such center, the team pooled participant demographics across the qualifying studies to see who enrolled.

Of 4,552 articles screened, 26 trials met the inclusion rules for the pooled analysis. Hispanic participants made up a pooled share of 0.35 of enrollees, and Black or African American participants 0.36 of the total pooled. Women accounted for 0.58, uninsured participants for 0.25, and people with at most a high school education for 0.54 in the same pooling. The Asian share stayed low at 0.03. Barsha argues center-based trials beat typical diversity benchmarks.
pmc-13376707:
Petr Potměšil and co-authors report a 30-year-old woman with rapid cycling bipolar disorder type 1 whose nine-month episode resisted an unusual number of treatments. Her illness began with mania at fourteen, and she had been hospitalised five times. The 2026 case report explains that the episode started after valproate was stopped ahead of a planned pregnancy, with depression and mania alternating every one to two weeks.

During a depressive phase she attempted suicide by strangulation. Successive regimens failed, including lamotrigine, high-dose lithium, quetiapine, monthly aripiprazole injections, olanzapine, carbamazepine, and electroconvulsive therapy. In hospital, one drug interaction complicated dosing: carbamazepine sped up breakdown of the new drug lurasidone, preventing target blood levels. The report's title records the eventual successful combination: lurasidone, clozapine, and valproate, which stabilised this treatment-resistant rapid cycling case after standard options had been exhausted.
pmc-13377307:
Natalie Lanners and co-authors probe the womb-heart link in a 2026 study. The afterbirth organ and the heart grow at the same weeks in the womb, which hints at shared roots. The set held 521 babies with heart faults and 122 sound peers from two centers.

Afterbirth cuts were classed by set rules and set next to heart type. Heart fault cases held far more poor flow marks in the afterbirth than sound cases. In the fault sets, marks were near even by heart type. The link backs joint checks: a bad afterbirth read may flag a heart to scan with care.
pmc-13377407:
Yan Liu and co-authors back built germ teams as green farm aids in a 2026 paper. Climate hits — dry, flood, heat — shake farm yields round the world. Most green farm plans lean on plant genes and farm craft, and skip the germs that live with crops.

Plants that thrive in harsh wild spots hold germs shaped by that stress, the team notes. Teams built from those germs can feed crops and tune how they bend with stress. The paper lays a road map to build and test such teams. The aim is crops that hold yield when the sky turns harsh.
pmc-13382307:
Aymane Bouzidi and a very large team present a 2026 study of the largest known family with dominant optic atrophy. That inherited disease slowly destroys the nerve cells carrying vision from eye to brain. Members of the same family can differ widely in how badly they are affected. Only about a third of cases get a genetic answer.

The family, from western France, included 64 people with the condition linked to a newly found deletion in a gene called OPA1, which helps run the cell's energy centres. Thirty-nine people were studied in detail, including five healthy controls. The authors map how the same deletion produced varied eye disease across the family, helping future counselling.
pmc-13383007:
Taoudi and colleagues made magnesium aluminate spinel nanopowders in 2026, a hard ceramic with high heat resistance, and tested them as cleaners for polluted water. A solid-state route reacted magnesium and aluminum nitrates with oxalic acid to form the fine powder. Seven lab methods then checked its crystal structure, shape, surface, and heat behavior to confirm the material formed as intended.

The powders were tested on Rhodamine B, a bright dye used as a stand-in pollutant, under a xenon lamp that mimics strong light. Removal combined surface uptake with light-driven breakdown, and the light-driven route worked best, clearing 95 percent of the dye within 120 minutes. The team presents the spinel as a low-cost, reusable option for treating dye-laden wastewater, a common problem for textile and printing plants.
pmc-13386907:
Robert M. Fusco and colleagues evolve a viral helper protein to boost gene therapy vector release in 2026 work. Adeno-associated viruses need the accessory protein MAAP to exit host cells efficiently. Guided evolution across three libraries selected variants that raised secretion of new virus particles.

Winning variants clustered in the protein's tail end and favored helix shapes with water-shunning faces. Unlike the natural protein, they gathered near the Golgi and skipped the nucleus entirely. Tests tied their strength to tighter engagement with SNARE fusion proteins, most notably VAMP3, which may speed vector production for therapy.
pmc-13387007:
Yu and colleagues review how viruses damage the heart, in a 2026 cardiology synthesis. Cardiotropic viruses covered include SARS-CoV-2, influenza, HIV, dengue and arboviruses, coxsackievirus B3, and cytomegalovirus. Their fallout ranges across myocarditis, pericarditis, rhythm disturbances, heart failure, and complications. The review organizes mechanisms into direct viral attack on heart cells, immune activation, and dysregulated inflammation that continues after the virus clears.

Evidence is weighed virus by virus, since each reaches the heart by its own route and leaves its own pattern of injury. Coxsackievirus B3 remains the classic myocarditis model, while SARS-CoV-2 broadened the picture to vascular and thrombotic injury. Yu argues clinicians meet heart disease in survivors of infection, yet diagnostics and treatments lag behind the mechanistic knowledge. The review calls for virus-specific cardiac checks after infections and for trials of immune-calming therapies timed to the injury phase.
pmc-13392907:
Sohaib Ahmed and four co-authors report a 31-year-old man whose red blood cells began breaking down about two months after starting etrasimod, a daily pill for ulcerative colitis. His bowel disease had been well controlled on the drug, which tunes immune cell traffic. Blood work showed anaemia with oversized red cells, a flood of young replacement cells, and fragmented cells under the microscope.

A direct antiglobulin test flagged immune attack on the red cells, and checks ruled out infection, metabolic faults, and inherited causes. Stopping the drug plus transfusions helped only partly, and full recovery of blood counts and an end to the breakdown came after high-dose steroids. The authors present the case as the first linking this drug to immune haemolytic anaemia, and urge awareness as use of its drug family grows.
pmc-13394207:
Mitch Lomax, Josh Osofa, Nicola Armstrong, Michael Tipton, and Gemma Milligan examined how the choice of statistic changes what researchers conclude about breathing muscle strength tests. The tests, maximal inspiratory and expiratory mouth pressures, use a handheld meter and serve as stand-ins for respiratory muscle strength. Thirty-one healthy men repeated the tests across visits with three raters of differing experience, and the team computed a battery of reliability statistics each way.

Agreement coefficients looked excellent throughout, and variation stayed low, yet the smallest change a clinician could trust ranged widely depending on the metric and whether repeatability or reproducibility was being judged. Reproducibility between raters actually beat repeatability within them, and trained raters' experience made no difference to values. The authors warn that interpretation hinges on the statistic chosen, not just on the numbers.
pmc-13395307:
Tzu-Chiao Lu and Hongjie Li comment, in 2026, on a study that tracks stem cell families in the ageing fly gut. Young guts hold a wide, mixed pool of stem cells. Over life that pool narrows, a drift long known in blood but hard to film in a living organ. The new study reads mutation barcodes that daughter cells inherit and add to.

With those barcodes, models judged which families last and which fade. Loss of families struck early in life, not just in old age. Early-born lines were more likely to persist and spread. The fruit fly gut offers a fast window on human gut ageing. The authors frame the work as a map for later studies.
pmc-13395507:
Mulford and colleagues wrote a 2026 review on a basic gap in knee care. By the time surgeons see worn knees, the wear has often run for decades. That late view makes the full course of knee osteoarthritis hard to trace. The authors survey how researchers track joints over long spans of life.

The review leans on two large long-running cohorts that supply most existing data. It covers scans, shape studies, and grouping tools used to map joint change. Early care and joint-saving steps may slow the path toward knee replacement surgery. New cohorts and computer tools could sharpen forecasts of which knees fail first. The authors urge care plans built on joint history, not single visits. Such long views also help patients weigh surgery against watchful waiting.
pmc-13396407:
Nayan Suryawanshi and co-authors developed a faster way to watch which protein recipes a brain cell uses right after it fires, and applied it in a 2026 study. Protein production at synapses underpins learning, yet the tools for catching it usually lag hours behind the activity that triggers it.

Their method tags and purifies ribosomes, the cell's protein factories, without waiting for slow protein turnover, giving readings within one hour of stimulation. In mouse hippocampus slices undergoing long-term potentiation, they found hundreds of switched-on reading frames. Potentiation is a strengthening of connections tied to memory. Among the finds was a previously unknown short upstream frame in the gene Egr1 that may tune its output.
pmc-13396607:
Ivan Scriabine and co-authors studied kidney transplant patients struck by norovirus, the stomach bug that can drag on for months when the immune system is suppressed. Their 2026 multicenter study asks a practical question: which patients are most likely to die or lose the graft?

Records covered 159 infected patients from 2017 to 2022, plus 96 matched transplant patients whose diarrhea had other causes. The norovirus group lost far more body weight, and severe undernutrition was about three times as common at diagnosis. Death and graft loss climbed step by step with undernutrition, and severe undernutrition alone nearly quadrupled the death hazard in adjusted models.
pmc-13396707:
Abbey Elsbernd and co-authors surveyed how children's hospitals use blood thinners during the first admission for acute myeloid leukemia, a cancer where clots are a real danger. Their 2026 report opens with two findings: clots in these young patients come with longer stays, higher costs, and more deaths in hospital.

Against that risk, practice varies widely. Some centers give anticoagulants and others do not, and the choice of drug differs too, with no shared standard to lean on. Mapping that variation is the first step toward a guideline, since children with leukemia walk a narrow line between clotting and bleeding and cannot simply borrow adult protocols.
pmc-13397907:
Georgiana Ciobanu and fellow authors present an older patient whose tick-borne brain infection hid behind a pile of misleading signs. Their 2026 case report follows a hospital stay that began with gut and breathing complaints, then chest pain and deep weakness. Blood tests added raised liver enzymes, a heart strain marker and low sodium, pointing at several rival diagnoses at once.

Only when nerve symptoms appeared, and a careful history covered tick exposure, did suspicion land on tick-borne encephalitis, and antibody tests confirmed it. The authors stress that in older adults this infection often wears many masks at once. Slow, broad detective work, they argue, beats chasing each abnormal number on its own.
pmc-13399407:
Amal Adel Alzu'bi and co-authors built a deep learning system that tells vitiligo apart from postinflammatory hypopigmentation, two conditions that both leave pale patches on the skin, in a 2026 diagnostic study. The distinction matters because their causes and treatments differ, yet even clinicians can struggle to separate them visually. The team also wanted the program to show its reasoning.

Their dataset held 332 clinical photographs, 176 of vitiligo and 156 of the inflammatory condition, from a Jordanian university hospital and public online sources. A lightweight MobileNetV2 network, fine-tuned on the images, was tested with patient-wise five-fold cross-validation. The model reached 94.88 percent accuracy overall, with an area under the curve of 0.9885 in the validation results. Three explanation methods were blended into one visual rationale, which reviewers judged clinically meaningful in 98.48 percent of a 66-image check set. The authors offer the tool as transparent support for dermatologists.
pmc-13399707:
Cory J. Call and co-authors surveyed hip arthroscopy surgeons three times over five years to track how they handle the hip capsule, in a 2026 study. The 29-question survey went to surgeons identified from the hip arthroscopy literature and, in later rounds, a sports medicine society mailing list.

Responses numbered 74 in 2018, 78 in 2020, and 83 in 2023. The interportal capsulotomy, a cut between the two standard portals, stayed the favorite access technique at every time point, with the T-shaped cut second. Closure was already common and grew commoner: half of surgeons said they always closed in 2018 and 2020, rising to 67 percent in 2023. Among 52 postoperative dislocations reported across respondents, 27 happened in cases where the capsule had been closed. The authors include that nuance against any simple story that closure alone prevents dislocation.
pmc-13399807:
Yi-Shan Teng and colleagues tell the story of a chin lump that turned out to be a tooth problem in disguise, in a 2026 case report. A woman aged 66 was referred to dermatology with a painful, protruding red nodule on her left lower chin. A biopsy showed abscess and granulomatous inflammation without explaining why the lesion would not heal.

The missing piece was a matching ulcer on the gum inside her mouth. A panoramic X-ray revealed a dark halo around the root tip of the left lower canine, the root-treated tooth. That confirmed a chronic periapical infection that had tunneled through to the skin as an odontogenic cutaneous fistula. The nodule resolved within a month. The authors stress that such fistulas are often mistaken for cysts or boils, and that a dental history should accompany any stubborn lower-face lesion.
pmc-13400307:
Jenna E AbuSalim and many co-authors show in 2026 that the body itself, not only gut bacteria, can make many indole and phenol compounds. These small molecules come from amino acids such as tryptophan and tyrosine. Some switch on gut immune signals, while others link to body weight or build up as toxins in kidney disease.

Using labeled atoms in cells, mice and rats, the team traced which compounds host tissue can build alone. Blood levels of many stayed steady even when gut microbes were disturbed, in both mice and patients. Bacteria were still needed for a smaller set, including free indole, phenol and p-cresol.
pmc-13400507:
Husameldin Elsawi Khalafalla leads a team translating, in 2026, a diabetes stigma questionnaire into Arabic for adults with type 1 diabetes in Saudi Arabia. Stigma can harm mood, self-care and blood sugar control. Despite high diabetes rates in the region, no validated Arabic tool existed to measure that stigma.

The team adapted the 19-item scale following standard cross-cultural steps and gave it to 299 adults at a diabetes center in Jazan. All items loaded well onto the three expected themes: being treated differently, blame and judgment, and identity concerns. Consistency scores were excellent. However, none of the tested structures met the usual statistical fit cutoffs, so the authors advise care in how total scores are interpreted.
pmc-13400807:
Tran Thanh Nam and colleagues run, in 2026, a randomized trial of an online behavioral parent training program for Vietnamese families of children with ADHD. Parent training is an established help for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, but evidence from lower-income Asian countries is scarce. The program was adapted to local culture.

Eighty-six parents of children aged six to eleven joined, half receiving the blended program and half usual care plus educational materials. The program mixed six weekly online group sessions, individual home support and twelve weeks of phone check-ins. Parenting skills improved substantially in the program group and stayed ahead at three-month follow-up. Parents also rated child symptoms lower within the program group, though adjusted differences between groups were small.
pmc-13400907:
Lauro and colleagues interview consumers who bought testing through a provider mediated service, where a person orders online but a doctor must sign off, about the counseling offered. Counseling is where a gene panel becomes decisions, yet here it is required only after positive results. Their 2026 study speaks with twenty nine customers of a 59 gene cancer and heart risk panel. A survey asks whether they used counseling and what stopped them.

Most never spoke with a counselor. Half of those who had not done so wanted a session, an unmet demand behind low uptake. People who did use counselors rated them helpful for grasping results, clarifying risk, and choosing steps. Time pressure was the barrier named most. The gap, the authors argue, is a design flaw rather than disinterest. Counseling should be woven into the testing path, not left as an extra most customers never reach.
pmc-13401307:
Rehab Elmeazawy and co-authors published a 2026 prospective study comparing lung ultrasound with chest X-ray for children with lower respiratory tract infections at a tertiary hospital. X-ray is the usual tool but involves radiation and can miss disease, while ultrasound is quick, radiation-free, and done at the bedside.

The study enrolled 338 children aged one month to 18 years with suspected infections, and every child received clinical assessment, X-ray, and ultrasound on admission and again at follow-up. Ultrasound sensitivity for lung pathology was high, at just under 96 percent on admission and a similar level later. Its specificity was weak at first, under 30 percent, but improved to about 63 percent at follow-up. Agreement between the two methods rose from fair to substantial over the same span.
pmc-13401407:
Scott Fong and co-authors wrote a 2026 database study of results after acromioclavicular joint reconstruction. That surgery rebuilds the joint between collarbone and shoulder blade, and the study takes a close look at differences between women and men. They drew on the TriNetX national database.

Patients treated between January 2015 and October 2022 were followed for 90-day and two-year results. The revision rate was just under 4 percent, while loss of reduction affected about 13 percent and distal clavicle fractures about 16 percent within two years. In propensity-matched comparisons, women reported postoperative antidepressant use more often than men, at about 16 versus 11 percent, and female sex carried a higher fracture risk. A Kaplan-Meier analysis compared revision probability by sex across the two years.
pmc-13401607:
John Chwen-Yu Chen and a large team report a 2026 study giving fast pain fibres, the myelinated A-nociceptors, a central role in mechanical pain behaviour. Slow unmyelinated C fibres have led pain research, while their fast cousins stayed unexplored.

In mice, light-based switching of these fibres on triggered rapid, precise withdrawal reflexes plus place aversion and facial changes consistent with pain feelings. Switching them off strongly blunted withdrawal from mechanical stimuli. Prolonged activation produced lasting mechanical pain that is easily triggered, plus a wound-up central response. Human evidence aligned: a rare person lacking thick A-beta fibres, and healthy volunteers under a nerve block favouring those fibres, both lost mechanical withdrawal reflexes and felt less mechanical pain. The findings redraw the wiring diagram of pain that protects.
pmc-13401707:
Maedeh Amini and co-authors analysed sex differences in the burden of diarrhoeal disease among children under five in a 2026 population study using Global Burden of Disease 2021 data. Global burden has fallen sharply over three decades, but gaps between boys and girls and across Asian regions remain poorly charted, especially for non-fatal outcomes.

The team extracted sex-split data on incidence, prevalence, deaths, and disability-adjusted life years from 1990 to 2021 and measured trends with estimated annual percentage changes. For Asian countries, three-level statistical models hunted for factors tied to burden, and forecasting models projected sex-specific patterns thirty years ahead to 2050. Burden fell substantially for both sexes on every measure across the study window, although boys carried the heavier share. The projections aim to steer child health policy toward fairer outcomes.
pmc-13402707:
Jiyuan Piao and colleagues isolate a dormancy factor from hibernating snails, copy it in the lab, and show it shields mouse hearts from the damage that follows restored blood flow. Hibernators remodel metabolism and switch on autophagy, the cell recycling system, to survive oxygen starvation that wrecks other animals. Named SNAP for its activation of the phosphatase PHLPP1, the molecule pushes stressed cells toward a protected dormant state.

In snail tissue and mouse cells alike, SNAP moved PHLPP1 signaling onto mitochondria, quieted growth pathways, raised autophagy, and helped cells resist death after oxygen returned. Perfused hearts gained protection too, with a key enzyme of fuel burning preserved and membranes holding their charge. Hearts lacking that enzyme in heart cells lost the benefit entirely. The authors float SNAP as a guard for donor hearts awaiting transplant.
pmc-13403007:
Thinh Tran Xuan and colleagues rank cheap prognostic markers for sepsis in central Vietnam, where costly tests cannot be assumed. Their cross-sectional study covered 146 adults meeting Sepsis-3 criteria at two Hue hospitals; average age was 67, about 62 percent had septic shock, and overall mortality reached 51.4 percent. Candidate markers included the lactate to albumin ratio, platelet count, and standard blood values.

The lactate-albumin ratio at a cutoff of 2.1 forecast death best, with an area under the curve of 0.76, sensitivity of 58.7 percent, and specificity of 88.7 percent in the reported results, beating lactate, albumin, platelets, and several rivals that scored near chance. Adjusted models kept the ratio, platelet count, and SOFA score as significant predictors. The authors recommend the ratio as a bedside tool matched to resource-limited wards.
pmc-13406707:
Alexander S Atalay, Benjamin T Newman and T Jason Druzgal link screen time to brain development paths in a huge teenage cohort, in a 2026 study. Scans from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development study were taken at two time points across thousands of young people. Advanced diffusion imaging measured cell-level structure beyond standard scans.

More screen time tracked with faster maturation in reward-linked cortex and slower maturation in control-linked cortex, the authors report. The sensitive imaging method picked up links that grey matter density and standard diffusion measures missed or showed weakly. The findings raise the possibility that heavy screen use bends normal teenage brain trajectories. Association is not proof of cause, a limit inherent in the design.
pmc-13407707:
Katie Hutchinson and co-authors report, in 2026, fourteen patients whose breastbone infections surfaced long after heart surgery, treated with combined orthopaedic and plastic surgery principles. Late sternal infection with non-union is poorly understood. It is also handled inconsistently. A specialist bone infection unit applied the pathway used for infected fractures. That means radical cleaning, deep sampling, stabilisation, and reconstruction. Targeted antibiotics complete the package.

Patients averaged about 64 years and carried heavy other illness; the gap from original surgery to definitive cleaning ranged from 25 days to nearly nine years. Eleven were rebuilt in a single operation and three in stages. Skin staphylococcus species and acne bacteria dominated the cultures, often mixed. Single-stage patients stayed about ten and a half days, and only one recurrence appeared over roughly 410 days of follow-up.
pmc-13407807:
Konstantinos Triantafyllias and co-authors test, in 2026, shining light through fingers to detect hand osteoarthritis. Optical transmission imaging promises a fast, examiner-free read on joint inflammation. The team measured thousands of finger joints with a dedicated hand scanner. Ninety-seven patients and 100 healthy controls took part. A subset also had examinations, blood markers, and ultrasound.

Light values ran clearly higher in patients, 10.39 against 7.51 on average, and the gap survived adjustment for other influences. At the small end joints of the fingers, values correlated weakly but significantly with both ultrasound types, and a discrimination analysis reached moderate accuracy for separating patients from controls. Hand size itself correlated moderately with readings in both groups, a caveat for interpretation. The authors offer the scan as a possible adjunct, not a replacement.
pmc-13408007:
Simone Cerciello and co-authors describe, in 2026, a step-by-step arthroscopic stitch, nicknamed the tie stitch, for anchoring the long head of the biceps tendon during shoulder surgery. Fixing that tendon is often added to rotator cuff repair in younger, active patients when the tendon is worn or inflamed. The same tendon has lately been drafted to rebuild the shoulder's superior capsule after massive, irreparable cuff tears. There, rock-solid initial fixation is mandatory.

Existing stitches can slacken a degenerated tendon or prove fiddly through the scope. The tie stitch is presented as easy to perform while gripping firmly enough to prevent slackening during healing. The technique paper walks through the procedure in sequence for surgeons weighing tenodesis against simply cutting the tendon.
pmc-13408807:
Wenhan Li, Craig Peeples, Juan Rey, Juan Perilla, and Reidun Twarock bring geometry to bear in 2026 on the cone-shaped shell that packages HIV's genome. Textbook models draw such capsids as perfect fullerene lattices, like a football's panels. Real HIV cores, the authors show, only approximate that tiling: the boundaries of their hexamer and pentamer building blocks form a pseudo-tiling with measurable local deviations.

pmc-13410607:

Mixing them up can trigger needless worry or missed screening.

The grouped type follows a wedge pattern and keeps the outer retina intact under scans. A side-by-side framework in the review helps clinicians decide who needs gene testing.
pmc-13410807:

Chemo-brain, as patients call it, blights life during and after therapy, and no effective medicine exists. pmc-13410907:

Each rise in the ratio also tracked with worse recorded disease grade, weaker heart pumping, and a wider right heart chamber. The cheap ratio may help staff sort patients by risk on arrival.
pmc-13413307:
Paschalis Theotokis, Soultana Meditskou, and Maria Eleni Manthou open a 2026 special issue that links how humans grow before birth with the health of whole groups. The set of papers runs from stem cells and embryo growth to birth defects and newborn health. Their editorial walks through the main themes. Stem cells come first, as tools that might one day mend fertility and help women have children.

More papers weigh the mother's vitamin D, gut germs, and swelling in slow fetal growth. Screening and registry work rounds out the set.
pmc-13415207:
Ricardo Lopes and colleagues stretch the World Health Organization fungal priority list toward animal health, in a 2026 review of Portuguese lab records. They checked every yeast positive find sent to one veterinary lab from 2019 onward. Naming used looks, an automated system, and mass spectrometry.

Of 2,033 fungal finds, 219 grew yeast, and 82 matched critical or high priority types. Candida albicans led the priority group, then came other Candida kin and Cryptococcus. Priority yeasts came mostly from ornamental birds, plus dogs, cats, and marine mammals. Routine animal testing already catches fungi that threaten people, supporting shared surveillance.
pmc-13415607:
Diego Romano Perinelli and colleagues sort out which factors matter when making nanoemulsions with high energy ultrasound, in 2026. These are tiny oil drops in water, used in foods, skin creams, and drugs. The team screened oil traits, soap type, heat, and machine settings, then let a neural net rank each one.

Oil thickness ruled both drop size and size spread, with thick oils fighting breakup into tiny drops. More heat helped, since warm oil thins. pmc-13415707:
Mohammed AlSarhan and colleagues review dental implant outcomes against patient traits and surgical choices, in a 2026 retrospective study. Records held 218 implants in 109 adults treated between 2015 and 2023, each with X-rays at least six months after the crown was fitted. Bone loss around implants was judged by whether implant threads showed on X-ray.

Most implants were bone level type placed in native bone. Grafting clustered at sites where decay had destroyed the tooth and in patients with good oral hygiene. Age tracked with poorer hygiene, while education and smoking did not. Bone loss and complications were rare overall, and grafting showed no link to bone loss.
pmc-13417707:
Gouli and colleagues present a 2026 study on how pulling force breaks carbon-carbon bonds in polymers, and how side groups change the force needed. In stretched plastics these bonds often snap even when weaker-looking bonds are present. The team used a computer method that mimics applied force to compare many side groups on plain bonds.

The calculations showed which side groups lower or raise the force at which a bond breaks, through electronic effects and crowding around the bond. The team also built a lab test for breaks that give no clear signal, using a polymer that unzips once cut as a reporter. Together, the work turns a side reaction into a design tool.
pmc-13418207:
Hannah A Burkhardt and colleagues describe Truveta, a health system governed platform that turns electronic records into continuously updated research data, in a 2026 article. Real world data have long suffered from fragmentation and delay. The platform gathers de identified records for 130 million patients, about one in three Americans, from member health systems.

Daily processing standardises notes, images, and pathology text using artificial intelligence, and links claims, death, and social data. Over 100 publications have used the resource, spanning treatment effects, device safety, vaccine safety, and equity. The partnership model makes health systems active partners rather than passive data suppliers.
pmc-13418507:
Tao Li and co-authors tune single iridium atoms with a sulfur neighbour to make a multifunctional enzyme mimic, in a 2026 study. Most artificial enzymes top out at modest activity. Adding sulfur beside each iridium atom shifted its electronic centre and lowered the energy barrier for activating oxygen, according to computer models.

The material mimicked three enzyme activities at once, including one not seen in the sulfur free version. Strong oxidising action allowed colour based sensing of antioxidants and organophosphate pesticides without added peroxide, with high sensitivity in messy real samples. Coordination tuning is offered as a general recipe for stronger single atom catalysts.
pmc-13418707:
Zhanfeng Yan, Dapeng Jing, and Zhenying Wang propose an evidence to action framework for managing insect resistance in Bt crops, in a 2026 article. Crops expressing bacterial insect toxins need stewardship after sale, yet signals of resistance vary in strength and meaning. Field injury, lab assays, and molecular markers can each mislead through confounding factors.

Their framework sorts findings into four states, from baseline susceptibility to practical resistance that breaks control. Each state carries minimum verification steps and proportionate responses, from watching to replacing failed components. Worked examples from maize and cotton pests show how refuge planting and deployment history shape fair decisions.
pmc-13419307:
Mulu Negesse and colleagues chart how Boutourlini's blue monkeys divide their day across two zones of Saja Forest in southwest Ethiopia. How a primate splits time among feeding, moving, and resting reveals how it copes with its habitat. The study sits inside the Kafa Biosphere Reserve, where this monkey's daily patterns had not been compared across forest zones before.

Watchers logged 19,725 behavior records from August 2024 to October 2025 using timed scan sampling. Monkeys in the core zone spent the most time feeding, at 33.0 percent of the records in that group, while the transition-zone group led on movement at 29.5 percent across its scans. Both gaps were firm in statistical terms. The split shows forest zone shaping daily life even within one reserve.
pmc-13419607:
Iris Becene and colleagues map what is known about mental health after a pregnancy complicated by heart and vessel disease. Such disease affects 1 to 4 percent of pregnancies in the United States and raises risks for the mother around birth. Their scoping review searched without limits on year, study type, or publication form.

Heart disease itself has been linked to a 70 percent higher risk of depression in the cited work. The review sorts which symptoms were measured, in whom, and where the blanks in the record sit. That map can guide clinics that now check the heart but rarely ask about mood.
pmc-13420207:
Xu and co-authors test a blood biomarker in this 2026 study of rheumatoid arthritis, an autoimmune disease where responses to the drug etanercept vary in ways no one can predict. They measured peripheral helper T cells, a recently recognized immune cell type marked by high PD-1 and no CXCR5, in 58 arthritis patients alongside osteoarthritis patients and healthy controls.

The helper cells were far more frequent in rheumatoid arthritis blood and tracked with several disease activity measures. Among 25 patients starting etanercept, nonresponders began with higher cell levels, at 13.23 percent of the measured T cells against 10.82 percent among later responders in the study's flow cytometry. Responders' levels then fell to 7.97 percent on treatment, moving with a related immune signal, interleukin-21. The authors propose the cell count as a way to forecast who will benefit, pending larger prospective validation.
pmc-13420307:
Ali Mirzaei and colleagues review stem cell therapy as a shield against heart damage from doxorubicin, a strong cancer drug whose use is capped by its harm to the heart. Their narrative review gathers the record on several stem cell types, with mesenchymal stem cells at the center. Heart injury from this drug can surface during treatment or years later, and no settled prevention exists.

The collected evidence suggests the cells calm inflammation, cut oxidative stress, and help repair the power units of heart cells. Those three routes match the main ways the drug injures the heart in the first place. The authors sort cell types and delivery routes by strength of support. A working cell shield would let oncologists use full drug doses without trading away the patient's heart.
pmc-13421207:
Bassant Ehab and Ekram Saleh review, in a 2026 paper, how pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma rewires its use of fatty acids to survive in a harsh, oxygen-poor tumour environment. Fatty acids serve the cancer as fuel, building material and signalling molecules, so their handling is closely tied to growth and treatment resistance.

The authors catalogue the enzymes and regulators that control fatty acid synthesis, uptake, storage and burning, and they explain how genetic changes push the tumour toward making or scavenging lipids. They also describe how surrounding tissue supplies extra lipid and supports the cancer's metabolism. The review ends with drugs that interfere with these pathways, presented as a route to weakening the tumour and improving response to existing therapy.
pmc-13421307:
Frank Cichocki and four colleagues ask directly, in the title of their 2026 review, whether natural killer cells can cure leukaemia. Natural killer cells are immune cells that attack tumours without the graft-versus-host disease and severe inflammatory reactions that make T-cell therapy risky.

By 2025, around 140 companies were developing some 160 natural-killer strategies. Their ideas ranged from donor cell products to molecules that unleash the patient's own cells. Thousands of patients have been treated in trials over two decades. The review weighs strong anti-tumour activity and off-the-shelf manufacturing against stubborn limits, notably poor persistence and weak antigen targeting. The authors' verdict is measured: the safety case is proven, while the durability needed for cures is not yet.
pmc-13421607:
Minet and colleagues reported in 2026 that human stem cells copy parts of their DNA twice on purpose while they specialise. Copying DNA twice, called re-replication, was known in flies as a way to amplify genes during development. The team used DNA sequencing and fibre imaging to watch for re-replication as stem cells turned into muscle, fat, bone, cartilage, and nerve cells.

Re-replication appeared in set time windows during every specialisation path they tested. Cells that had re-replicated showed higher expression of genes lying in the copied regions. Some of the extra DNA was found outside the nucleus, which hints it may be shared with neighbouring cells. The authors propose that cells use this old mechanism to raise gene copy numbers and meet the high protein demands of differentiation.
pmc-13421807:
Kaiyuan Shen and six colleagues investigate, in a 2026 study, how an excess of one small regulatory RNA harms the ovarian cells that nurture eggs. Diminished ovarian reserve, a common cause of infertility, had already been linked to distinctive microRNAs carried in follicular fluid, and one of them — miR-483-3p — stood out as sharply raised.

Flooding the cells with the microRNA cut proliferation, weakened mitochondrial membrane potential and lowered the mark's level. A chemotherapy drug and an enzyme-blocking compound produced comparable effects. The authors frame the excess as acutely toxic to granulosa cells.
pmc-13422107:
Robert Fekete reports, in a 2026 case study, a 42-year-old woman with Tolosa-Hunt syndrome whose blood carried strikingly high levels of the inflammatory signal interleukin-6. The syndrome is a rare, unexplained inflammation behind the eye that causes pain and double vision, and her episodes had begun ten years earlier, recurring four years ago.

Scans during the later episode showed a mass in the cavernous sinus that later vanished, and both bouts settled after about five weeks of steroid tablets. She now controls milder pain with short steroid courses twice a year. Her interleukin-6 measured far above normal both in remission and mid-episode, the lower reading possibly reflecting steroid use. Fekete suggests the cytokine may illuminate how this disorder works.
pmc-13422807:
Charlotte Lambrechts leads a seven-author team setting out, in a 2026 protocol, a non-invasive work-up of calf muscle in children with spastic cerebral palsy. These children's muscles change under altered nerve control and unusual loading, yet research has mostly measured size alone, leaving stiffness and composition — and how the three interact — largely unmapped.

Their study pairs children with cerebral palsy against typically developing peers across ages. Freehand three-dimensional ultrasound measures muscle size, quantitative MRI reads composition, and shear-wave elastography gauges passive stiffness. Grip-style dynamometry and functional tests add strength. The authors plan to compare groups property by property and then examine the relations among properties within the same muscle.
pmc-13423907:

pmc-13424007:
Montgomery and Harcourt interviewed in 2026 eighteen adults with inheritable conditions that visibly affect appearance, such as neurofibromatosis and craniofacial conditions, about deciding whether to have children. Most participants were women who had considered children, were trying, were pregnant, or had recently given birth.

Four themes emerged. Parents moved from early distress to practical coping, treating their own experience as both burden and resource. Memories of stigma shaped views on natural conception, embryo screening, and ending a pregnancy. Testing offered a sense of control but raised ethical strain. Participants asked for unbiased counseling and peer contact. The authors urge counselors to name stigma openly in such talks.
pmc-13424607:

pmc-13424907:

pmc-13425007:

Models adjusted for age, sex, social position, parental asthma, and siblings compared the multi-allergic group against people with no atopic disease. Delivery mode, birthweight, breastfeeding, smoke exposure, pet type and timing, and living conditions all entered the exposure list.
pmc-13425607:

Oil from red-quinoa-fed larvae held the most protective plant compounds and scored best on three antioxidant tests, with rice bran oil close behind. pmc-13425807:

Delivering the drug through the vagina, using a ring device, produced about a tenfold lower metabolite-to-parent ratio in their comparisons.

pmc-13426007:

pmc-13426407:

pmc-13426507:

pmc-13426707:
Chad G. Ball, Sean Gregg, and Edward J. Harvey examine Canada's unregulated private health care market in a 2026 French-language commentary on Alberta's new law. Legislation in force from 18 December 2025 created a legal framework for dual practice, letting Alberta physicians work in both private and public sectors. Debate was heated, with many Canadian health coalitions calling the bill a violation of the Canada Health Act.

Supporters see a chance to improve access and expand system capacity, while critics warn of drift toward a two-tier system shut to citizens who cannot pay. The authors situate the fight within wider frustration among patients who already feel poorly served.
pmc-13427907:
Kunal Dhankhar and colleagues report a 30-year-old woman with a shattered pelvis and hip socket plus a hidden internal skin-tearing injury after high-energy trauma. The tearing, called degloving, rips fat and skin layers apart under unbroken-looking skin near the groin.

Scans showed an unstable pelvic ring break and a fracture across the right hip socket. Care came in stages: early wound cleaning, temporary pelvis stabilising, infection control, and only later the final metal fixation. A pin-site infection was beaten without spreading deep, a key risk in such open injuries. By four months the bones were knitting, and at one year healing was complete with strong hip and pelvis scores.
pmc-13428107:
Chen and colleagues published a 2026 study on a triple treatment for advanced liver cancer. Their patients faced a hard outlook: tumors in the portal vein and spread to the lungs. The team compared two drug pairs against the same pair plus artery-delivered chemotherapy. Data came from several hospitals, with matching used to balance the groups.

After matching, 96 pairs of patients were compared head to head. The triple group lived a median of about 15 months versus 7 months. Tumors shrank in nearly half the triple group, versus about one fifth otherwise. Side effects came more often with triple therapy but stayed manageable for most. The authors call for a randomized trial to confirm the gain.
pmc-13428407:

Rhythm diagnoses rested on cardiology reports with tracing proof. pmc-13430207:

Nearly half the women reported at least one such hard event across their pregnancies. A pregnancy with a hard event carried about 27 percent higher odds of depression or anxiety after birth. The link held after the team adjusted for other known risk factors. The authors frame hard births as possible sources of trauma. pmc-13430607:

Warming the new compound drove off hydrogen and left a four-sided form with an even lower charge state. Giving that form hydrogen restored the prior compound in a clean way. pmc-13432907:

One fierce, drug-proof chicken strain anchors the work. Family trees of gene marks show clear place clusters and lead groups, with strains from unlike hosts mixed overall yet clumped by place.
