The team also proved a fresh poison-guard pair, carried on a loose DNA ring, that boosts slime mats, cell survival, and drug endurance. pmc-13434607:

Alcohol strength showed for 83.3 percent of drinks. Sugar showed for just 33.0 percent, and fewer than three in one hundred listed other nutrients or contents. Beer labels varied most, while spirits scored lowest. Mixed ready drinks stayed low and uniform. The authors urge rules that force full nutrition labels on all drinks.
pmc-13434707:

One protein also weaves into corkscrew fibers of unknown duty. Blocking wake up could stop gut illness before it starts.
pmc-13434807:

pmc-13435107:

pmc-13437507:

Combined results showed little to no difference between users and non-users on heart rate, breathing, or a key inflammation marker. Body composition and metabolic readings also ran alike in the two groups. The authors take this as a lack of consistent harm, reassuring for active women and their coaches. Larger, tighter studies would be needed before anyone claims the pills are provably neutral for sport.
pmc-13437607:

Their 2026 study gave the mixture into a vein of hypertensive rats and recorded pulse waves, while artery strips were tested in a tension rig.

The aorta did the opposite and tightened, a response softened by antioxidant enzymes, pointing to reactive oxygen as its trigger. pmc-13437807:

Family harmony linked directly with social responsibility, and the link held even after the middle factors entered the model. Part of the link ran through stronger emotion-management skills, which alone carried the largest middle share. A smaller part ran through problem social media use, and a chain through both factors also counted, Ercengiz reports.
pmc-13437907:

Forty-seven participants finished the cough testing, and 17 of them, or 36.17 percent, fell below the 270 liters per minute threshold considered effective for clearing airways. Lower cough flow tracked with younger age, earlier symptom onset, and weaker respiratory muscles across the measured group. Cough flow correlated strongly with inspiratory pressure, expiratory pressure, and vital capacity percentages in the statistical analysis. Regression singled out inspiratory pressure and age at onset as the primary predictors, and the authors argue cough flow beats vital capacity as a direct gauge of clearance ability.
pmc-13438607:
Shuo Liu and a large team built a transistor merging sight and sound the way a brain does, inside the device rather than in software. Perception gains power when senses agree: a voice plus moving lips beats either alone. Artificial systems usually fuse such streams with clumsy algorithms. Their 2026 device uses a ferroelectric semiconductor coupling light, charge, and memory, letting one component weigh and blend the two inputs directly.

The device obeyed the classic rules of multisensory neurons. Combined inputs overshot the sum of parts, a superadditive gain of twenty-eight-fold. Weak inputs gained the most help, matching the brain's inverse effectiveness rule. Wired into a spiking network on a chip, the system recognized fuzzy objects at over ninety-eight percent accuracy. The authors pitch the work as a physics-first route to self-adjusting edge intelligence, where sensors think a little before they report.
pmc-13439307:
Sung Eun Kim discusses how doctors should handle small lumps found by chance under the stomach lining, writing in South Korea in 2026. Biennial stomach screening for adults over 40 has raised detection of these subepithelial lesions, most of which cause no symptoms. New Korean guidance suggests watchful scope checks alone for likely harmless lumps under one centimetre. Bigger lumps with unclear identity get a repeat scope at six months, then yearly checks if stable.

Kim highlights a screening study of more than 30,000 adults that put the frequency near two in a hundred, matching a larger multi-centre count. Follow-up data on which lumps grow help doctors judge who can safely wait. The piece favours calm monitoring over quick removal for small, quiet lesions, while keeping surgery for lumps that change or worry.
pmc-13439607:
D Natasha Owitipana and colleagues brew antibody-shaping enzymes in common bacteria to cut the cost of tailored antibody sugars, reporting in 2026. Sugar chains on antibodies steer how strongly they rally immune attack, so drug makers want uniform sugar forms. The enzymes that add those sugars normally come from mammal cells and cost dearly. The team produced human and cow versions of a galactose-adding enzyme, plus single-change variants, as fusion proteins in Escherichia coli with high yields.

Human enzyme versions far outperformed the cow ones at adding sugars to whole antibodies. The enzymes built an unusual sugar ending, LacdiNAc, in place of the standard one. Follow-up enzymes could cap that ending with sialic acid, and a single change in the antibody itself freed a stubborn spot for capping. Receptor tests showed the new forms kept key immune binding, opening cheaper routes to designer antibodies.
pmc-13440107:
Shi and colleagues followed in 2026 the gut microbes of ovarian cancer patients through chemotherapy, asking whether change over time links to later relapse. Past work mostly took single snapshots in other cancers. In a prospective cohort of 91 patients, the team sequenced stool samples from 33 patients across early, middle, and late chemotherapy, one hundred samples in all, and modelled the trajectories against recurrence.

Shi found gut diversity rose steadily through the course, with fringe species turning over faster than core ones. Severe side-effect burden did not predict relapse. The clear signal was one genus, Fusicatenibacter, draining away over time in patients who later relapsed, a pattern that survived every sensitivity check the team ran. Predicted pathway shifts and a microbe network tied to those pathways added support. The authors flag the disappearing genus as a candidate early marker of relapse risk.
pmc-13442007:
Moritz A Knolle and colleagues audit medical AI models patient by patient and find privacy risk hiding beneath reassuring averages, reporting in 2026. Membership inference attacks ask whether a given person's records trained a model, a direct privacy threat when training data are sensitive scans. Past audits averaged attack success across whole datasets. Across varied medical datasets, the team instead scored the attack separately for every contributing patient.

For individual patients, attacks often succeeded almost perfectly, even where the dataset average hovered near coin-flip level. Patients contribute multiple similar records, which is part of what exposes them. Bigger models widened the exposed group further. Underrepresented patients, sorted by sex, insurance, self-reported race, disease status, or imaging protocol, faced disproportionately high attack success. The authors warn that average-case privacy metrics can badly understate the risk borne by the most exposed patients.
pmc-13442607:
Joel Ravichandar and colleagues report use of a new sleep drug, remimazolam, for a heart scan in a 16-month-old girl in a 2026 case report. Her heart muscle worked poorly due to a primary muscle illness, so standard sleep drugs posed real risk to her breathing and blood flow. She needed a CT vessel scan while fully still and calm.

Care ran remimazolam as a steady drip, topped with small ketamine doses as needed. The drug wears off in minutes, since body enzymes break it down fast, which limits pile-up in the blood. The report walks through her course and then weighs past reports of the drug in heart-sick patients. The authors present the pairing as a workable path for scans in small children with weak hearts, while case counts stay low.
pmc-13443107:
Cristina Antich and colleagues print a living placenta model in 3D to mimic pregnancy stages in a 2026 paper. The placenta feeds the unborn child, yet faults in it drive early birth and growth harm. Real tissue is hard to get, and animal models predict human faults poorly.

Their printed tissue joins primary human trophoblasts with stroma cells and blood vessel paths. Builds in a 96-well plate copy early and late pregnancy states. Tests show wall guard duty, food uptake, carrier work, and hormone release like the real organ. The team offers the plate as a screen for drugs and for goods that may harm the unborn. Deep trait checks back the claim that stage marks match human pregnancy well.
pmc-13444007:
Alakram and Hedding measure how a South African port coastline is moving and what a major surge would flood. Their 2026 study of Richards Bay integrates satellite analysis and modelling. It uses 45 years of shoreline positions, from 1977 to 2022, through the standard digital shoreline analysis system. The trends are then extrapolated ten and twenty years forward.

The harbour splits the coast's behaviour: persistent erosion to its north, and accretion, shoreline growth, to its south. About eighty percent of South Africa's coast is erodible sandy beach, much of it sensitive dune, which makes the pattern consequential for planning. The storm surge analysis delivered the starkest figure: a ten-metre surge would inundate 82 percent of the study area. The authors offer the shoreline history and flood mapping as an information base for flood risk analysis and disaster management around the port.
pmc-13444607:
Danielle P. Uhl and colleagues present a single-cell atlas of blood immune cells in dogs at each stage of leishmaniosis, a parasite disease spread by sand flies. Published in 2026, the work maps dogs with no infection beside dogs with mild through severe illness from Leishmania infantum. Dogs matter here because they carry the parasite and pass it on to people, so their illness mirrors a wider public health risk.

The team used single-cell RNA sequencing to track how cell types shift as disease grows worse. Blood moved from a lymphoid-heavy mix toward a myeloid-heavy one, helper T cells showed growing signs of exhaustion, and monocytes took on more inflamed states. Readers gain a shared reference, named the LeishDog Atlas, for comparing immune change across stages and for later work on treatment.
pmc-13445507:
Dominik Hlauschek and colleagues warn of common traps in studies that track tumor DNA in the blood over time, in a 2026 viewpoint. Such DNA can flag cancer that lingers after treatment, guide care, and track response. Yet the numbers these studies report can mislead when time itself is mishandled.

Three traps get close looks: how lead time before relapse is defined, test accuracy that shifts as months pass, and a bias that creeps in when patients are classed by later results. Worked toy cases, computer runs, and fresh looks at past data show each trap in action. The authors offer design and reporting guidance, while noting that firm fixes await more proof.
pmc-13446107:
Anna Kubota and colleagues test whether work performance sits between sleep quality and wellbeing in high-stress office workers in Japan, in a 2026 survey study. Poor sleep is known to drag wellbeing down, yet the steps in between are less clear. Showing up sick or drained, called presenteeism, was their candidate middle step.

One hundred twenty-nine workers filled tested scales for sleep, performance loss, and wellbeing. Poor sleep went with both worse performance and lower wellbeing. Mediation checks found performance loss carried part of the sleep effect, and the indirect path held after adjusting for age, hours, rank, smoking, and drinking. The authors say sleep programs at work may pay off twice, lifting both output and felt health.
pmc-13446307:
Savvas Teloni and Yiorgos Apidianakis present a protocol for counting odd features of gut stem cells in the fruit fly, meant as early warnings of later tumors, published in 2026. The adult fly gut renews itself through stem cells that can cluster wrongly when a key signal weakens. Such clusters grow with age and track rare true tumors late in life.

Steps cover labeling the clusters, staining, and counting cell number and size by gut region as flies age. Further steps give division rate and DNA content per clustered cell. Scores can then be set across gene types and conditions and matched to each group's late tumor rate. The authors offer the counts as a forecast tool for gut aging studies.
pmc-13447307:
Ana Isabel González-Hernández and fellow editors introduce a 2026 collection on polyamines in plant stress and development. Polyamines are small nitrogen-rich molecules found in all living cells, where they steer growth and buffer plants against drought, heat and attack. Climate change makes that buffering role urgent for crops facing harsher conditions.

One study covered here built a precise measurement toolkit that tracks two key enzyme routes and related compounds in a single run. Gene-edited tomato plants showed one route is essential for flower formation, since plants lacking it made no buds at all. Another line of work shows a specific polyamine fine-tuning wood vessel growth through two balancing proteins. Further papers cover chemical priming and nano-delivery ideas aimed at multi-stress resilience in the field.
pmc-13447707:
Sommer reviews how purified and reshaped cellulose, the fiber that stiffens plant walls, serves modern winemaking and wine testing. Cellulose is a chain of glucose, a simple sugar, and makers can tune its water behavior by chemical tweaks. His 2026 review covers plain cellulose as a filter aid, treated forms that pull unwanted compounds from wine, and cellulose gums used to keep wine stable in the bottle.

In production, cellulose filters wine and helps stop crystals and haze that form in cold or heat. Carboxymethyl cellulose, a treated gum, guards against cold instability, a cloudy fault in white wines. Methylcellulose is barred as a wine additive but earns its place in the lab, where it measures condensed tannins, the bitter plant compounds that shape red wine taste. Sommer closes on a green note: plant based cellulose can replace several mined or animal based aids.
pmc-13448507:
Kizilkilic and colleagues use a special MRI method to look at the walls of brain arteries in neuro-Behçet syndrome, an inflammatory disease long known for vein problems. Standard scans show the channel inside a vessel, not its wall, so early wall disease can hide. Their 2026 study scans 39 patients, some during an attack and some between attacks, and rates 1,170 artery segments for wall thickening and contrast uptake, a sign of active inflammation.

Wall involvement appeared in 16 patients, about two in five, and sat mostly in the back of the brain's circulation. The common pattern was even, ring like thickening without contrast uptake. Patients scanned during attacks showed wall changes far more often than patients scanned in quiet periods, and contrast uptake appeared only during attacks. Worse disability scores tracked with wall disease across three or more back circulation segments, a clue for grading severity.
pmc-13448707:
Peijin Li and colleagues present in 2026 a flat optical device that creates and measures complex states of light. The states mix polarization with orbital angular momentum, giving photons a larger space of possible forms. Such high-dimensional states could carry more information for communication and quantum uses.

A single-layer metasurface built from four-atom unit cells shapes amplitude, phase, and polarization at once to make any chosen state in a four-dimensional space. The team also reads back the full state from just three interference patterns. Their analysis reveals a parity rule in the patterns that holds regardless of how the modes are weighted, plus controlled transformations driven by geometric phase.
pmc-13448807:
K. A. Yashaswini and co-authors propose in 2026 a phone-based framework for flagging bipolar disorder near its onset. Called IDMBD, the system collects five kinds of information through a mobile computing device and profiles each participant in fine detail. A standard severity scale anchors its forecasts of how critical a person's state may be.

The profiled features pass through several analysis steps before reaching a deep neural network that learns patterns linked to the disorder. The team tested many pairings of machine learning and deep learning methods against standard performance measures. The framework performed best when random forest and decision tree models were integrated with it. The authors frame the tool as a faster alternative to repeated questionnaire and interview visits, which can delay early detection.
pmc-13449507:
Yousafzai and co-authors test whether teaching nurses suctioning technique changes what they know and do. Their 2026 single-group study covers sixty intensive care nurses in three public hospitals in Peshawar, Pakistan. Knowledge was measured by questionnaire and practice by an observational checklist. Both were assessed before and after training on endotracheal tube suctioning. That is the airway-clearing procedure for ventilated patients.

Both measures jumped. Knowledge scores rose from about 6.6 to about 10.2, and practice scores from about 12.7 to about 16.4, each with very large effect sizes and strong statistical significance. The authors conclude the training was associated with substantial improvement, a result relevant to preventing ventilator-associated pneumonia. They also flag the design honestly: with no control group, some of the gain could reflect testing effects or concurrent changes, so controlled confirmation is needed.
pmc-13449807:
Saima Armana and colleagues report in 2026 a case of Lemierre syndrome whose damage kept unfolding months after the initial infection. The syndrome classically follows a throat infection with sepsis, a clot in the jugular vein, and infection seeded around the body, usually by Fusobacterium bacteria. Their patient, a previously healthy seventeen-year-old, arrived with a week of sore throat and worsening neck pain, then developed a retropharyngeal abscess.

The infection ate into the skull base and cervical spine, injuring the twelfth cranial nerve and loosening the junction where skull meets spine. Five months after hospitalization, scans showed atlanto-axial instability and the skull settling downward, a combination that threatens the spinal cord itself. The patient is being managed without surgery for now and has been told to avoid contact sports. The authors urge long follow-up imaging whenever this syndrome touches the skull base.
pmc-13449907:
Shangyi Fu, Danny Huynh, and Milcah Poothakary write in 2026 to estimate how many people in the United States live with myelodysplastic syndrome. The bone marrow disorder is sometimes called preleukemia because its faulty blood-cell production can precede leukemia. They mined the national SEER cancer registry, which held records for nearly 44 million people at the time of collection. Their calculation put the number living with primary disease of this type at roughly 5,747.

Prevalence climbed steadily with age and peaked in people aged eighty-five and older. By race, the estimate ran highest in White individuals, at 0.03 percent, against 0.02 percent in Black, American Indian and Alaska Native, and Asian or Pacific Islander groups. The authors caution that the registry's own mix skews Whiter and more Asian than the country. Patients missed by the census or by healthcare access could push the true count higher.
pmc-13450607:
Jipeng Huang and a large team probe in 2026 how hearing and attention grow in children with ADHD, using brain wave tests. They enrolled 80 children with ADHD and 80 peers with typical growth, all aged seven to twelve. Each child did a listening task with rare odd tones while scalp sensors traced fast brain replies.

One early brain reply grew steadily with age in typical children, yet in the ADHD group it stayed weak in the older years and traced a U shape. A later reply tied to focus was weak in the youngest ADHD children. The team reads the pattern as a late-stage effort to catch up, and they offer the brain marks as leads for longer studies.
pmc-13451407:
Attiq ur Rehman and co-authors test in 2026 gene-based forecasts of mildew resistance for strawberry breeding stock. They crossed two wild strawberry kin and scored the young plants for leaf and fruit resistance to powdery mildew. Forecast models used gene markers from thirteen families.

Leaf resistance was easier to forecast than fruit resistance across years. Close family ties lifted accuracy a lot, and a training set of two fifths of the plants proved steady. Adding the big known resistance spots as fixed parts of the model raised accuracy for both traits. Field and greenhouse checks held up, so the team gives breeders working rules for set size and marker counts.
pmc-13451807:
Junchao Xu and co-authors lay out in 2026 a plan to build mRNA vaccines as one joined system, carrier and message tuned together. Most work tunes the fat carrier and the message ends apart, yet only a sliver of a shot reaches the cells that spark immunity. Their summary draws on a study that screened both parts at scale.

A search of 96 carrier fats picked a lead fat that homes to the immune starter cells. Fine-tuning the mix routed the shots through lymph paths, while a screened message frame lifted output and tilted immunity toward a virus-fighting type. The joined design aims for strong shots at lower doses, with less soreness as a hoped gain.
pmc-13452107:
Kazem Habibi-Tanha and co-authors scan in 2026 work on learning models fed with body marks to guess which mouth sores will turn to cancer. Mouth cancers often grow out of such sores, yet the shift is hard to call and tissue grading wobbles between readers. The review gathered ten past studies that paired machine learning with marks from genes, proteins, or tissue images.

The models showed strong promise, and image-based tissue traits looked most ready for clinic use. Yet methods varied, no study had tested its model on fresh patients ahead of time, and age and sex reporting was patchy. The authors urge mixed-mark models, trials that run forward in time, and checks across wider groups.
pmc-13452307:
Gutierrez-Aguirre and colleagues compare in 2026 drugs that speed blood recovery after autologous stem cell transplantation. That procedure returns a patient's own stem cells after high-dose chemotherapy, done here as an outpatient treatment for lymphoma or myeloma.

Thirty transplant patients were randomly given a single dose of either the original pegfilgrastim or its biosimilar version. Their results were set against 53 earlier patients who received daily filgrastim instead. White cell recovery took a median of ten days with the original drug, nine with the biosimilar, and eleven with filgrastim. Platelet recovery took ten days against twelve in the same comparison across the groups. Fever with low white cells struck far fewer pegfilgrastim patients than filgrastim patients. The original drug cost the most and filgrastim the least.
pmc-13452407:
Meseret Bekele and seven co-authors survey how homes in Harar, Ethiopia handle chicken and tomatoes safely in the kitchen. Their 2026 study visited 252 urban households and built a hygiene index from 39 habits and conditions. The index gives town programs a single score for how safely a home prepares food.

Risky habits were common: 74 percent of homes used one cutting board for both meat and vegetables, and 35 percent cleaned surfaces only now and then. Homes with better scores tended to sit in areas with stronger services and to get food safety news from television. Scores for chicken and for tomatoes tracked each other closely, which suggests the same daily habits shape safety for both foods. The authors back TV campaigns and better local services as the next steps.
pmc-13453507:
Aiyang Tong and six co-authors build a nanoparticle that floods cancer cells with calcium until they die in a fiery, immune waking way. The death mode, called PANoptosis, blends several cell death paths and rouses the immune system against the tumor. Their 2026 particle stacks a calcium peroxide core inside a manganese oxide shell, coated with hyaluronic acid to home in on tumor cells.

In the tumor's acidic, glutathione rich setting, the shell breaks down and frees a drug, fingolimod, that jams calcium channels. Calcium then floods the cell while a Fenton like reaction, a burst of chemical stress, wrecks its inner balance. Manganese freed in the process also trips an immune alarm that helps immune cells mature. Tumors shrank hard in tests, and pairing the particle with a checkpoint drug spread the effect to distant tumors.
pmc-13453607:
Itzick Nahmoud, Karli Monahan, Eric A Woodcock, and Alana C Conti review a tryptophan breakdown path that may link brain injury to lasting pain and depression. The path, named for its first product kynurenine, is stirred up by the swelling that follows a traumatic brain injury. Their 2026 review weighs the path's products in blood, spinal fluid, and brain tissue from patients.

Two products pull in opposite directions: quinolinic acid, which can excite and harm nerve cells, and kynurenic acid, which calms them. Injury skews their levels, and the same skew shows in depression and in pain states such as fibromyalgia and nerve pain. The review maps which enzymes steer the path at each fork. The authors point to those enzymes as drug targets that might ease two of the heaviest burdens after brain injury.
pmc-13453707:
Yuxuan Qi builds a prediction model to tell whether a lone lung nodule is cancerous, using scans, personal facts, and blood tests. Their 2026 study reviews 516 patients seen between December 2022 and August 2025, of whom 402 had benign nodules and 114 had cancer. Two modeling methods competed to pick the strongest warning signs.

Five signs stood on their own in the classic model: older age, smoking history, larger nodule size, a lobed edge, and spiky strands reaching out from the nodule. A second method swapped in a blood marker, carcinoembryonic antigen, for age and lobed edge. The classic model won on both accuracy and fit, so Qi turned it into a nomogram, a chart that gives each patient a personal risk score. The tool aims to spare benign cases from needless surgery.
pmc-13453807:
Zhiyue Zhu and four co-authors ask how extraordinary landscapes restore national park visitors, tracing the path through awe. Their 2026 study surveys 457 visitors at Sanjiangyuan and Qinghai Lake parks in China. A chain model links how striking the scene feels to awe, then to how broadly people think, then to felt closeness with nature.

More extraordinary scenes came with more awe, more closeness to nature, and stronger restoration. Awe itself lifted broad thinking and closeness, and closeness in turn lifted restoration. Statistical resampling backed the chain, with the direct scene effect only partly explained by the links. The authors advise park designers to stage the moments that spark awe, since awe starts the whole chain. The study extends earlier work from plain green space to grand wild settings.
pmc-13454107:
Lili Wang and five co-authors profile the cardiology voices who lead opinion on Xiaohongshu, a Chinese social platform. Their 2026 study screens accounts by set rules and scores them on 14 signs of credibility, reach, and style. In all, 150 accounts with 46,616 posts form the set, and clustering sorts them into four types.

Public Health Educators share plain language prevention posts, while Clinical Narrators mix case stories with emotional support. Academic Interactors won the highest engagement and pushed research news hardest. Authoritative Experts held the largest followings and the strongest credentials, yet drew lower engagement per post. The authors describe the four types as a complementary ecosystem that spreads heart health facts, comfort, and debate. The map could help health agencies pick the right partners for campaigns.
pmc-13454207:
Yan Guo and nine co-authors sort the causes of chest pain in children and teenagers in the Shihezi area of Xinjiang, China. Their 2026 study reviews 243 patients aged 8 to 17 seen at one university hospital in 2023 and 2024 with non traumatic chest pain. Each case is classed as heart related, non heart related, or unexplained.

Non heart causes led at 47.7 percent, heart causes took 20.6 percent, and 31.7 percent stayed unexplained. Work and rest patterns, pain scores, shortness of breath, and palpitations differed across the three groups. Heart markers ran higher in the heart group, though the authors warn those markers helped make the class call, so the link is partly circular. Lung tests ran most abnormal in the non heart group. The authors back careful history and exams, with tests chosen by risk signs.
pmc-13454307:
Elena Papamichael, Irene-Chrysovalanto Themistocleous, Stelios Hadjisavvas, and Christina Michailidou published a 2026 review of game-like exercise programs for people with dementia. Most earlier work covered mild memory problems, leaving open how such programs serve people with deeper decline. The team gathered randomized trials from three databases and pooled their results.

Nine trials with 717 people in total met the entry rules. Pooled results showed a clear gain in overall thinking scores on one common test. Gains on a second thinking test, daily living skills, and a short physical test did not reach clear levels. Programs differed widely in length and intensity, and most used flat-screen rather than immersive systems. The authors call the thinking benefit real but the body benefits unproven.
pmc-13455307:
Halliday and co-authors interviewed women and physiotherapists inside a feasibility trial of a bespoke elastic fabric support garment. The garment targets chronic pelvic girdle pain after pregnancy. That pain lingers beyond three months in roughly 10 to 30 percent of postpartum women. The parent trial randomized women across three English trusts to standard advice and exercise, with or without the garment.

Seven of the 24 trial participants, five from the garment arm and two controls, plus five of seven physiotherapists, gave interviews for the sub-study. The web-based data collection and remote delivery were broadly acceptable, though both groups would have preferred at least one face-to-face session during the trial. Women said the garment held them together, heightened body awareness, and enabled more physical activity in daily life. Physiotherapists found fitting acceptable but wanted a wider range of garment options available.
pmc-13457007:
Laura Saad, Eileen Roesler, Elizabeth Phillips, and J. Gregory Trafton introduce, in a 2026 article, a database of the questionnaires used to measure people in human-robot interaction research. Robots are judged not only by task speed but by how users feel: trust, comfort, and perceived smarts hide inside the mind and must be asked about. Surveys of two major conferences found most papers lean on such scales.

The problem the database answers is sprawl. Scales multiply across labs, often tweaked or renamed, so findings resist comparison and good instruments get reinvented. A shared, searchable home lets researchers find a scale's source, its items, and what it truly measures before adopting it. The authors frame measurement hygiene as a foundation for cumulative science: if the field cannot agree on how it asks people about robots, its claims about better robots rest on sand.
pmc-13457107:
Meiying Shen and six colleagues compare, in a 2026 study, seven machine learning methods for forecasting breast cancer return or spread. The team reviewed 1,056 patients treated at one center from 2012 to 2021, splitting them into training and validation groups. Classic statistics first singled out the factors that matter on their own.

Tumor size, node surgery, hormone receptor levels, a growth index, and HER2 status each predicted disease-free survival independently. Among the seven algorithms, random forest and a boosting method led the field with steady accuracy. The forest's discrimination scores in validation ran from about 0.76 to 0.85 across one, three, and five years. Error scores stayed low and calibration looked honest. Explanation values showed which inputs drove each forecast. The authors offer the winning model as a decision aid, pending outside testing.
pmc-13457307: When nurses feel supported, they act safer — decent work and job embeddedness mediate. Huihua Tang, Qianming Xie, and others model the sequence. The 2026 Europe PMC paper is nursing organizational behavior. It tests the sequential mediating roles in the safety behavior model.
pmc-13459007:
Maxim Wilkinson and a team of Scottish public health researchers used linked hospital records in 2026 to ask how often blood-borne viruses are diagnosed late. Late HIV meant a low CD4 count soon after diagnosis, while late hepatitis meant cirrhosis or liver cancer appearing near diagnosis. The cohort covered 543 people with HIV and several thousand with hepatitis B or C.

Many late cases had already passed through emergency departments or hospital wards in the five years before diagnosis, often more than once. Among late HIV cases, 44 percent had attended an emergency department earlier, and late hepatitis C cases reached 61 percent on that measure. The authors argue that secondary care visits are missed chances to test earlier.
pmc-13459207:
Stephanie Shiau and co-authors examined DNA methylation, chemical tags on DNA that tune gene activity, in young people who acquired HIV around birth. Their 2026 study compared 32 such youth with seven peers who were exposed to HIV before birth but not infected. Blood samples were taken twice, at least three years apart, and the team searched genome-wide for tag differences linked with the virus, drug treatment, or inflammation markers like C-reactive protein.

No genome-wide methylation differences separated the groups at either time point. One targeted gene involved in immune protein processing, PSMB9, did differ at both visits, however. Within the HIV group, neither viral load nor immune cell counts explained methylation patterns. Inflammation did: C-reactive protein tracked with seventeen sites at the first visit and eighteen at the second. The authors frame inflammation as a possible early intervention target.
pmc-13459407:
Jonathan Annan-Asare and co-authors looked at nutrition and mental health among adults living with disabilities in Accra, Ghana's capital, a group facing layered disadvantage in low income settings. Their 2026 study signed up 350 adults whose disabilities were physical, visual, hearing related, or intellectual between May and July 2024. It measured body size by World Health Organization rules and rebuilt diet from repeated day recalls and food questionnaires. Depression and anxiety were screened with the standard PHQ-9 and GAD-7 tools.

A double burden of malnutrition appeared: 28.9 percent of participants were underweight while 31.4 percent were overweight or obese. Mental health strain was heavy, with 22.9 percent showing moderate to severe depressive symptoms and 55.4 percent reporting serious anxiety on the screening tools. Statistical tests found no significant associations between specific sociodemographic factors and the outcomes examined. The combined burden is a neglected priority, the authors say.
pmc-13459607:
Kiran Nilangekar, Nidhi Murmu, Govind Sahu, and Bhupendra V. Shravage published a 2026 correction to their article on fruit fly reporters for autophagy and mitochondrial reactive oxygen species in the germline. The error sat in the methods section on western blotting, where the recipe for RIPA buffer, a solution used to break open cells, listed wrong concentrations for several ingredients.

The corrected recipe lowers sodium chloride from one molar to a much smaller concentration and adjusts Tris, while sodium deoxycholate and SDS percentages also drop sharply. One sentence about preparing fly lysates is corrected with the same revised values. Readers are told that the original article itself has been updated, so anyone repeating the blotting procedure should follow the corrected composition.
pmc-13460107:
De-An Wu, Hong-Xia Qi, He-Jing Wang, Long Wang, and Xiao-Ju Liu surveyed in 2026 the literature linking air pollution with health outcomes in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Their bibliometric study pulled more than eleven thousand articles and reviews from the Web of Science, spanning 1964 to May 2025. It mapped collaborations, journal influence, keyword clusters, and bursts of new topics with standard tools.

Output climbed quickly after 1990. The United States, China, and the United Kingdom led production, Harvard stood out among institutions, and three respiratory journals anchored the field. Major themes included disease burden, exposure-response questions, indoor biomass smoke, and oxidative stress. China and climate change appeared as the newest frontiers, which the authors flag for prevention planning.
pmc-13460207:
Jinfeng He and a team of co-authors investigated in 2026 the RNA-binding protein LARP7 in non-small cell lung cancer, where it appears to act as a brake on tumors. Database checks showed LARP7 levels run low in lung cancer tissue. Laboratory experiments then raised its levels in cancer cells and watched growth, movement, invasion, and cell death, with mouse experiments extending the test to living tumors.

Boosting LARP7 slowed proliferation, migration, and invasion while encouraging cancer cells to die, and tumors grew less in animals. Single-cell sequencing revealed that the protein raises particular splice variants of two genes, FN1 and ADAR, hinting at how it works. The authors offer LARP7 as a candidate marker for diagnosis and prognosis and a possible treatment target.
pmc-13461607:
Grant Steiner and colleagues compared two sister algae, the record-fast Chlorella ohadii and its slower cousin Chlorella sorokiniana, in weak and extreme light. Ohadii withstands extreme light, and the team asked which inner differences give it its edge.

Pushed with extra CO2 and extreme light, sorokiniana doubled in just under 1.7 hours, nearing its cousin's speed. In low light, both species split water at nearly the same rate, the tests showed. Under extreme light, sorokiniana's water-splitting cycles faltered as charges recombined wastefully, while ohadii's kept working well. Electron flow detours differed too, yet turnover speed and antenna size matched between the species. Steiner concludes the edge lies in how photosystem II is built, not in raw turnover speed.
pmc-13462307:
Tadesse and colleagues counted in 2026 the autism load in Eastern Sub-Saharan Africa across three decades, from a world health bank. Autism is a life long brain growth state that shapes talk, social ease, and acts. Counts from this region were thin and split. The team drew on the Global Burden of Diseases 2023 bank. Math models filled gaps by age, place, and year, and gave rates per head with doubt bands.

In 2023 the region held more than four million folk living with autism. The age fair rate sat near eight in ten thousand folk. Years lived with the ill's drag came near a million in sum. Rates held near flat from 1990 to 2023, with no clear split by sex or land. The team urges early spotting, home based aid in local ways, and far better count systems.
pmc-13463107:
DeLisio, Young, and McClelland ran in 2026 a California case study on school meals, using dairy as the lens for the whole food chain. Rules set meal worth and fairness, but a vast chain must make them real each day. The team used a three step frame: what is, so what, now what. Nineteen phone talks with meal heads and dairy works came first. A meet of forty chain folk then shaped the next steps.

Talks laid bare the grind: buy rules, food worth, and form loads. The meet turned those facts to shared sense and fresh dairy ideas. The plan that came out leans on farm to tray lessons for kids. It adds dairy foods from more food ways, to fit all pupils. Local farm ties and staff growth round it out. The authors pitch the frame for other meal chains.
pmc-13463407:
Mohamed I Mabrouk leads a 2026 randomized trial comparing two hands-on therapies for moderate carpal tunnel syndrome in women. Carpal tunnel syndrome squeezes the median nerve at the wrist, causing numbness and weakness. One group received neurodynamic techniques, movements that glide and tension the nerve. The other received desensitization maneuvers, exercises calming an oversensitive nerve area. The trial enrolled 380 women aged 45 to 55, treated for three months, then followed for a year.

Both groups improved in nerve conduction, pain, symptom severity, and daily function. The desensitization group improved more on every head-to-head measure, including sensory and motor nerve conduction and questionnaire scores. Grip strength, whole-hand and pinch, improved in the desensitization group. Gains in pain and function held at the one-year check. The authors conclude both manual approaches help women with moderate disease, while desensitization maneuvers give larger, lasting gains.
pmc-13463707:
Bill Tiger Lam and three co-authors survey how well young Australian adults follow healthy, planet-friendly diets. Adults aged eighteen to twenty-five often eat poorly, which makes them a key group for change. The team polled 297 young adults online, and 107 of them also logged their meals over several days.

Scores for diet quality and low impact averaged under half of the scale top. Plant-based eaters scored higher than meat eaters. Most respondents had never heard the guidelines and saw such diets as costly, hard to reach, or awkward to keep. Taste for meat and dairy ranked as the chief block, more so for men than for women.
pmc-13463907:
Huimin Zhang and three co-authors study how marriage quality shapes the link between stress and low mood in urban Chinese women. The team drew on a 2020 family and health survey from Chengdu and Beijing, covering 1,865 married women. Marriage quality was split into warm interaction on one side and disagreement on the other.

Higher felt stress tracked with stronger depressive symptoms across the group. Warm interaction softened that link, so stress hurt less where marriages felt close. Disagreement did the opposite and deepened the harm stress caused. The authors argue that family-focused support and better marriage quality could guard women's mental health under pressure.
pmc-13465007:
Li Xiao and three co-authors argue that exercise works as whole-body medicine against Alzheimer's disease. Plaque-led drug hunts have disappointed, which pushes attention to system-wide failure with age: liver, vessels, hormones, and immunity all drift together. Movement, the review shows, pushes each system back toward balance.

Active muscles and liver release signal compounds and tiny vesicles that reach the brain. Blood flow, oxygen delivery, and waste clearance in the brain all improve with regular training. New neuron growth in the memory hub also gets support from exercise signals. Chronic inflammation and oxidative stress fall at the same time. The authors present training as a low-cost, multi-path prevention and care tool.
pmc-13465307:
Zhuang and colleagues sorted primary Sjögren's syndrome into molecular subtypes in 2026 using gene data from salivary glands. The disease is an autoimmune condition that dries the eyes and mouth and can involve many organs. It also raises lymphoma risk. The team combined single-cell and bulk gene sequencing. A factorization method then separated the tangled signals into distinct patterns.

Four subtypes emerged. The authors named them the Classical Immune Type, the Ion Channel Type, the Fibrotic Senescent Type, and the Immune Desert Type. Each carried its own characteristic gene set. Scores for those gene sets can be computed from a patient's gland tissue. The subtypes differed in clinical features and in the local immune mix around the glands. The authors suggest the labels could guide personal treatment choices. They could also help select patients for future clinical trials.
pmc-13467007:
Şencan and colleagues reported a 2026 case of a rare blood vessel link found during lung surgery on a 77-year-old woman. She had the upper lobe of her right lung removed for a two-centimeter tumor. It proved to be a mix of adenocarcinoma and large-cell neuroendocrine carcinoma, two forms of lung cancer, at an early stage. Vessel variants occur in roughly 5 to 15 percent of people and can cause heavy bleeding during camera-guided surgery.

During the operation the surgeons found a direct link, matching an arteriovenous fistula, between the upper lung vein and the artery running between the lobes, and they tied it off safely. The authors say such links have not been described in the English-language literature before. Careful review of scans before surgery and alert checking during it are their route to safe removal in cases like this one.
pmc-13467207:
Abudureyimujiang Aosimanjiang, Mo Chen, Zhiyu Wang, and Qunyi Huang study bolted steel joints loaded along a frame's weaker axis. Their 2026 analysis asks how much bending such joints take before yielding under construction overloads. A detailed three-dimensional computer model with contact behavior and layered material rules was checked against published test curves.

Random sampling mapped into a fast surrogate model let the team scan many designs for scatter and capacity. Plasticity theory produced formulas for two competing yield patterns, tested against the numerical grid. Two column traits, web thickness and section depth, dominated the outcome, together driving about three fifths of the joint's elastic capacity.
pmc-13467307:
Israel Casanova-Méndez and co-authors report a small clinical study, published in 2026. It treats allergic conjunctivitis with a bacterial suspension. This is the itchy allergic eye inflammation common in children. The suspension was given as an immune-modulating add-on therapy. Five children aged seven to nine received the treatment. All had moderate-to-severe persistent disease. Their skin allergy tests were negative.

After ninety days, the children had less itching. Light sensitivity and burning also fell. Eye inflammation dropped markedly on examination. Quality-of-life scores improved across all domains. Blood tests showed an increase in a regulatory immune cell type. The authors read this as early support for the approach. The group was very small and uncontrolled, though.
pmc-13467907:
Liu, Sun, and Xie review a laboratory technology for testing whether chemicals harm male fertility, in this 2026 article. The technology is testicular organoids. These are three-dimensional clusters of testicular cells grown in dishes. Male reproductive health has declined for decades. The standard tools, rodent studies and flat cell cultures, miss many effects that matter in human tissue.

Drawing on studies published between 2010 and 2024, the review explains how organoids are built. They are made from primary cells or stem cells. Studies have used them to test hormone-disrupting chemicals and chemotherapy drugs. Several studies detected harm at doses well below those needed in flat cultures. This was especially true under long, low-dose exposure. The authors also list what still blocks regulatory use. Barriers include incomplete barrier structures, unstable long-term culture, and donor variability. Poor production of mature sperm is another gap.
pmc-13468307:
He and colleagues reviewed in 2026 fabrics that move on their own, treating textiles as active engineering systems. The newer approach builds actuation into the fibres themselves, using active polymers and shape memory alloys. The review organises the field in four tiers: fibre, yarn, fabric, and system.

It analyses how weaving, knitting, braiding, and non-woven structures amplify, redirect, or constrain the stroke and force of active materials. Liquid crystal elastomers, coiled polymer actuators, and shape memory polymers are covered, plus alloy-polymer hybrids. The authors bridge fibre-level mechanics with fabric-level design, a gap they say has slowed the field. Design strategies in the review target engineers building garments that bend, squeeze, or change shape on cue. The authors frame intrinsic actuation as the next paradigm for smart clothing and soft machines.
pmc-13468407:
İbrahim Türkmen and co-authors review in 2026 the hardened performance of 3D-printed geopolymer mortars, a low-carbon construction material that pairs digital printing with alkali-activated binders. Judging these mortars is tricky because strength depends not just on chemistry but on printing settings, curing, layer bonding, and pore structure. The review closely examines printing studies for strength, durability, and practical rollout.

Across the literature, precursor type, activator choice, sand ratios, printing conditions, and curing regime strongly shape bond strength, often differently by loading direction. Durability follows the same coupled pattern, with layer voids and directional pores affecting shrinkage, water uptake, chloride penetration, and carbonation. The authors also cover sustainability claims and the missing standards that slow adoption, giving builders a sober map of what printed geopolymer can already bear.
pmc-13468507:
Vineela Vepakomma and colleagues survey in 2026 the blood nutrients and neuronal injury markers of older adults with mild cognitive impairment in Hyderabad, India. The community study enrolled 184 adults aged 55 to 85 between January 2024 and March 2025, testing cognition with the Montreal Cognitive Assessment and measuring vitamins, metabolic indices, and brain-related proteins.

Mild cognitive impairment was found in 36.4 percent of participants, a high share. That group showed higher blood sugar marker HbA1c and systolic blood pressure, plus elevated neuronal markers including beta-amyloid, tau, and neurofilament light. Vitamin D and several B vitamins ran significantly lower, with a heavier deficiency burden, and higher vitamin levels correlated with better cognitive scores. In a country facing a steep dementia climb, cheap blood panels that flag risk early are exactly what community screening needs.
pmc-13468807:
Sanger and Pietras advance a testable hypothesis in this 2026 theory article about why suggestion-based treatments, including hypnosis-like procedures, struggle to win acceptance in psychiatric care. Their proposal is to reframe such treatments around phenomenological control. The term names the patient's own capacity to steer subjective experience deliberately. That framing replaces the image of something done to a passive patient.

The article makes separate predictions for patients and clinicians. For patients, the new framing should raise perceived agency and acceptability while lowering fears about losing control during treatment. For providers, it should improve scientific credibility and willingness to recommend, refer, or train in these methods. The authors are careful to claim no boost in actual treatment effectiveness, only in uptake. They note the predictions may hold unevenly across people and settings. That unevenness is exactly what future trials should test.
pmc-13469107:
Cichutek and colleagues report a 2026 study of FGL-1, a liver-made protein that damps T cell activity, in COVID-19 patients. The protein interacts with LAG-3, an immune checkpoint that rises on T cells in severe infection. The team measured blood FGL-1 in 65 patients and 33 healthy donors and tracked it against clinical measures and disease course.

FGL-1 levels correlated with inflammation markers and with severe disease, as the study's title reports, placing the protein inside the COVID immune picture rather than beside it. Because blocking the FGL-1 and LAG-3 interaction can free T cells in cancer research, the same axis is a candidate drug target in infection. A liver protein that rises with severity could also serve as a blood marker for triage, if larger cohorts confirm the link the team found.
pmc-13469207:
Elis Kouki and colleagues mine a Finnish nationwide registry in 2026 to ask whether blood sugar control at the moment atrial fibrillation is found predicts what happens next. The FinACAF study covered all 157,658 patients with new atrial fibrillation in Finland between 2010 and 2017. Diabetes was present in 23 percent. A baseline HbA1c was available for 17,519 of those patients. Outcomes were death, ischemic stroke, heart attack, and bleeding.

Diabetes itself raised the hazards of every outcome. Among patients with diabetes, higher HbA1c tracked with progressively higher risk. At the worst control level, above 63 millimoles per mole, the hazard reached 1.56 for death, 1.38 for ischemic stroke, and 1.70 for heart attack against patients without diabetes. The gradient message is blunt: in fibrillating hearts, sugar control is not a side issue but a main predictor of who fares badly.
pmc-13469707:
Skvorcova and co-authors hunt for new malaria drugs by taking apart old enzyme blockers in this 2026 study. Malaria parasites need an enzyme called plasmepsin V. It prepares proteins they export into host cells. Its shape differs enough from human enzymes to allow selective drugs. The team mined known blocker structures for the small pieces that grip the enzyme's active center.

They built a focused library around three ring-shaped cores and tested the pieces in a fluorescence-based assay. One pyrrolidine-based fragment blocked the enzyme at a concentration of 70 micromolar, and refining its attachments improved potency to roughly 10 micromolar in the best compounds. Versions with two aromatic groups on a sulfonamide arm worked best, giving the team a fresh, non-peptide scaffold to develop further.
pmc-13469907:
Qian Li, Xin Xiang, Yuan Liang, and Hu Mao propose in 2026 a fairer way to grade computer generated radio signals. Judging synthetic radio frequency data has leaned on borrowed image metrics with no agreed baselines. Their framework stacks ten measures in six layers and calibrates each one against pairs of genuine recordings, which set the ceiling a generator could hope to reach.

Scores for generated signals are then expressed relative to that ceiling, and results are split by signal strength. Applying the framework uncovered two quirks of common training setups. A standard preprocessing step starved one loss term and wrecked amplitude modulated signals until a compression fix was applied. The usual training objective also quietly suppressed gradients for those signals. Switching the prediction target largely repaired the damage at small cost elsewhere.
pmc-13470207: Batten and colleagues published a correction in 2026 to their study of how emotional words trigger the release of brain chemicals in the human thalamus and cortex. Two sets of map coordinates in the methods, giving virus injection sites for supporting mouse work, held typos. Corrected coordinates are given for midbrain dopamine cells and for cells of the locus coeruleus. The authors state the errors have no impact on the results. The notice is the lasting fix, since the article itself can no longer be changed.
pmc-13470407:
Lingayat and a team in India set in 2026 two graft picks for knee ligament rebuild side by side. The front cruciate ligament, a key knee band, is most often rebuilt with a hamstring cord from the back of the thigh. That pick can come out thin and can sap knee bend strength. The rival pick takes a cord from the outer ankle, the peroneus longus, long spared in the past. Fifty patients split near half by pick, and were tracked for two years.

The ankle cord group won on most counts. Their work took less time, the graft came out thicker, and knee scores at two years ran higher. They bent the knee wider at three months, went back to daily life weeks sooner, and reached sport months ahead. Their knees also held more firm on a lax gauge. The authors back the ankle cord as a sound swap.
pmc-13470507:
Marybel R. Gonzalez leads a large ABCD Study team reviewing in 2026 how family, friends, and community shape adolescent development. The ABCD Study follows young people for over a decade, gathering brain, health, and social data at many levels. The reviewers selected sixty four high impact papers from that literature and asked how often social context measures were woven into each health outcome.

Family, peer, and community measures appeared most often beside brain imaging and thinking outcomes, and beside mental health outcomes. Far fewer papers used them for physical health or substance use questions. Where studied, social measures acted as both risks and protections depending on the setting. The authors urge fuller use of the long term data now maturing, since most work so far rests on single time point snapshots.
pmc-13470607:
Zhang and co-workers in China showed in 2026 how cigarette smoke juice pushes lung cancer cells to spread form, through one gene switch. Smoke is the top driver of lung cancer deaths, yet its cell paths stay murky. The team bathed a lung cancer line in smoke juice and grew the cells as tumors in mice. Both sets grew, crawled, and broke bounds faster than plain kin.

Smoke had raised PRMT6, an enzyme that tags proteins, and its tag mark in the cells. Shape marks of spread rose with it: grip marks fell away, cut enzymes climbed, and two shape drivers woke. A growth path of three linked switches ran hot in step. One drug that blocks PRMT6 wiped the whole set clean, in dishes and in mice alike. The authors name PRMT6 a drug mark for smoke linked lung cancer, and urge tests in patient samples next.
pmc-13471307:
Ren and colleagues showed in 2026 that eye alignment one week after surgery for intermittent exotropia, a drifting-out eye condition, forecasts whether the drift returns. The study followed 91 children, mean age about eight, after one-sided muscle surgery combining a weakening and a tightening procedure. Alignment was measured at set times over a mean follow-up near 17 months, with recurrence meaning outward drift beyond a threshold at six months.

Thirty-one children recurred early; sixty held success. The recurrence group already showed larger leftover outward drift at near and distance in the first week. Adjusted models confirmed week-one alignment predicted six-month recurrence and final failure. A six-month near measurement predicted final outcome even more strongly. Children in the success group kept binocular fusion, the eyes working as one, more often at final review, and the authors suggest week-one readings can flag children for closer monitoring.
pmc-13471507:
HeeKyung Chang, MinJi Park, JuHee Seo and YoungJoo Do published this 2026 validation study of the World Health Organization's ICOPE Step 1 screening tool in Korean older adults. The tool is meant to catch decline in intrinsic capacity, the body's physical and mental reserves, across mobility, nutrition, mood and cognition. The authors tested four non-sensory domains against reference tests in 464 adults from eleven sites in Jinju.

The screen caught 89.0 percent of people with decline in a domain, but its specificity was only 45.1 percent, so many flagged people were fine. Mobility screening looked most accurate, though part of that edge was overlap with its reference test. Cognition screening had the weakest specificity, clearing only about half of healthy people. Adding a low body-mass cut-off to the nutrition domain lifted its sensitivity from 59.0 to 68.2 percent cheaply. The authors support the tool for first-pass case finding, with local adjustments.
pmc-13473107:
Sorjonen and colleagues published a comment in 2026 challenging a study that claimed food insecurity and poor mental health fuel each other. Baek and Yoon had analysed survey data from 13,893 Korean adults with a statistical model that tracks within-person change over time. They found food insecurity predicted lower self-esteem and more depressive symptoms, and vice versa, and called it a vicious cycle.

The alternative models gave divergent results: some effects decreased, others increased, instead of the original clean pattern. The authors argue the original model is prone to spurious findings because it cannot adjust for confounders that change over time. Hence the vicious-cycle conclusion may be premature. They recommend researchers always fit alternative models to panel data. Conclusions should rest on comparing findings across models, not on one model's output.
pmc-13473507:
Fox and co-authors show that a bacteriophage genome can be sequenced the same day from a single plaque. A plaque is the clear spot a virus leaves in a bacterial lawn, and the method needs no DNA extraction step. Their 2026 method adapts a Nanopore rapid PCR barcoding kit to crude plaque material, using tagmentation and amplification to build the sequencing library directly.

Across their phage set, assemblies from the shortcut matched traditional Illumina sequencing at 99.88 to 100% average nucleotide identity, with a mean of 99.97% across the set. Two phages, CabbageMan and MaterMagnus, came through at a perfect 100% identity match. The trade-off is plain: PCR-based reading cannot see chemical changes on the phage DNA, a capability nanopore reading normally offers. For routine naming and host-range work, the same-day route is enough.
pmc-13473807:
Panagiotou and colleagues in Cyprus asked in 2026 how food allergies in babies and toddlers weigh on the whole family's life. Most past work dealt with school age children. Their study mixed two tools: a set form filled by mothers of one hundred allergic children under three, and long talks with twelve of those mothers. The form had been shaped to fit Greek tongue and ways.

Scores pointed to mild to mid harm on the whole. The sore spots were fear of new foods, tight food rules, and lost social ease. Three in four mothers feared a stray bite or a bad attack. The talks told of watch that never rests, days rebuilt round food safety, and strain from mixed word by doctors. Care at clinics split in worth, and folk at large knew little of the risk. The authors urge one clear care plan from the start.
pmc-13474707:
Zuber and co-authors mined the All of Us research database for 40,585 adults with depression but no diabetes, following them a median of 8.15 years to see which familiar risk factors actually deliver type 2 diabetes in this already vulnerable group. Their 2026 retrospective cohort fitted adjusted survival models to demographics, body mass, and income.

The classic factors all held, with measurable force. Each ten-unit rise in body mass index carried a hazard ratio of 1.76 for new diabetes, Black race carried 1.79 against the reference group, male sex 1.38, and each year of age 1.03 on the model's scale. Household income carved a clean socioeconomic gradient in the opposite direction. The authors argue endocrine screening in depressed patients should be systematic and weighted toward those with obesity and social disadvantage.
pmc-13478507:
Ke and co-authors used a national Chinese aging cohort in 2026 to test how sleep quality and depressive symptoms together predict new digestive disease. The study followed 3,711 adults who began free of digestive disease, scoring their sleep from questionnaire items and their mood with a ten-item depression scale. Models then estimated who went on to report digestive disease, adjusting for social, lifestyle, and health factors.

Poor sleep alone carried a hazard ratio of 1.67 for later digestive disease, and depressive symptoms alone carried 1.33 in the separate models fitted. Against the best-off group, people with poor sleep but no depressive symptoms faced a hazard ratio of 1.91, and those with both problems faced 1.80 in fully adjusted results. Nearly half the mood effect, 47.3 percent in the mediation analysis, ran through poor sleep, suggesting sleep care may protect the gut too.
pmc-13478607:
Yang and colleagues interviewed 16 women with gestational diabetes at a large hospital in Hefei, China, in 2026 about what health information they actually need. Gestational diabetes, high blood sugar first found in pregnancy, affects 14.8 percent of pregnant women in China and depends heavily on daily self-management. The women described needs across food, exercise, glucose checks, emotions, and life after birth, which the team sorted using a needs theory framework.

The needs fell into three domains and ten topics, covering the disease itself, treatment and tests, childbirth, and social support. Growth needs were the most detailed, spanning diet management, exercise, blood glucose control, emotional coping, and postnatal care plans for mother and baby. Women with this condition face a 7.7-fold higher risk of later type 2 diabetes, the authors note, and they call for staged, plain-language information services shaped to each woman.
pmc-13479407:
Chen-xi Li, Di-shu Huang, and Zhong-cheng Gong report a 2026 case of partial facial duplication in a newborn boy, linked to a newly found variant in the PAX7 gene. Diprosopus, meaning duplication of facial structures, is an extremely rare malformation related to conjoined twinning. Its causes remain poorly understood, so genetic findings in single cases carry unusual weight.

The baby, from a Kazak family, had a complete left cleft lip plus an accessory upper lip mass with a small sinus tract, and scans showed duplicated, displaced upper jaw arches. Surgeons repaired the lip and removed the duplicated jaw in operations at eleven months and four years, with feeding and speech developing normally. Gene sequencing of the child and his mother found a shared single-copy PAX7 variant, offered as a candidate explanation.
pmc-13480107:
Sancho Pedro Xavier and colleagues present a 2026 pooled review of antibiotic prescribing for children across Africa. The team searched six databases in May 2025 for studies on drug choice, route, and fit with the World Health Organization AWaRe grouping, which sorts antibiotics into Access, Watch, and Reserve tiers.

About seventy-six percent of child patients got an antibiotic, and a like share got at least one drug by injection or drip. Children received about one and a half antibiotics each on average. Rates ran highest in Central and West Africa and lower in the East and South. Access drugs made up about two-thirds of orders, Watch drugs just over a quarter, and Reserve drugs appeared only in South Africa. Wide gaps between studies urge care in reading the totals, yet the pattern supports stronger stewardship programs.
pmc-13480507:
Laura Trapani and co-authors report a 2026 case series on a targeted drug for slow-growing brain tumours in children. Three children with a gene condition called NF1 had tumours on the visual pathway that kept growing. Standard chemotherapy can halt such tumours but brings heavy side effects and rarely restores sight. Each child took a daily drug that blocks a growth signal switch downstream of the faulty gene.

Scans showed each tumour shrank or held steady. Vision improved in a clear way for all three, and one child regained near-full sight. Side effects stayed mild, mostly skin complaints, with no severe body-wide harm. One child had the drug after chemotherapy failed, while two got it first by special access. Three cases cannot settle policy, yet sight recovery marks a gain chemotherapy seldom delivers.
pmc-13482007:
Alarcón-Sánchez and co-workers in Mexico and Spain combed in 2026 the record for gene variants of two immune receptors. The receptors are tied to periodontitis, a gum disease that eats the tissue holding teeth. Genes can be cut and rejoined in mixed ways, called splicing, to yield variant proteins. The pair of receptors, IL-23R and IL-17RA, catch immune signals that drive gum swelling. The team searched six databases and also ran computer checks on protein shapes.

Of a hundred plus finds, twelve studies fit. The IL-23R gene showed thirty two known splice variants. Its partner gene showed just one. The variants make twenty three distinct protein forms, from loose decoy copies to cut down chains. All kept studies scored low for bias risk. What the forms do in gum disease is still not clear, and wet lab work must come next.
pmc-13482307:
Hong and colleagues test in 2026 whether a dye-based ultrasound scan before retinal reattachment surgery can forecast how well a patient will see afterward. Their prospective study enrolled 52 patients with detached retinas, all treated with vitrectomy, and measured blood flow in the eye using contrast-enhanced ultrasound before the operation. Six months later patients were split by whether their corrected vision had improved, 39 in the improved group and 13 not.

Improvers showed richer blood flow before surgery, with higher peak intensity and total flow area under the curve, and faster dye arrival than the non-improvement group in the scans. Peak intensity, how brightly the eye tissue lights up with dye, stood alone as the ultrasound predictor, scoring 0.844 on the standard discrimination curve. It explained 34.7 percent of the differences in recovery, and the authors caution that the small single-center sample needs multicenter confirmation before clinical use.
pmc-13482607:
Ermler and colleagues investigate in 2026 whether the hepatitis B drug bepirovirsen does double duty, attacking the virus directly while also waking up the liver's innate immune defenses. The drug, an antisense molecule now in phase III trials, had triggered a burst of immune signals right after dosing in an earlier patient study. The team checked patient blood samples and then hunted the responsible sensor in cells and specially bred mice.

Patients on the drug showed rises in multiple pro-inflammatory cytokines, the messenger proteins that recruit and activate immune cells, echoing the original trial observation. In sensor-equipped test cells, only the presence of human TLR8, a viral-pattern detector, produced a significant response, at a probability value of 0.00085 in the analysis. Mice engineered to carry human TLR8 responded with the same cytokine pattern while normal mice did not, and liver Kupffer cells and macrophages were the main responders identified.
pmc-13483407:
Dilip Shettigar and co-authors present a 2026 systematic review of long-term exercise habits, brain shape, and thinking skills in adults. Staying inactive counts among the changeable risks for dementia, so the team gathered follow-up studies that tracked activity for at least a year and then measured the brain. Twenty studies from five databases, all in adults free of cognitive trouble at entry, passed the screen.

Across the set, busier people kept more grey matter in the memory hub and the planning region, and their wiring decayed more slowly. Planning skill and processing speed showed the steadiest links, growing with total lifetime dose. The pattern ran stronger in carriers of a known risk gene. Caution runs through the review: every study carried some bias concerns, and people with healthier brains also stayed busier later, so cause could flow both ways.
pmc-13483607:
Enyuan Fang and colleagues examine spine spread from sarcomatoid carcinoma, an aggressive cancer type with few dedicated studies. Published in 2026, the retrospective series covers 25 patients with clinical, imaging, pathology, treatment, and survival details. Most patients first came to attention because of symptoms from the spine lesions themselves.

No clear survival difference appeared by original tumor site, and scans showed no signature look that sets these deposits apart. Only targeted drugs and immune therapy showed a trend toward longer survival among treatments tried. Three factors predicted survival on their own, namely number of deposits, a clotting marker called D-dimer, and a blood inflammation ratio. A scoring chart and a simplified grouping built from those factors may help surgeons judge who could benefit from an operation.
pmc-13483707:
Canavati and team described sixteen patients from ten Palestinian families who share one inherited gene change behind a rare disorder. The condition, TANGO2 deficiency, causes repeated metabolic crises, muscle breakdown, seizures, and dangerous heart rhythms. Their 2026 study sequenced the gene in the first families, then checked relatives with a targeted test, and compared DNA markers around the gene to test for a common ancestor.

Every affected person carried two copies of the same spelling change in TANGO2, and the change appears in no public database. Symptoms varied widely even within this shared genetic picture, from developmental delay to heart involvement. Marker patterns around the gene matched across families, confirming a founder effect, meaning all inherited the change from one distant ancestor. Canavati urges wider genetic testing in under-studied groups.
pmc-13483907:
Son Hoang, Vinh Quang Pham, and Cong Chi Tran optimize injection molding for a curved shin guard plate where accuracy and weight pull against each other. Their 2026 framework varies packing pressure, melt temperature, and cooling time in a structured experiment, then fits predictive surface models for size deviation and part weight. Packing pressure proved the strongest lever of the three.

An evolutionary search over the fitted models produced a spread of best-trade-off settings, with an adaptive version exploring the frontier more thoroughly than the standard one. A weighted ranking method then picked a single compromise setting for the factory floor. Test runs at the chosen setting and two alternatives matched predictions closely, with size errors under 7.41 percent and weight errors under 1.70 percent. The recipe transfers to other curved molded parts.
pmc-13486507:
Sharma and team used fractal mathematics to stretch India's crop production records before training forecasting networks, arguing the jagged year-to-year swings carry information smooth models miss. Their 2026 study covered millet, maize, wheat, and rice output from 1961 to 2023. Fractal interpolation creates extra plausible data points that preserve the series' roughness, measured by its Hurst exponent, a statistic for long-memory behavior in data.

Variable-scaling interpolation produced rougher, more faithful series than the constant-scaling version across all four crops. Networks trained on the stretched data clearly outperformed those trained on raw records. The best model, a memory network with variable scaling, forecast millet, maize, and wheat with errors under about five percent on the percentage error measure used. Sharma says fractal pretreatment deserves a place in agricultural forecasting for climate-stressed regions.
pmc-13487607:
Jos Borkent simulates what happens to vitamin and mineral intake when Dutch older adults eat less or no animal food. Published in 2026, the modeling uses two-day food diaries from 607 community-dwelling seniors in the national consumption survey. Five scenarios replace meat and fish at forty and eighty percent, then remove seafood only, all animal flesh, or all animal products.

Even on their current diet, seniors already ran low on riboflavin, vitamin B6, folate, and calcium, with women also low on vitamin A and selenium. Gentle forty-percent replacement added no new problem nutrients. Deeper cuts made niacin low across scenarios, while the fully vegan pattern left nearly every micronutrient low. Sustainability advice for older adults must pair protein swaps with deliberate micronutrient cover.
pmc-13487907:
Gad Murenzi and colleagues examine HIV viral load testing in Rwanda in a 2026 observational study. Paired blood samples from the same people were sent to two laboratories that used different test kits. Participants were adults aged 40 years or older who had received HIV care for many years, most of them on modern treatment.

Results agreed well at higher cutoffs used for clinical decisions, yet they differed sharply near the lowest measurable levels. One laboratory reported far more low-level quantifiable results than the other did on the same samples. The authors conclude that very low thresholds can misclassify people, so higher cutoffs for judging viral suppression are safer in routine programs.
pmc-13488007:
Reneigh Morley-Hart and colleagues run a sham-controlled trial of joint manipulation for squat strength in a 2026 crossover study. Twenty-four resistance-trained adults with limited ankle bend, measured as dorsiflexion range, received quick thrust manipulations of lower limb joints and, on another occasion, a sham procedure that mimicked the treatment. Each person served as their own comparison, with squat one-repetition maximum and ankle motion captured by three-dimensional cameras.

Strength rose slightly after both real and sham sessions, with no clear difference between them in the reported tests. Ankle range also failed to change more after real treatment. The authors conclude that a single manipulation session does not meaningfully boost squat performance in this group.
pmc-13490407:
Xiuxiu Liu and co-authors study a ribosome-building protein in fruit fly development in a 2026 genetics investigation. Ribosomes are the cell's protein factories, and a nucleolar protein called nucleostemin helps assemble them in growing cells. The team depleted its fly version, Ns1, in the wing imaginal disc, a growing tissue that becomes the adult wing, and tracked protein production, ribosome parts, and cell death signals.

Loss of Ns1 triggered widespread cell death without using the classic p53 route seen in mammals, and global protein production fell in the reported measures. Sixty-five ribosomal proteins dropped in abundance, while a stress-sensing complex rose and switched on a death signal pathway. The authors name Ns1 a guardian of ribosome supply in growing tissue.
pmc-13490507:
Kazymbetova and team built a lithium-sulfur battery cathode from buckwheat-derived carbon threaded with carbon nanotubes, attacking the chemistry's notorious shuttle problem. Sulfur batteries promise high energy but fade as dissolved sulfur species wander between electrodes. Their 2026 cathode traps those species in porous hard carbon baked from buckwheat at high temperature, while a small nanotube share wires the structure electrically.

The cathode delivered an initial capacity near 1,250 milliamp-hours per gram at a gentle discharge rate in the reported tests. After one hundred cycles it kept about sixty percent of that capacity, with charging efficiency near one hundred percent throughout. Six percent nanotubes proved the sweet spot among the loadings varied. Kazymbetova pitches the biomass-based design as cheap, scalable, and sustainable compared with engineered carbon hosts.
pmc-13491607:
Ali Tadayon and nine colleagues present a 2026 case series on aortopexy, an operation that lifts the aorta away from a soft, collapsing windpipe in infants. The condition, tracheomalacia, often stems from blood vessels pressing on the airway. All six infants also had several other birth defects, which made their outlook hard to separate from the surgery itself.

Symptoms began between six days and one year of age, and diagnosis rested on direct airway inspection. Surgery used chest incisions in five babies and a neck incision in one, each paired with removal of some or all of the thymus gland. No major early complications occurred, though two children later needed further procedures and two died from their other conditions. Survivors often kept lasting problems, so the authors credit underlying defects more than the operation.
pmc-13491707:
