Richmond Balinia Adda and five colleagues measure in 2026 how strongly pregnant women in northern Ghana react to one piece of a malaria parasite protein tied to pregnancy infection. The protein VAR2CSA lets infected red blood cells stick in the placenta, and vaccine designers hope its steadier regions can train protection. The team focused on one such region, called DBL5, in blood from 156 women.

Those infected with the malaria parasite showed the strongest antibody response to DBL5, ahead of women infected with hepatitis B and women carrying both infections. Responses to DBL5 tracked closely with responses to the whole protein, suggesting the fragment captures much of what the immune system sees. Computer predictions also flagged conserved stretches likely to be recognized widely, though the authors call for longer studies with functional tests.
pmc-13491807:
Ziliang Yu leads a fourteen-author team overturning in 2026 assumptions about interleukin-35, an immune signal usually described as purely calming in rheumatoid arthritis. The group found IL-35 signaling disturbed in patients and tested the protein in arthritic mice and in the fibroblast cells that overgrow joint linings in the disease. The surprise was what happened to those fibroblasts directly.

Giving IL-35 eased arthritis in mice, and in dishes the protein pushed joint fibroblasts into senescence, a retired state where cells stop dividing. The route ran through an internal alarm pathway, cGAS-STING, and blocking that pathway erased the effect. Lowering the body's own IL-35 worsened disease unless an activator of the same pathway was added. Turning pathogenic fibroblasts senescent, the authors argue, is a new therapeutic lever.
pmc-13492407:
Megan E LaBreck and four colleagues evaluate in 2026 the safety of giving dofetilide through a feeding tube instead of as a swallowed capsule. Dofetilide is a rhythm-control drug with a notoriously narrow safety margin. Some patients who need the drug cannot swallow, because of ventilation or other illness. Opening the capsule and flushing the contents through a tube could change how the drug is absorbed or how fast it acts, and no earlier study had examined the practice.

The report walks through why caution is warranted: the drug stretches the heart's electrical recovery time, and excess effect can trigger a dangerous rhythm called torsades de pointes. Risk depends on the patient's own repolarization traits, on drug levels, and on interacting medicines. Standard care starts the drug in hospital with continuous monitoring for the first doses, a safeguard the authors carry into their tube-administration evaluation.
pmc-13493807:
Zheng and colleagues address a practical tunnelling problem: knowing rock quality ahead of a tunnel boring machine helps crews build safely and quickly. Each new project, though, starts with little data of its own. Earlier methods leaned on physics definitions that wobble when sensor data get noisy, or on fitted curves that fail when geology changes. Their 2026 approach computes features from boring machine data in a knowledge-guided way, then feeds them to learning models trained across projects.

The authors compared five algorithms and found CatBoost strongest on accuracy and F1-score, a combined measure of precision and recall. Tested on three separate tunnel projects, the method predicted rock class with accuracies in the mid-to-high eighties. Because the features transfer between sites, a new tunnel can borrow strength from finished projects instead of gathering its own long history. That supports real-time decisions at the tunnel face.
pmc-13493907:
Ticha and colleagues developed a three-dimensional cell model for toxicity testing, growing human nerve-like cells as hundreds of tiny balls called spheroids instead of flat sheets. In their 2026 work, coating wells with poly-D-lysine coaxed SH-SY5Y cells into forming spheroids. The balls showed higher levels of proteins linked to cell connection and nerve identity, signs the cells had matured further than in flat growth.

The team then dosed both formats with three heavy metal salts, cadmium, mercury, and lead, for one to two days. Flat-grown cells suffered more on every measure, including energy stores and protective glutathione levels, while spheroids resisted better. Spheroid numbers per well settled over a week of growth, from roughly three hundred down to about half that count. The authors offer the model as a more tissue-like tool for safety testing.
pmc-13499607:
Samarelli and a team in Italy swabbed in 2026 the skin and vents of 28 pet lizards at a southern zoo park, hunting for yeasts they might carry. Pet reptiles are known germ hosts, but yeast loads and drug strength had not been gauged in them. The set held nine species of lizard. Lab growth and gene tests named each yeast found, and drug tests checked how well antifungal drugs could stop them.

Three in four lizards grew yeast, and more than half of all swabs did too. The lab named 113 yeast strains from 17 species. One kind, Arthrographis kalrae, made up more than a third of finds. Eight kinds are known to sicken people. Many strains stood up to top drugs: most shrugged off one front line drug at high dose, and three kinds showed frank resistance. The authors urge hygiene and routine checks in zoo reptile houses.
pmc-13500707:
Mastoureh Naddafi and Thumu Udayabhaskararao ask in 2026 whether two plant flavonoids can rescue rat livers poisoned by diazinon. The widely sprayed farm insecticide hits the liver first and blocks a key enzyme. Both candidate compounds, rutin and quercetin, are known antioxidants, so poisoned Wistar rats received each at the same dose. Liver markers of oxidative damage, antioxidant enzymes, and the blocked enzyme's activity were tracked against healthy controls.

Both compounds lowered the damage marker and improved the other readings in the reported results, yet quercetin clearly outperformed its partner. It restored antioxidant enzyme levels and the blocked enzyme to near control values, credited to stronger radical-scavenging power and better uptake by the body. The authors present quercetin as a promising candidate antidote for this poisoning while stressing that animal, cell, and clinical studies must come before any human use.
pmc-13500807:
Orkan Telhan leads a six-author team introducing a 2026 computing material grown from fungal mycelium. The chips infuse mycelium, the root-like network of fungi, with a conductive polymer called PEDOT:PSS, forming resistors, capacitors, and nonlinear elements whose shapes can be tuned during growth. The work uses physical reservoir computing, where a physical system turns time-varying inputs into rich internal patterns and only a simple readout layer needs training.

Grown hyphal networks handled a standard sequence task called NARMA-10, and the team measured memory capacity, fading-memory behaviour, and variation between chips. Growth complexity changed how charge moved through the material and how much it remembered. The authors stress practical advantages: the non-living chips are cheap, biodegradable, and compatible with mushroom farming methods, with yields above three million chips per growth cycle.
pmc-13501607:
Seungjun Lee leads a seven-author team with a 2026 flexible biosensor that tracks inflammation signals inside healing wounds in real time. The device uses laser-induced graphene, a carbon material written directly by a laser, set into a soft elastomer so it bends with tissue. Tuning the laser settings produced stable, low-resistance graphene networks that survived repeated bending and sticking stresses. Antibodies attached to the surface gave the sensor its targeting of three cytokines, interleukin-6, CXCL12, and TGF-beta1, at picogram-per-millilitre levels.

Sensitivity matched the standard laboratory ELISA test. Placed in a chronic wound model, the sensor followed each cytokine's distinct time course across the inflammatory, growth, and remodelling phases of healing, and conventional assays confirmed the readings. The authors frame the platform as a step toward continuous, gentle monitoring of wound inflammation, and possibly of brain disorders driven by it.
pmc-13501807:
Saha and colleagues describe a synthetic peptide, a short chain of amino acids, that coaxes breast cancer cells into digesting themselves. The story starts with a receptor called PAR1. Switched on the usual way by thrombin it feeds tumour growth, but a bacterial protease switches it on differently, quieting a growth pathway and triggering autophagy, the cell's self-cleaning programme. Their 2026 study isolated the receptor fragment responsible and copied it as a peptide, testing it in two breast cancer cell types and in mice.

The peptide triggered autophagy on its own in both hormone-sensitive and triple-negative cancer cells grown in dishes. In mice carrying low-grade malignant breast tumours, peptide-driven autophagy significantly slowed tumour growth and delayed progression. Normal breast cells lack the receptor, which suggests the approach could spare healthy tissue, a specificity most autophagy drugs miss.
pmc-13503107:
Sheila Murunga and colleagues compared two urine protein measures head to head in 2026 for predicting progression of chronic kidney disease in children. Both the albumin-based ratio and the total protein ratio are used for risk sorting, but their relative strength was unclear. The study tracked 596 children aged 6 to 17 with moderate to advanced disease, most with congenital kidney and urinary tract anomalies.

A standard-step rise in the albumin ratio came with more than double the risk of the combined bad outcome of halved kidney function, near-total failure, or replacement therapy. The same step in the protein ratio came with a smaller rise. The albumin measure's link was about 28 percent stronger, though the two did not differ on the yearly rate of function decline overall. The authors back current guidance that favors the albumin measure for risk sorting and monitoring.
pmc-13503507:
Feiteira, Tavares, and Ribeiro review the stubborn gap between what biosimilar medicines can do and how little they are used. Biosimilars are near-copies of expensive biologic drugs for immune diseases such as psoriasis, lupus, and inflammatory bowel disease, and regulators approve them only after proving close similarity. Their 2026 review assembles trial and real-world switching evidence. It then asks why patients and doctors still hesitate, pointing at three brakes: doubts about swapping and extrapolation, poor communication, and the nocebo effect, where negative expectations themselves cause symptoms.

The evidence they summarise is reassuring across the board: no study found switching, even repeatedly or in reverse, raised immune reactions, lost effectiveness, or created new safety problems in these diseases. Success in practice, they argue, hinges on managing expectations as carefully as the pharmacology, with honest conversations before any switch.
pmc-13503707:
Shoutaro Tsuji reports a new gene carrier for making antibodies in cells, in this 2026 paper. An antibody needs two parts, a light chain and a heavy chain, made in matched amounts. Older carriers often make the two parts at uneven rates or leave stray tags on the end product.

The new carrier uses splicing, the cut-and-join step that edits gene messages, to yield two message forms from one start signal. A refined build worked with three common start signals and in several mammal cell lines. It made eight times more antibody than a standard carrier of the older type. The system also produced Fab pieces, the binding arms of antibodies, which widens its use in screening and drug work.
pmc-13504007:
Yiwei Lin and Jiatong Zhou sort prostate cancers by immune gene patterns to forecast relapse after surgery, in a 2026 study. Relapse is tracked by a rising blood marker after the gland is removed. The team asked whether gene activity in tumor and nearby healthy tissue could flag who relapses.

Scoring gene sets across both tissues, they split patients into three subtypes; one group stayed relapse-free far longer than the others. Two gene sets in tumor tissue, tied to cell division and energy use, carried the forecast weight. Machine learning then narrowed the field to 36 risk genes, with one gene shared by both methods. Lab tests showed its partner gene drives tumor growth in prostate cells, which backs the forecast role.
pmc-13504207:
Siti Gusti Ningrum leads a team hunting bacteria and their viruses in swiftlet houses in Indonesia, in a 2026 study. The team took 80 samples of droppings, pond water, soil, and nests from four houses in Central Kalimantan. Culture and gene tests confirmed fifteen Nitrobacter strains. One steady strain hosted a virus hunt: spot tests found four viruses able to kill it. The authors call this a first step toward biological control, with lab and on-site checks still to come.
pmc-13505007:
Tetsuro Tago leads a team reporting the first human PET scans with a tracer that images a brain enzyme called HDAC6, in a 2026 study. The enzyme helps clear damaged proteins and is tied to brain diseases like Alzheimer's. A safe tracer would let doctors watch it at work in living brains.

Three healthy men had whole-body scans to gauge radiation dose, which came out within accepted bounds; the gallbladder wall took the highest dose. Five more men had two-hour brain scans with blood sampling. Models fit the tracer's brain kinetics well, with the richest signal in the cerebellum and the leanest in white matter. No safety problems appeared. The team judges the tracer ready for patient studies.
pmc-13506107:
Shengli Guo, Luokai Huangfu, and Guangyu Qiao report salvage surgery for twenty-one patients whose first operation for Chiari I malformation had failed. In these patients the skull-base problem was driven by instability between the top two neck vertebrae, which the first decompression had missed. Their salvage approach fixed the C1 and C2 vertebrae together with screws and rods from behind.

Scans afterward showed near-complete realignment in about ninety percent of patients. Average function scores rose markedly by six months, and the angle between skull and spine improved on imaging. Every patient with follow-up imaging achieved solid bone fusion, with no implant failure or new nerve damage. The authors present the technique as a reliable rescue that reduces, decompresses, and stabilises in one operation.
pmc-13506607:
Renato Souza Lima Sant'Anna, Alejandro G Marangoni, and Erica Pensini study, in 2026 work, how salts and metals change the behavior of cresols in polluted groundwater. Cresols are industrial chemicals that often occur near chloride and sulfate salts of sodium, zinc, iron, and copper. The team used bottle tests, microscope views, lab spectra, and computer models.

Salt levels in the tested range made cresols mix less with water and form droplets of many sizes. Some metal and salt mixes created distinct cresol-metal forms, more often with chloride than sulfate. Droplet size then governed how cresols drift, float, sink, or get trapped in fine soil pores. Site cleanup plans need to allow for those shifts.
pmc-13507107:
Fumihiro Kayamori and colleagues test, in 2026 work, whether microwaves can steer drug-like peptides toward mitochondria, the energy hubs inside cells. Peptides were built from known mitochondria-targeting sequences and tracked with glowing tags under microwave exposure at a standard frequency. Microscope imaging and cell sorting measured uptake and overlap with mitochondria stains.

One peptide design showed a clearly stronger glow rise after exposure than without it, while cell survival stayed high. Overlap with mitochondria rose too, though match scores stayed low overall. The authors treat the result as an early sign, not proof, and call for direct mitochondria function tests. Physical steering could one day complement chemical delivery tags.
pmc-13507307:
Hanpeng Liao leads a 2026 team that catalogs carbon-breaking enzymes carried by prophages, viruses dormant inside soil bacteria, and gauges their climate role. Soils hold more carbon than the atmosphere, and microbes release much of it with carbohydrate-active enzymes. Whether resident viruses quietly donate such enzymes was unmapped at global scale. The catalog holds 4708 viral enzymes targeting plant fiber, lignin, and pectin, including newly found oxidative types. Lab soil tests confirmed the genes switch on with temperature and speed carbon release by host bacteria. Models project a notable rise in soil carbon metabolism potential by 2100 under high emissions. Dormant viruses join the climate ledger.
pmc-13508007:

Heavy gaming often came with poor sleep, low activity, mood symptoms, weaker school results, and family conflict. Rates varied a lot between studies because definitions and tools differed. Cutting screen time helps, the author argues, but on its own it is not enough.
pmc-13508207:

Parent genomes were read in full, and the lines were scored with a dense marker chip. The team built family maps and one combined map of gene positions. Tests on flowering time, flower color, and seed protein showed the population can locate trait genes. Filling in missing markers from the map produced millions of extra data points and sharpened gene hunts. The datasets are public for breeders and researchers.
pmc-13508307:

It tracked 213 transports involving 110 professionals, roughly half before and half after implementation, and scored the effort with the RE-AIM implementation framework.

Professionals engaged strongly, with participation and compliance measures running high, and the evaluation found real gains: staff knowledge and guideline-following improved, transport-related adverse events fell, and handovers between teams ran more efficiently. Two blemishes stood out. Only a third of eligible children were actually reached by the new process, and transports took longer, the price of fuller preparation. The authors call the trade worthwhile but say reach and duration need work.
pmc-13509407:

Blood tests showed strong lupus-linked antibodies, marked inflammation, anemia, and low albumin, while scans found fluid in the abdomen yet urine protein stayed normal.

That mix led the team to suspect protein loss through the gut or irritation of tissue linings, though tests to confirm either were not available. The case warns clinicians that eye swelling alone, paired with low albumin and fluid, can open a lupus workup in teenagers.
pmc-13510707:

Without it, germ cells died by apoptosis, meiosis stalled, and sperm came out fewer and weaker, with short tails and poor swimming. Fertility was badly compromised as a result. pmc-13511707: The Reports Editorial Office issued this 2026 notice as an expression of concern only, tied to a published case report by Messina on breast cancer radiation injury to the lumbosacral nerve plexus. After publication, concerns reached the office about the accuracy of the reported data and how the findings were read. The editor-in-chief opened an investigation and sought clarification from the author. Readers are told an update will follow once the process ends, with any change to the paper announced under the publisher's updating policy.
pmc-13514407:

pmc-13515707:
Muralidaran and colleagues review how to deposit aluminum nitride, a piezoelectric material that generates voltage when squeezed, as thin films for electronics, in a 2026 survey of sputtering methods. Looking ahead, the authors point to 6G radio, harsh-environment sensors, biomedical ultrasound, and energy harvesting for small devices. pmc-13515807:
Youssef O Al-Ghamdi, Amani Chrouda, Nicole Jaffrezic-Renault, and Hamdi Ben Halima build a small sensor for glyphosate, the world's most used weedkiller, in a 2026 study. The authors present the platform as a simple, cheap tool for watching glyphosate in environmental samples.
pmc-13516207:

All three products came out highly pure and gripped the receptor tightly. In cell tests they entered only receptor-carrying cells, and the therapy pair killed cells in a dose-dependent way. In mice bearing myeloma grafts, all three reached tumours with low spill into other tissues. Imaging over seven days showed the therapy agent washing out of tumours over time, though.
pmc-13516407:

The authors suggest pairing such materials with standard antibiotics in future work.
pmc-13516907:
Safa Q Alfattani and Mahfuzur R Sarker test how essential oils attack a food-poisoning bacterium in a 2026 study. The treated cells also soaked up more of a dye that slips through damaged membranes. Electron microscopy sealed the case, showing far greater membrane wreckage in treated cells. pmc-13518107:

Through a single small incision at the navel, the surgeons freed the bowel with a water jet. They closed the hernia opening by pulling the lining inward and tying it with a pre-tied loop, avoiding mesh entirely. A hidden hernia on the other side was closed the same way. The operation took about an hour with almost no blood loss. The woman ate on day two, went home on day five, and stayed well at three months.
pmc-13518807:

One insertion lowered GPC6 activity in northern Chinese pigs, possibly aiding local adaptation. Another deletion cut PLAG1 activity in muscle and linked to body weight, connecting variants to farm traits.
pmc-13518907:
Farhad Javid and a team including Robert Langer and Giovanni Traverso present in 2026 a swallowable drug carrier folded like origami, designed to stay in the stomach and release medicine for weeks. Its ring shape resists being swept away yet carries up to forty percent of its weight as drug, releasing it at a near steady rate. Parts that dissolve at intestinal acidity ensure safe exit. In pigs, devices stayed in the stomach from one to three weeks and passed without injury, which imaging and scope checks confirmed.
pmc-13520407:
Nevnihal Akbaytürk and Tayfun Aygün test in 2026 flipped learning for teaching facial nerve anatomy to second-year dental students, where learners study material before class and practise during class. A comparison group received traditional teaching on the same topic.

Fifty-nine students took knowledge tests before teaching, right after, and at follow-up. Scores improved over time in both groups, with no clear difference between flipped and traditional groups at any point. Flipped learners still rated the method as beneficial on feedback forms. The even result cautions against assuming newer formats automatically beat well-delivered conventional teaching for anatomy.
pmc-13521907:
Yao Mu and colleagues probe in 2026 a signalling axis that drives inflammatory activation of brain immune cells after stroke blood flow returns. Rat artery blockage models plus oxygen-starved microglia in dishes were treated with blockers of two linked proteins, MST1 and Drp1.

Blocking either protein calmed inflammatory markers, lowered TNF, IL-6 and IL-1β release, and shrank infarct size with better neurological scores. Combined blockade helped further on several measures, nominating the axis for stroke therapy research.
pmc-13522307:
Mokhtar Rejili, Kasim Sakran Abass and Farid Hashemi review in 2026 how circular RNAs steer autophagy, the cell recycling system, in lung cancer. Circular RNAs are unusually stable ring-shaped molecules that tune growth, death and stress responses, making them attractive as markers.

Coverage gathers which circular RNAs raise or lower recycling flow, through which signalling routes, and with what effects on tumour survival, spread and chemotherapy sensitivity. Most evidence remains preclinical, drawn from cell and animal work rather than patient trials. The authors frame these molecules as candidate diagnostic and prognostic markers plus possible drug targets, pending stronger clinical validation.
pmc-13522507:
Daniela Chanci and collaborators test open-source language models on pediatric critical care questions in a 2026 benchmark study. One hundred board-style multiple-choice questions across six domains were written by specialists. Eight models ranging from small to large were scored for accuracy and for quality of clinical reasoning, and six trainee physicians answered the same set for comparison.

The largest model scored highest at seventy-eight percent, yet a much smaller model reached seventy-five percent with nearly equal reasoning scores. Both performed close to the trainee group overall. Models did well on ethics questions and poorly on calculations. The authors argue that smaller, locally run models merit further study for secure decision support and trainee education, provided calculation weaknesses are addressed.
pmc-13522807:
Jing Peng and a large team report a pain neuroscience study, published in 2026, searching for receptor switches that can quiet pain-sensing nerve cells. Screening receptors found on pain neurons in mice and humans, they focused on a serotonin receptor called Htr1b, already targeted by migraine medicines known as triptans.

In cell tests, triptan drugs calmed the pain neurons, and in animals they eased several kinds of pain including nerve pain. Deleting the receptor from one fibre type removed the benefit, showing the pain relief runs through those fibres, while some side effects did not depend on the receptor. The work nominates this receptor family for new painkillers.
pmc-13523207:
Jin Woo Choi and Ji Eun Kim compare fracture predictors in kidney disease patients in a 2026 retrospective study. Nine hundred eighteen adults with chronic kidney disease, split between those on dialysis and those not, had bone density scans and blood markers of bone metabolism between 2010 and 2024. Fractures were tracked over a median follow-up of about four and a half years.

Eighty-three fractures occurred. Neither blood marker, parathyroid hormone nor a bone enzyme, predicted fractures in either group. Bone density did: each one-unit rise in the density score was linked to roughly forty-five percent lower fracture risk in both groups, and density clearly outperformed the markers for five-year prediction. The authors support bone density assessment for fracture risk in kidney disease regardless of dialysis status.
pmc-13523307:
Tanliu Wang and colleagues trace a metabolic clue to pollen failure in a sterile rapeseed line in a 2026 study. The Ogura male-sterile line is widely used to produce hybrid seed, yet its sterility mechanism is incompletely understood. Flower buds of the sterile line and its fertile maintainer were grouped by size, and their pollen-producing organs underwent gene and metabolite profiling across three stages.

One pathway, propanoate metabolism, stood out as abnormal in the sterile line. A compound in that pathway, 3-hydroxypropanoic acid, was consistently higher in sterile buds across all comparisons and in a second sterile pair. Applying the compound to plants disturbed starch buildup in pollen grains. The authors conclude that abnormal accumulation of this compound is closely tied to pollen abortion in this sterility system.
pmc-13523407:
Antonio Terrón and colleagues report the first known case of native valve endocarditis caused by an obscure bacterium in a 2026 case report. A sixty-seven-year-old man, whose heart valves had been damaged by rheumatic fever, arrived with fever and a purple rash. Kidney and skin findings first suggested body-wide vessel inflammation. Heart ultrasound, however, revealed a large growth on the mitral valve, pointing instead to infection of the heart lining.

Advanced identification methods named Staphylococcus condimenti in blood cultures, a species previously dismissed as harmless, and the same organism grew from the removed valve. Urgent valve replacement plus targeted antibiotic treatment brought full recovery, with the immune-related complications resolving as well. The authors warn that rare staphylococci should not be waved off as contaminants when the clinical picture fits endocarditis.
pmc-13523507:
Diana Carolina Tiga-Loza leads a large team in a 2026 protocol for the INTERCOG pilot trial, testing a non-drug program with several parts for mild cognitive impairment with families involved. Such decline can progress to dementia, so home-based help that supports both patient and family partner is attractive. The program pairs thinking tasks with food and exercise.

The pilot will randomize 102 pairs, each an older adult with mild memory problems plus a family study partner. The intervention group gets twelve weeks of home visits twice weekly, covering thinking training, food advice, and exercise, while family members learn care and self-care skills. Controls get standard care plus infection prevention messages. The pilot checks recruitment, data collection, and acceptability, with thinking scores, quality of life, and caregiver burden as early results.
pmc-13525507:
Liu and colleagues asked whether low cholesterol in late pregnancy is linked to congenital heart defects in newborns. Their 2026 study covered 36,633 mother-child pairs at a Fujian maternity hospital. The pairs were treated between 2016 and 2020. Maternal blood fats were measured a week before delivery, and babies received heart ultrasound within three days of birth to detect defects.

Liu found congenital heart disease in about one in forty babies. Lower total cholesterol and both major cholesterol fractions were linked to higher overall defect risk, with the good cholesterol fraction showing the strongest protective association. For patent ductus arteriosus, all three measures stayed protective. A patent ductus arteriosus is a fetal blood vessel that fails to close after birth. For wall holes between heart chambers, only total cholesterol reached significance. Triglycerides showed no reliable link. The authors call for prospective multicenter work before any dietary guidance changes.
pmc-13526307:
Williams and colleagues present a 2026 case series of seven patients with anti-IgLON5 disease, a rare autoimmune condition tied to striking sleep problems. Antibodies attack IgLON5, a protein that helps nerve cells stick together, and patients often develop trouble swallowing, unsteady walking, movement problems, and memory decline.

Sleep studies in these patients showed abnormal dream and non-dream sleep behaviors, noisy breathing called stridor, and obstructive sleep apnea, where breathing stops briefly during sleep. The authors stress that sleep complaints should prompt a full neurological exam, since they may be the first sign of this disease. Early diagnosis matters because immune treatment can help, yet the condition stays under-recognized, with few reports from Asia so far.
pmc-13526807:
Florian Van Oers and others systematically score, in a 2026 review, candidate targets for CAR-T cell therapy in acute myeloid leukemia. Engineered T cells transformed care for B-cell cancers, yet leukemia targets are scarce because most markers also appear on healthy blood stem cells, risking their destruction. Early trials against three popular targets gave few lasting remissions.

The team evaluated sixty-three leukemia-associated antigens for which CAR constructs exist. They used five criteria covering expression across patients, uniformity within a patient's disease, presence on leukemic stem cells, and sparing of normal stem and mature blood cells. A twenty-point framework elevated thirteen antigens as most promising, including ADGRE2, SIGLEC-6, and IL1RAP. Advantages, limits, and risk-reduction strategies are discussed for each, offering a prioritized map for next-generation designs.
pmc-13528007:
Sei Morinaga and six colleagues review a cement-assisted nailing technique for thigh bone weakened by cancer spread in a 2026 case series. A gun injects bone cement through the hollow bone before a metal nail is placed. The cement should add stability and allow early weight bearing. The series covers eleven patients treated between 2008 and 2025. Seven faced likely fractures and four had already fractured.

Average age was about 72 years. Performance scores improved sharply after surgery. Nine of eleven patients could walk one month later. Blood loss averaged about 319 milliliters and operations took about 191 minutes. One implant broke after a fall and needed reoperation. One-year implant survival was ninety percent. The authors call the method a useful option, while asking for larger studies.
pmc-13528107:
Víctor Siles-Guerrero and nine colleagues test a body signal as a marker in severe anorexia nervosa in a 2026 study. The signal, phase angle, comes from a body impedance scan. It reflects cell mass and fluid balance. Forty-two female inpatients at a specialist unit were measured at admission. Patients were split into thirds by their phase angle value.

Body weight barely differed across the thirds. Cell mass rose steadily from low to high thirds. Thigh muscle area and grip strength were clearly better at the top. Fluid sat more inside cells in the high group. Hospital stays shrank from a median near fifty-eight days to about forty-one. Estimated costs fell in step. The authors call the signal a promising severity marker. They note the study is small and the cost link follows stay length.
pmc-13530707:
Horowitz and colleagues present in 2026, as conference paper 49, a cadaver study testing whether patients could bear weight immediately after a new type of medial meniscus root repair. The question was whether early weight bearing would tear the repair loose. Root tears wreck the meniscus's hoop function, yet standard protocols ban weight bearing for weeks on caution alone.

Seven cadaver knees were fitted with metal tracers in the shin bone and meniscus, then loaded with about two and a half times body weight. Cutting the root let the meniscus marker drift significantly outward under load. After repair with the novel onlay all-suture anchor, the marker position matched the intact knee, and it stayed matched after 250 weight-bearing cycles in the straightened leg. The authors argue the result supports allowing protected weight bearing in a brace locked in extension.
pmc-13531207:
Choi wrote a 2026 editorial on using catheter-based techniques to stabilize the smallest premature babies born with congenital heart disease. Infants under fifteen hundred grams who also have heart defects die more often than similar babies without them. Yet surgical repair in this group has produced mixed results, and the best timing is unknown. Catheter closure of a fetal vessel has become standard even at these sizes.

Choi discusses a case in which an infant had both that open vessel and a large hole between the heart's pumping chambers. The baby received a closure device plus flow restrictors in both lung arteries through catheters, the first such report at very low birth weight. The baby was off the ventilator within five days, went home weeks later and had surgical repair without lung artery procedures. The editorial presents the case as effective bridge palliation and urges operators to publish their experiences.
pmc-13531807:
Julius Kyomya and colleagues explore in 2026 how pharmacy students in southwestern Uganda view team-based simulation training. Interviews reached 14 final-year students and three faculty members at Mbarara University during October 2025. Current clinical teaching suffers from few placements, scarce supervisors, and separate training by profession.

Students named hierarchy, low confidence, timetable clashes, and thin simulation capacity as barriers. Skilled guidance, curriculum room, leadership backing, and the safe practice setting counted as enablers. Clear speaking, role clarity, teamwork, and drug-care skills topped the training wish list for joining mixed health teams.
pmc-13531907:
Sunita and co-authors compare fat-tissue hormone signals by body weight during heart attacks in a 2026 Indonesian study. Blood from 105 patients, split into non-obese and obese groups by body mass, was tested for four adipokines, fat-derived messengers that steer inflammation and metabolism. Heart injury levels were similar across groups.

Non-obese patients carried higher levels of all four messengers, a counterintuitive pattern. Across everyone, the best-known messenger moved opposite to cholesterol and blood fat measures while tracking the protective cholesterol fraction. Subgroup checks blurred several links, urging cautious reading of weight-based metabolic snapshots.
pmc-13532007:
Emilly V Figueiredo and colleagues review in 2026 how sex shapes the brain resident immune cells called microglia in Alzheimer disease. Women make up about two-thirds of cases, a gap that longer life alone cannot explain. Microglia clear debris, trim connections, and fan or calm inflammation, and they differ by sex from early life.

Hormone shifts at menopause, sex chromosome effects on immunity, and interactions with major risk genes all steer microglial states differently in each sex. The review maps candidate mechanisms and gaps, arguing prevention and treatment should be designed sex-aware.
pmc-13534507:
Xia Jing and colleagues study in 2026 whether low eosinophil counts predict death within 30 days in hospital patients with aspiration pneumonia. The lung infection follows inhaled food or fluid and mainly strikes older adults, yet reliable risk signs are lacking. A single-centre study followed 841 patients grouped by eosinophil level.

Death within 30 days was far more common in the low-count group than in the higher group. The link held after matching and weighting methods that balanced other patient traits. Readers gain a simple blood sign that may flag patients who need closer care.
pmc-13536707:
Sachin Acharya and colleagues review methods for learning from uneven multi-group data in a 2026 methodological survey. Many health tasks sort cases into several groups where some groups are rare, such as uncommon diseases. Standard models then favor common groups and miss rare ones. The review gathers 75 studies found through major databases and citation tracing to compare fixes and measures of success.

Common fixes reshape data by distance, clustering, or distribution, or split multi-group tasks into paired tasks. A simple ratio of group sizes remains the most used gauge of unevenness. Results depend heavily on data size, number of groups, and severity of the imbalance. The authors warn that stacking fixes at several stages can add bias, and that weak reporting of data details blocks fair comparison across studies.
pmc-13540807:
Wajahat Mirza and colleagues weigh two surgical robots in a 2026 review. The newer Hugo system faces the long-established da Vinci system. Both remove the prostate in localised cancer. Hospitals need head-to-head evidence before they buy the cheaper challenger. The authors also graded the certainty of that evidence.

Six databases were searched through January 2026. Only three prospective studies qualified. Each arm held 145 patients. No outcome differed in a clear way between the robots. The outcomes covered surgical complications, margins, and operating time. They also covered blood loss, hospital stay, and catheter days. Wide ranges and thin data kept certainty low.
pmc-13540907:
Junzhe Liu leads a 2026 study unveiling a tool that boosts protein production from chosen genes without touching DNA or the gene's own switches. Most gene regulators act at transcription, the first step, while this system works at translation, where proteins are actually assembled.

Short guide RNAs steer a small engineered protein complex to a target message, recruiting the cell's protein-making machinery. In glioblastoma cells the system switched on two tumor suppressors, p53 and PTEN, slowing growth and invasion. Delivered by virus into mouse brain tumors, it extended survival by roughly five to six weeks. Protein surveys found no off-target effects, and the tool worked in mouse and cattle cells too.
pmc-13543007:
Zhang, in a 2026 perspective, warns phage researchers against calling every blocked infection an immune defence. High-throughput screens increasingly find bacteria that restrict bacteriophages, the viruses of bacteria, before anyone knows the mechanism. A lower plaque count or slower lysis is a phenotype, the author argues, and labelling it immunity by default corrupts databases and engineering plans built on them.

The piece distinguishes three explanations. Immune-gated defences act after a virus enters. Replication-niche barriers stop infection earlier, through surface states that block entry or cell states that cannot support a viral factory. Assay-limited phenotypes are artefacts of the test conditions themselves. Zhang proposes a decision tree using native context, matched physiology, stage-specific readouts, triggers, and rescue tests to sort them. The practical stakes include phage therapy and biocontrol, where the right label dictates the right fix.
pmc-13543607:
Peng Deng and colleagues published a 2026 study of a protein that stabilises the contact sites where mitochondria meet the endoplasmic reticulum. They asked what its loss does after a subarachnoid haemorrhage, bleeding around the brain. Early brain injury after such bleeding involves failing mitochondria and dying neurons. In mouse models and cultured neurons, the team tracked the protein PDZD8, raised it, deleted it, and mutated one chemically vulnerable site to test the mechanism.

After haemorrhage the protein fell sharply in neurons, contact sites broke down, mitochondria breathed poorly, and oxidative damage mounted. Restoring PDZD8 preserved the contacts, calmed the damage, and improved behaviour scores. The injury marked the protein for destruction through a chemical tag at one cysteine site, feeding it to the cell's disposal machinery; blocking that site prevented the loss. A single tagged amino acid may thus decide how much injury follows the bleed.
pmc-13546707:
Ari Retnowati, Sugiharto Sugiharto, and Dian Wahyu Harjanti set out in 2026 to check whether the two main rulebooks for judging antibiotic resistance agree. Their test samples were bacteria from Indonesian broiler chickens. They tested 390 Escherichia coli isolates with a standard lab panel and read the results under both the American CLSI rules and the European EUCAST rules, each in its 2025 edition.

Resistance to ampicillin was highest under both systems, near 78 percent, while every isolate stayed sensitive to meropenem. The two rulebooks agreed almost fully for five drugs, yet they clashed sharply on colistin, where agreement was almost none, and differed on ciprofloxacin. The authors argue that such reports should state both readings to avoid misleading policy.
pmc-13547607:
Lyu and colleagues reported in 2026 high-pressure experiments that may solve a deep-Earth puzzle. Two huge slow zones sit at the base of the mantle, and why they survive instead of being stirred away was unclear. These zones, spotted by earthquake waves, feed volcanic plumes and steer the mantle's slow churn. Heat and water inside them should make them weak and easy to mix, yet they persist.

The team grew bridgmanite, the main mineral of the lower mantle, under mantle-like pressure and found that water makes its crystals grow much larger. Bigger crystals make rock far stiffer. By their estimate, the water-rich zones could flow more than twenty times more slowly than the mantle around them. That hidden stiffness, they argue, is what lets the zones endure as long-lived anchors of the deep Earth.
pmc-13547907:
Sofianos Andrikopoulos leads the author group of this 2026 joint statement from diabetes societies in Australia and New Zealand. It sets out why continuous glucose monitors, wearable sensors that track sugar levels day and night, need shared minimum standards for safety and accuracy.

The statement argues that treatment choices, including insulin doses, now rest directly on sensor readings, so weak accuracy puts patients at risk. It recommends that devices sold in either country must prove they meet set levels of precision before approval. The authors link good monitoring to fewer dangerous low-sugar events and better long-term control. Their aim is to give clinicians and patients confidence that any approved device performs to the same trusted standard.
pmc-13548307:
Fulden Eratam and colleagues used X-ray spectroscopy to examine single copper atoms parked on an iron oxide surface. The surface is a model for a class of catalysts that spread their active metal one atom at a time. How the lone atom is gripped by the surface decides its chemistry. Yet reading that grip from spectra is tricky, because a surface atom is undercoordinated compared with atoms inside a bulk material.

The copper atoms, each held by two bonds, produced a spectrum closely resembling copper oxide, plus one extra feature ahead of the main edge. The team traced that feature to the adsorption geometry itself, and showed it grows stronger when carbon monoxide sticks to the atom and bends its surroundings. The work warns against reading single-atom spectra by simple comparison with bulk standards.
pmc-13548707:
Padet Siriyasatien and colleagues survey mosquitoes across Thailand for two viruses and map their genetic variety, in a 2026 descriptive study. Aedes aegypti spreads dengue and chikungunya, both entrenched in the country, yet broad surveillance of the mosquito itself was sparse. The team collected 303 adults from eight provinces in five regions, screened them for viral RNA, and read a mitochondrial gene to build family trees of the populations.

Chikungunya RNA turned up in about one mosquito in six, across four provinces, with the highest rates near Bangkok and in Prachuap Khiri Khan. Dengue RNA appeared in none. Gene patterns showed moderate to high diversity, with some family lines shared widely and others unique to one province, and most variation sat within local populations. The authors offer the map as a foundation for future vector watching.
pmc-13550407:
Sarah M Alhammad and colleagues pair a forecasting transformer with a herd-inspired search algorithm to project water use far into the future, in a 2026 study. Countries need long-range estimates of freshwater withdrawal and desalination per person as populations grow and climates shift, yet transformer models succeed or fail on their settings. The team built per-capita indicators from national time series and tuned the model's knobs with an improved horse herd optimizer, racing it against rival optimizers on equal budgets.

The tuned model won, correlating with observed values at near zero point nine nine and converging faster and steadier than competitors. Extra tests held up across longer horizons, disturbed inputs, different time aggregations, and missing-data fixes. The authors present the framework as a transparent planning tool for water stress policy, bound to the data and budget they evaluated.
pmc-13550607:
Yaren Dincoglu, Suyash Verma, and Arman Hemmati published a 2026 engineering simulation of how a shaped insert inside a pipe disturbs turbulent flow. Inserts of three thicknesses, measured against pipe diameter, were tested at a Reynolds number of 25,000, a standard index of flow intensity. The authors tracked how turbulence and average speed recovered downstream of the insert.

Thicker inserts stirred the flow more, and the extra turbulence drifted away from the wall following a power-law pattern tied to thickness. Each case showed a local drop in skin friction that faded at different distances. The thickest insert cut friction most yet raised overall pressure loss, a trade-off the authors flag for pipeline design.
pmc-13550807:
Ruby Lister-Whelan, leading thirteen colleagues, published a 2026 protocol for the INVEST trial, which tests giving immunotherapy directly into the bladder before major bladder surgery. High-risk bladder cancer that has not invaded muscle is hard to control, and current options are poorly tolerated or in short supply. The trial delivers atezolizumab either by slow instillation or by injection into the bladder wall.

Run at a single United Kingdom center, the open-label phase Ib study first confirms a safe dose, then expands that dose to check safety further. Main outcomes are dose-limiting toxic effects and adverse events, with survival, complete response, and drug levels in blood and urine as secondary measures. Patients of all stages heading for bladder removal may join.
pmc-13551707:
Jiawei Yan, with five colleagues, published a 2026 genetics study of eastern cottonwood, a valuable timber poplar whose breeding still relies on slow crossing and selection. The team genotyped 209 trees with a 60K SNP chip, a panel of single-letter DNA differences, and measured fifteen growth and leaf traits. Association analysis hunted for DNA markers tied to those traits.

After quality checks, 46,031 markers yielded 219 significant associations, narrowed to 57 target markers and 77 candidate genes. The authors then built 48 working KASP assays, quick tests for single markers, and 25 of them separated trees with clearly different trait values. They offer those markers as practical tools for selecting promising poplars early.
pmc-13551807:
Petch Rawdaree, Nisita Jirawutkornkul, Parnnaphat Luksameesate, and Dilok Piyayotai published a 2026 scoping review of obesity policy and drug reimbursement worldwide, aimed at lessons for Thailand. The team searched three databases for documents from 2004 to mid-2024 and reviewed gray literature on payment for obesity treatment, mapping policies thematically.

Nineteen policy themes grouped into three broad domains: government policy, food access and healthier surroundings, and support inside the health system. High-income countries ran more comprehensive, integrated strategies than middle-income ones in the authors' comparison. Surgery was reimbursed more widely than anti-obesity medicines, and newer GLP-1 drugs were paid for weight loss only in selected rich countries, elsewhere mainly for diabetes. The authors urge integrated prevention plus treatment with interagency collaboration.
pmc-13554107:
Mohammad-Taghi Hamzaban and two colleagues compare flat and full three-dimensional checks of slope safety at an Iranian copper pit in a 2026 study. Flat checks are common in mining yet can miss how a curved slope truly fails. The team built a detailed three-dimensional model of the Sungun pit, with ground layers and water levels included. Flat slices were then cut from that model for side-by-side testing.

The full model foresaw a rotating slide with a safety score just above the danger line. Cracks and movement seen in the field matched that picture. Flat slices gave wildly mixed scores, from near failure to very safe, depending on where they were cut. Slices facing the main slide direction came closest, yet none caught the slide's true shape and reach.
pmc-13554307:
Jaden Wise leads an eleven-author team reviewing how tuning choices shape artificial intelligence tools for spine surgery in a 2026 paper. Such tools now help with diagnosis, planning, guidance during surgery, and outcome forecasts. Yet strong test scores do not always mean trusty clinic performance. The team searched three databases for work from 2015 to early 2025 and grouped findings by tuning theme.

Settings such as learning pace, feature choice, and safeguards against overfitting steered every stage of care. Reported scores swung widely with task, dataset, and checking method. Most studies were small, single-centre, and backward-looking, with patchy reporting of settings. The authors call for standard reporting, fairness checks, forward trials, and watch for drift after launch.
pmc-13554907:
Praneeth Katrapati leads a six-author team reporting a rescue burn procedure after a valve replacement blocked the heart's outflow in a 2026 case report. Their seventy-eight-year-old patient had received a catheter-based mitral valve for a narrowed valve. Afterward, the new valve choked the path blood takes leaving the heart, a known hazard of this procedure. Standard preventive tricks are applied before surgery, not after trouble strikes.

The team used a standard radiofrequency catheter to burn away part of the heart's dividing wall, thinning it and freeing the outflow path. No earlier report described this fix used after the valve was already in place. The authors present it as a feasible bailout when other options fail or cannot be used, expanding the rescue toolkit.
pmc-13557707:
Alice Accorroni, Christine Clavien, and Giovanni B. Frisoni explored in 2026 how the words used to define Alzheimer's disease change what doctors tell patients. Two leading frameworks read the same brain biomarker results differently, especially for people whose thinking is still normal. Using case-based simulated conversations, refined with input from clinical experience and a narrative literature review, the authors compared the stories each framework produces.

Under one framework, a positive amyloid result in a symptom-free person is spoken of as the disease itself, which the authors call a deterministic story that invites misunderstanding. The rival framework treats the same result as a risk state, since many such people never decline, and allows a more complex yet more honest conversation. Careful word choice, they argue, supports patient engagement, follow-through with advice, and public trust in medicine.
pmc-13558707:
Ma Jun and six colleagues wired shoppers with eye trackers in 2026 to learn how livestream hosts and product types jointly steer buying. Livestream selling pairs a presenter, called an anchor, with goods that buyers either research by specification or judge by experience. Their experiment crossed five anchor arrangements, from single presenters to mixed-gender pairs, with product type and the audience each product targets, in ninety-five participants whose gaze and pupil size were recorded.

Two routes to a decision emerged. A bottom-up route handled product information, while a top-down route handled social judgement of the anchor, and the eye measures separated from stated intentions along that split. Pairing matters: the authors advise brands to match anchor combinations to product attributes, and they single out mixed-gender pairing as insurance against audience mismatch. Questionnaires completed the picture that gaze data began.
pmc-13560107:
Yifan Hu and colleagues test whether measurements from a special MRI method can forecast survival after surgery for esophageal squamous cell carcinoma. Their 2026 retrospective study included eighty patients who had intravoxel incoherent motion imaging before resection. The technique separates water diffusion from blood perfusion inside tumors, yielding four parameters that standard staging cannot capture.

Models built on the imaging values predicted overall survival better than models using clinicopathological factors alone. Combining both sets performed best of all, reaching an area under the curve of 0.827 for one-year survival in their analysis. Similar gains appeared for time without the cancer returning, and risk scores split patients into groups with clearly different outcomes. The authors argue the scans add information beyond pathology reports. They propose the combined model as a sharper tool for sorting patients after surgery.
pmc-13561107:
Romy, Alcántara, and Bedolla analyze in 2026 the one hundred most popular mental health podcasts on Apple Podcasts. They ask what the hits share while treatment access stays limited and audio fills the gap. Little was known about what separates top shows from the rest.

Three trained coders scored each show against a credibility framework covering content, hosts, and production. The hits kept a tight topical focus, a consistent episode structure, and a conversational delivery, with episodes typically running thirty to sixty minutes. Hosts often told personal stories, showed emotion openly, and displayed professional credentials or affiliations. Content mixed advice, facts, and personal discussion, and production quality was high with predictable release schedules. The authors offer the pattern as practical guidance for creators and as groundwork for scholarship on digital mental health communication.
pmc-13562207:
Tian Hao and colleagues compare two wrist access points for invasive blood pressure monitoring catheters: the conventional radial site and the newer distal radial site in the hand. Their 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis follows PRISMA guidance and pools twelve randomized trials with 1,790 participants published through the end of 2025. Evidence quality was graded formally.

Distal access produced fewer hematomas, fewer catheter blockages, and less bleeding than the conventional route, with risk ratios well under one for each complication in the pooled estimates. Insertion took longer, by roughly twenty-seven seconds on average. Pressure tracing stability improved and bleeding stopped faster with distal access, while first-attempt success and pain scores matched overall. Patients sixty-five and under actually succeeded more often at first attempt distally. The authors call distal access a feasible alternative needing longer-term confirmation.
pmc-13562307:
Viktoria Mertin and three colleagues review whether heart ultrasound before non-cardiac surgery earns its place, weighing new diagnoses found, management changes triggered, and outcome effects. Their 2026 narrative review also lines up the freshest European and North American guideline advice side by side. Postoperative heart complications rank among the commonest serious harms of surgery worldwide.

Scanning does surface new diagnoses in a relevant share of patients, findings suggest, but studies on effectiveness stay limited. Data on how often findings actually change management are scarce, and proof of outcome benefit remains inconclusive. Both guideline families endorse scanning for symptomatic patients and reject routine use, though real differences between them persist. The authors catalog the knowledge gaps and propose research priorities, from yield studies to trials on whether scan-driven decisions help patients at all.
pmc-13562707:
Paul Elliott and two colleagues tune soft metal pastes that harden without a furnace, aiming for low-temperature bonding and repair parts. Copper particles stirred into liquid gallium set into a framework of intermetallic crystals, but the result can snap brittly. The 2026 study varied the recipe: pure gallium, plus blends with indium, tin, or both, each set at room temperature or at 100 degrees Celsius. Four-point bending tests measured strength, and surfaces were inspected to read the failure mode.

Heat helped the gallium and gallium-tin pastes, lifting both to about 7 megapascals, while indium-bearing mixes weakened. Fractures in the strong pair split cleanly through plate-like crystals, evidence of an unbroken rigid frame. Indium mixes tore softly where indium-rich pockets interrupted that frame. Gallium-tin won on balance of strength, consistency, and cost. The authors frame composition and setting temperature as the dials for these systems.
pmc-13563707:
Muli Wudu and nine colleagues examine a little-studied membrane protein, TMEM33, as a driver of lung adenocarcinoma. This common lung cancer still lacks enough targets. The 2026 team screened gene datasets with network analysis to find hub genes, then checked TMEM33 against a large cancer atlas. The protein ran high in tumour tissue and marked patients with worse outlooks. Lab assays measured what happens when cancer cells are made to produce extra TMEM33 or lose it.

Extra protein sped cell growth, colony formation, and migration through test membranes, and it switched on the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway. In nude mice, tumours carrying extra TMEM33 grew larger. Blocking that pathway cancelled the advantage, which ties the protein's mischief to one named circuit. The authors classify TMEM33 as an oncogene in this cancer and propose it as a therapeutic target, pending the long road from mouse work to patients.
pmc-13563807:
Jianfeng Gan and nine colleagues let a clustering algorithm sort preeclampsia, the dangerous blood-pressure disorder of pregnancy, into types based on blood fats. The condition varies bafflingly between women, and the placenta's handling of lipids may drive some of that variety. Their 2026 study reviewed 1,124 affected women treated between 2018 and 2022. Four standard third-trimester lipid measures fed an unsupervised k-means method, which settled on four subtypes: low metabolic, high HDL, high triglyceride, and high metabolic.

Surprises followed. The high triglyceride group, despite the heaviest mothers, recorded the lowest preterm birth rate at 3.1 percent and the least low birth weight. The high metabolic group carried the worst blood pressure and protein leakage. The authors argue that fat-based sorting exposes real biological variety inside one diagnosis, and that treatment trials should stop averaging across it.
pmc-13563907:
Djeneba B. Fofana and thirteen colleagues take hepatitis B viral load testing out of the laboratory and into Malian antenatal clinics, where mothers pass the virus to babies at birth. Knowing a pregnant woman's viral load decides who needs antivirals, yet DNA testing means a distant lab. Their 2026 study screened 2,952 pregnant women at referral and community sites between June 2024 and May 2025. The 205 who tested surface-antigen positive, a 6.9 percent prevalence, gave blood for the Xpert assay, run on site at two centres and centrally for the rest.

After spoilage, 191 women were tested: 64.0 percent had detectable virus, most below 2,000 units per millilitre, while 5.7 percent carried the high loads that endanger newborns. On-site testing returned same-day results for 23.5 percent of women against 4.4 percent centrally, though most results in both routes took over four days. The authors call decentralised testing feasible and faster, with system delays the barrier to clear.
pmc-13564207:
Aaron N. Gillman and colleagues map, in a 2026 study, how HIV-1 escapes the approved drug temsavir, which blocks the virus's envelope protein. Screening found eighteen envelope changes that raised resistance, yet only some of them actually appeared in patients who failed treatment.

Which changes emerged depended on how easily the needed genetic spelling changes arise and on whether the altered virus stayed fit and hidden from immunity. Common non-neutralizing antibodies blocked several escape routes, funneling the virus toward a narrow set of options. The framework could help forecast resistance before a drug reaches wide use, a useful step for HIV treatment design.
pmc-13566407:
Jessica L. Bloom and Indira Sriram review, in a 2026 article, immune system problems in children and adults with Down syndrome, whose extra chromosome reshapes immunity toward inflammation and autoimmunity. Arthritis linked to Down syndrome is described as a distinct, aggressive illness, separate from other childhood arthritis forms.

Risks include severe lung disease tied to systemic arthritis and bleeding into the lungs. Standard drugs can be hard to tolerate or less effective in this group, with poor tolerance of one common drug and weaker responses to another class. Early trials of a newer drug family that calms interferon signaling look promising across skin, joint, and regression symptoms.
pmc-13576107:
Jenny Guo leads a 2026 study of laser prostate surgery in men who had already been treated for an enlarged prostate. Minimally invasive options can wear off, leaving some men needing a second procedure. Holmium laser enucleation removes prostate tissue completely and works at any gland size, yet results after earlier treatment were unclear.

The study matched 418 re-treatment patients with 418 first-time patients by tissue weight removed. Surgery time, laser energy, and problems during surgery were similar in both groups. Complications at 90 days were close, at 6.5 against 5.5 percent, though re-treatment patients visited emergency care more often. Symptom and quality of life gains matched between groups. Leakage symptom scores were slightly better in the re-treatment group. The authors support the laser option after prior treatment.
pmc-13576307:
Akbiyik and colleagues measured in 2026 how visible modern flowable resin composites, the runny tooth-filling materials, appear on X-rays. Radiopacity, how bright a material shows against tooth, decides whether dentists can spot fillings, gaps, and decay at follow-up. The team made discs of six current formulations, from universal injectable to fiber-reinforced, and imaged them with an aluminum step wedge and tooth slices to convert brightness into aluminum-equivalent values.

The materials differed significantly. One universal injectable composite topped the scale, while a bulk-fill product sat at the bottom at about half its value. Every product still outshone dentin and passed the international minimum for radiopacity, so all are clinically usable on that score. The authors advise dentists to weigh radiopacity alongside handling and strength when choosing a flowable composite, especially where later X-ray reading matters.
pmc-13577107:
Minkyung Kim, Yong-Joon Cho, and Ok-Sun Kim argue that bacterial genome assemblies need checking, not just completing, in a 2026 review. Long-read sequencing now delivers near-complete or circular bacterial genomes as a matter of routine. A smooth assembly can still hide errors, from collapsed repeats and wrong joins to botched plasmid rebuilds and single-letter mistakes.

The review traces where those errors come from: repeated genome stretches, quirks of each sequencing platform, and limits of the assembly software. It then offers a decision framework that links the choice of sequencing plan, assembly route, and polishing effort to how much checking a project needs. A tiered confidence scale helps readers grade how far an assembly can be trusted for its intended use. The authors urge the field to prize accuracy and transparent reporting over completeness alone.
pmc-13577907:
Eugene Vorontsov and colleagues built PRISM2, an artificial intelligence model that reads whole pathology slides and talks through cases in clinical language. Pathology slides are the stained tissue samples doctors study under a microscope to diagnose disease, often cancer.

The model trained on 2.3 million whole slide images and 14 million question and answer pairs drawn from 700,000 pathology reports. This dialogue training tied what tissue looks like to how doctors reason about a diagnosis. In prompt-based tests, PRISM2 matched or beat approved clinical products at spotting cancer in prostate, breast, and lymph node slides. Its slide summaries also never fell behind earlier models across diagnosis, marker, and survival test sets.
pmc-13584507:
Gul and colleagues published a 2026 study on a gene family that loosens plant cell walls in sorghum. Expansins let walls stretch so plants can grow and adapt to stress. Sorghum is a hardy grain, yet its expansin family had gone unmapped. The team catalogued the full set across the sorghum genome.

They found 68 expansin genes, mostly in two large subfamilies overall. Gene copies grew through both small and large duplications over time. Many expansins switched on strongly in roots and fast-growing tissues. Under drought tests, a subset rose sharply, confirmed by a second method. Three hub genes may lead breeding work for drought-tough sorghum. Wall loosening under drought may help roots keep drinking longer.
pmc-13586507:
Waratchaya Tirasarnvong and colleagues built a prediction model for whether gut stromal tumours return or grow after surgery. These tumours, called GISTs, arise in the digestive tract wall, and their risk grading leans on counting dividing cells under a microscope.

The team reviewed 150 patients operated on at a Thai hospital between 2009 and 2021, grading each tumour two ways. The older method, counting across 50 microscope fields, overstated the standard risk class in about 14 percent of cases. A model using tumour size, site, rupture, the newer area-based count, and a blood inflammation score scored highest. Its accuracy reached 0.939 on a scale where one is perfect, beating the older count in every model tried.
pmc-13587107:
Justine Münsterberg and a large team sample blood straight from the blocked artery of stroke patients to catch inflammation in its first hours. The strokes came from large vessel blockages, and patients were having the clot pulled out by a catheter. In 54 patients, the team compared blood trapped behind the clot with blood from elsewhere in the same person, using wide molecular profiling.

Immune cells on the spot were already switched on. Monocytes were primed to release interleukin-1 beta, a master alarm signal, within the first few hours, helped by high levels of an energy molecule in the blood. Neutrophils alongside them spun out web-like traps that gum up vessels, and post-mortem tissue showed those webs inside the starved brain. The authors name this fast local storm as a target for calming drugs added to clot removal.
pmc-13587407:
Ignacio Ventura and colleagues review a rare X-linked syndrome and argue that one of its forms deserves its own name. Mohr-Tranebjaerg syndrome begins with early deafness and moves on to movement and vision loss, driven by faults in a gene called TIMM8A. In some patients the damage also wipes out a neighbor gene, BTK, which the immune system needs to make antibodies. Their 2026 review gathered 75 confirmed patients from three decades of reports.

Every patient with the double deletion had the immune failure, and none with the single-gene form did. Language delay was far more common in the double form, while progressive blindness was far more common in the classic form. The authors name the double form XLA-MTS and urge wider gene testing for children with syndromic deafness and slow development, so the immune side is never missed.
pmc-13587507:
Beibei Zhang and colleagues compare two ways of clearing cysts from the jaw in a randomized trial. Jaw cysts hollow out bone and loosen teeth, and the standard fix scrapes the cyst out through an opening in the bone. The rival bone lid method lifts that bone plate off, cleans the cyst, and sets the plate back, keeping the jaw's outer wall. Sixty patients were assigned by chance, thirty to each method, and followed with 3D scans for nine months.

The bone lid group refilled their defects faster, with bigger drops in hole volume and surface area and denser new bone on scans. Gum measures around nearby teeth also improved more, and teeth steadied sooner, with a clearly higher chance of stable teeth at nine months. The authors add one caution: the groups differed a little in starting lesion shape, which softens the surface-area result.
pmc-13588807:
Bin Chen and eleven colleagues test whether a parent's gut microbes can echo into the next generation's brain. Autism is known to involve both genes and environment, and gut bacteria have been linked to its risk. In their 2026 mouse study, adults given antibiotics were colonized with stool microbes from children with autism or from typically developing children, then bred, and their pups were watched for autism-like behavior.

Parents stayed behaviorally normal, but pups of the autism-microbe group showed autism-like changes, plus gut inflammation and neuron loss in two brain regions. Chemical tags on DNA, called methylation marks, shifted in parents' brain, blood, and colon, and a subset of those shifts appeared in the pups. The patterns ran through sex-specific networks tying microbes to genes and behavior. The authors read this as a route by which unaffected parents might pass risk along.
pmc-13592307:
Lee and colleagues report in 2026 a reaction that builds tetrahydrofuran rings, five-membered oxygen rings common in natural products and drug candidates. The reaction controls the rings' three-dimensional shape precisely. Shaping four stereocenters, the atoms whose arrangement defines handedness, in one step is a prized result.

The reaction joins allylsilanes with glyoxal partners through a formal cycloaddition followed by a hydrogen shift, steered by a chiral catalyst that acts as a Lewis acid, an electron-pair acceptor. Yields reached the high eighty percent range at their best. The desired handedness was produced almost exclusively, and one ring shape was favored more than twenty to one over its rival in the best cases. Earlier versions of this reaction relied on chirality already built into the starting materials; this one creates the asymmetry from scratch.
pmc-13592607:
Md Parvej Hussain leads a team linking low birth weight to child malnutrition across five South Asian countries. Survey data from Bangladesh, India, Pakistan, Nepal, and the Maldives gave 147,332 complete child records. Matching methods paired similar children who differed mainly in birth weight, then compared five outcomes: stunting, wasting, underweight, any malnutrition, and several forms at once.

About one child in six was born underweight, with Pakistan highest and Nepal lowest. Matched comparisons tied low birth weight to every malnutrition form in the pooled data and in nearly every country. Wasting alone broke the pattern in Bangladesh and the Maldives. Hussain and the team press for country specific action on birth weight as a lever against early childhood malnutrition.
pmc-13592707:
Amanda R. Young leads a team asking how myelin sheaths know how long to grow. Sheath length tunes signal timing in the brain, and thicker axons carry longer sheaths, yet the sensing trick was unknown. Using lab grown fibers and mice, the group tested whether each sheath reads its own fiber's width locally. A pressure sensing channel called Piezo1, found in the sheath making cells, stood as the prime suspect.

Each sheath did respond to its own fiber's diameter alone. Mice lacking Piezo1 in those cells grew sheaths too short on thick axons, matching the dish results, while sheath thickness stayed normal. Young and the team propose that Piezo1 turns width into length, hard wiring timing patterns across circuits.
pmc-13593707:
Mathias Busch, Gerrit Bredeck, Hans Bouwmeester, and Roel P. F. Schins review how inhaled or swallowed particles and fibers switch on the NLRP3 inflammasome, a protein assembly inside immune cells that drives inflammation. Their 2026 review gathers laboratory and animal work on materials from asbestos and quartz to microplastics and desert dust.

The chain from particle exposure through inflammasome activation to disease is firmly established for workplace mineral dusts. For the low-level environmental exposures people meet daily, that chain is still being traced. The authors argue that testing whether a new material activates NLRP3 should become a routine part of hazard assessment. The response appears across very different materials, and it sits upstream of lasting harm. Emerging materials such as nanocomposites could then be screened before wide use.
pmc-13595707:
Julia Naganuma-Carreras and co-authors analyzed survey data from 1,360 post-9/11 American veterans to see which post-deployment struggles predict arrest and charge, and whether the pattern differs for women and men. Their 2026 study defined justice involvement as arrest after deployment and tested mental health, substance use, anger, and housing factors together.

Fifteen percent reported justice involvement overall, with men higher than women. Younger age and a probable alcohol use disorder raised the odds in both sexes. Other risks split by gender: problematic anger mattered for women, while a history of homelessness mattered for men. The authors argue for gender-responsive prevention that treats mental health, drinking, and housing as one tangle, with the mix tuned to the different risk profiles they found.
pmc-13598007:
Madelaine Hettler leads a seventeen-author pilot study combining two imaging lenses on high-grade soft tissue sarcoma. One lens is a PET tracer. It lights up fibroblast activation protein, a marker of the tumor's supporting tissue. The other is MRI diffusion measures of how crowded the cells are. Nine patients underwent thirteen combined scans, some after treatment.

Every tumor took up the tracer distinctly. Neither tracer uptake nor diffusion separated grade two from grade three tumors, disappointing one hope. Two measures did talk to each other: denser cell packing on diffusion went with stronger tracer uptake, an inverse correlation. Tissue staining agreed with imaging, since stained-positive tumors showed far higher uptake. Responders to treatment showed steep uptake falls and looser diffusion before size changed. The authors call the pairing complementary and worth larger study.
pmc-13599907:
Mukhethwa Netshiombo and four colleagues map how African health systems are responding to climate change, and how far global climate pledges have entered national law in southern Africa. African health services produce few emissions yet face heavy climate shocks. The scoping review gathered research from six databases plus policy documents, keeping 78 research papers and 15 grey publications for analysis.

Most research clustered on training a climate-ready health workforce and on greener buildings, technology, and supply chains. Among Southern African Development Community members, only South Africa and Mauritius had passed a Climate Change Act. Four countries had a national health adaptation plan, and Madagascar alone had measured emissions across its public hospitals. Because immediate threats dominate, adaptation clearly outweighs emission cutting in both research and policy. The authors urge planners to weave climate goals into everyday health system planning so resilient, low-carbon care can actually be built.
pmc-13601507:
Ramya Lakshmi Rajendran and colleagues review in 2026 a cell-free approach to healing wounds that refuse to close. Chronic wounds stall amid lasting inflammation, poor blood vessel growth, and faulty tissue rebuilding. Stem cells can nudge these processes along, yet their use is held back by poor survival after transplant, uneven quality, and safety worries. Tiny parcels released by stem cells, called extracellular vesicles, might deliver the benefit without the cells.

The review weighs natural vesicles against artificial nanovesicles built to imitate them. In animal wound models, vesicle treatments calmed inflammation, encouraged vessel growth, and improved closure and tissue appearance. Proof is still missing for harder endpoints: lasting function, less scarring, and wounds staying closed. Delivery route, dose, and trial endpoints all remain unsettled. The authors supply a framework for the studies needed before vesicle therapy can claim a place in routine wound care.
pmc-13612207:
Junlin Pu and three colleagues map five years of publishing on brain fog after COVID-19. Cognitive dysfunction is among the most disabling features of post-COVID-19 condition, and work on it has exploded. Their analysis pulled papers from 2021 to 2025 out of Web of Science and Scopus, screening to 746 and 1,117 papers respectively. Output, teamwork, and themes were then charted with standard mapping tools.

Publication counts climbed steadily across the five years. The United States produced the most, the University of London led the institution list, and the Journal of Clinical Medicine stood out on publication and citation measures. Keywords clustered into three domains: psychological factors, oxidative stress, and neuroinflammation.
